lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The electronegativity of beryllium is approximately equal to that of aluminium.
  • Lithium forms only the normal oxide with oxygen, while the larger alkali metals form peroxides or superoxides.
  • Fluorine, F2, is the strongest oxidizing agent among the halogens, ahead of Cl2, Br2 and I2.
  • Barium sulphate is not soluble in water.
  • NaF has the highest melting point among the sodium halides NaCl, NaBr, NaF and NaI.
  • HF has the highest boiling point among the hydrogen halides because of the highest electronegativity of fluorine.
  • The inert pair effect dominates in lead, the heaviest Group-IVA element listed.
  • Carbon and silicon have no tendency to form dichlorides in Group-IVA.

Solved Exercises

Exercise: Multiple Choice Questions

Q: 1. Electronegativity of Be is approximately equal to that of

Options: (a) Al (b) Mg (c) B (d) Na

Correct answer: Al

Q: 2. The elements which are most abundant in earth crust are:

Options: (a) Si and Al (b) Ca and Mg (c) B and Ar (d) B and Al

Correct answer: Si and Al

Q: 3. Carbonates of Li are not stable like that of sodium due to

Options: (a) low electronegativity (b) low electropositivity (c) high charge density of Li+ (d) low charge density of Li+

Correct answer: high charge density of Li+

Q: 4. Which one of the following metal sulphates is not soluble in water

Options: (a) Na2SO4 (b) K2SO4 (c) BaSO4 (d) ZnSO4

Correct answer: BaSO4

Q: 5. Which of the following alkali metal forms only normal oxide with O2?

Options: (a) Li (b) K (c) Na (d) Rb

Correct answer: Li

Q: 6. Strongest oxidizing agent among the halogens is (Note: the printed answer key gives (d) for this question, which is wrong.)

Options: (a) Cl2 (b) F2 (c) Br2 (d) I2

Correct answer: F2

Q: 7. Which of the following has the lowest electron affinity?

Options: (a) F (b) I (c) Cl (d) Br

Correct answer: I

Q: 8. Which of the following halide has the highest melting point?

Options: (a) NaCl (b) NaBr (c) NaF (d) NaI

Correct answer: NaF

Q: 9. The highest boiling point of HF amongst the hydrogen halides is due to

Options: (a) lowest electronegativity of F (b) highest electronegativity of F (c) lowest atomic weight of F (d) lowest atomic radius of F

Correct answer: highest electronegativity of F

Q: 10. Which of the following is acidic in nature?

Options: (a) Al2O3 (b) CO2 (c) SnO2 (d) CaO

Correct answer: CO2

Q: 11. Third period element that initially reacts rapidly with oxygen to form a protective oxide coating that prevents further reactions is

Options: (a) Na (b) Al (c) Si (d) Mg

Correct answer: Al

Q: 12. Which of the following has a greater affinity for oxygen?

Options: (a) B (b) Na (c) K (d) Mg

Correct answer: K

Q: 13. Which of the following is the strongest base

Options: (a) Si(OH)4 (b) Be(OH)2 (c) Mg(OH)2 (d) Al(OH)3

Correct answer: Mg(OH)2

Q: 14. The inert pair effect dominates in

Options: (a) Pb (b) Sn (c) C (d) Si

Correct answer: Pb

Q: 15. The elements of Group-IVA which have no tendency to form a dichloride are

Options: (a) C and Si (b) P and Sn (c) Ga and C (d) Sn and Si

Correct answer: C and Si

mcqs.q: Electronegativity of Be is approximately equal to that of
mcqs.why: Beryllium and aluminium are diagonally related, and the solved answers note their similar charge density, so the electronegativity of Be is approximately equal to that of Al.

mcqs.q: The elements which are most abundant in earth crust are:
mcqs.why: Silicon and aluminium are the most abundant metals/metalloid elements named for the earth crust in this exercise, ahead of the other pairs listed in the options.

mcqs.q: Carbonates of Li are not stable like that of sodium due to
mcqs.why: The small Li+ ion has a high charge density and strongly polarizes the carbonate ion, so lithium carbonate breaks up much more easily than sodium carbonate.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following metal sulphates is not soluble in water
mcqs.why: Barium sulphate is insoluble in water, whereas the sulphates of sodium, potassium and zinc listed here dissolve in water.

mcqs.q: Which of the following alkali metal forms only normal oxide with O2?
mcqs.why: The small Li+ ion stabilizes only the small oxide ion O2-, so lithium forms only the normal oxide Li2O, while the larger alkali metals form peroxides or superoxides.

mcqs.q: Strongest oxidizing agent among the halogens is
mcqs.why: The printed answer key gives (d) I2 for this question, which is wrong. Fluorine is the strongest oxidizing agent because the F-F bond enthalpy is very low and the small F- ion has a very high hydration energy, so F2 gains electrons most readily; the order is F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2.

mcqs.q: Which of the following has the lowest electron affinity?
mcqs.why: Electron affinity decreases overall down the halogen group as the atom grows larger, so iodine, the largest halogen listed, has the lowest electron affinity.

mcqs.q: Which of the following halide has the highest melting point?
mcqs.why: NaF has the strongest ionic attraction and the highest lattice energy among the sodium halides listed, so it has the highest melting point.

mcqs.q: The highest boiling point of HF amongst the hydrogen halides is due to
mcqs.why: Fluorine has the highest electronegativity, so HF is strongly hydrogen bonded, and this extra attraction gives HF the highest boiling point among the hydrogen halides.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is acidic in nature?
mcqs.why: Carbon dioxide is an acidic oxide that reacts with alkalis to form carbonates, while Al2O3 and SnO2 are amphoteric and CaO is basic.

mcqs.q: Third period element that initially reacts rapidly with oxygen to form a protective oxide coating that prevents further reactions is
mcqs.why: Aluminium reacts rapidly with oxygen at first, but the aluminium oxide layer formed is protective and prevents any further reaction of the metal below it.

mcqs.q: Which of the following has a greater affinity for oxygen?
mcqs.why: Potassium is the most reactive metal among the options and has the greatest affinity for oxygen, forming its oxide most readily.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is the strongest base
mcqs.why: Mg(OH)2 is a basic hydroxide, while Be(OH)2 and Al(OH)3 are amphoteric and Si(OH)4 is acidic in character, so Mg(OH)2 is the strongest base listed.

mcqs.q: The inert pair effect dominates in
mcqs.why: The inert pair effect grows down Group-IVA and dominates in lead, the heaviest element listed, making the +2 state of Pb the most stable.

mcqs.q: The elements of Group-IVA which have no tendency to form a dichloride are
mcqs.why: Carbon and silicon show no tendency to form dichlorides; the dichlorides become stable only for the heavier Group-IVA elements because of the inert pair effect.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Thermal stability of Group-IIA nitrates and carbonates increases down the group as the M2+ ion grows larger and its polarizing power falls.
  • Group-IIA elements have the outer configuration ns2, show the fixed oxidation state +2, and give flame colours such as Ca brick red, Sr crimson and Ba green.
  • Group-IA carbonates are more thermally stable than Group-IIA carbonates because the M+ ion polarizes the carbonate ion only weakly.
  • BeCl2 is covalent, polymeric in the solid, dimeric in the vapour and readily hydrolysed, unlike the ionic chlorides of its group.
  • CCl4 does not hydrolyse because carbon has no vacant d-orbitals, whereas SiCl4 hydrolyses completely to SiO2 and HCl.
  • Fluorine is a stronger oxidizing agent than chlorine because the F-F bond enthalpy is very low and the F- ion has a very high hydration energy.
  • Be(OH)2 is amphoteric: it dissolves in dilute HCl and also in excess NaOH, forming Na2[Be(OH)4].
  • Argon appears to have the largest radius in the third period because its radius is a van der Waals radius, not a covalent radius.

Solved Exercises

Exercise: Short Answer Questions

Q: i. Give the reason that the nitrates and carbonates of Group-IIA elements are thermally stable.

Ans: The nitrates and carbonates of Group-IIA elements need strong heating before they decompose, and their thermal stability increases down the group. The reason is the size of the metal ion. On going down the group the M2+ ion becomes larger, so its charge density and polarizing power decrease. A large cation distorts the electron cloud of the nitrate or carbonate ion only slightly, so the anion is not weakened and more heat is needed to break it up into the oxide. Hence the stability increases in the order Mg < Ca < Sr < Ba salts.

Q: ii. Write down at least four characteristics of Group-IIA elements.

Ans: (1) They are reactive metals with the outer electronic configuration ns2, and they show the fixed oxidation state of +2 in their compounds. (2) Their atomic radius increases and ionization energy decreases down the group, so reactivity increases from Be to Ba. (3) Their oxides and hydroxides are basic in nature; BeO and Be(OH)2 are amphoteric. (4) They form ionic compounds which are mostly colourless, and their salts give characteristic flame colours, e.g. Ca brick red, Sr crimson and Ba green. (5) The solubility of their hydroxides increases down the group while that of their sulphates and carbonates decreases.

Q: iii. Give reason(s) that why carbonates of Group-IA elements are more thermally stable than those of Group-IIA.

Ans: The cation of a Group-IA carbonate carries a single positive charge (M+), while that of a Group-IIA carbonate carries a double charge (M2+). The M2+ ion is also smaller, so it has a much higher charge density and polarizing power. It strongly distorts the electron cloud of the large carbonate ion, weakens the C-O bonds and helps the carbonate to break up into the oxide and CO2 on heating. The M+ ion polarizes the carbonate ion only weakly, so Group-IA carbonates (except Li2CO3) do not decompose even at very high temperature.

Q: iv. Justify that beryllium chloride is different from the chlorides of its group.

Ans: The chlorides of Mg, Ca, Sr and Ba are ionic solids with high melting points which conduct electricity in the molten state. BeCl2 is different in every way. Because the Be2+ ion is very small and has a high polarizing power, BeCl2 is covalent in nature. In the solid state it has a polymeric chain structure with bridging chlorine atoms, in the vapour it exists as the dimer Be2Cl4, and it is monomeric and linear only at high temperature. It has a low melting point, dissolves in organic solvents, does not conduct electricity when molten, and is readily hydrolysed by water giving an acidic solution.

Q: v. Explain the structure and stability of chlorides of Group-IVA elements.

Ans: The tetrachlorides CCl4, SiCl4, GeCl4 and SnCl4 are covalent liquids with a tetrahedral structure formed by sp3 hybridization of the central atom. PbCl4 is also covalent but is very unstable and decomposes on warming: PbCl4 -> PbCl2 + Cl2. The dichlorides become more stable down the group because of the inert pair effect, so SnCl2 is a reducing agent while PbCl2 is an ionic, sparingly soluble solid. CCl4 does not hydrolyse because carbon has no vacant d-orbitals to accept a lone pair from water, whereas SiCl4 hydrolyses completely: SiCl4 + 2H2O -> SiO2 + 4HCl. Thus the +4 chlorides become less stable and the +2 chlorides more stable down the group.

Q: vi. Why fluorine is stronger oxidizing agent than chlorine?

Ans: An oxidizing agent gains electrons and is itself reduced. Fluorine is the most electronegative element and the formation of the F- ion is the most energetically favourable reduction among the halogens. Although the electron affinity of fluorine is slightly less than that of chlorine, the F-F bond enthalpy is very low and the small F- ion has a very high hydration energy, so the overall change X2 -> 2X-(aq) releases the most energy for fluorine. Hence the order of oxidizing power is F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2, and fluorine can oxidize even chloride ions.

Q: vii. How would you test and confirm the amphoteric nature of Be(OH)2?

Ans: Prepare white beryllium hydroxide by adding alkali to a solution of a beryllium salt and divide it into two parts. To the first part add dilute hydrochloric acid; the precipitate dissolves forming beryllium chloride: Be(OH)2 + 2HCl -> BeCl2 + 2H2O, which shows basic behaviour. To the second part add excess sodium hydroxide solution; the precipitate also dissolves forming soluble sodium tetrahydroxoberyllate: Be(OH)2 + 2NaOH -> Na2[Be(OH)4], which shows acidic behaviour. Since Be(OH)2 reacts with both an acid and an alkali, it is amphoteric.

Q: viii. Why the atomic radius of argon is larger than all the member of third period?

Ans: For all the other elements of the third period the atomic radius is measured as a covalent radius, i.e. half the distance between the nuclei of two bonded atoms. Argon is a noble gas and does not form covalent bonds, so its radius can only be measured as a van der Waals radius, i.e. half the distance between the nuclei of two neighbouring non-bonded atoms in the solid. The van der Waals radius is always much larger than the covalent radius of a similar atom, so argon appears to have the largest atomic radius in the period, although its atoms are not really the biggest.

Q: ix. Why there is a fall in ionization energy at Al and Si in same period?

Ans: Ionization energy generally increases across the third period because the nuclear charge increases while the electrons enter the same shell. There is a fall at aluminium because the electron removed from Al comes from the higher-energy 3p subshell, which is shielded by the filled 3s subshell, so it is removed more easily than the 3s electron of magnesium. A second small fall occurs after phosphorus (at sulphur) because in sulphur the 3p electron is removed from an orbital which already contains a paired electron, and the electron-electron repulsion makes its removal easier. Between Al and Si the value rises again because of the increased nuclear charge of Si.

Q: x. Give the reason(s) that the compounds of Sn4+ are covalent in nature while those of Sn2+ are ionic.

Ans: This is explained by Fajans rules. The Sn4+ ion is smaller in size and carries a charge of +4, so it has a very high charge density and a strong polarizing power. It distorts the electron cloud of the anion towards itself, which gives the bond a largely covalent character, e.g. SnCl4 is a covalent liquid. The Sn2+ ion is larger and carries only a +2 charge, so its polarizing power is weak, the anion is hardly distorted and the compounds remain ionic, e.g. SnCl2 is an ionic solid. The inert pair effect also makes the +2 state of tin the more stable ionic state.

mcqs.q: Why does the thermal stability of Group-IIA nitrates and carbonates increase down the group?
options: The M2+ ion becomes larger, so its charge density and polarizing power decrease
The M2+ ion becomes smaller and polarizes the anion more strongly
The nitrate and carbonate ions become smaller down the group
The metals become less reactive down the group
mcqs.why: Down the group the M2+ ion grows larger, distorts the nitrate or carbonate ion less, and more heat is needed to decompose the salt, in the order Mg < Ca < Sr < Ba.

mcqs.q: What is the outer electronic configuration and fixed oxidation state of Group-IIA elements?
mcqs.why: Group-IIA elements have the outer configuration ns2 and show the fixed oxidation state of +2 in their compounds, as stated in the solved short answers.

mcqs.q: Which flame colours are correctly matched in the solved answers?
options: Ca crimson, Sr brick red, Ba blue
Ca green, Sr brick red, Ba crimson
Ca brick red, Sr crimson, Ba green
Ca lilac, Sr green, Ba brick red
mcqs.why: The solved answers give characteristic flame colours for Group-IIA salts: calcium brick red, strontium crimson and barium green.

mcqs.q: Why are Group-IA carbonates more thermally stable than Group-IIA carbonates?
options: The M+ ion has a higher charge density than M2+
Group-IA carbonates contain no carbonate ion
The M2+ ion is larger than the M+ ion of the same period
The M+ ion carries a single charge and polarizes the carbonate ion only weakly
mcqs.why: A Group-IA cation carries only a +1 charge, so it distorts the carbonate ion weakly, while the smaller, doubly charged M2+ ion polarizes it strongly and helps it decompose to the oxide and CO2.

mcqs.q: Which statement about BeCl2 is correct?
options: It is an ionic solid that conducts electricity when molten
It is covalent, polymeric in the solid and exists as the dimer Be2Cl4 in the vapour
It is monomeric and linear in the solid state
It is not hydrolysed by water
mcqs.why: Because Be2+ is very small and strongly polarizing, BeCl2 is covalent: it has a polymeric chain structure in the solid, exists as Be2Cl4 in the vapour and is readily hydrolysed by water.

mcqs.q: Why does CCl4 not hydrolyse, while SiCl4 hydrolyses completely?
options: Carbon is more electronegative than silicon
SiCl4 is ionic and CCl4 is covalent
Carbon has no vacant d-orbitals to accept a lone pair from water
CCl4 has a tetrahedral structure and SiCl4 does not
mcqs.why: The solved answer states that carbon has no vacant d-orbitals to accept a lone pair from water, whereas SiCl4 hydrolyses completely to SiO2 and HCl.

mcqs.q: What is formed when Be(OH)2 dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide solution?
mcqs.why: Be(OH)2 reacts with excess NaOH to form soluble sodium tetrahydroxoberyllate, Na2[Be(OH)4], which proves the acidic side of its amphoteric behaviour.

mcqs.q: Why does argon appear to have the largest atomic radius in the third period?
options: Its atoms contain the most electrons in the period
It forms covalent bonds longer than any other element
Its radius is measured as a van der Waals radius, which is much larger than a covalent radius
Its nucleus has the weakest charge in the period
mcqs.why: Argon forms no covalent bonds, so only its van der Waals radius can be measured, and a van der Waals radius is always much larger than the covalent radius of a similar atom.

mcqs.q: Why is there a fall in ionization energy at aluminium in the third period?
options: The electron removed from Al comes from the higher-energy 3p subshell, shielded by the filled 3s subshell
Aluminium has a smaller nuclear charge than magnesium
The 3s electron of aluminium is removed
Aluminium forms a stable +3 ion before ionization
mcqs.why: The electron lost by aluminium comes from the higher-energy 3p subshell and is shielded by the filled 3s subshell, so it is removed more easily than the 3s electron of magnesium.

mcqs.q: According to Fajans rules, why are Sn4+ compounds covalent while Sn2+ compounds are ionic?
options: Sn4+ is larger than Sn2+ and distorts the anion more
Sn2+ has a very high charge density
Sn4+ is smaller and carries a +4 charge, so its polarizing power is strong
SnCl4 is a solid and SnCl2 is a liquid
mcqs.why: Sn4+ is small and highly charged, so it strongly distorts the anion and gives covalent compounds such as SnCl4, while the larger Sn2+ ion polarizes weakly and its compounds stay ionic.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Halide ions are reducing agents and their reducing strength increases in the order F- < Cl- < Br- < I-.
  • With concentrated H2SO4, bromide reduces sulphur from +6 to +4 (SO2) and iodide reduces it from +6 to -2 (H2S), while chloride does not reduce it.
  • Hydrogen halide bond enthalpies fall from H-F +568.2 to H-I +298.3 kJ/mol, so thermal stability decreases HF > HCl > HBr > HI.
  • Lithium forms only the normal oxide Li2O, sodium forms mainly the peroxide Na2O2, and K, Rb and Cs form superoxides such as KO2.
  • The inert pair effect makes the +2 state more stable down Group-IVA, so PbCl4 decomposes to PbCl2 and Cl2.
  • Group-IIA nitrates and carbonates decompose on heating to the oxide, and their thermal stability increases in the order Mg < Ca < Sr < Ba.
  • Third-period oxides change from basic Na2O and MgO, through amphoteric Al2O3, to strongly acidic SO3 and Cl2O7.
  • The F-F bond enthalpy (+158 kJ/mol) is lower than Cl-Cl (+242 kJ/mol) because lone pairs on the small fluorine atoms repel strongly.

Solved Exercises

Exercise: Detailed Answer Questions

Q: 1(a). Explain halide ions as reducing agents and discuss their trends in reducing strength.

Ans: A reducing agent loses electrons and is itself oxidized. Halide ions act as reducing agents by losing an electron to form the halogen: 2X- -> X2 + 2e-. The larger the halide ion, the farther its outer electron is from the nucleus and the more weakly it is held, so the electron is lost more easily. Therefore the reducing strength increases down the group in the order F- < Cl- < Br- < I-, and iodide is the strongest reducing agent. This is the reverse of the oxidizing power of the halogens, F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2. The trend is confirmed by the reactions with concentrated sulphuric acid: Cl- is not oxidized by it, Br- reduces H2SO4 to SO2 (sulphur falls from +6 to +4), while I- reduces H2SO4 all the way to H2S (sulphur falls from +6 to -2).

Q: 1(b). Why the bond enthalpy is important in the thermal stability of hydrogen halides?

Ans: On heating, a hydrogen halide decomposes into hydrogen and the halogen, and for this the H-X bond must be broken. The energy needed is the bond enthalpy of the H-X bond. Down the group the halogen atom becomes larger, the bond becomes longer and the attraction between the bonding pair and the nucleus becomes weaker, so the bond enthalpy decreases: H-F +568.2, H-Cl +431.9, H-Br +366.1 and H-I +298.3 kJ/mol. Hence HF and HCl are stable to heat and do not decompose easily, HBr decomposes slightly on heating and HI decomposes to a much greater extent. Thermal stability therefore decreases in the order HF > HCl > HBr > HI, exactly following the bond enthalpies.

Q: 2(a). Give the reason(s) that why simple oxides, peroxides and superoxide of Group-II A elements are formed?

Ans: When the alkali metals burn in oxygen, the type of oxide formed depends on the size of the metal ion, because the lattice energy is greatest when the cation and anion are of comparable size and the charges are well matched. Small Li+ stabilizes the small oxide ion O2-, so lithium forms only the normal oxide: 4Li + O2 -> 2Li2O. The larger Na+ stabilizes the bigger peroxide ion O2^2-, so sodium forms mainly the peroxide: 2Na + O2 -> Na2O2. The still larger K+, Rb+ and Cs+ stabilize the large superoxide ion O2-, so they form superoxides: K + O2 -> KO2. Thus normal oxides, peroxides and superoxides are formed by different metals according to the size of their ions.

Q: 2(b). What is meant by inert pair effect? Explain inert pair effects in formation of ionic and covalent bond.

Ans: The inert pair effect is the non-participation of the two s-electrons of the outermost shell in bonding, shown by the heavier p-block elements. Down Group-IVA the ns2 electrons become increasingly reluctant to be shared or lost, so the oxidation state two less than the group oxidation state (+2 instead of +4) becomes more stable, e.g. Pb2+ is more stable than Pb4+. In ionic compounds this means the lower oxidation state forms stable ionic compounds such as PbCl2 and SnCl2, and compounds of the higher state, like PbO2 and PbCl4, become strong oxidizing agents which readily change to the +2 state. In covalent compounds the effect explains why the tetrachlorides become less stable down the group (PbCl4 decomposes to PbCl2 and Cl2) while the covalent dichlorides and monoxides (CO is an exception, SnO and PbO) become more important for the heavier elements.

Q: 3(a). Discuss the effect of heat on nitrates, carbonates and hydrogen carbonates of Group-II A elements?

Ans: All Group-IIA nitrates decompose on heating to the metal oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen, e.g. 2Mg(NO3)2 -> 2MgO + 4NO2 + O2. The carbonates decompose to the oxide and carbon dioxide: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2. In both cases the temperature needed for decomposition increases down the group, because the larger cation has a smaller polarizing power and distorts the anion less; thus MgCO3 decomposes easily while BaCO3 needs a very high temperature. The hydrogen carbonates of these elements exist only in solution (temporary hardness of water) and on boiling they decompose to the carbonate: Ca(HCO3)2 -> CaCO3 + CO2 + H2O. So thermal stability of all these salts increases in the order Mg < Ca < Sr < Ba.

Q: 3(b). Discuss in detail acid base behaviour of Group-IVA oxides.

Ans: Group-IVA elements form monoxides (CO, SiO, GeO, SnO, PbO) and dioxides (CO2, SiO2, GeO2, SnO2, PbO2). CO2 is an acidic oxide which reacts with alkalis to form carbonates, while SiO2 is weakly acidic and reacts only with hot concentrated alkali and with HF. On going down the group the oxides become less acidic and more basic in character: GeO2, SnO2 and PbO2 are amphoteric, reacting with both acids and strong alkalis. The monoxides show the same trend: CO is a neutral oxide, while SnO and PbO are amphoteric with basic character predominating, dissolving readily in acids to form salts. In general the +2 oxides are more basic than the +4 oxides of the same element, and the overall trend down the group is acidic -> amphoteric -> basic, as the elements become more metallic.

Q: 4(a). Explain acid-base behaviour of oxides of third period elements.

Ans: Across the third period the oxides change from strongly basic through amphoteric to strongly acidic, following the change from metal to non-metal. Na2O and MgO are basic oxides: Na2O reacts with water to give the strong alkali NaOH, and MgO gives the weakly alkaline Mg(OH)2; both react with acids to form salts. Al2O3 is amphoteric and reacts with both acids and alkalis: Al2O3 + 6HCl -> 2AlCl3 + 3H2O and Al2O3 + 2NaOH -> 2NaAlO2 + H2O. SiO2 is weakly acidic, P4O10 and SO3 are strongly acidic oxides which form phosphoric acid and sulphuric acid with water, and Cl2O7 is the most strongly acidic, forming perchloric acid. Argon forms no oxide.

Q: 4(b). Enlist the properties of hydroxides of third period elements.

Ans: (1) NaOH is a strong base, completely ionized in solution, very soluble in water and corrosive. (2) Mg(OH)2 is a weak base, only sparingly soluble in water, and its suspension (milk of magnesia) is mildly alkaline. (3) Al(OH)3 is insoluble in water and amphoteric: it dissolves in acids to give aluminium salts and in excess alkali to give aluminates. (4) The hydroxides of the non-metals are in fact oxo-acids: silicic acid H2SiO3 (or Si(OH)4) is a very weak acid, phosphoric acid H3PO4 is a medium-weak acid, sulphuric acid H2SO4 is a strong acid and perchloric acid HClO4 is the strongest of all. Thus basic strength decreases and acidic strength increases across the period from Na to Cl.

Q: 5(a). Explain the bond enthalpies in halogens and bond enthalpies in hydrogen halides.

Ans: In the halogen molecules the bond enthalpy generally decreases down the group because the atoms become larger and the bonding electrons are farther from the nuclei: Cl-Cl +242, Br-Br +193 and I-I +151 kJ/mol. The F-F bond is an exception; its bond enthalpy (+158 kJ/mol) is lower than that of Cl-Cl because the fluorine atom is so small that the lone pairs on the two atoms repel each other strongly and weaken the bond. In the hydrogen halides the bond enthalpy decreases steadily down the group: H-F +568.2, H-Cl +431.9, H-Br +366.1 and H-I +298.3 kJ/mol. As the halogen atom grows, the H-X bond becomes longer and weaker, which is why the thermal stability of the hydrogen halides decreases from HF to HI.

Q: 5(b). Analyse the halide ions as reducing agents and trends in reducing strength of halides ions.

Ans: Halide ions are reducing agents because they can donate an electron and be oxidized to the halogen. Their reducing power depends on how easily the ion loses that electron. Down the group the ionic size increases (F- < Cl- < Br- < I-), the nuclear attraction for the outer electron decreases and the electron is lost more readily, so reducing strength increases in the order F- < Cl- < Br- < I-. The reactions with concentrated H2SO4 prove the trend: chloride ions do not reduce H2SO4 at all (only HCl gas is evolved), bromide ions reduce it to SO2 in which sulphur falls from +6 to +4: H2SO4 + 2H+ + 2Br- -> Br2 + SO2 + 2H2O, and iodide ions, the strongest reducing agents, reduce it to H2S in which sulphur falls from +6 to -2: 8HI + H2SO4 -> 4I2 + H2S + 4H2O. Chlorine, being a stronger oxidizing agent, also oxidizes Br- and I- to the free halogens, which confirms the same order.

mcqs.q: What is the order of reducing strength of the halide ions?
mcqs.why: The larger halide ion holds its outer electron more weakly and loses it more easily, so reducing strength increases down the group and iodide is the strongest reducing agent.

mcqs.q: How far does iodide reduce concentrated sulphuric acid?
options: It does not reduce sulphuric acid at all
It reduces sulphur from +6 to +4, forming SO2
It reduces sulphur from +6 to -2, forming H2S
It reduces sulphur from +6 to 0, forming sulphur
mcqs.why: Iodide is the strongest reducing halide: it reduces H2SO4 all the way to H2S, in which sulphur falls from +6 to -2, while bromide stops at SO2 and chloride does not reduce it.

mcqs.q: Which hydrogen halide has the largest bond enthalpy, and what is its value in the solved answers?
mcqs.why: The solved answers list H-F +568.2, H-Cl +431.9, H-Br +366.1 and H-I +298.3 kJ/mol, so HF has the largest bond enthalpy and is the most thermally stable hydrogen halide.

mcqs.q: Which oxide does sodium form mainly when it burns in oxygen?
mcqs.why: The larger Na+ ion stabilizes the bigger peroxide ion O2^2-, so sodium forms mainly the peroxide, 2Na + O2 -> Na2O2, while lithium forms only the normal oxide.

mcqs.q: What does the inert pair effect make more stable for lead?
options: The +2 oxidation state, as in PbCl2
mcqs.why: The inert pair effect makes the ns2 electrons reluctant to bond, so Pb2+ is more stable than Pb4+ and PbCl4 decomposes on warming to PbCl2 and Cl2.

mcqs.q: What happens when a Group-IIA hydrogen carbonate solution is boiled?
options: It forms the metal hydroxide and hydrogen
It forms the free metal and CO2
It decomposes to the carbonate, CO2 and water
mcqs.why: Group-IIA hydrogen carbonates exist only in solution and on boiling they decompose to the carbonate, for example Ca(HCO3)2 -> CaCO3 + CO2 + H2O.

mcqs.q: How do the Group-IVA oxides change in acid-base character down the group?
options: They become more acidic down the group
CO2 is basic and PbO2 is acidic
They change from acidic through amphoteric towards basic
They are neutral oxides in every case
mcqs.why: CO2 is acidic and SiO2 weakly acidic, GeO2, SnO2 and PbO2 are amphoteric, and the monoxides SnO and PbO are amphoteric with basic character predominating down the group.

mcqs.q: Which third-period oxide is amphoteric?
mcqs.why: Al2O3 reacts with both acids and alkalis, forming AlCl3 with HCl and NaAlO2 with NaOH, while Na2O and MgO are basic and SiO2, P4O10 and SO3 are acidic.

mcqs.q: Which hydroxide or oxo-acid of the third period is described as the strongest acid?
mcqs.why: Across the third period basic strength falls and acidic strength rises: NaOH is a strong base, H2SO4 is a strong acid and perchloric acid HClO4 is the strongest acid of all.

mcqs.q: Why is the F-F bond enthalpy (+158 kJ/mol) lower than that of Cl-Cl (+242 kJ/mol)?
options: Fluorine atoms are larger than chlorine atoms
The F-F bond is ionic in character
Fluorine has no d-orbitals in its valence shell
The fluorine atom is so small that the lone pairs on the two atoms repel each other strongly and weaken the bond
mcqs.why: The solved answers explain the exception by the very small size of fluorine: the lone pairs on the two bonded atoms repel strongly, weakening the F-F bond below the Cl-Cl value.

lessons.title: Project
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • In a flame test the wire is cleaned in concentrated HCl, dipped in the salt and held in the blue Bunsen flame.
  • Lithium salts give a crimson red flame, sodium salts an intense golden yellow flame and potassium salts a lilac flame.
  • Calcium gives a brick red flame, strontium a crimson red flame and barium an apple green flame.
  • Beryllium and magnesium salts give no colour to the flame.
  • Observations are recorded in a table of salt name, colour of the salt, colour of the flame and element identified.

Solved Exercises

Project

Q: Project: Perform an experiment that will enable you to differentiate and identify the elements present in salt using flame test. Record your observation in the table form (Salt name, Colour of the salt, Colour of the flame, Element identified).

Ans: Clean a nichrome or platinum wire in concentrated HCl, dip it in the salt and hold it in the blue Bunsen flame. Each Group-IA and Group-IIA element gives its characteristic colour, by which it is identified: lithium salts give a crimson red flame, sodium salts an intense golden yellow flame, potassium salts a lilac flame, rubidium salts a red-violet flame and caesium salts a blue flame. Among Group-IIA salts, calcium gives a brick red flame, strontium a crimson red flame and barium an apple green flame, while beryllium and magnesium salts give no colour to the flame. Record the salt name, the colour of the salt, the flame colour observed and the element identified in the four columns of the table.

chapters.title: Unit 14: d and f-Block Elements: Transition Elements

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Cu+ is diamagnetic because it has the configuration [Ar] 3d10 with all electrons paired.
  • Potassium ferrocyanide is a complex salt containing the [Fe(CN)6]4- ion.
  • The oxidation state of chromium in CrO2Cl2 is +6.
  • Paramagnetism depends on the number of unpaired electrons in the substance.
  • Ligands are electron pair donors that form co-ordinate bonds with the central metal ion.
  • The co-ordination number of iron in [Fe(CN)6]4- is 6.
  • The oxalate ion C2O4^2- is a bidentate ligand.
  • Potassium dichromate acts as a strong oxidizing agent, and copper is a constituent of German silver.

Solved Exercises

Exercise: Multiple Choice Questions

Q: 1. The diamagnetic ion is

Options: (a) Ni2+ (b) Cr3+ (c) Mn2+ (d) Cu+

Correct answer: Cu+

Q: 2. Potassium ferrocyanide is a

Options: (a) normal salt (b) mixed salt (c) double salt (d) complex salt

Correct answer: complex salt

Q: 3. The co-ordination compound [CuCl4]2- exists in the shape of

Options: (a) tetrahedral (b) octahedral (c) square planner (d) rhombic

Correct answer: tetrahedral

Q: 4. The oxidation state of chromium in CrO2Cl2 is

Options: (a) +2 (b) +3 (c) +4 (d) +6

Correct answer: +6

Q: 5. [BeF4]2- is an example of

Options: (a) square planar (b) tetrahedral complex (c) bent structure (d) octahedral complex

Correct answer: tetrahedral complex

Q: 6. Which of the following is a typical transition element

Options: (a) Zn (b) Cd (c) Ra (d) Co

Correct answer: Co

Q: 7. The paramagnetic nature of a substance depends on

Options: (a) the number of electron in the outer most orbit (b) the number of electron that are easily ejected (c) the number of un-paired electrons (d) the number of lone pair of electrons

Correct answer: the number of un-paired electrons

Q: 8. Ligands are

Options: (a) electron pair donors (b) electron pair acceptors (c) neutral (d) donor and then acceptor

Correct answer: electron pair donors

Q: 9. Which one is not ferromagnetic?

Options: (a) Fe (b) Co (c) Sb (d) Ni

Correct answer: Sb

Q: 10. The co-ordination number of iron in [Fe(CN)6]4- is

Options: (a) 9 (b) 3 (c) 4 (d) 6

Correct answer: 6

Q: 11. Select ligand which is bidentate?

Options: (a) H2O (b) NH3 (c) CO (d) C2O4^2-

Correct answer: C2O4^2-

Q: 12. Cu2+ salt solution is blue in colour due to transition of electron from

Options: (a) s to p orbital (b) d to d orbital (c) p to d orbital (d) p to p orbital

Correct answer: d to d orbital

Q: 13. Potassium dichromate acts as a strong

Options: (a) oxidizing agent (b) reducing agent (c) bleaching agent (d) dehydrating agent

Correct answer: oxidizing agent

Q: 14. One of the constituent of German silver is

Options: (a) Ag (b) Au (c) Cu (d) Al

Correct answer: Cu

Q: 15. The names which remains unchanged in naming co-ordination compounds are

Options: (a) anionic ligands (b) cationic ligands (c) neutral ligands (d) none of these

Correct answer: neutral ligands

mcqs.q: The diamagnetic ion is
mcqs.why: Cu+ has the configuration [Ar] 3d10 with all electrons paired, so it is diamagnetic, while Ni2+, Cr3+ and Mn2+ all have unpaired d electrons.

mcqs.q: Potassium ferrocyanide is a
mcqs.why: Potassium ferrocyanide, K4[Fe(CN)6], contains the complex ion [Fe(CN)6]4-, so it is a complex salt, not a normal, mixed or double salt.

mcqs.q: The co-ordination compound [CuCl4]2- exists in the shape of
mcqs.why: The four chloride ligands around copper in [CuCl4]2- are arranged tetrahedrally, giving the complex ion a tetrahedral shape.

mcqs.q: The oxidation state of chromium in CrO2Cl2 is
mcqs.why: In CrO2Cl2 the two oxygen atoms contribute -4 and the two chlorine atoms -2, a total of -6, so chromium must be in the +6 oxidation state.

mcqs.q: [BeF4]2- is an example of
mcqs.why: [BeF4]2- has four fluoride ligands arranged around beryllium, so it is a tetrahedral complex rather than square planar or octahedral.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a typical transition element
mcqs.why: Cobalt is a typical transition element with a partially filled d subshell, while Zn and Cd have full d subshells and Ra is an s-block element.

mcqs.q: The paramagnetic nature of a substance depends on
options: the number of electron in the outer most orbit
the number of electron that are easily ejected
the number of lone pair of electrons
mcqs.why: Paramagnetism is caused by unpaired electrons being attracted into a magnetic field, so it depends on the number of unpaired electrons present.

mcqs.q: Ligands are
mcqs.why: Ligands donate a lone pair of electrons to the central metal ion to form co-ordinate bonds, so ligands are electron pair donors.

mcqs.q: Which one is not ferromagnetic?
mcqs.why: Iron, cobalt and nickel are ferromagnetic, but antimony, Sb, is not ferromagnetic, so Sb is the odd one out in this list.

mcqs.q: The co-ordination number of iron in [Fe(CN)6]4- is
mcqs.why: Six cyanide ligands surround the iron in [Fe(CN)6]4-, so the co-ordination number of iron in this complex is 6.

mcqs.q: Select ligand which is bidentate?
mcqs.why: The oxalate ion C2O4^2- donates through two oxygen atoms at once, so it is a bidentate ligand, unlike H2O, NH3 and CO.

mcqs.q: Cu2+ salt solution is blue in colour due to transition of electron from
mcqs.why: The blue colour of Cu2+ solutions arises when an electron is promoted between split d-orbitals, that is a d to d orbital transition absorbing part of the visible light.

mcqs.q: Potassium dichromate acts as a strong
mcqs.why: Potassium dichromate readily gains electrons and oxidizes other substances, so it acts as a strong oxidizing agent.

mcqs.q: One of the constituent of German silver is
mcqs.why: German silver is an alloy of copper, zinc and nickel, so copper is one of its constituents, while Ag, Au and Al are not.

mcqs.q: The names which remains unchanged in naming co-ordination compounds are
mcqs.why: In naming co-ordination compounds the names of neutral ligands remain unchanged, while anionic ligand names end in -o and cationic ligand names end in -ium.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Cu+ is [Ar] 3d10, diamagnetic and colourless, while Cu2+ is [Ar] 3d9, paramagnetic and coloured.
  • The first transition series runs from scandium to zinc, with chromium [Ar] 3d5 4s1 and copper [Ar] 3d10 4s1 as exceptions.
  • Transition elements act as catalysts because of variable oxidation states, vacant d-orbitals and the large surface of finely divided metals.
  • Transition metals show variable oxidation states because the (n-1)d and ns electrons are very close in energy.
  • Sc3+ is [Ar] 3d0, so scandium compounds are colourless and diamagnetic.
  • The oxidation state of chromium in [Cr(H2O)6]3+ is +3 because water is a neutral ligand.
  • Iron is not used in the Contact process because arsenic oxide impurities poison it, so V2O5 is used instead.
  • Zn2+ salts are white because the 3d10 subshell is full, while Cu2+ salts are coloured because of d-d transitions.

Solved Exercises

Exercise: Short Answer Questions

Q: i. Give the reason that why Cu+ is diamagnetic but Cu2+ is paramagnetic.

Ans: Copper(I) has the configuration [Ar] 3d10. All the 3d electrons are paired, so Cu+ has no unpaired electron and is repelled by a magnetic field, i.e. it is diamagnetic, and its compounds are colourless. Copper(II) has the configuration [Ar] 3d9. One electron in the 3d subshell is unpaired, so Cu2+ is attracted by a magnetic field, i.e. it is paramagnetic, and its compounds are coloured.

Q: ii. Write down the electronic configuration of the first transition series.

Ans: The first transition series runs from scandium to zinc, and the 3d subshell is filled progressively: Sc [Ar] 3d1 4s2, Ti [Ar] 3d2 4s2, V [Ar] 3d3 4s2, Cr [Ar] 3d5 4s1, Mn [Ar] 3d5 4s2, Fe [Ar] 3d6 4s2, Co [Ar] 3d7 4s2, Ni [Ar] 3d8 4s2, Cu [Ar] 3d10 4s1, Zn [Ar] 3d10 4s2. Chromium and copper are exceptions to the expected pattern because the half-filled (3d5) and completely filled (3d10) configurations are extra stable.

Q: iii. Why the transition elements show the catalytic behaviour?

Ans: Transition elements act as catalysts for several reasons. They show variable oxidation states, so they can form unstable intermediate compounds with the reactants which then break up to give the products and regenerate the catalyst, e.g. V2O5 in the Contact process. Their ions have vacant d-orbitals and can form co-ordination compounds with the reactant molecules, bringing them close together. Their finely divided metals also provide a large surface area on which the reactant molecules are adsorbed and their bonds are weakened, e.g. iron in the Haber process.

Q: iv. Give the reason that transition elements form the co-ordination compounds.

Ans: Transition metal ions form co-ordination (complex) compounds readily because (1) they are small in size and carry a high positive charge, so they have a high charge density and strongly attract the lone pairs of the ligands; (2) they have vacant d-orbitals of suitable energy which can accept the lone pairs donated by the ligands and form co-ordinate covalent bonds; and (3) they can accommodate a definite number of ligands (co-ordination number 2, 4 or 6) around them in a regular geometry.

Q: v. Explain why transition metals have variable oxidation states.

Ans: In transition metals the (n-1)d and ns electrons are very close to each other in energy. Under different conditions either the ns electrons alone, or the ns electrons together with one or more (n-1)d electrons, can be used for bonding. Energy is needed to unpair and promote the d electrons, but this is recovered by the stronger bonds formed. So the metals show several oxidation states differing by one unit, e.g. iron shows +2 and +3, and manganese shows +2, +3, +4, +5, +6 and +7.

Q: vi. Justify the statement that "Scandium forms colourless and diamagnetic compounds".

Ans: Scandium (Z = 21) has the configuration [Ar] 3d1 4s2 and its only common ion is Sc3+, formed by losing all three outer electrons, which has the configuration [Ar] 3d0. The Sc3+ ion has no electron in the d subshell, so no d-d transition is possible and its compounds absorb no visible light; they are therefore colourless. It also has no unpaired electron, so its compounds are diamagnetic. Hence scandium forms colourless and diamagnetic compounds.

Q: vii. How do transition elements differ from s and p-block elements?

Ans: Transition (d-block) elements are all hard metals with high melting points, densities and tensile strength, whereas the s and p-blocks contain non-metals and gases as well. They show variable oxidation states, while s-block elements show only +1 or +2 and p-block elements a limited range. Their compounds are generally coloured and paramagnetic because of partially filled d-orbitals and unpaired electrons, while s and p-block compounds are usually colourless and diamagnetic. Transition elements form co-ordination compounds and alloys and act as catalysts, which s and p-block elements generally do not. In the s-block the differentiating electron enters the s-orbital and in the p-block the p-orbital, while in transition elements it enters the (n-1)d orbital.

Q: viii. What is the oxidation state of chromium in [Cr(H2O)6]3+?

Ans: Water is a neutral ligand, so it contributes no charge. Let the oxidation state of chromium be x. Then x + 6(0) = +3 (the charge on the complex ion), so x = +3. The oxidation state of chromium in [Cr(H2O)6]3+ is +3.

Q: ix. Give the reason that Fe is a catalyst in Haber process but not in the preparation of sulphuric acid.

Ans: In the Haber process the gases nitrogen and hydrogen are pure, so finely divided iron works well as a catalyst for N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3. In the manufacture of sulphuric acid by the Contact process, the sulphur dioxide is made by burning sulphur or roasting sulphide ores and contains impurities such as arsenic oxide, which permanently poison an iron (and even a platinum) catalyst and make it useless. Therefore iron is not used for the oxidation of SO2 to SO3; instead vanadium(V) oxide, V2O5, is used because it is not poisoned by these impurities and remains active for a long time.

Q: x. Zn2+ salts are white while Cu2+ salts are coloured. Why?

Ans: Zn2+ has the configuration [Ar] 3d10, i.e. a completely filled d subshell. There is no vacant d-orbital of the same set into which an electron can be promoted, so no d-d transition can take place and no visible light is absorbed; zinc salts are therefore white (colourless). Cu2+ has the configuration [Ar] 3d9 with an incomplete d subshell. In its compounds the d-orbitals are split by the ligands and an electron absorbs part of the visible light to jump from the lower to the higher d level (d-d transition). The remaining transmitted light gives copper(II) salts their blue or green colour.

mcqs.q: Why is Cu+ diamagnetic while Cu2+ is paramagnetic?
options: Cu+ is [Ar] 3d10 with all electrons paired, while Cu2+ is [Ar] 3d9 with one unpaired electron
Cu+ has one unpaired electron and Cu2+ has none
Both ions have completely filled d subshells
mcqs.why: Copper(I) is 3d10 with no unpaired electron, so it is diamagnetic and colourless, while copper(II) is 3d9 with one unpaired electron, so it is paramagnetic and coloured.

mcqs.q: Which two elements of the first transition series are exceptions to the expected filling pattern?
mcqs.why: Chromium is [Ar] 3d5 4s1 and copper is [Ar] 3d10 4s1, because the half-filled and completely filled d subshells have extra stability.

mcqs.q: Why can transition elements act as catalysts through variable oxidation states?
options: They form unstable intermediate compounds with the reactants that break up to give the products and regenerate the catalyst
They are used up completely in the reaction
They lower the temperature of every reaction to room temperature
They never form bonds with the reactants
mcqs.why: The solved answers give V2O5 in the Contact process as the example: the catalyst forms an intermediate by changing oxidation state and is then regenerated.

mcqs.q: Which set of reasons explains why transition metal ions form co-ordination compounds readily?
options: Large size, low charge and no vacant orbitals
They are all diamagnetic and colourless
Small size, high charge density and vacant d-orbitals that accept lone pairs from ligands
They have completely filled d subshells only
mcqs.why: Transition metal ions are small and highly charged and have vacant d-orbitals of suitable energy, so they strongly attract and accept the lone pairs donated by ligands.

mcqs.q: Why do transition metals show several oxidation states differing by one unit?
options: Their s and p electrons have very different energies
The (n-1)d and ns electrons are very close in energy, so either or both can be used in bonding
They lose electrons only from the p subshell
Each metal has only one stable ion
mcqs.why: Because the (n-1)d and ns energies are close, the ns electrons alone or together with d electrons can bond, so iron shows +2 and +3 and manganese shows +2 up to +7.

mcqs.q: Why are scandium compounds colourless and diamagnetic?
options: Sc3+ is [Ar] 3d1 with one unpaired electron
Sc forms only the Sc2+ ion
Sc3+ is [Ar] 3d0, so no d-d transition is possible and there is no unpaired electron
Scandium has a completely filled 3d10 subshell
mcqs.why: Sc3+ loses all three outer electrons to give a 3d0 ion: with no d electron there can be no d-d transition and no unpaired electron, so its compounds are colourless and diamagnetic.

mcqs.q: What is the oxidation state of chromium in [Cr(H2O)6]3+?
mcqs.why: Water is a neutral ligand and contributes no charge, so x + 6(0) = +3 for the complex ion, giving the oxidation state of chromium as +3.

mcqs.q: Why is iron not used as the catalyst in the Contact process for sulphuric acid?
options: Iron does not catalyse any gas reaction
Iron melts at the temperature of the process
Vanadium(V) oxide is cheaper than iron in every case
Impurities such as arsenic oxide in the SO2 permanently poison an iron catalyst
mcqs.why: The SO2 made by burning sulphur or roasting sulphide ores contains arsenic oxide impurities that poison iron (and platinum), so V2O5 is used because it is not poisoned and stays active.

mcqs.q: Why are Zn2+ salts white while Cu2+ salts are coloured?
options: Zn2+ is 3d10, so no d-d transition can occur, while Cu2+ is 3d9 and absorbs part of the visible light
Zinc salts contain no ligands around the metal ion
Copper salts are coloured because they are paramagnetic only
mcqs.why: Zn2+ has a completely filled 3d10 subshell with no vacant d-orbital for promotion, so no visible light is absorbed, while the incomplete 3d9 subshell of Cu2+ allows d-d transitions.

mcqs.q: How do transition elements differ from s and p-block elements in their compounds?
options: Their compounds are usually colourless and diamagnetic
They show only +1 and +2 oxidation states
Their compounds are generally coloured and paramagnetic because of partially filled d-orbitals
They never form co-ordination compounds or alloys
mcqs.why: The solved answers contrast the blocks: transition compounds are generally coloured and paramagnetic with variable oxidation states, while s and p-block compounds are usually colourless and diamagnetic.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • In the 3d series the 4s electrons are lost first on ion formation, so Fe2+ is [Ar] 3d6 and Fe3+ is [Ar] 3d5.
  • Colour in co-ordination compounds comes from d-d transitions between split d-orbitals; ions with 3d0 or 3d10 configurations are colourless.
  • Transition elements are hard metals with high melting points, variable oxidation states, coloured and paramagnetic compounds, and strong catalytic behaviour.
  • V2O5 catalyses the Contact process by changing between vanadium(V) and vanadium(IV), while finely divided iron catalyses the Haber process by adsorption.
  • In complex names the ligands are named first in alphabetical order, anionic ligands end in -o, and the metal oxidation state is shown as a Roman numeral.
  • KMnO4 is a powerful oxidizing agent and is self-indicating in acid titrations because its purple colour is discharged on reduction.
  • Alloys are harder and stronger than their component metals because atoms of different size distort the lattice and stop layers sliding.
  • Cu+ disproportionates in aqueous solution to Cu and Cu2+, and Cu2+ is the most stable state of copper in water.

Solved Exercises

Exercise: Detailed Answer Questions

Q: 1(a). Write down the electronic structure of 3d elements.

Ans: The 3d elements are Sc, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu and Zn, with atomic numbers 21 to 30. Their electronic structures are: Sc [Ar] 3d1 4s2; Ti [Ar] 3d2 4s2; V [Ar] 3d3 4s2; Cr [Ar] 3d5 4s1; Mn [Ar] 3d5 4s2; Fe [Ar] 3d6 4s2; Co [Ar] 3d7 4s2; Ni [Ar] 3d8 4s2; Cu [Ar] 3d10 4s1; Zn [Ar] 3d10 4s2. In each case the 4s subshell is filled before the 3d subshell is complete, because the 4s orbital is of lower energy, but when ions are formed the 4s electrons are lost first, e.g. Fe2+ is [Ar] 3d6 and Fe3+ is [Ar] 3d5.

Q: 1(b). Explain why the electronic configuration for chromium and copper differ from those assigned using the Aufbau principle.

Ans: According to the Aufbau principle, chromium (Z = 24) should be [Ar] 3d4 4s2 and copper (Z = 29) should be [Ar] 3d9 4s2. In fact chromium is [Ar] 3d5 4s1 and copper is [Ar] 3d10 4s1. One 4s electron moves into the 3d subshell in each case. This happens because a half-filled subshell (3d5, with one electron in each orbital) and a completely filled subshell (3d10) have extra stability, due to their symmetrical distribution of charge and the large exchange energy when many electrons have parallel spins. The energy gained from this stability is more than the small energy needed to promote the 4s electron into the 3d subshell.

Q: 2(a). Explain the origin of colour in coordination compounds.

Ans: In a free transition metal ion all five d-orbitals have the same energy. When ligands approach the metal ion in a complex, the d-orbitals split into two sets of different energies. An electron in the lower set can absorb energy from visible light equal to the energy gap and jump to the upper set; this is called a d-d transition. The colour absorbed is removed from white light and the complex shows the complementary colour, e.g. [Cu(H2O)6]2+ absorbs orange-red light and appears blue. The colour depends on the metal, its oxidation state and the ligands present. Ions with empty (3d0, e.g. Sc3+) or full (3d10, e.g. Zn2+) d subshells cannot show d-d transitions and are colourless.

Q: 2(b). What are the general characteristics of transition elements?

Ans: (1) They are hard, strong metals with high melting points, boiling points and densities. (2) They show variable oxidation states. (3) Most of their compounds are coloured, due to d-d transitions. (4) Many of them and their compounds are paramagnetic because of unpaired d electrons. (5) They form co-ordination compounds with ligands. (6) They and their compounds act as good catalysts, e.g. Fe in the Haber process and V2O5 in the Contact process. (7) They readily form alloys with one another and with other metals because their atoms are of similar size and can replace one another in the lattice. (8) They form interstitial compounds with small atoms like H, C and N, and their binding energies, oxidation states and paramagnetism increase with the number of unpaired electrons.

Q: 2(c). Assess the catalytic nature of vanadium and iron.

Ans: Vanadium acts as a catalyst through its compound V2O5 in the Contact process for making sulphuric acid. Vanadium(V) oxidizes SO2 to SO3 and is itself reduced to vanadium(IV): SO2 + V2O5 -> SO3 + V2O4; the vanadium(IV) is then re-oxidized by oxygen: V2O4 + 1/2 O2 -> V2O5, so the catalyst works by changing its oxidation state between +5 and +4. Iron is the catalyst of the Haber process: finely divided iron provides a large surface on which N2 and H2 molecules are adsorbed, their bonds are weakened, and they combine stepwise to form NH3. Iron compounds are also used as catalysts in other reactions, e.g. FeCl3. Both metals catalyse reactions because of their variable oxidation states and their ability to form temporary bonds with the reactants.

Q: 3. Discuss in detail the nomenclature of co-ordination compounds with suitable examples.

Ans: Rules: (1) The cation is named first and the anion second. (2) Within the complex, the ligands are named first, in alphabetical order, and the metal last. (3) Anionic ligands end in -o, e.g. chloro (Cl-), cyano (CN-), hydroxo (OH-); neutral ligands keep their names, with special names aqua (H2O), ammine (NH3) and carbonyl (CO); cationic ligands end in -ium, e.g. hydrazinium. (4) The number of each ligand is shown by di, tri, tetra, penta, hexa (bis, tris for complicated ligands). (5) The oxidation state of the metal is written as a Roman numeral in brackets. (6) If the complex is an anion, the metal name ends in -ate. Examples: [Co(NH3)6]Cl3 is hexaamminecobalt(III) chloride; K4[Fe(CN)6] is potassium hexacyanoferrate(II); [Cu(NH3)4]SO4 is tetraamminecopper(II) sulphate; [CoCl2(NH3)4]Cl is tetraamminedichlorocobalt(III) chloride.

Q: 4(a). Explain and write the reactions of Potassium Manganate (VII) as an oxidizing agent in organic chemistry.

Ans: Potassium manganate(VII), KMnO4, is a powerful oxidizing agent because MnO4- is readily reduced. In acid solution the half-equation is: MnO4- + 8H+ + 5e- -> Mn2+ + 4H2O, and the purple colour is discharged. With organic compounds it oxidizes oxalic acid on warming to carbon dioxide and water: 2KMnO4 + 5H2C2O4 + 3H2SO4 -> K2SO4 + 2MnSO4 + 10CO2 + 8H2O; this reaction is used in titrations and needs no indicator because KMnO4 is self-indicating. In alkaline or neutral solution cold dilute KMnO4 (Baeyer reagent) oxidizes an alkene to a diol and is itself reduced to brown MnO2, which is a test for a C=C double bond. It also oxidizes primary alcohols and aldehydes to carboxylic acids on heating. The book also notes that manganate(VII) ions oxidize ethene-type compounds and, in inorganic work, Fe2+ to Fe3+, H2O2 to O2 and sulphite ions to sulphate ions.

Q: 4(b). What are alloys? Describe some properties of an alloy that are different from the metals that compose it.

Ans: An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or of a metal with a non-metal, prepared by mixing the molten components and cooling the mixture. Because the atoms of the added element are of a different size, they distort the regular lattice of the host metal and stop the layers of atoms from sliding over one another. As a result an alloy is generally harder and stronger than the metals composing it, e.g. steel is harder than pure iron and brass is harder than copper. Alloys often have a lower melting point than the constituent metals (solder melts below the melting points of lead and tin), they are more resistant to corrosion (stainless steel does not rust like iron, and German silver, an alloy of Cu, Zn and Ni, resists tarnishing), and their colour and electrical conductivity also differ from those of the pure metals.

Q: 5(a). Explain the oxidation states of copper.

Ans: Copper (Z = 29) has the configuration [Ar] 3d10 4s1 and shows the oxidation states +1 and +2 (and rarely +3). In the +1 state copper is [Ar] 3d10; Cu(I) compounds such as Cu2O and CuCl are colourless and diamagnetic because the d subshell is full. In aqueous solution Cu+ is unstable and disproportionates: 2Cu+(aq) -> Cu(s) + Cu2+(aq). In the +2 state copper is [Ar] 3d9; Cu(II) is the most stable state in aqueous solution, and its compounds such as CuO and CuSO4.5H2O are coloured and paramagnetic because of the one unpaired d electron. The +2 state is stabilized by the high hydration energy of the small Cu2+ ion.

Q: 5(b). Write down some important reactions of hexaaquacopper (II) with hydroxide ions, ammonia and carbonate ions.

Ans: In water, copper(II) exists as the pale blue hexaaquacopper(II) ion, [Cu(H2O)6]2+. With hydroxide ions a pale blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide is formed: [Cu(H2O)6]2+ + 2OH- -> Cu(OH)2(s) + 6H2O. With ammonia solution the same pale blue precipitate of Cu(OH)2 first appears, but it dissolves in excess ammonia because the water ligands are replaced by ammonia, forming the deep blue tetraammineaquacopper(II) ion: Cu(OH)2 + 4NH3 + 2H2O -> [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+ + 2OH-. With carbonate ions the hexaaqua ions are not acidic enough to release CO2 from the carbonate; instead a precipitate of copper(II) carbonate is formed: Cu2+(aq) + CO3^2-(aq) -> CuCO3(s).

mcqs.q: When transition metal ions are formed, which electrons are lost first?
options: The 4s electrons are lost first, so Fe2+ is [Ar] 3d6 and Fe3+ is [Ar] 3d5
Electrons are lost equally from 3d and 4s
mcqs.why: Although the 4s subshell fills before 3d is complete, the solved answers state that on ion formation the 4s electrons are lost first, giving Fe2+ as 3d6 and Fe3+ as 3d5.

mcqs.q: Why does one 4s electron move into the 3d subshell in chromium and copper?
options: The 3d subshell repels the 4s electrons out of the atom
The Aufbau principle does not apply to metals
A half-filled 3d5 and a completely filled 3d10 subshell have extra stability from symmetrical charge distribution and exchange energy
Chromium and copper have extra protons in the 3d subshell
mcqs.why: The stability gained by the symmetrical half-filled or completely filled d subshell, with its large exchange energy, is more than the small energy needed to promote the 4s electron.

mcqs.q: What colour change is used as the example of a d-d transition for [Cu(H2O)6]2+?
options: It absorbs blue light and appears orange
It absorbs orange-red light and appears blue
It absorbs green light and appears red
It absorbs no light and appears colourless
mcqs.why: When ligands split the d-orbitals, an electron absorbs energy equal to the gap; [Cu(H2O)6]2+ absorbs orange-red light, so the complex shows the complementary colour, blue.

mcqs.q: Which pair of ions cannot show d-d transitions and are colourless?
mcqs.why: Ions with an empty d subshell such as Sc3+ (3d0) or a full one such as Zn2+ (3d10) cannot undergo d-d transitions, so their compounds are colourless.

mcqs.q: How does V2O5 catalyse the oxidation of SO2 to SO3 in the Contact process?
options: Vanadium(V) is reduced to vanadium(IV) as it oxidizes SO2, and oxygen then re-oxidizes it to V2O5
V2O5 dissolves the SO2 in water
V2O5 supplies the oxygen atoms permanently and is used up
V2O5 works only by providing a large surface area
mcqs.why: The solved cycle is SO2 + V2O5 -> SO3 + V2O4 followed by V2O4 + 1/2 O2 -> V2O5, so vanadium changes between the +5 and +4 oxidation states and the catalyst is regenerated.

mcqs.q: What is the correct name of K4[Fe(CN)6] under the nomenclature rules given?
mcqs.why: The cation is named first; in the anionic complex the metal name ends in -ate and its oxidation state is shown in Roman numerals, giving potassium hexacyanoferrate(II).

mcqs.q: Why does a KMnO4 titration need no separate indicator?
options: KMnO4 is colourless throughout the titration
KMnO4 is self-indicating because its purple colour is discharged as it is reduced
Oxalic acid changes colour at the end point
Mn2+ formed in the titration is deep purple
mcqs.why: In acid solution MnO4- + 8H+ + 5e- -> Mn2+ + 4H2O, so the purple colour disappears as the manganate(VII) is reduced, making KMnO4 its own indicator.

mcqs.q: What does cold dilute KMnO4 (Baeyer reagent) do to an alkene?
options: It reduces the alkene to an alkane
It oxidizes the alkene to a carboxylic acid and stays purple
It oxidizes the alkene to a diol and is itself reduced to brown MnO2
It has no reaction with alkenes
mcqs.why: Cold dilute alkaline KMnO4 oxidizes an alkene to a diol and is reduced to brown MnO2, which is the Baeyer test for a C=C double bond described in the solved answers.

mcqs.q: Why are alloys generally harder and stronger than the metals composing them?
options: Alloy atoms are all the same size, so the layers slide more easily
The added atoms distort the regular lattice and stop the layers of atoms sliding over one another
Alloys have higher melting points than every pure metal
mcqs.why: Atoms of the added element are of a different size and distort the host lattice, preventing the layers from sliding, so steel is harder than pure iron and brass is harder than copper.

mcqs.q: What happens to Cu+ ions in aqueous solution, and why is Cu2+ the stable state there?
options: Cu+ is stable and Cu2+ disproportionates to Cu+
Cu+ gains an electron to form only copper metal
Cu+ disproportionates, 2Cu+(aq) -> Cu(s) + Cu2+(aq), and Cu2+ is stabilized by its high hydration energy
Cu+ forms a deep blue solution that never changes
mcqs.why: Copper(I) is unstable in water and disproportionates into copper metal and Cu2+, and the +2 state is stabilized by the high hydration energy of the small Cu2+ ion.

lessons.title: Project
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • On heating, blue hydrated copper sulphate loses its water of crystallization and forms white anhydrous copper sulphate, CuSO4.5H2O -> CuSO4 + 5H2O.
  • The blue colour is due to water molecules acting as ligands around the Cu2+ ion, allowing d-d transitions.
  • Adding water to the cooled white anhydrous salt turns it blue again and heat is evolved, so the change is exothermic and reversible.
  • Anhydrous copper sulphate is used as a chemical test for the presence of water.

Solved Exercises

Project

Q: Project 1. Observe the colour change after heating and see what happened after heating.

Ans: On heating, the deep blue crystals of hydrated copper sulphate, CuSO4.5H2O, lose their water of crystallization in stages and finally form white anhydrous copper sulphate: CuSO4.5H2O -> CuSO4 + 5H2O. The colour fades gradually during heating and disappears completely when all the water has been driven off.

Q: Project 2. Why the deep blue colour of the copper disappears.

Ans: The deep blue colour of hydrated copper sulphate is due to the water molecules acting as ligands around the Cu2+ ion. When the water of crystallization is removed by heating, the ligand field around Cu2+ disappears, d-d transitions are no longer possible in the same way, and the salt becomes white anhydrous CuSO4.

Q: Project 3. Can you explain the reason of colour change?

Ans: The colour change is caused by the loss of water of crystallization on heating. The blue colour belongs to the hydrated [Cu(H2O)6]2+-type environment of the Cu2+ ion in the crystals; removing the water changes the environment of the ion, so the light absorbed changes and the solid appears white.

Q: Project 4. Add some water to the heated copper sulphate and observe what happened.

Ans: When a few drops of water are added to the cooled white anhydrous copper sulphate, it becomes blue again and heat is evolved, i.e. the change is exothermic. This is why anhydrous copper sulphate is used as a chemical test for the presence of water.

Q: Project 5. Explain why the deep blue colour reappears.

Ans: The deep blue colour reappears because the anhydrous copper sulphate takes up the added water and is converted back into hydrated copper sulphate, CuSO4.5H2O. The water molecules again surround the Cu2+ ions as ligands, the d-orbitals are split again and d-d transitions again absorb part of the visible light, so the blue colour returns. The reaction is reversible: CuSO4 (white) + 5H2O -> CuSO4.5H2O (blue).

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The first organic compound prepared in the laboratory was urea.
  • Graphite is an allotrope of carbon and is not an organic compound.
  • Anthracite contains the highest percentage of carbon among the types of coal.
  • Petroleum is mainly a mixture of saturated hydrocarbons, and the major component of natural gas is methane.
  • Refinery gas is not obtained by destructive distillation of coal; coal tar, coal gas and coke are obtained from it.
  • Coal can be converted to petroleum by the Fischer-Tropsch process, which forms alkanes from carbon monoxide and hydrogen.
  • Pyridine is a heterocyclic compound containing nitrogen, and the functional group of amides is -CONH2.
  • Oxygen cannot be detected directly in an organic compound, while Lassaigne's solution is used to test for nitrogen, sulphur and halogens.

Solved Exercises

Exercise: Q I. Choose the Correct One from the Given Options

Q: 1. The first organic compound prepared in the laboratory was

Options: (a) peat (b) urea (c) sugar (d) alcohol

Correct answer: urea

Q: 2. All the substances are organic except

Options: (a) graphite (b) urea (c) methane (d) acetic acid

Correct answer: graphite

Q: 3. The type of coal containing highest percentage of carbon is

Options: (a) Anthracite (b) Lignite (c) Peat (d) Bituminous

Correct answer: Anthracite

Q: 4. Petroleum is mainly a mixture of

Options: (a) heterocyclic compounds. (b) aromatic Hydrocarbons. (c) saturated hydrocarbons. (d) unsaturated hydrocarbons.

Correct answer: saturated hydrocarbons.

Q: 5. The major component of natural gas is

Options: (a) butane (b) ethane (c) propane (d) methane

Correct answer: methane

Q: 6. All of the following fractions are obtained by destructive distillation of coal except

Options: (a) coal tar. (b) refinery gas. (c) coal gas. (d) coke.

Correct answer: refinery gas.

Q: 7. Coal can be converted to petroleum by

Options: (a) Haber process. (b) Destructive distillation. (c) Fischer-Tropsch process. (d) Fractional distillation.

Correct answer: Fischer-Tropsch process.

Q: 8. Pyridine belongs to which class of organic compounds

Options: (a) heterocyclic (b) hydrocarbon (c) alicyclic (d) homocyclic

Correct answer: heterocyclic

Q: 9. Which of the following represents the functional group of amides?

Options: (a) -COOR (b) -NH2 (c) -C≡N (d) -CONH2

Correct answer: -CONH2

Q: 10. Which of the following elements can not be detected in a given organic compound, directly?

Options: (a) Chlorine (b) Phosphorous (c) Nitrogen (d) Oxygen

Correct answer: Oxygen

Q: 11. Lassaigne's solution is used to test the presence of

Options: (a) nitrogen. (b) halogen. (c) sulphur. (d) all of these.

Correct answer: all of these.

Q: 12. Lassigne's solution plus silver nitrate gives yellow precipitate which is insoluble in ammonium hydroxide. This shows the presence of

Options: (a) nitrogen (b) sulphur (c) iodine (d) carbon

Correct answer: iodine

Q: 13. Fischer-Tropsch synthesis involve the formation of alkanes by the combination of

Options: (a) CO and H2 (b) CO2 and H2 (c) C and H2 (d) All of these

Correct answer: CO and H2

Q: 14. Bucky balls consists of .................... carbon rings

Options: (a) tetragonal (b) pentagonal (c) hexagonal (d) b and c both

Correct answer: b and c both

Q: 15. Pyridine

Options: (a) is homocyclic compound. (b) contains nitrogen. (c) is heterocyclic compound. (d) both b and c.

Correct answer: both b and c.

mcqs.why: A deep yellow precipitate with silver nitrate that is insoluble in ammonium hydroxide indicates iodine in the halogen test of the unit.

mcqs.why: The Fischer-Tropsch equation (2n + 1)H2 + nCO -> CnH2n+2 + nH2O shows that alkanes form by the combination of carbon monoxide and hydrogen.

mcqs.why: Bucky ball is built of hexagonal rings like graphite and also pentagonal rings, so both pentagonal and hexagonal carbon rings are present.
