mcqs.why: Pyridine has a nitrogen atom in its six-membered ring, so it contains nitrogen, and because a non-carbon atom is part of the ring it is a heterocyclic compound; both facts hold together.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Organic compounds contain carbon as the major element and are obtained from living things as well as synthesized in the laboratory.
  • In Lassaigne's test, Prussian blue or green colouration after adding FeSO4, FeCl3 and concentrated HCl confirms the presence of nitrogen.
  • A homologous series has members with similar structures and chemical properties, each differing from the next by a -CH2- group, with a general formula such as CnH2n+2 for alkanes.
  • Bucky ball (C60) is a hollow spherical cage of 60 carbon atoms made of hexagonal and pentagonal rings.
  • Metal carbonates, cyanides, oxides of carbon and allotropes of carbon contain carbon but are not considered organic compounds.
  • Partial synthesis starts from intermediates isolated from natural sources, while total synthesis builds a molecule from small, cheap and readily available molecules.
  • Carbon forms a very large number of compounds because of catenation, stable single and multiple bonds, and isomerism.
  • Acyclic compounds have open carbon chains, while cyclic compounds have rings that are homocyclic if made only of carbon and heterocyclic if the ring contains another atom.

Solved Exercises

Exercise: Q2. Write Short Answers of the Following Questions

Q: i. What is meant by organic compounds and organic chemistry?

Ans: Organic compounds are the compounds containing carbon which are obtained from living things (plants and animals) as well as synthesized in the laboratory. They contain carbon as a major element along with other elements like hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, sulphur etc. Organic chemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with the scientific study of the structure, properties, composition, reactions and preparations of carbon-based compounds, i.e. hydrocarbons and their derivatives.

Q: ii. Write down the procedure for the test of presence of nitrogen in organic compound.

Ans: First Lassaigne's solution (sodium extract) is prepared by heating the substance strongly with sodium metal in a fusion tube till the tube becomes red hot and plunging it into distilled water in a china dish; the contents are boiled and filtered. For nitrogen: take a part of Lassaigne's solution in a test tube, add a few drops of sodium hydroxide and then a few millilitres of freshly prepared ferrous sulphate (FeSO4) solution and boil it. After cooling, add a few drops of ferric chloride (FeCl3) solution and excess of concentrated HCl solution. The formation of Prussian blue or green colouration confirms the presence of nitrogen.

Q: iii. What is homologous series? Give the characteristics of homologous series.

Ans: A series of organic compounds in which all members possess similar structural features and similar chemical characteristics, but each member differs from the next member by a methylene (-CH2-) group, is called a homologous series; its members are called homologues. Characteristics: (1) each class of organic compounds has its own homologous series having a general formula, e.g. alkanes CnH2n+2; (2) all members have similar chemical properties and the same general methods of preparation, similar structural features and the same functional group; (3) physical properties like melting point, boiling point and density increase down the series due to increase in molecular masses.

Q: iv. Although bucky ball is an allotropic form of carbon, but it is included in organic chemistry.

Ans: Bucky ball (Buckminster fullerene, C60) is a hollow spherical shaped cage made of 60 carbon atoms, built of hexagonal rings like graphite and also pentagonal rings. Although it is an allotrope of carbon like diamond and graphite, it exists as discrete covalent molecules of carbon atoms joined in rings, and its chemistry is the chemistry of a carbon cage molecule which can be studied and derivatized like other carbon compounds. That is why fullerenes, which have significantly expanded the number of known allotropes of carbon, are included in organic chemistry.

Q: v. Mention those compounds which although contain carbon but are not considered organic.

Ans: The carbon containing alloys (including steel), metal carbonates, bicarbonates, carbonyl, cyanides (NaCN), cyanates (KOCN, NH4OCN), oxides and sulfides of carbon (CO, CO2, CS2), as well as the allotropes of carbon (diamond, graphite and amorphous forms), although contain carbon, are not organic compounds. They are inorganic in nature either by their source or properties or nature of bonding.

Q: vi. Differentiate between partial and total synthesis?

Ans: Partial synthesis is the process in which the intermediate product or compounds, isolated from natural sources (e.g. coal, petroleum, natural gas, plants, animals or microorganism etc.) are used as a starting material to produce other organic molecules, e.g. formation of soap from oil or fat obtained from plants or animals, and production of alcohol from sugar by fermentation. Total synthesis is the process in which an organic molecule is synthesized from small, cheap and readily available molecules, the desired product being obtained by converting the starting material through many steps, e.g. production of urea from methane, air and water through a number of chemical steps.

Q: vii. How coal can be converted into petroleum?

Ans: Coal gas, obtained from the destructive distillation of coal, can be converted into petroleum by the Fischer-Tropsch (FT) process. It is a set of chemical reactions that convert a mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen into liquid hydrocarbons, mainly alkanes: (2n + 1)H2 + nCO -> CnH2n+2 + nH2O. The conversion involves hydrogenolysis of the C-O bond and formation of C-C bonds, and takes place in the presence of transition metal catalysts (cobalt, iron, ruthenium or nickel etc.) at a temperature range of 150-300 C.

Q: viii. Discuss the reasons for the presence of large number of organic compounds?

Ans: The abundance of organic compounds is due to the unique behaviour of carbon. Carbon has the property of self-linkage (catenation): it can link with hundreds and thousands of other carbon atoms to form long C-C chains or rings. Carbon can also form stable single and multiple bonds with each other and with other atoms like hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, halogens, sulphur etc. In addition, compounds with the same molecular formula can have different structures (isomerism). As a result carbon forms a large number of organic compounds.

Q: ix. Differentiate between acyclic and cyclic organic compounds.

Ans: In acyclic (open chain) organic compounds the carbon atoms are linked to each other in open chains, which may be a straight chain, e.g. n-butane CH3-CH2-CH2-CH3, or a branched chain, e.g. isobutane. In cyclic (closed chain) organic compounds the carbon atoms are arranged in closed chain (ring) form. Cyclic compounds may be homocyclic, in which the ring is made only of carbon atoms (alicyclic compounds like cyclopropane and cyclohexane, and aromatic compounds containing a benzene ring), or heterocyclic, in which the ring contains at least one atom other than carbon, e.g. pyridine, furan and pyrrole.

mcqs.q: According to the solved answers, organic compounds always contain which element as the major element?
mcqs.why: Organic compounds contain carbon as the major element, along with other elements like hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and sulphur.

mcqs.q: In Lassaigne's test for nitrogen, which colour confirms the presence of nitrogen?
mcqs.why: After adding freshly prepared FeSO4 solution, then FeCl3 and excess concentrated HCl to the sodium extract, Prussian blue or green colouration confirms nitrogen.

mcqs.q: By what group does each member of a homologous series differ from the next member?
mcqs.why: Members of a homologous series possess similar structural features, but each member differs from the next member by a methylene (-CH2-) group.

mcqs.q: How many carbon atoms are present in a bucky ball (Buckminster fullerene, C60)?
mcqs.why: Bucky ball is a hollow spherical shaped cage made of 60 carbon atoms, built of hexagonal rings and also pentagonal rings.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT considered an organic compound although it contains carbon?
mcqs.why: Cyanides such as NaCN, along with carbonates, oxides of carbon and the allotropes of carbon, are inorganic in nature and are not considered organic compounds.

mcqs.q: Formation of soap from oil or fat obtained from plants or animals is an example of which type of synthesis?
mcqs.why: Partial synthesis uses an intermediate product isolated from natural sources as the starting material, as in the formation of soap from oil or fat obtained from plants or animals.

mcqs.q: The Fischer-Tropsch conversion of coal gas into petroleum takes place in the presence of which catalysts?
mcqs.why: The Fischer-Tropsch conversion takes place in the presence of transition metal catalysts such as cobalt, iron, ruthenium or nickel, at a temperature range of 150-300 C.

mcqs.q: The property of carbon to link with hundreds and thousands of other carbon atoms to form long chains or rings is called
mcqs.why: Self-linkage of carbon is called catenation, and together with stable multiple bonds and isomerism it explains the presence of a large number of organic compounds.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is the branched-chain acyclic compound given in the solved answers?
mcqs.why: Isobutane is given as the branched open-chain (acyclic) example, while cyclohexane and pyridine are closed-chain (cyclic) compounds.

mcqs.q: In which type of cyclic compound does the ring contain at least one atom other than carbon?
mcqs.why: Heterocyclic compounds are cyclic compounds in which the ring contains at least one atom other than carbon, e.g. pyridine, furan and pyrrole.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Fossil fuels, namely coal, petroleum and natural gas, form by anaerobic decomposition of buried plant and animal remains.
  • Anthracite is the highest rank coal with more than 91.5% carbon, and petroleum is a mixture of alkanes, cycloalkanes and aromatic hydrocarbons.
  • Carbon is detected when the CO2 produced on heating with cupric oxide turns lime water milky, and hydrogen when water droplets turn white anhydrous copper sulphate blue.
  • Sulphur is confirmed by a black precipitate of lead sulphide, and halogens by silver nitrate precipitates whose colour and solubility in ammonium hydroxide identify chlorine, bromine or iodine.
  • Oxygen has no direct test in an organic compound and is detected indirectly through oxygen-containing functional groups.
  • Destructive distillation of coal gives coke, coal tar, ammoniacal liquor and coal gas.
  • Most organic compounds are covalent and non-ionic, insoluble in water but soluble in non-polar solvents, and their reactions are slow.
  • A functional group is the chemically active part of a molecule, and each functional group defines a class of organic compounds with its own general formula.

Solved Exercises

Exercise: Q3. Write Detail Answers of the Following Questions

Q: 1. What are fossil fuels? Discuss different types of fossil fuels.

Ans: Fossil fuels are the natural sources of organic compounds formed under the earth surface from plant and animal remains by the anaerobic (without oxygen) decomposition of buried plants and animals. Petroleum, coal and natural gas are called fossil fuels. (1) Coal: an important solid fossil fuel of black or brownish-black colour, normally occurring in rock strata in layers called coal beds. It is mainly composed of carbon along with hydrogen, oxygen, sulphur and nitrogen, and is formed from plant matter buried under the soil millions of years ago, first converted into peat which under high pressure and temperature gets converted into coal. Its forms are lignite (low percentage of carbon), sub-bituminous coal, bituminous coal and anthracite (highest rank coal, more than 91.5% carbon). It is mainly used as a fuel to produce electricity and heat through combustion. (2) Petroleum: the word is derived from Latin 'Petra' (rock) and 'oleum' (oil), i.e. rock oil, also called mineral oil, crude oil or liquid gold. It is a viscous liquid having dark brown colour with a strong unpleasant smell, and is a mixture of mostly alkanes, cycloalkanes and aromatic hydrocarbons, with trace amounts of compounds containing nitrogen, oxygen, sulphur and metals like nickel, copper and vanadium. (3) Natural gas: a gaseous form of fossil fuel which is a mixture of low boiling hydrocarbons, methane, ethane, propane and butane, formed by the decay of dead animal matter and usually found above the underground deposits of petroleum.

Q: 2. Elaborate the detection of various elements in organic compound.

Ans: The main elements present in organic compounds are carbon and hydrogen as well as oxygen, nitrogen, sulphur and halogens. Carbon: the organic substance is mixed with dry cupric oxide in 1:3 ratio and heated in a test tube fitted with a delivery tube dipping into lime water, Ca(OH)2. Carbon converts to carbon dioxide, which turns lime water milky due to formation of calcium carbonate: Ca(OH)2(aq) + CO2(g) -> CaCO3(s) + H2O(l). Hydrogen: if hydrogen is present, it is oxidized to water vapours which condense in small droplets on the cooler end of the test tube; the water is further confirmed by passing the issuing gases over anhydrous copper sulphate (white), which turns blue as it converts to the hydrated form (CuSO4.5H2O). Nitrogen, sulphur and halogens are detected by Lassaigne's test: the substance is heated strongly with sodium metal in a fusion tube till it becomes red hot, plunged into distilled water, boiled and filtered; the filtrate is Lassaigne's solution or sodium extract. Nitrogen: to a part of the extract add a few drops of NaOH and freshly prepared FeSO4 solution and boil; after cooling add FeCl3 solution and excess concentrated HCl; Prussian blue or green colouration confirms nitrogen. Sulphur: to another portion add acetic acid and then lead acetate solution; a black precipitate of lead sulphide confirms sulphur. Halogens: boil a portion of the extract with concentrated nitric acid and add silver nitrate solution; a white precipitate soluble in ammonium hydroxide indicates chlorine, a pale yellow precipitate slightly soluble in NH4OH indicates bromine, and a deep yellow precipitate insoluble in NH4OH shows iodine. Oxygen: it has no direct test; the substance is heated alone in a dry test tube usually in nitrogen atmosphere and formation of water droplets on the cooler part shows oxygen, or tests are applied for oxygen containing functional groups like alcohol (-OH), ketone (-CO-), aldehyde (-CHO) and carboxylic acid (-COOH); detection of any one confirms oxygen.

Q: 3. Write the different fractions obtained by the destructive distillation of coal. Give their importance.

Ans: When coal is heated in the absence of air, it does not burn but produces many by-products; this process is called destructive distillation of coal. The main products are: (i) Coke: a fuel used in homes and factories, but mainly used in industries as a reducing agent for the extraction of metals from their ores. (ii) Coal tar: a mixture of organic compounds which can be separated by fractional distillation and used for making soap, fats, dyes, plastics, perfume, drugs, pesticides and explosives; on fractional distillation it gives important organic compounds like benzene, toluene, xylene, phenol, cresol, naphthalene and anthracene. (iii) Ammoniacal liquor: an ammonia solution used for making fertilizers like ammonium sulphate and ammonium superphosphate. (iv) Coal gas: a mixture of hydrogen and carbon monoxide, which is combustible, making coal gas an excellent fuel; it is also converted into petroleum by the Fischer-Tropsch process.

Q: 4. Explain some of the important characteristics of organic compounds.

Ans: (1) Unique properties of carbon: carbon has the property of self-linkage (catenation), linking with hundreds and thousands of carbon atoms to form long chains or rings, and forming stable single and multiple bonds with itself and other atoms, so it forms a large number of compounds. (2) Isomerism: two or more compounds having the same molecular formula but different structures are called isomers, and this phenomenon is isomerism. (3) Non-ionic character: most organic compounds involve covalent bonds between C-C and C-H, therefore they are generally non-polar and have non-ionic character. (4) Solubility: following 'like dissolves like', most organic compounds are insoluble in water but readily soluble in non-polar solvents like ether, benzene and carbon tetrachloride. (5) Rates of organic reactions: bonds in organic molecules are formed by mutual sharing of electrons, and for a reaction the existing bonds must be broken and new bonds formed, therefore organic reactions are slow. (6) Similar structural features and behaviour: organic compounds have similar structural features (functional groups) and similar physical and chemical properties, so they are grouped into a few classes or homologous series. (7) Polymerization: some organic compounds exhibit polymerization, e.g. ethylene polymerizes to polyethylene.

Q: 5. Define functional group. How organic compounds are classified on the basis of functional group?

Ans: An atom or a group of atoms or multiple bonds that gives certain characteristic properties to an organic compound is called a functional group, because it is the chemically active or functional part of a molecule; each functional group represents a different class of organic compounds. On this basis compounds are classified, with general formula and example, as: alkanes (no functional group, CnH2n+2, CH4 methane); alkenes (C=C double bond, CnH2n, C2H4 ethene); alkynes (-C≡C- triple bond, CnH2n-2, C2H2 ethyne); alkyl halides (-X = F, Cl, Br, I, halo group, R-X or CnH2n+1X, CH3-Cl methyl chloride); alcohols (-OH hydroxyl, R-OH, CH3-OH methanol); amines (-NH2 amino, R-NH2, CH3-NH2 methyl amine); ethers (-O- oxygen/oxa, R-O-R, CH3-O-CH3 dimethyl ether); ketones (C=O carbonyl/keto group, (CnH2n+1)2CO, acetone); aldehydes (-CHO formyl, R-CHO, CH3-CHO ethanal); carboxylic acids (-COOH carboxyl, R-COOH, CH3-COOH acetic acid); acid halides (-COX halo carbonyl, R-COX, CH3-COCl acetyl chloride); acid amides (-CONH2 amide, R-CONH2, acetamide); esters (-COOR ester/alkoxy carbonyl, methyl acetate); and alkyl cyanides or nitriles (-C≡N cyano, R-CN, CH3CN methyl cyanide). Each class has its own homologous series represented by its general formula.

Q: 6. Give old classification of organic compounds based on arrangement of carbon atoms in the molecule.

Ans: This classification is based on the arrangement of carbon atoms in molecules, and organic compounds are broadly divided into two groups. (i) Open chain or acyclic organic compounds: the carbon atoms are linked to each other in open chains, which may be a straight chain, e.g. n-butane CH3-CH2-CH2-CH3, or a branched chain, e.g. isobutane CH3-CH(CH3)-CH3. (ii) Closed chain or cyclic organic compounds: the carbon atoms are arranged in closed chain (ring) form. They may be homocyclic or heterocyclic. Homocyclic (carbocyclic) compounds, in which the cycle or ring is made only of carbon atoms, are further divided into alicyclic compounds, having properties similar to open chain compounds, e.g. cyclopropane, cyclobutane and cyclohexane, and aromatic compounds, in which a benzene ring is present, e.g. benzene, toluene and naphthalene. Heterocyclic compounds are those cyclic compounds in which the ring contains at least one atom other than carbon, e.g. pyridine, thiophene, furan and pyrrole.

mcqs.q: Fossil fuels are formed from buried plant and animal remains by decomposition
options: In the presence of excess oxygen
mcqs.why: Fossil fuels are formed under the earth surface from plant and animal remains by the anaerobic, that is without oxygen, decomposition of buried plants and animals.

mcqs.q: Anthracite, the highest rank coal, contains more than what percentage of carbon?
mcqs.why: The solved answer states that anthracite is the highest rank coal, containing more than 91.5% carbon.

mcqs.q: In the detection of carbon, the gas evolved turns lime water milky because of the formation of
mcqs.why: Carbon is oxidized to carbon dioxide, which reacts with lime water to form calcium carbonate: Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O, turning the lime water milky.

mcqs.q: A black precipitate with lead acetate in Lassaigne's test confirms the presence of
mcqs.why: To a portion of the sodium extract, acetic acid and then lead acetate solution are added; a black precipitate of lead sulphide confirms sulphur.

mcqs.q: Which halogen gives a deep yellow precipitate with silver nitrate that is insoluble in ammonium hydroxide?
mcqs.why: In the halogen test, chlorine gives a white precipitate soluble in NH4OH, bromine a pale yellow precipitate slightly soluble in NH4OH, and iodine a deep yellow precipitate insoluble in NH4OH.

mcqs.q: Coke obtained by the destructive distillation of coal is mainly used in industries as
options: A reducing agent for the extraction of metals from their ores
mcqs.why: Coke is a fuel, but it is mainly used in industries as a reducing agent for the extraction of metals from their ores.

mcqs.q: Ammoniacal liquor obtained from coal is used for making fertilizers such as
mcqs.why: Ammoniacal liquor is an ammonia solution used for making fertilizers like ammonium sulphate and ammonium superphosphate.

options: Non-polar solvents like ether, benzene and carbon tetrachloride

mcqs.q: Ethylene polymerizes to form which product?
mcqs.why: Polymerization is one of the characteristics of organic compounds; ethylene polymerizes to polyethylene.

mcqs.why: In the functional group classification, alkenes containing a C=C double bond have the general formula CnH2n, while alkanes are CnH2n+2 and alkynes are CnH2n-2.

lessons.title: Project
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Urea is mixed with dry cupric oxide in about 1:3 ratio and heated strongly to test for carbon and hydrogen.
  • Carbon is confirmed when the carbon dioxide produced turns lime water milky by forming calcium carbonate.
  • Hydrogen is confirmed when water vapours condense as droplets and turn white anhydrous copper sulphate blue.
  • Nitrogen in urea is confirmed by Lassaigne's test, in which the sodium extract gives a Prussian blue or green colouration.

Solved Exercises

Project

Q: Perform tests for detection of carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen in Urea (or any other available organic compound containing C, H and N) by following the procedure discussed in section 15.7.

Ans: Carbon and hydrogen: mix a little urea with dry cupric oxide (CuO) in about 1:3 ratio in a hard glass test tube fitted with a delivery tube dipping into lime water, and heat strongly. The carbon of urea is oxidized to CO2, which passes into the lime water and turns it milky (Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O), confirming carbon. The hydrogen is oxidized to water vapours, which condense as small droplets on the cooler upper part of the test tube; passing the gases over white anhydrous copper sulphate turns it blue (formation of CuSO4.5H2O), confirming hydrogen. Nitrogen: prepare Lassaigne's solution by fusing a little urea with a small piece of sodium metal in a fusion tube till red hot, plunging it into distilled water, boiling and filtering. To a part of the filtrate add a few drops of NaOH and freshly prepared FeSO4 solution and boil; cool, then add a few drops of FeCl3 and excess concentrated HCl. A Prussian blue (or green) colouration appears, confirming the presence of nitrogen in urea.

lessons.title: Self-Assessment
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • In propane every carbon is sp3 hybridized, with C-C sigma bonds from sp3-sp3 overlap and C-H sigma bonds from sp3-s overlap, bond angles about 109.5 degrees, C-C bond length about 154 pm and C-H bond length about 109.5 pm.
  • Bromohydration of but-2-ene with bromine in aqueous solution gives 3-bromobutan-2-ol through a cyclic bromonium ion intermediate.
  • In drawing an alkyne, the longest chain containing the triple bond is drawn first and the triple bond is given the lowest possible position numbers.
  • In chlorobenzene, delocalization of the chlorine lone pair makes the ortho and para positions electron rich, while in benzaldehyde the ortho and para positions carry positive charge character.

Solved Exercises

Self-Assessment

Q: Draw orbital hybridization model of propane and show different types of overlaps in formation of carbon-carbon and carbon-hydrogen sigma bonds.

Ans: In propane (CH3-CH2-CH3) every carbon atom is bonded to four other atoms, so each carbon uses sp3-hybrid orbitals, as in ethane. The C-C sigma bonds are formed by linear (head-on) overlap of an sp3-hybrid orbital of one carbon atom with an sp3-hybrid orbital of the neighbouring carbon atom (sp3-sp3 overlap). Each C-H sigma bond is formed by overlap of an sp3-hybrid orbital of carbon with the 1s orbital of a hydrogen atom (sp3-s overlap). All the C-C and C-H bonds are therefore sigma bonds, the bond angles are about 109.5 degrees (tetrahedral geometry), with C-C bond length about 154 pm and C-H bond length about 109.5 pm, exactly as described for ethane in the unit.

Q: Predict the product of bromohydration of but-2-ene and write the complete reaction.

Ans: Bromohydration means addition of Br and OH across the double bond when the alkene is treated with bromine in aqueous solution, because water competes as a nucleophile for the cyclic bromonium ion. For but-2-ene: CH3-CH=CH-CH3 + Br2 + H2O -> CH3-CH(OH)-CH(Br)-CH3 + HBr. The product is 3-bromobutan-2-ol (butane-2,3-bromohydrin), formed through a cyclic bromonium ion intermediate which is attacked by water, followed by loss of H+.

Q: Draw the structures of the following alkynes: (i) 3,3,4-trimethylpent-1-yne (ii) 3-methylhexa-1,4-diyne (iii) 4-ethyl-3,5-dimethylhex-1-yne

Ans: (i) 3,3,4-trimethylpent-1-yne: HC≡C-C(CH3)2-CH(CH3)-CH3. (ii) 3-methylhexa-1,4-diyne: HC≡C-CH(CH3)-CH2-C≡CH. (iii) 4-ethyl-3,5-dimethylhex-1-yne: HC≡C-CH(CH3)-CH(CH2-CH3)-CH(CH3)-CH3. In each case the longest chain containing the triple bond(s) is drawn first, the triple bond is given position 1 (or 1 and 4), and the methyl and ethyl substituents are placed on the numbered carbons shown in the name.

Q: Draw the possible resonance structures for chlorobenzene and benzaldehyde.

Ans: Chlorobenzene: besides the two Kekule forms of the ring, the lone pair of electrons on chlorine is delocalized into the ring, giving contributing structures in which Cl forms a double bond with the ring carbon (Cl bearing a positive charge) and a negative charge appears at an ortho position, at the other ortho position, and at the para position; this is why the ortho and para positions become electron rich. Benzaldehyde: the ring gives the usual Kekule contributing forms, and the pi electrons of the -CHO group are also involved: contributing structures place a positive charge on the carbonyl carbon (C=O polarized as C+-O-) and, by delocalization through the ring, positive charge character at the ortho and para positions of the ring, while the carbonyl oxygen carries the negative charge; the actual molecule is the resonance hybrid of all these contributing (canonical) forms.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Pentane, C5H12, has 3 isomers, and C2H6O has 2 isomers.
  • Heating a tetrahalide such as 2,2,3,3-tetrabromobutane with zinc dust gives an alkyne, but-2-yne.
  • Lindlar's catalyst converts but-2-yne into cis-but-2-ene, and excess HCl adds to acetylene to give 1,1-dichloroethane.
  • Homolytic fission of a C-H bond in an alkane gives an alkyl free radical.
  • The -Cl group deactivates the benzene ring but is ortho/para directing.
  • But-2-ene can exhibit geometrical isomerism, while but-1-ene cannot.
  • Dehydrohalogenation of an alkyl halide is carried out with alcoholic KOH, and sec-butyl bromide contains a chiral centre.
  • Nitrobenzene on chlorination in the presence of AlCl3 gives m-chloronitrobenzene as the major product.

Solved Exercises

Exercise: Q I. Choose the Correct One from the Given Options

Q: 1. The number of possible isomers for an alkane having the molecular formula C5H12 is

Options: (a) 2 (b) 3 (c) 4 (d) 5

Correct answer: 3

Q: 2. 2,2,3,3-tetrabromobutane when heated with zinc dust, yields

Options: (a) but-1-yne (b) but-2-yne (c) isobutylene (d) pent-1-yne

Correct answer: but-2-yne

Q: 3. But-2-yne can be converted into cis-but-2-ene by using

Options: (a) H2/Ni (b) Lindlar's catalyst (c) Na/liq. NH3 (d) Zn/HCl

Correct answer: Lindlar's catalyst

Q: 4. When excess of HCl is added to acetylene, the product is

Options: (a) vinyl chloride. (b) ethyl chloride. (c) 1,2-dichloroethane. (d) 1,1-dichloroethane.

Correct answer: 1,1-dichloroethane.

Q: 5. The homolytic fission of C-H bond in an alkane results in

Options: (a) carbanion. (b) carbocation. (c) alkyl free radical. (d) all of these.

Correct answer: alkyl free radical.

Q: 6. The groups that deactivate benzene ring and is o/p-directing

Options: (a) -NH2 (b) -OH (c) -OCH3 (d) -Cl

Correct answer: -Cl

Q: 7. Alkene that can be expected to exhibit geometrical isomerism

Options: (a) but-1-ene (b) 2-methylbut-2-ene (c) 2-methylpropene (d) none of these

Correct answer: none of these

Q: 8. How many isomers are possible for C2H6O?

Options: (a) 2 (b) 4 (c) 8 (d) 5

Correct answer: 2

Q: 9. Addition of HBr to isobutylene mainly gives

Options: (a) n-butyl bromide. (b) isobutyl bromide. (c) sec-butyl bromide. (d) tert-butyl bromide.

Correct answer: tert-butyl bromide.

Q: 10. An alkene upon ozonolysis yield a mixture of acetone and acetaldehyde. The alkene is

Options: (a) isobutylene (b) but-2-ene (c) 2-methylbut-2-ene (d) pent-2-ene

Correct answer: 2-methylbut-2-ene

Q: 11. Dehydrohalogenation of alkylhalide is carried out in presence of

Options: (a) Zn dust. (b) conc. H2SO4. (c) alcoholic KOH. (d) aqueous KOH.

Correct answer: alcoholic KOH.

Q: 12. Which of the following molecules contain chiral center?

Options: (a) n-butyl bromide (b) isobutyl bromide (c) sec-butyl bromide (d) tert-butyl bromide

Correct answer: sec-butyl bromide

Q: 13. In the following reaction C6H5CH3 + Cl2 --(U.V. light)--> C6H5CH2Cl + HCl, what type of reaction has taken?

Options: (a) Electrophilic substitution (b) Electrophilic addition (c) Free radical substitution (d) Free radical addition

Correct answer: Free radical substitution

Q: 14. A compound when treated with sodium amide yields a salt. The compound is

Options: (a) C2H4 (b) C3H4 (c) C6H6 (d) C6H12

Correct answer: C3H4

Q: 15. Nitrobenzene reacts with chlorine in presence of AlCl3. The major product obtained is

Options: (a) o-chloronitrobenzene. (b) m-chloronitrobenzene. (c) p-chloronitrobenzene. (d) no reaction occurs at all.

Correct answer: m-chloronitrobenzene.

mcqs.q: The number of possible isomers for an alkane having the molecular formula C5H12 is
mcqs.why: C5H12 can be arranged as a straight chain and in branched forms, giving three structural isomers in total, as keyed in the book.

mcqs.q: 2,2,3,3-tetrabromobutane when heated with zinc dust, yields
mcqs.why: Dehalogenation of tetrahalides with zinc dust forms an alkyne; removing the four bromine atoms from 2,2,3,3-tetrabromobutane leaves a triple bond between carbons 2 and 3, giving but-2-yne.

mcqs.q: But-2-yne can be converted into cis-but-2-ene by using
mcqs.why: Partial hydrogenation of but-2-yne with Lindlar's catalyst stops at the alkene stage and adds the hydrogen atoms from the same side, giving cis-but-2-ene.

mcqs.q: When excess of HCl is added to acetylene, the product is
mcqs.why: Excess HCl adds to acetylene in two Markovnikov steps, both chlorine atoms going to the same carbon, giving 1,1-dichloroethane.

mcqs.q: The homolytic fission of C-H bond in an alkane results in
mcqs.why: Homolytic fission splits the C-H bond evenly, each fragment keeping one electron, so an alkyl free radical is formed, as in the free radical chlorination mechanism.

mcqs.q: The groups that deactivate benzene ring and is o/p-directing
mcqs.why: Halogens withdraw electrons by their -I effect and deactivate the ring, yet delocalization of their lone pair directs the incoming electrophile to the ortho and para positions.

mcqs.q: Alkene that can be expected to exhibit geometrical isomerism
mcqs.why: The book keyed 'none of these', replaced here by the explicit correct fact: but-2-ene has two different groups on each doubly bonded carbon, so it shows cis-trans geometrical isomerism, while but-1-ene cannot because its terminal carbon carries two identical hydrogens.

mcqs.q: How many isomers are possible for C2H6O?
mcqs.why: C2H6O can be arranged in two different ways, as an alcohol and as an ether, giving two isomers, as keyed in the book.

mcqs.q: Addition of HBr to isobutylene mainly gives
mcqs.why: Addition of HBr to isobutylene follows Markovnikov's rule; the bromine goes to the more substituted carbon, giving tert-butyl bromide as the main product.

mcqs.q: An alkene upon ozonolysis yield a mixture of acetone and acetaldehyde. The alkene is
mcqs.why: Ozonolysis cleaves each doubly bonded carbon into a carbonyl carbon; 2-methylbut-2-ene gives acetone from its (CH3)2C end and acetaldehyde from its CH-CH3 end.

mcqs.q: Dehydrohalogenation of alkylhalide is carried out in presence of
mcqs.why: Dehydrohalogenation removes HX from an alkyl halide using alcoholic KOH, as in the conversion of ethyl bromide into ethene given in the unit.

mcqs.q: Which of the following molecules contain chiral center?
mcqs.why: In sec-butyl bromide the second carbon bears four different groups, H, Br, CH3 and C2H5, so it contains a chiral centre, unlike the other butyl bromides listed.

mcqs.q: In the following reaction C6H5CH3 + Cl2 --(U.V. light)--> C6H5CH2Cl + HCl, what type of reaction has taken?
mcqs.why: In ultraviolet light chlorine forms free radicals which substitute a hydrogen atom of the methyl side chain, so the reaction is a free radical substitution.

mcqs.q: A compound when treated with sodium amide yields a salt. The compound is
mcqs.why: C3H4 is propyne, a terminal alkyne whose acidic hydrogen is removed by sodium amide to form a sodium alkynide salt; the other compounds listed have no such acidic hydrogen.

mcqs.q: Nitrobenzene reacts with chlorine in presence of AlCl3. The major product obtained is
mcqs.why: The -NO2 group is a meta directing deactivator, so chlorination of nitrobenzene in the presence of AlCl3 gives mainly m-chloronitrobenzene.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Aliphatic hydrocarbons are open chain or cyclic hydrocarbons such as alkanes, alkenes and alkynes, while aromatic hydrocarbons contain a benzene ring and resemble benzene in their properties.
  • Unsaturation in an alkene is detected by the bromine test, in which the brown colour of bromine is rapidly discharged.
  • Benzene is less reactive than ethene because its pi electrons are delocalized over the ring, but more reactive than ethane, which has only sigma bonds.
  • Halogens are ortho/para directing by resonance but deactivate the ring by their electron-withdrawing inductive effect.
  • A chiral carbon bears four different substituents, while chirality is the property of a whole molecule whose mirror images are not superimposable.
  • Cyclopropane is more reactive than propane because its 60 degree bond angle causes angle strain and weak bent bonds.
  • Terminal alkynes are distinguished by a red copper alkynide precipitate with ammoniacal cuprous chloride and a white silver alkynide precipitate with ammoniacal silver nitrate.
  • Tautomers are real isomers that interconvert, whereas resonance forms are only contributing representations of one real structure.

Solved Exercises

Exercise: Q2. Write Short Answers of the Following Questions

Q: i. What is the difference between aliphatic and aromatic hydrocarbons?

Ans: Aliphatic hydrocarbons are the open chain (acyclic) or cyclic hydrocarbons derived historically from fats and oils (Greek aleiphar, fat); they include the saturated alkanes and cycloalkanes and the unsaturated alkenes and alkynes, e.g. methane, ethene, ethyne and cyclohexane. Aromatic hydrocarbons (arenes) are benzene and those compounds which resemble benzene in their chemical properties; they contain a benzene ring with delocalized pi electrons, show resonance stabilization, and prefer electrophilic substitution over addition, e.g. benzene, toluene and naphthalene.

Q: ii. What is plane polarized mono chromatic light?

Ans: Monochromatic light is light of a single wavelength. Ordinary light consists of waves vibrating in all planes perpendicular to the direction of propagation. When such unpolarized light is passed through a polarizing filter, the randomly vibrating waves are filtered so that most of the light passing through vibrates in one direction only. Light of a single wavelength vibrating in only one plane is called plane polarized monochromatic light.

Q: iii. How do you detect the unsaturation in alkenes?

Ans: Unsaturation (a C=C double bond) in an alkene is detected by the bromine test. When a dilute solution of bromine (bromine water, or bromine in CCl4) is added to a compound containing a carbon-carbon double bond, the brown colour of bromine is rapidly discharged as the colourless dibromo addition compound (a vicinal dihalide) is formed: -CH=CH- + Br2 -> -CHBr-CHBr-. Rapid decolourisation of bromine, without evolution of HBr, confirms the presence of a double bond.

Q: iv. Why benzene is less reactive than ethene but more reactive than ethane?

Ans: In ethene the pi bond is localized between the two carbon atoms, its electron cloud lies above and below the bond axis, exposed and easily accessible to an electrophile, and the weak pi bond breaks easily in addition reactions, so ethene is very reactive. In benzene the pi electrons are delocalized over the whole ring as a continuous sheet above and below the ring, which gives benzene extra (resonance) stability; addition would destroy this aromatic delocalization, so benzene reacts less readily than ethene and prefers substitution. Ethane, on the other hand, has only strong, non-polar C-C and C-H sigma bonds and no pi electrons at all, so it is inert towards polar reagents and reacts only by free radical substitution under special conditions; hence benzene is more reactive than ethane.

Q: v. Why halogens are deactivating groups although they are ortho/para directing?

Ans: Halogens have two opposing effects. By their strong electron-withdrawing inductive effect (-I effect) they withdraw electron density from the ring, making the ring electron deficient and less reactive towards a second electrophile than benzene itself, so they are ring deactivators. At the same time, a lone pair of electrons on the halogen can be delocalized into the ring by resonance, which increases the electron density at the ortho and para positions and makes the arenium ion more stable when the electrophile attacks at the ortho or para position than at the meta position. Therefore halogens are ortho/para directing although they deactivate the ring; they are the exception mentioned in the unit, e.g. -Cl is a weak deactivator but an ortho/para director.

Q: vi. What is the basic difference between a chiral carbon and chirality?

Ans: A chiral carbon is one particular tetrahedral carbon atom in a molecule which bears four different substituents; it is also called an asymmetric carbon atom and is designated by an asterisk (*), e.g. the central carbon of lactic acid bonded to -H, -OH, -CH3 and -COOH. Chirality is a property of the whole molecule: a molecule is chiral if its two mirror-image forms are not superimposable in three dimensions (it has no plane of symmetry). Thus a chiral carbon is a centre (cause), while chirality is the property of the entire molecule; a molecule may be chiral because it contains a chiral centre, and its non-superimposable mirror images are enantiomers.

Q: vii. Why there are no geometrical isomers of but-1-ene?

Ans: Geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism is possible only when each doubly bonded carbon atom is attached to two different atoms or groups, because rotation about the double bond is restricted. In but-1-ene, CH3-CH2-CH=CH2, the terminal doubly bonded carbon carries two identical hydrogen atoms. Interchanging the groups on that carbon gives the same compound, so no cis and trans forms exist; hence but-1-ene has no geometrical isomers.

Q: viii. Why cyclopropane is more reactive than propane?

Ans: In cyclopropane each carbon is sp3 hybridized, so the C-C-C bond angle should be 109.5 degrees, but the three carbon atoms occupy the corners of an equilateral triangle and the ring bond angle is only 60 degrees. The sp3-sp3 overlap is therefore not maximum and does not take place along the internuclear axes; the orbitals overlap outside their axes and form weak 'bent bonds'. This deviation of 49.5 degrees from the normal tetrahedral angle causes angle strain in the molecule, so its C-C bonds are weaker than those of propane, which has normal tetrahedral angles and maximum overlap. Cyclopropane therefore readily undergoes ring opening reactions, while propane is unreactive.

Q: ix. How can you distinguish 1-alkyne from other non-terminal alkynes?

Ans: A 1-alkyne (terminal alkyne) has an acidic hydrogen attached to the triply bonded carbon, so it reacts with ammoniacal solutions of cuprous chloride and silver nitrate to form metal alkynides: acetylene and 1-alkynes give a red precipitate of copper alkynide with ammoniacal Cu2Cl2, e.g. CH≡CH + Cu2Cl2 + 2NH4OH -> CuC≡CCu (red ppt) + 2NH4Cl + 2H2O, and a white precipitate of silver alkynide with ammoniacal AgNO3, e.g. HC≡CH + 2AgNO3 + 2NH4OH -> AgC≡CAg (white ppt) + 2NH4NO3 + 2H2O. Non-terminal (internal) alkynes have no such hydrogen, do not form alkynides, and give no precipitate, so the two can be distinguished by this test.

Q: x. What is the main difference between tautomerism and resonance?

Ans: Tautomerism is a special type of functional group isomerism in which two real, actually existing isomers (tautomers), differing in the position of a proton (and a pi bond), are in dynamic equilibrium with each other and interconvert, e.g. the keto and enol forms of acetone, propanone and propen-2-ol; each tautomer can in principle be separated and has its own properties. Resonance, in contrast, is only a way of representing one real structure as a weighted average of two or more contributing (canonical) structures which differ only in the placement of pi electrons; the contributing forms are not real molecules, do not exist separately, do not interconvert, and the actual molecule (the resonance hybrid) has a single fixed structure with delocalized electrons.

mcqs.why: Aliphatic hydrocarbons were derived historically from fats and oils; aleiphar is the Greek word for fat.

options: A methyl and an ethyl group
mcqs.why: Geometrical isomerism requires two different groups on each doubly bonded carbon; in but-1-ene the terminal carbon carries two identical hydrogen atoms, so interchanging them gives the same compound.

mcqs.why: The three carbon atoms of cyclopropane occupy the corners of an equilateral triangle, so the ring bond angle is only 60 degrees instead of the tetrahedral 109.5 degrees, causing angle strain.

mcqs.why: Acetylene and 1-alkynes give a red precipitate of copper alkynide with ammoniacal Cu2Cl2, and a white precipitate of silver alkynide with ammoniacal AgNO3; non-terminal alkynes give no precipitate.

mcqs.q: The keto and enol forms of acetone are an example of
mcqs.why: Tautomers are real, actually existing isomers differing in the position of a proton and a pi bond and interconverting in dynamic equilibrium, e.g. the keto and enol forms of acetone.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Chlorination of methane is a free radical substitution in ultraviolet light with initiation, propagation and termination steps, giving CH3Cl, CH2Cl2, CHCl3 and CCl4 in succession.
  • Alkanes C1-C4 are gases, C5-C17 are liquids and C18 and above are wax-like solids, and straight chain alkanes have higher boiling points than their branched isomers.
  • Ethene is prepared by dehydrating ethyl alcohol with concentrated sulphuric acid at 170 C or by dehydrohalogenation of ethyl bromide with alcoholic KOH.
  • The more alkyl groups attached to the doubly bonded carbons, the more stable the alkene, and trans isomers are more stable than cis isomers.
  • Terminal alkynes are acidic because the sp-hybridized carbon has 50% s-character, and they form sodium alkynides with sodium amide in liquid ammonia.
  • In benzene each carbon is sp2 hybridized, all bond angles are 120 degrees, the C-C bond length is 139 pm, and six pi electrons are delocalized over the ring.
  • Electrophilic substitution in benzene proceeds through a resonance stabilized arenium ion (sigma-complex), which then loses a proton to restore the aromatic system.
  • Ortho/para directing groups such as -OH and -NH2 generally activate the ring, meta directing groups such as -NO2 deactivate it, and halogens are ortho/para directing deactivators.

Solved Exercises

Exercise: Q3. Write Detail Answers of the Following Questions

Q: 1. (a) Describe the mechanism of chlorination of methane in detail. (b) Explain the structure and reactivity of cycloalkanes. (c) Write down the physical properties of alkanes and cycloalkane.

Ans: (a) Chlorination of methane is a free radical substitution reaction carried out in ultraviolet light: CH4 + Cl2 --(U.V. light)--> CH3Cl + HCl. Its mechanism has three steps. Step 1, Initiation: a chlorine molecule undergoes homolytic fission in the presence of ultraviolet light to give two chlorine free radicals: Cl-Cl --(U.V. light)--> Cl. + Cl. Step 2, Propagation: (i) a chlorine free radical attacks the methane molecule to give a methyl free radical and HCl: Cl. + CH4 -> .CH3 + HCl; (ii) the methyl free radical attacks a chlorine molecule to form methyl chloride and a new chlorine free radical: .CH3 + Cl-Cl -> CH3Cl + Cl. These propagation steps are repeated again and again in a chain. Step 3, Termination: the chain ends when any two free radicals combine to form stable products: Cl. + Cl. -> Cl2; .CH3 + Cl. -> CH3Cl; .CH3 + .CH3 -> CH3-CH3. In practice the reaction does not stop at the methyl chloride stage; the remaining hydrogens are successively replaced: CH3Cl + Cl2 -> CH2Cl2 (dichloromethane) + HCl; CH2Cl2 + Cl2 -> CHCl3 (chloroform) + HCl; CHCl3 + Cl2 -> CCl4 (carbon tetrachloride) + HCl, so a mixture of all four substitution products is obtained, the proportions depending on the relative amounts of methane and chlorine. (b) Structure of cycloalkanes: in cycloalkanes, like alkanes, each carbon is bonded to four other atoms and uses sp3-hybrid orbitals to form sigma bonds. In cyclopropane the C-C-C bond angle is 60 degrees instead of the tetrahedral 109.5 degrees, so the sp3-sp3 overlap is not along the internuclear axes and bent bonds are formed; the deviation causes angle strain. In cyclobutane the strain is less, and in higher cycloalkanes the rings can pucker so the angles are close to tetrahedral. Reactivity: cycloalkanes resemble alkanes in chemical behaviour except cyclopropane and cyclobutane. Because of greater angle strain, cyclopropane is unstable and undergoes ring opening reactions with several reagents to give open chain addition products; cyclobutane, having less angle strain, is more stable and undergoes ring opening only under severe conditions, e.g. hydrogenation of cyclopropane and cyclobutane to the corresponding open chain alkanes over nickel catalyst occurs at 80 C and 200 C respectively. Higher members are even more stable, do not undergo ring opening, and resemble open chain alkanes, undergoing only radical substitution reactions. (c) Physical properties of alkanes: the first four members (C1-C4) are colourless gases at room temperature; straight chain alkanes up to seventeen carbons (C5-C17) are colourless liquids, and higher unbranched alkanes with eighteen or more carbons are wax-like colourless solids. Boiling points increase with molecular mass, and straight chain alkanes have higher boiling points than their branched isomers (n-pentane 36 C, isopentane 28 C). Melting points also increase with molecular mass, but not regularly. Alkanes are non-polar, insoluble in water, but soluble in non-polar solvents like ether and benzene. Their density increases with molecular weight up to a maximum of 0.81 g/mL, so they are lighter than water. Physical properties of cycloalkanes: cyclopropane and cyclobutane are gases at room temperature and atmospheric pressure, while the remaining cycloalkanes are mostly liquids. Their boiling points increase gradually with molecular mass and are higher than those of the corresponding open chain alkanes. Their melting points do not increase regularly, the alternation between odd and even numbers of carbon atoms being more pronounced than in open chain alkanes. They are insoluble in water but dissolve in ether, benzene and carbon tetrachloride due to their non-polar nature, and their densities increase with molecular mass but remain less than 1 g/mL.

Q: 2. (a) What are hydrocarbons? Explain the different classes of hydrocarbons. (b) Give methods for preparation of ethene from; (i) ethyl alcohol (ii) ethyl bromide (c) Explain the relative stabilities of different alkenes.

Ans: (a) Hydrocarbons are the organic compounds which contain carbon and hydrogen only, e.g. methane (CH4), ethylene (C2H4), acetylene (C2H2) and benzene (C6H6); all other organic compounds are considered derivatives of hydrocarbons. They are divided into two major classes. (1) Aliphatic hydrocarbons: (i) saturated hydrocarbons, in which carbon atoms are joined only by single bonds - the open chain alkanes (CnH2n+2) and the cyclic cycloalkanes (CnH2n); (ii) unsaturated hydrocarbons, which contain a carbon-carbon multiple bond - alkenes containing a double bond (CnH2n) and their cyclic forms (cycloalkenes), and alkynes containing a triple bond (CnH2n-2) and cycloalkynes. Aliphatic hydrocarbons may be open chain (acyclic) or cyclic. (2) Aromatic hydrocarbons (arenes): benzene (C6H6) is the parent member; they contain a benzene ring, resemble benzene in chemical properties, and include toluene and naphthalene. (b) Preparation of ethene: (i) From ethyl alcohol (dehydration): when ethyl alcohol is heated at 170 C in the presence of concentrated sulphuric acid, a water molecule is eliminated: CH3-CH2-OH --(H2SO4, 170 C)--> CH2=CH2 + H2O. Industrially, dehydration is carried out by passing vapours of alcohol over alumina (Al2O3) at 400 C. (ii) From ethyl bromide (dehydrohalogenation): when ethyl bromide is heated with an alcoholic solution of KOH (or NaOH), hydrogen and bromine are eliminated: CH3-CH2-Br + KOH --(alcohol, 60 C)--> CH2=CH2 + KBr + H2O. (c) Relative stability of alkenes depends upon the position of the double bond and the number, nature and relative position of substituents on the doubly bonded carbons. In general, the greater the number of alkyl groups attached to the double bonded carbons, the greater is the stability of the alkene. For geometric isomers, the trans-isomer is always more stable than the cis-isomer, and for isomeric dienes the conjugated dienes are more stable than non-conjugated ones. Stability is compared by heats of hydrogenation or heats of combustion: stable alkenes evolve a smaller amount of heat. For the four isomeric butylenes (C4H8), but-1-ene evolves the largest heat of combustion (2719 kJ/mol) and is the least stable; cis-but-2-ene evolves 2712 kJ/mol, trans-but-2-ene 2707 kJ/mol, and isobutylene (2-methylpropene) the lowest, 2703 kJ/mol, so isobutylene is the most stable of the four isomers.

Q: 3. (a) Describe any two methods for preparation of alkynes. (b) Discuss the acidity of terminal alkynes. How terminal alkynes can be distinguished from non-terminal alkynes? (c) Starting from an alkene how would you prepare the following compounds? (i) Vicinal dihalide (ii) Alcohol (iii) Aldehydes and ketones (iv) Epoxide

Ans: (a) Two methods of preparation of alkynes by elimination reactions: (1) Dehydrohalogenation of vicinal dihalides: vicinal and geminal dihalides, when treated with alcoholic potassium hydroxide or sodium amide in liquid ammonia, form alkynes in two steps; the vinyl halide formed in the first step is treated with the stronger base sodium amide to remove another molecule of HX, e.g. 1,2-dibromoethane + KOH (alcohol, 80 C) -> bromoethene (vinyl bromide) + KBr + H2O, and bromoethene + NaNH2 (liq. NH3, -33 C) -> HC≡CH (ethyne) + NaBr + NH3. (2) Dehalogenation of tetrahalides: tetrahalides having two halogen atoms on each of two adjacent carbons are heated with zinc dust in alcohol to form alkynes, e.g. 1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane + 2Zn --(alcohol)--> HC≡CH (acetylene) + 2ZnBr2. (b) Acidity of terminal alkynes: alkynes in which the triple bond is at the end of the chain (terminal or 1-alkynes, R-C≡C-H) are slightly acidic and readily donate a proton to a strong base; treated with sodium amide in liquid ammonia they give sodium alkynides: R-C≡C-H + NaNH2 --(liq. NH3)--> R-C≡C-Na+ + NH3. Their acidity is due to the sp-hybridization of the triply bonded carbon: an sp orbital has 50% s-character, so the carbon is more electronegative than sp2 (33.33%) and sp3 (25%) carbons and pulls the electrons of the C-H bond strongly towards itself, making the hydrogen slightly acidic (pKa: ethane 50, ethene 44, ethyne 25). Distinguishing terminal from non-terminal alkynes: terminal alkynes react with ammoniacal cuprous chloride to give a red precipitate of copper alkynide and with ammoniacal silver nitrate to give a white precipitate of silver alkynide, e.g. HC≡CH + 2AgNO3 + 2NH4OH -> AgC≡CAg (white ppt) + 2NH4NO3 + 2H2O; non-terminal alkynes do not form alkynides and give no precipitate. (c) From an alkene: (i) Vicinal dihalide - by halogenation: the alkene adds chlorine or bromine in an inert solvent such as CCl4 through a cyclic halonium ion: CH2=CH2 + Br2 --(CCl4)--> CH2Br-CH2Br (1,2-dibromoethane, a vic-dihalide). (ii) Alcohol - by hydration: water adds across the double bond at 100 C with sulphuric or phosphoric acid catalyst, following Markovnikov's rule for asymmetric alkenes: CH2=CH2 + H2O --(H2SO4, 100 C)--> CH3-CH2-OH (ethyl alcohol); propene similarly gives propan-2-ol. (iii) Aldehydes and ketones - by ozonolysis: ozone is passed through the alkene solution in an inert solvent at low temperature (-80 C) to form an ozonide, which is decomposed with zinc dust and water to carbonyl compounds: CH2=CH2 + O3, then Zn/H2O -> 2HCHO (formaldehyde); in general each doubly bonded carbon becomes a carbonyl carbon, giving an aldehyde or a ketone according to its substitution, and the reaction is used to locate the position of the double bond. (iv) Epoxide - by epoxidation: the alkene reacts with a peroxyacid (peracid), most commonly peracetic acid, to give a cyclic ether called an epoxide (oxirane): CH2=CH2 + CH3COOOH -> ethylene oxide (oxirane) + CH3COOH. Industrially ethylene oxide is prepared by oxidation of ethene with oxygen over silver oxide catalyst at 300 C.

Q: 4. (a) Describe the structure of benzene on the basis of MOT. (b) Describe mechanism of electrophilic substitution reaction in benzene. (c) How would you prepare the following compounds from benzene? (i) Acetophenone (ii) Toluene (iii) Nitrobenzene (iv) Benzenesulphonic acid (v) Chlorobenzene (vi) Cyclohexane

Ans: (a) Structure of benzene on the basis of molecular orbital theory: each carbon atom of the ring is linked to the others by sp2-hybrid orbitals and with the 1s orbital of a hydrogen atom, forming six C-C and six C-H sigma bonds. Since the sigma bonds result from overlap of planar sp2-hybrid orbitals, all carbon and hydrogen atoms in benzene lie in the same plane and all bond angles are 120 degrees. Each carbon atom also possesses a half-filled unhybridized p orbital perpendicular to the plane of the sigma bonds. The sidewise overlap of these p orbitals produces delocalized pi molecular orbitals containing six electrons, associated with all six carbon atoms; the electron cloud of the delocalized pi electrons lies half below and half above the ring. This extensive pi electron delocalization is responsible for the greater stability of benzene; the carbon-carbon bond length is 139 pm (1.39 A) and the carbon-hydrogen bond length is 108 pm (1.08 A). (b) Mechanism of electrophilic substitution in benzene: Step 1 - formation of an electrophile: E-B + catalyst -> E+ + B- (catalyst). Step 2 - the electrophile attacks the aromatic ring to produce a non-aromatic carbocation called an arenium ion or sigma-complex; this step is slow. The arenium ion is resonance stabilized and is a hybrid of three structures, and is called a sigma-complex because the electrophile is joined to the ring by a new sigma bond. Step 3 - the unstable, non-aromatic arenium ion loses a proton (fast) to the base/catalyst, restoring the stable aromatic system: arenium ion -> substituted benzene + H-B + catalyst. The overall reaction is the substitution of a proton of the ring by an electrophile. (c) From benzene: (i) Acetophenone - Friedel-Crafts acylation: benzene + acetyl chloride (CH3COCl) --(AlCl3)--> acetophenone (C6H5-CO-CH3) + HCl; the electrophile is the acylium ion CH3-C+=O formed from acetyl chloride and AlCl3. (ii) Toluene - Friedel-Crafts alkylation: benzene + methyl chloride (CH3Cl) --(AlCl3)--> toluene (methylbenzene) + HCl; the electrophile is the methyl cation CH3+. (iii) Nitrobenzene - nitration: benzene + conc. HNO3 --(conc. H2SO4, 60 C)--> nitrobenzene + H2O; the electrophile is the nitronium ion NO2+, produced by HNO3 + 2H2SO4 -> NO2+ + 2HSO4- + H3O+. (iv) Benzenesulphonic acid - sulphonation: benzene + conc. H2SO4 --(120 C)--> benzenesulphonic acid + H2O, or with fuming sulphuric acid (SO3) at 25 C; the electrophile is sulphur trioxide, SO3. (v) Chlorobenzene - halogenation: benzene + Cl2 --(FeCl3, 25 C)--> chlorobenzene + HCl; the electrophile is the chloronium ion Cl+ formed from Cl2 + FeCl3 -> Cl+ + FeCl4-. (vi) Cyclohexane - catalytic hydrogenation (addition of hydrogen): benzene + 3H2 --(Ni, 250-300 C, or Pt or Pd)--> cyclohexane.

Q: 5. (a) Explain the directing and activitating effect in mono substituted benzene derivatives. (b) Write the systematic names for the following organic compounds. (i) CH3-CH(CH2-CH3)-CH2-CH3 (ii) CH3-CH2-CH2-CH(CH(CH3)2)-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH3, the CH(CH3)2 group being attached to the fourth carbon of the chain (iii) CH3-CH2-C(=CH2)-CH2-CH2-CH3 (iv) (CH3CH2)2C=CHCH3 (v) (CH3)3C-C≡C-CH(CH3)CH2CH3 (vi) a cyclohexane ring joined by a single bond to a cyclobutane ring (vii) a benzene ring carrying -NO2, -Cl, -NO2 and -Br on four consecutive carbons in this order (viii) a benzene ring carrying -OH and -OH at the 1,4-positions and -CH3 next to one -OH (ix) a cyclohexane ring carrying -CH3, -C2H5 and -CH3 groups, the -C2H5 group being adjacent to one -CH3 group (x) three benzene rings fused in a straight row

Ans: (a) Directing (orientation) effect: the first substituent on the benzene ring may direct the incoming electrophile to the ortho, meta or para position. Ortho/para directing substituents direct the second substituent to the ortho and para positions simultaneously, e.g. -OH, -NH2, -NHR, -NR2, -R and -X (halogens); their effect is explained by charge distribution (the lone pair of the substituent is delocalized over the ring, making the ortho and para positions more electron rich than the meta position) and by the relative stability of the arenium ion, which is more stable for ortho/para attack. Meta directing substituents direct the second substituent to the meta position, e.g. -NO2, -CN, -CHO, -COR and -COOH; these groups withdraw electron density from the ortho and para positions, leaving the meta position relatively electron rich, and the arenium ion is more stable for meta attack. Activating and deactivating (reactivity) effect: ortho/para directing groups generally release electrons to the ring, making it electron rich and more reactive than benzene itself, so they are ring activators (strong: -OH, -NH2, -NHR, -NR2; moderate: -OCOR, -NHCOR, -NRCOR; weak: -R). Halogens are the exception: they are ortho/para directing but, because they withdraw electrons, they are weak ring deactivators. All meta directing groups withdraw electrons from the ring, making it electron deficient and slower to react, so they are deactivators (moderate: -CHO, -COR, -COOH, -CONH2, -COOR; strong: -NO2, -+NH3, -+NR3). For example, benzene needs conc. HNO3/H2SO4 at 60 C for nitration, phenol is nitrated even by dilute HNO3 at 25 C (activating -OH), while nitrobenzene needs conc. acids at 100 C and reacts even more slowly (deactivating -NO2). (b) Systematic names: (i) 3-methylpentane - the longest chain has 5 carbons; numbering from the end nearer the branch puts the methyl group on carbon 3. (ii) 4-isopropyloctane - the longest chain has 8 carbons and the -CH(CH3)2 (isopropyl) group is on carbon 4. (iii) 2-ethylpent-1-ene - the longest chain containing the double bond has 5 carbons, the double bond starts at carbon 1 (the =CH2 carbon), and an ethyl group is on carbon 2. (iv) 3-ethylpent-2-ene - a 5-carbon chain with the double bond between carbons 2 and 3 and an ethyl group on carbon 3. (v) 2,2,5-trimethylhept-3-yne - the longest chain containing the triple bond has 7 carbons, the triple bond is between carbons 3 and 4, with two methyl groups on carbon 2 and one methyl group on carbon 5. (vi) Cyclobutylcyclohexane - a cyclohexane ring joined by a single bond to a cyclobutane ring; the larger ring is taken as the parent and the smaller ring as the cyclobutyl substituent. (vii) 4-bromo-2-chloro-1,3-dinitrobenzene - the four substituents are on four consecutive ring carbons; numbering to give the lowest locants puts -NO2 at 1 and 3, -Cl at 2 and -Br at 4. (viii) 3-methylbenzene-1,4-diol - the two -OH groups are at the 1 and 4 (para) positions of the ring and the -CH3 group is at position 3. (ix) 1-ethyl-2,5-dimethylcyclohexane - on the cyclohexane ring the ethyl group is given position 1, and numbering in the direction of the nearer methyl group puts methyl groups at positions 2 and 5, the lowest locant set. (x) Anthracene - three benzene rings fused together in a straight (linear) row, a polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon.

Q: 6(a). Draw the structural formula of the following organic compounds. (Printed numbering: i, ii, iii, iv, iv, v, vi, vii, viii, ix - the book prints two items as iv.) i. 3-ethyl-4-methyloctane ii. 4-isopropyldecane iii. sec-butylcycloheptane iv. 2,3-dimethyl-4-propylnonane iv. 2,4,4-trimethylhex-2-ene v. cis-hex-3-ene vi. phenanthrene vii. hex-2-yne viii. 1,2-dimethyl-4-propylbenzene ix. cyclopropylbenzene

Ans: (i) 3-ethyl-4-methyloctane: CH3-CH2-CH(CH2CH3)-CH(CH3)-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH3 - an 8-carbon chain with an ethyl group on carbon 3 and a methyl group on carbon 4. (ii) 4-isopropyldecane: CH3-CH2-CH2-CH(CH(CH3)2)-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH3 - a 10-carbon chain with an isopropyl group, -CH(CH3)2, on carbon 4. (iii) sec-butylcycloheptane: a seven-membered cycloheptane ring bearing a sec-butyl group, -CH(CH3)-CH2-CH3, on one ring carbon. (iv) 2,3-dimethyl-4-propylnonane: CH3-CH(CH3)-CH(CH3)-CH(CH2CH2CH3)-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH3 - a 9-carbon chain with methyl groups on carbons 2 and 3 and a propyl group on carbon 4. (v) 2,4,4-trimethylhex-2-ene: CH3-C(CH3)=CH-C(CH3)2-CH2-CH3 - a 6-carbon chain with the double bond between carbons 2 and 3, one methyl group on carbon 2 and two methyl groups on carbon 4. (vi) cis-hex-3-ene: CH3-CH2-CH=CH-CH2-CH3, drawn with both ethyl groups (the higher groups on the two doubly bonded carbons) on the same side of the double bond. (vii) Phenanthrene: three benzene rings fused together in an angular (bent) arrangement, not in a straight row. (viii) Hex-2-yne: CH3-C≡C-CH2-CH2-CH3 - a 6-carbon chain with the triple bond between carbons 2 and 3. (ix) 1,2-dimethyl-4-propylbenzene: a benzene ring carrying -CH3 groups on carbons 1 and 2 and a -CH2CH2CH3 (propyl) group on carbon 4. (x) Cyclopropylbenzene: a benzene ring joined by a single bond to one carbon of a cyclopropane (three-membered) ring.

mcqs.q: In the chlorination of methane, the initiation step involves homolytic fission of which molecule in ultraviolet light?
mcqs.why: In the initiation step a chlorine molecule undergoes homolytic fission in the presence of ultraviolet light to give two chlorine free radicals.

mcqs.why: Cyclobutane has less angle strain and undergoes ring opening only under severe conditions; hydrogenation of cyclopropane and cyclobutane over nickel occurs at 80 C and 200 C respectively.

mcqs.why: The first four alkanes are colourless gases at room temperature, alkanes up to seventeen carbons are colourless liquids, and those with eighteen or more carbons are wax-like colourless solids.

mcqs.why: When ethyl alcohol is heated at 170 C in the presence of concentrated sulphuric acid, a water molecule is eliminated and ethene is formed.

mcqs.why: Dehalogenation of tetrahalides with zinc dust in alcohol removes the halogen atoms and forms an alkyne, e.g. 1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane gives acetylene.

mcqs.why: The sp-hybridized carbon has 50% s-character and is more electronegative, so ethyne has pKa 25, compared with 44 for ethene and 50 for ethane.

mcqs.why: Each carbon of benzene forms sigma bonds with planar sp2-hybrid orbitals, so all carbon and hydrogen atoms lie in the same plane and all bond angles are 120 degrees.

mcqs.why: The electrophile joins the ring by a new sigma bond to produce a resonance stabilized, non-aromatic carbocation called an arenium ion or sigma-complex, which then loses a proton.

mcqs.why: Meta directing substituents include -NO2, -CN, -CHO, -COR and -COOH; these groups withdraw electron density and direct the second substituent to the meta position.

lessons.title: Project
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The bromine test is used to detect a carbon-carbon double bond in an organic compound.
  • The compound is dissolved in water if it is water soluble, or in carbon tetrachloride if it is water insoluble, and the bromine reagent is added drop by drop without adding an excess.
  • The brown colour of the bromine reagent is discharged and the solution becomes colourless when a double bond is present.
  • Bromine adds across the carbon-carbon double bond to form a colourless vicinal dibromide: -CH=CH- + Br2 -> -CHBr-CHBr-.

Solved Exercises

Project

Q: Set up one small test tube in a test tube rack in the hood. Add 10 mg of a solid or 10 mL of a liquid organic compound containing carbon-carbon double bond. Add 1-3mL of distilled water (if compound is water soluble) or carbon tetrachloride (if compound is water insoluble), shake the mixtures for 2 minutes. Add bromine water reagent (5mL of bromine dissolved in 100 mL of water) for water soluble compound, or bromine in CCl4 (5mL of bromine dissolved in 100mL of CCl4) for water insoluble compound, drop by drop. Do not add an excess of the bromine reagent. The bromine reagent is brown or yellow-brown in color. Observe the dissipation of the brownish color of bromine.

Ans: This project is the bromine test for a carbon-carbon double bond. The compound is dissolved in distilled water (if water soluble) or in carbon tetrachloride (if water insoluble) and shaken; bromine water (for the water soluble compound) or bromine in CCl4 (for the water insoluble compound) is then added drop by drop, without adding an excess. Observation: the brown (yellow-brown) colour of the bromine reagent is dissipated, i.e. it is discharged and the solution becomes colourless. This happens because bromine adds across the carbon-carbon double bond of the unsaturated compound to form a colourless vicinal dibromide: -CH=CH- + Br2 -> -CHBr-CHBr-. Disappearance of the brownish colour of bromine therefore confirms the presence of a carbon-carbon double bond (unsaturation) in the compound.

lessons.title: Self-Assessment
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Methylmagnesium bromide adds its methyl group to the carbonyl carbon of acetaldehyde and acetone.
  • With acetaldehyde, acid workup gives propan-2-ol (isopropyl alcohol), a secondary alcohol.
  • With acetone, acid workup gives 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tert-butyl alcohol), a tertiary alcohol.
  • In both reactions the carbonyl oxygen first takes MgBr, and hydrolysis converts it into the -OH group.

Solved Exercises

Self-Assessment

Q: Write the reaction of methylmagnesium bromide with acetaldehyde and acetone, followed by acid workup. Also write the names of products.

Ans: With acetaldehyde: CH3-MgBr + CH3-CHO -> CH3-CH(OMgBr)-CH3, and on acid workup (H3O+) it gives CH3-CH(OH)-CH3, propan-2-ol (isopropyl alcohol), a secondary alcohol. With acetone: CH3-MgBr + (CH3)2C=O -> (CH3)3C-OMgBr, and on acid workup it gives (CH3)3C-OH, 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tert-butyl alcohol), a tertiary alcohol. In both cases the methyl group of the Grignard reagent adds to the carbonyl carbon and the oxygen takes MgBr, which hydrolysis converts into the -OH group.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Alkyl iodides are the most reactive alkyl halides in nucleophilic substitution because the C-I bond is weakest.
  • A carbocation is a positively charged carbon bonded to three groups; it is sp2 hybridised and trigonal planar.
  • A Grignard reagent has the formula R-Mg-X and gives tertiary alcohols from ketones and higher esters.
  • SN1 reactions proceed through a planar carbocation and show partial racemization with first-order kinetics.
  • The SN1 rate does not depend on the nature of the nucleophile, only on ionisation of the substrate.
  • Acetone is a polar aprotic solvent, while water, ethyl alcohol and formic acid are polar protic solvents.
  • A Grignard reagent with CO2 and hydrolysis gives a carboxylic acid with one carbon more than the parent halide.
  • Crowding around the alpha-carbon of an alkyl halide favours elimination over substitution.

Solved Exercises

Exercise: Q I. Choose the Correct One from the Given Options

Q: Q1. The reaction of CH3MgI with acetone followed by hydrolysis gives

Options: (a) tert-butyl alcohol (b) sec-butyl alcohol (c) n-butyl alcohol (d) none of these

Correct answer: tert-butyl alcohol
