lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • In nucleophilic substitution a nucleophile replaces a leaving group on a polar carbon-halogen bond; in electrophilic substitution an electrophile replaces hydrogen on benzene.
  • Carbocation stability increases as tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl because of the +I effect and hyperconjugation.
  • SN1 and E1 share the same slow ionisation step to a carbocation, so they have equal rates for the same tertiary halide.
  • Fluoride is a weak nucleophile in protic solvents because hydrogen bonding traps it, but strong in aprotic solvents where it stays nearly free.
  • SN2 attack is from the back side, opposite the leaving group, and gives inversion of configuration.
  • Carbon-halogen bond energies fall from C-F 467 to C-I 228 kJ/mol, so iodides are most reactive and fluorides least.
  • Secondary amines are the most basic amines in aqueous solution because solvation of the ammonium ion outweighs the +I effect.
  • Nucleophilicity is a kinetic measure of attack on carbon, while basicity is an equilibrium measure of attack on a proton.

Solved Exercises

Exercise: Q2. Write Short Answers of the Following Questions

Q: Q1 (i). Compare nucleophilic substitution reaction and electrophilic substitution reaction.

Ans: In nucleophilic substitution a nucleophile (electron-pair donor) attacks an electron-deficient carbon and replaces a leaving group, e.g. R-X + OH- -> R-OH + X-; it is typical of alkyl halides where the carbon-halogen bond is polar (C delta+ - X delta-). In electrophilic substitution an electrophile (electron-deficient species) attacks an electron-rich centre, usually the pi system of an aromatic ring, and replaces a hydrogen atom, e.g. nitration and halogenation of benzene. Thus the attacking species, the substrate and the group replaced (halide ion versus H) are different in the two reactions.

Q: Q2 (ii). Why alkyl halides undergo nucleophilic substitution while benzene undergo electrophilic substitution reactions?

Ans: In alkyl halides the carbon-halogen bond is polar because halogen is more electronegative, so the alpha-carbon carries a partial positive charge and is attacked by nucleophiles, and the halide ion is a good leaving group. In benzene there is no such polar bond or leaving group; instead the ring has a cloud of delocalised pi electrons above and below its plane, which attracts electrophiles. Benzene therefore undergoes electrophilic substitution, which also preserves its stable aromatic pi system.

Q: Q3 (iii). Why tertiary carbocation is more stable?

Ans: A carbocation is stabilised by the electron-donating (+I) effect of the alkyl groups attached to the positively charged carbon, which push electron density towards it and disperse the positive charge. A tertiary carbocation has three alkyl groups donating electrons, a secondary has two and a primary only one, so the order of stability is tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl. Hyperconjugation from the neighbouring C-H bonds further stabilises the tertiary carbocation.

Q: Q4 (iv). In a polar protic solvent, the SN1 and E1 reaction for the same tertiary alkyl halide, have equal rates. Explain.

Ans: Both SN1 and E1 reactions of a tertiary alkyl halide begin with the same slow, rate-determining step: ionisation of the alkyl halide in the polar protic solvent to form the same carbocation intermediate. The rate therefore depends only on this common ionisation step, rate = k[R-X], and is the same for both. The reactions differ only in the fast second step, where the carbocation either combines with a nucleophile (SN1) or loses a beta-proton to a base (E1), which does not affect the overall rate.

Q: Q5 (v). Fluoride ion is weak nucleophile in polar protic solvent and strong nucleophile in polar aprotic solvent. Explain.

Ans: Fluoride ion is small and has a high charge density. In a polar protic solvent (e.g. water or alcohol) it is very strongly solvated by hydrogen bonding, so it is trapped in a solvent cage and cannot easily attack the substrate; it behaves as a weak nucleophile. In a polar aprotic solvent (e.g. acetone or DMSO) there is no hydrogen bonding to the anion, so F- remains almost free (naked) and highly reactive, and behaves as a strong nucleophile.

Q: Q6 (vi). Why in SN2 the nucleophile attack on opposite side of leaving group?

Ans: In the SN2 reaction the nucleophile donates its electron pair into the antibonding side of the C-X bond, so it must approach the carbon from the side opposite to the leaving group (back-side attack), where electron density is lowest and repulsion from the leaving group is minimum. Front-side attack is blocked by the leaving group itself. This back-side attack passes through a transition state in which carbon is bonded to both groups, and the product is formed with inversion of configuration.

Q: Q7 (vii). Alkyl fluorides are least reactive while alkyl iodides are more reactive towards nucleophilic substitution. Why?

Ans: Reactivity depends on the strength of the carbon-halogen bond, which must break during substitution. Bond energies decrease down the group: C-F 467 kJ/mol, C-Cl 346 kJ/mol, C-Br 290 kJ/mol and C-I 228 kJ/mol. The C-F bond is the strongest and fluoride is a poor leaving group, so alkyl fluorides are least reactive, while the C-I bond is weakest and iodide leaves most easily, so alkyl iodides are most reactive. The order is R-I > R-Br > R-Cl > R-F.

Q: Q8 (viii). Why secondary amines are more basic than tertiary in aqueous solution?

Ans: Basicity in aqueous solution depends on three factors acting together: the +I effect of alkyl groups (favours tertiary), solvation of the conjugate acid (ammonium ion) by water through hydrogen bonding (favours primary and secondary, whose ions have more N-H bonds and less crowding), and steric hindrance around nitrogen. In water the solvation effect outweighs the +I effect for tertiary amines, because their bulky ammonium ions are poorly solvated. The balanced result, also shown by the pKb values in Table 17.4, is that secondary amines are the strongest bases in aqueous solution, e.g. diethylamine pKb 3.01 versus triethylamine pKb 3.24.

Q: Q9 (ix). The structure of methyl carbocation is trigonal planar but not pyramidal. Why?

Ans: In the methyl carbocation, CH3+, the carbon atom is sp2 hybridised: its three sp2 orbitals form sigma bonds with the three hydrogen atoms in one plane at angles of about 120 degrees, while the remaining p orbital stays empty and perpendicular to this plane. Because all three bonds lie in a single plane with an empty p orbital, the shape is trigonal planar. A pyramidal shape would need sp3 hybridisation with a lone pair, which the carbocation does not have.

Q: Q10 (x). Explain briefly the difference between nucleophile and base.

Ans: A nucleophile is a species with an unshared pair of electrons which it donates to an electrophilic carbon atom, forming a new bond in substitution or addition reactions; its strength is called nucleophilicity and is a kinetic measure. A base donates its electron pair to a proton (H+), usually removing a beta-proton in elimination reactions; its strength is basicity, an equilibrium (thermodynamic) measure. All nucleophiles can act as bases and vice versa, e.g. OH- gives substitution with a primary halide but elimination with a tertiary halide; whether it behaves as nucleophile or base depends on the substrate and conditions.

mcqs.q: In nucleophilic substitution of an alkyl halide, what does the nucleophile replace?
options: A leaving group on an electron-deficient carbon
A pi bond of an alkene
mcqs.why: In nucleophilic substitution a nucleophile attacks the electron-deficient carbon of the polar C-X bond and replaces the leaving group, e.g. R-X + OH- gives R-OH + X-.

mcqs.q: Why does benzene undergo electrophilic substitution rather than nucleophilic substitution?
options: Its C-H bonds are strongly polar
It has no leaving group but a delocalised pi electron cloud that attracts electrophiles
Its ring carbon carries a partial positive charge
Its halide ion is a good leaving group
mcqs.why: Benzene has no polar bond or leaving group; its delocalised pi cloud attracts electrophiles, and substitution preserves the stable aromatic pi system.

mcqs.q: What is the correct stability order of carbocations?
mcqs.why: Alkyl groups stabilise a carbocation by their +I effect and hyperconjugation; three alkyl groups stabilise most, so tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl.

mcqs.q: Why do SN1 and E1 reactions of the same tertiary alkyl halide have equal rates in a polar protic solvent?
options: Both share the same slow ionisation step forming the same carbocation
Both are attacked by the same nucleophile
Both lose a beta-proton in the first step
mcqs.why: Both reactions begin with the same rate-determining ionisation to the same carbocation, rate = k[R-X]; they differ only in the fast second step, which does not affect the rate.

mcqs.q: Why is fluoride ion a weak nucleophile in water or alcohol?
options: It is too large to approach the carbon
It has no lone pair of electrons
It is strongly solvated by hydrogen bonding and trapped in a solvent cage
mcqs.why: Fluoride is small with high charge density, so protic solvents solvate it strongly by hydrogen bonding; trapped in a solvent cage it cannot easily attack the substrate.

mcqs.q: What stereochemical result follows from back-side attack in an SN2 reaction?
mcqs.why: Back-side attack passes through a transition state bonded to both groups and the product is formed with inversion of configuration.

mcqs.q: Which carbon-halogen bond energy is given for the C-I bond?
mcqs.why: Bond energies decrease down the group: C-F 467, C-Cl 346, C-Br 290 and C-I 228 kJ/mol, which is why alkyl iodides are most reactive.

mcqs.q: Which class of amine is most basic in aqueous solution?
mcqs.why: In water, solvation of the ammonium ion outweighs the +I effect for tertiary amines; diethylamine (pKb 3.01) is more basic than triethylamine (pKb 3.24), so secondary amines are strongest.

mcqs.q: What is the hybridisation and bond angle arrangement in the methyl carbocation CH3+?
options: sp2 hybridised with bonds in one plane at about 120 degrees
sp3 hybridised with a lone pair
mcqs.why: The methyl carbocation carbon is sp2 hybridised: three sp2 orbitals bond to hydrogens in one plane at about 120 degrees, leaving an empty p orbital, so it is trigonal planar.

mcqs.q: How do nucleophilicity and basicity differ as measures?
options: Nucleophilicity is an equilibrium measure; basicity is kinetic
Both measure attack on a proton
Nucleophilicity is a kinetic measure of attack on carbon; basicity is an equilibrium measure of attack on a proton
Basicity measures attack on carbon only
mcqs.why: A nucleophile donates its pair to an electrophilic carbon and its strength (nucleophilicity) is kinetic; a base donates its pair to a proton and basicity is a thermodynamic equilibrium measure.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Alkyl halides are prepared from alcohols with halogen acids, thionyl chloride or phosphorus trihalides; free-radical halogenation gives mixtures.
  • Elimination removes H from the beta-carbon and halide from the alpha-carbon to form an alkene; E1 is two-step and E2 is one-step.
  • SN1 is two-step with rate = k[R-X] and partial racemization; SN2 is one concerted step with rate = k[R-X][Nu-] and complete inversion.
  • Grignard reagents are made from an alkyl halide and magnesium in dry ether; formaldehyde gives primary, higher aldehydes secondary and ketones tertiary alcohols.
  • Esters of higher acids give tertiary alcohols with Grignard reagents because the ketone formed first reacts with a second molecule.
  • Amines are trigonal pyramidal with bond angles near 107.5 degrees, and primary amines give diazonium salts with nitrous acid.
  • A leaving group leaves the substrate with its bonding electron pair and is also called a nucleofuge.
  • Carbocations form by ionisation of alkyl halides and by protonation of alkenes or alcohols followed by loss of water.

Solved Exercises

Exercise: Q3. Write Detail Answers of the Following Questions

Q: Q1. (a) Discuss various methods of preparation of alkyl halides. (b) Explain elimination reaction in alkyl halides.

Ans: (a) Alkyl halides are prepared mainly by: (1) Reaction of alcohols with halogen acids: R-OH + H-X -> R-X + H2O; reactivity of HX is HI > HBr > HCl, anhydrous ZnCl2 is used as catalyst with HCl, and tertiary alcohols react most readily. (2) Reaction of alcohols with thionyl chloride: R-OH + SOCl2 (pyridine) -> R-Cl + SO2 + HCl, giving pure alkyl chlorides because the other products are gases. (3) Reaction of alcohols with phosphorus trihalides: 3R-OH + PX3 -> 3R-X + H3PO3; PBr3 and PI3 are generated in situ from red phosphorus and Br2 or I2. (4) Free-radical halogenation of alkanes with Cl2 or Br2 in ultraviolet light or at high temperature, which replaces hydrogen atoms by halogen but gives a mixture of haloalkanes, so it is not a good method for a pure alkyl halide. (b) In an elimination reaction a hydrogen halide is removed from an alkyl halide: a proton is removed from the beta-carbon and the halide ion leaves from the alpha-carbon, so a new pi bond forms between the alpha and beta carbons and an alkene is produced; it is therefore called 1,2-elimination or beta-elimination (dehydrohalogenation). Two strong sigma bonds (C-H and C-X) are broken and a weaker pi bond is formed. It occurs by two mechanisms: E1, unimolecular, a two-step mechanism through a carbocation, favoured by tertiary halides, weak bases and polar protic solvents, with first-order kinetics; and E2, bimolecular, a one-step concerted mechanism, favoured by primary halides and strong bases, with second-order kinetics. Elimination competes with substitution, and crowding around the alpha-carbon and strong bases favour elimination.

Q: Q2. (a) Discuss the mechanism of SN1 and SN2 reactions. (b) Define the following terms: (i) substrate (ii) leaving group (iii) carbocation.

Ans: (a) SN1 mechanism (unimolecular nucleophilic substitution) occurs in two steps and is followed by tertiary alkyl halides. Step 1 (slow, rate-determining): the substrate ionises and the halide ion leaves, forming a planar carbocation, e.g. (CH3)3C-Br -> (CH3)3C+ + Br-. Step 2 (fast): the nucleophile attacks the planar carbocation from either face, giving the product; attack from both faces gives partial racemization. The rate depends only on the substrate, rate = k[R-X], and polar protic solvents favour it. SN2 mechanism (bimolecular nucleophilic substitution) occurs in one concerted step and is followed by methyl and primary alkyl halides. The nucleophile attacks the carbon from the back side, opposite the leaving group; bond formation and bond breaking occur together through a single transition state in which carbon is partly bonded to both groups, and the product shows complete inversion of configuration. The rate depends on both reactants, rate = k[R-X][Nu-], and polar aprotic solvents favour it. (b) (i) Substrate: the molecule which undergoes the substitution reaction, i.e. the alkyl halide whose group is replaced. (ii) Leaving group: the group or species which leaves the substrate with its bonding electron pair and is replaced by the incoming nucleophile, e.g. the halide ion in R-X, also called nucleofuge. (iii) Carbocation: an ion in which a carbon atom carries a positive charge and is bonded to three other atoms or groups; it is sp2 hybridised, trigonal planar, and is formed when the halogen atom detaches from the carbon of an alkyl halide with its bonding electrons.

Q: Q3. (a) How can you prepare Grignard reagent? (b) Discuss the reaction of Grignard reagent with: (i) aldehydes (ii) ketones (iii) esters (iv) carbon dioxide.

Ans: (a) A Grignard reagent is prepared by the action of an alkyl or aryl halide on freshly prepared magnesium metal in anhydrous (dry) diethyl ether or tetrahydrofuran: R-X + Mg (ether) -> R-MgX. The reaction is heterogeneous; the reagent cannot be isolated, so its ethereal solution is used directly. Ease of formation increases from fluoride to iodide; alkyl iodides are most reactive, but bromides are commonly used as they are cheaper and less toxic. (b) The carbon-magnesium bond is polar, so the alkyl group behaves as a carbanion or nucleophile and adds to polarised carbonyl compounds; the addition product on acid workup gives the final product. (i) Aldehydes: formaldehyde gives a primary alcohol, while higher aldehydes give secondary alcohols, e.g. R-MgX + R'-CHO -> R-CH(OH)-R' after workup. (ii) Ketones: give tertiary alcohols, e.g. R-MgX + (R')2C=O -> R-C(OH)(R')2 after workup. (iii) Esters: formate esters give secondary alcohols, while esters of higher carboxylic acids give tertiary alcohols, because the first addition produces a ketone (after loss of alkoxide) which reacts with a second molecule of Grignard reagent. (iv) Carbon dioxide: the reagent adds to CO2 and the addition product on hydrolysis gives a carboxylic acid containing one carbon more than the parent alkyl halide, e.g. CH3-MgBr + CO2 -> CH3-COOH (acetic acid).

Q: Q4. (a) How amines are prepared? Discuss its structure and basicity. (b) Write down different reactions of amines.

Ans: (a) Preparation: (1) Alkylation of ammonia: ammonia heated with an alkyl halide gives a mixture of primary, secondary and tertiary amines and quaternary ammonium salt, because the hydrogens of ammonia are replaced successively by alkyl groups; an excess of alkyl halide gives the quaternary salt as the main product. (2) Reduction of nitriles: R-C triple bond N is reduced by H2/Ni, Pt or Pd, or by LiAlH4 in ether followed by workup, to a primary amine, e.g. CH3-C triple bond N -> CH3-CH2-NH2. (3) Reduction of nitroalkanes with H2/Ni or Fe or Sn in HCl, e.g. CH3-NO2 + 3H2 (Ni) -> CH3-NH2 + 2H2O. (4) Reduction of amides with LiAlH4 in ether: primary, secondary and tertiary amides give the corresponding primary, secondary and tertiary amines. Structure: amines are derivatives of ammonia in which one or more hydrogens are replaced by alkyl or aryl groups; nitrogen is sp3 hybridised with a lone pair in one sp3 orbital, giving a trigonal pyramidal shape with bond angles close to 107.5 degrees (108 degrees in trimethylamine). Basicity: due to the lone pair on nitrogen, amines accept a proton and are basic in nature, forming ammonium salts with acids: R-NH2 + H-X -> R-NH3+ X-. Aliphatic amines are stronger bases than ammonia because alkyl groups donate electrons (+I effect) and stabilise the conjugate acid; in aqueous solution secondary amines are the most basic because solvation of the ammonium ion also matters (see Table 17.4 pKb values). (b) Reactions of amines: (1) As bases, they react with acids to form salts. (2) Alkylation with alkyl halides (SN2) gives secondary and tertiary amines and finally quaternary ammonium salts. (3) With aldehydes and ketones, primary amines give condensation products called N-substituted imines or Schiff bases, with loss of water, in the presence of acid catalyst. (4) Preparation of amides: primary and secondary amines react with acid chlorides or acid anhydrides to give N-substituted (secondary) and N,N-disubstituted (tertiary) amides; tertiary amines do not react as they have no hydrogen on nitrogen. (5) Preparation of diazonium salts: primary amines react with nitrous acid (NaNO2 + dilute HCl, in situ) to give highly unstable diazonium salts; this is the diazotization reaction.

Q: Q5. (a) What are carbocations? Write any two methods for formation of carbocations. (b) Explain the stability order of different types of carbocations. (c) Write the systematic names for the following organic compounds: (i) H3C-CH2-CH(I)-C(CH3)(C2H5)-CH2-CH3 (ii) H3C-CH(Cl)-CH(CH3)-C(Br)(C2H5)-CH2-CH3 (iii) H3C-CH(Br)-CH(CH3)-C(Br)(F)-CH2-CH=CH2 (iv) H3C-CH(C2H5)-CH(CH3)-C(Br)(CH3)-CH2-CH3 (v) H3C-CH2-CH(NH2)-CH(CH3)-CH2-CH3 (d) Draw the structural formula of the following organic compounds: (i) 3-methylpentane-2,3-diamine (ii) 2,3-dimethylhexane-2,3-diamine (iii) 2-bromo-3-fluoro-2,3-dimethylpentane (iv) 4-bromo-4-chloro-3-fluoro-2,3-dimethylhexane (v) 2-chloro-3,3-dimethylpentan-2-amine.

Ans: (a) A carbocation is an ion in which a carbon atom carries a positive charge and three bonds; it is sp2 hybridised and trigonal planar with an empty p orbital. Two methods of formation: (1) Ionisation of an alkyl halide, in which the halogen atom leaves the carbon with its bonding electron pair, e.g. (CH3)3C-Br -> (CH3)3C+ + Br-, the slow step of SN1 and E1 reactions. (2) Protonation of an alkene or alcohol followed by loss of water or addition of H+ to the double bond, e.g. dehydration of alcohols in acid, where the -OH group is protonated and leaves as water forming a carbocation. (b) Stability order: tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl carbocation. Alkyl groups attached directly to the positively charged carbon stabilise it through their electron-donating (+I) effect and hyperconjugation, spreading the positive charge; three alkyl groups stabilise most, so tert-butyl cation is most stable and methyl cation, with no alkyl group, is least stable (Figure 17.3). (c) (i) 3-ethyl-4-iodo-3-methylhexane (longest chain of six carbons through the ethyl group on C-4). (ii) 4-bromo-2-chloro-4-ethyl-3-methylhexane. (iii) 4,6-dibromo-4-fluoro-5-methylhept-1-ene (chain numbered from the double-bond end). (iv) 3-bromo-3,4,5-trimethylheptane (longest chain of seven carbons through the ethyl group). (v) 4-methylhexan-3-amine. (d) (i) CH3-CH(NH2)-C(NH2)(CH3)-CH2-CH3. (ii) CH3-C(NH2)(CH3)-C(NH2)(CH3)-CH2-CH2-CH3. (iii) CH3-C(Br)(CH3)-CH(F)(CH3)-CH2-CH3. (iv) CH3-CH(CH3)-CH(F)(CH3)-C(Br)(Cl)-CH2-CH3. (v) CH3-C(Cl)(NH2)-C(CH3)(CH3)-CH2-CH3.

mcqs.q: Why does reaction of an alcohol with thionyl chloride give a pure alkyl chloride?
options: The other products, SO2 and HCl, are gases that escape
Thionyl chloride is a strong oxidising agent
The reaction forms no by-products at all
mcqs.why: R-OH + SOCl2 (pyridine) gives R-Cl + SO2 + HCl; because the other products are gases, the alkyl chloride obtained is pure.

mcqs.q: In beta-elimination (dehydrohalogenation) of an alkyl halide, from which carbons are H and X removed?
options: H and X from the same carbon
H from the alpha-carbon and X from the beta-carbon
H from the beta-carbon and X from the alpha-carbon
H and X from two separate molecules
mcqs.why: In 1,2-elimination a proton is removed from the beta-carbon and the halide leaves from the alpha-carbon, forming a pi bond between them to give an alkene.

mcqs.q: What is the rate law of an SN1 reaction?
mcqs.why: SN1 rate depends only on the substrate because the slow step is ionisation of the alkyl halide alone, so rate = k[R-X].

mcqs.q: Which conditions favour the E2 mechanism?
options: Tertiary halide, weak base, polar protic solvent
Primary halide and a strong base
mcqs.why: E2 is a one-step concerted bimolecular mechanism favoured by primary halides and strong bases, with second-order kinetics; E1 is favoured by tertiary halides and weak bases.

mcqs.q: How is a Grignard reagent prepared?
options: By heating an alkyl halide with sodium in water
By reacting an alcohol with magnesium in ether
By reacting magnesium with an alkyl halide in water
By the action of an alkyl or aryl halide on magnesium in anhydrous diethyl ether or THF
mcqs.why: R-X + Mg in dry ether or tetrahydrofuran gives R-MgX; the reagent cannot be isolated and its ethereal solution is used directly.

mcqs.q: What alcohol is obtained from a Grignard reagent and formaldehyde after workup?
mcqs.why: Formaldehyde gives a primary alcohol with a Grignard reagent, higher aldehydes give secondary alcohols and ketones give tertiary alcohols.

mcqs.q: Why do esters of higher carboxylic acids give tertiary alcohols with Grignard reagents?
options: The ester is reduced directly to an alcohol
Only one molecule of reagent reacts
The ketone formed first reacts with a second molecule of Grignard reagent
The alkoxide group adds to the carbonyl twice
mcqs.why: The first addition to the ester produces a ketone after loss of alkoxide, and that ketone reacts with a second molecule of reagent to give a tertiary alcohol.

mcqs.q: What is the shape of an amine molecule such as trimethylamine?
options: Trigonal pyramidal with bond angles close to 107.5 degrees
mcqs.why: Nitrogen in amines is sp3 hybridised with a lone pair in one sp3 orbital, giving a trigonal pyramidal shape; the angle in trimethylamine is about 108 degrees.

mcqs.q: What do primary amines give with nitrous acid (NaNO2 + dilute HCl)?
mcqs.why: Primary amines react with nitrous acid generated in situ to give highly unstable diazonium salts; this is the diazotization reaction.

mcqs.q: Which is a correct method of carbocation formation?
options: Ionisation of an alkyl halide in which halogen leaves with its bonding electron pair
Attack of a nucleophile on an alkane
Loss of a proton from an alkane
Addition of a halide ion to an alkene
mcqs.why: Carbocations form by ionisation of alkyl halides, e.g. (CH3)3C-Br gives (CH3)3C+ + Br-, the slow step of SN1 and E1 reactions.

lessons.title: Project
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Hinsberg's reagent is benzene sulfonyl chloride with aqueous sodium hydroxide, used to distinguish primary, secondary and tertiary amines.
  • Tertiary amines cannot form sulfonamides, while primary and secondary amines do.
  • A primary amine's sulfonamide dissolves in NaOH because it still has an acidic hydrogen on nitrogen and forms a soluble sodium salt, giving a single layer.
  • A secondary amine's sulfonamide is insoluble in NaOH, giving a double layer; the organic layer is then tested with 5% HCl to exclude a tertiary amine.

Solved Exercises

Project

Q: Project. Hinsberg's test is used to distinguish primary, secondary and tertiary amines. The Hinsberg's reagent is a solution of aqueous sodium hydroxide and benzene sulfonyl chloride. In the Hinsberg's test, an amine is reacted with benzene sulfonyl chloride. If a product forms, the amine is either a primary or secondary amine because tertiary amines can not form sulfonamides. If the sulfonamide that forms dissolves in aqueous sodium hydroxide solution, it is a primary amine. If the sulfonamide is insoluble in aqueous sodium hydroxide, it is a secondary amine. The sulfonamide of a primary amine is soluble in an aqueous base because it still possesses an acidic hydrogen on the nitrogen, which can be lost to form a sodium salt. Procedure: Add 4-5 mL of an amine to a large test tube. Add 5 mL of benzene sulfonyl chloride and 10 mL of 10% NaOH and shake vigorously to mix. Check for the presence of a single layer (primary amine) or a double layer (secondary amine) in the solution. If there is a double layer, draw off the lower aqueous layer with a separating funnel and check if the organic layer is soluble in 5% HCl. If yes, it is tertiary but if it is insoluble, then secondary amine is present.

Ans: Step 1: Take 4-5 mL of the given amine in a large test tube, add 5 mL of benzene sulfonyl chloride and 10 mL of 10% NaOH, and shake vigorously. Step 2: If a single layer is obtained, the sulfonamide formed has dissolved in the NaOH solution, so the amine is a primary amine; its sulfonamide still has an acidic hydrogen on nitrogen and forms a soluble sodium salt. Step 3: If a double layer is obtained, the sulfonamide is insoluble in NaOH, indicating a secondary amine. Step 4: Separate the layers with a separating funnel and test the organic layer with 5% HCl: if it dissolves, a tertiary amine is present (tertiary amines form no sulfonamide and the unchanged amine dissolves in acid as its salt); if it stays insoluble, the amine is secondary. In this way the three classes of amines are distinguished in one test.

lessons.title: Self-Assessment
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The method sets the sum of oxidation states in a neutral compound to zero, taking H as +1 and O as -2 and solving for iodine.
  • For HIO4: (+1) + x + 4 x (-2) = 0 gives 1 + x - 8 = 0, so iodine is +7.
  • For HIO3: (+1) + x + 3 x (-2) = 0 gives 1 + x - 6 = 0, so iodine is +5.
  • Iodine is +7 in HIO4 (periodic acid) and +5 in HIO3 (iodic acid).

Solved Exercises

Self-Assessment

Q: What are the oxidation states of the iodine in HIO4 and HIO3?

Ans: Given: In a neutral compound the sum of oxidation states is zero. Oxidation state of H is +1 and of O is -2.
For HIO4: Let the oxidation state of iodine be x.
Substitution: (+1) + x + 4 x (-2) = 0
Working: 1 + x - 8 = 0, so x = +7
For HIO3: Let the oxidation state of iodine be x.
Substitution: (+1) + x + 3 x (-2) = 0
Working: 1 + x - 6 = 0, so x = +5
Answer: Iodine is +7 in HIO4 (periodic acid) and +5 in HIO3 (iodic acid).

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Isopropyl alcohol is a secondary alcohol, and tertiary alcohols such as 2-methyl-2-propanol react fastest with Lucas reagent.
  • Lucas reagent is concentrated HCl with anhydrous ZnCl2, and cloudiness in the test is due to the insoluble alkyl chloride formed.
  • PCC oxidises a primary alcohol only as far as the aldehyde, while secondary alcohols oxidise to ketones.
  • Periodic acid cleaves 1,2-diols to two carbonyl compounds; ethylene glycol gives formaldehyde.
  • Protonated alcohols and ethers contain an oxonium ion, an oxygen with a positive charge bonded to three atoms.
  • Alcohols react with sodium to give alkoxides and hydrogen.
  • Benzenediazonium salts hydrolyse on warming with water to give phenol with loss of nitrogen.
  • Benzyl alcohol is an aromatic alcohol, whereas p-cresol, with -OH directly on the ring, is a phenol.

Solved Exercises

Exercise: Q I. Choose the Correct One from the Given Options

Q: Q1. Isopropyl alcohol is a type of

Options: (a) primary alcohol (b) secondary alcohol (c) tertiary alcohol (d) none of these

Correct answer: secondary alcohol

Q: Q2. Which of the following has the highest boiling point?

Options: (a) Dimethyl ether (b) Ethyl alcohol (c) n-propyl alcohol (d) Isopropyl alcohol

Correct answer: n-propyl alcohol

Q: Q3. Trimethylene glycol is a

Options: (a) vic-diol (b) gem-diol (c) triol (d) none of these

Correct answer: none of these

Q: Q4. The final product of oxidative cleavage of ethylene glycol with periodic acid is

Options: (a) formaldehyde (b) acetaldehyde (c) formic acid (d) mixture of formaldehyde and acetaldehyde

Correct answer: formaldehyde

Q: Q5. Oxygen carrying positive charge and bonded to three other atoms is called

Options: (a) oxide ion (b) oxonium ion (c) carbocation (d) carbanion

Correct answer: oxonium ion

Q: Q6. Which of the proper reagent used for oxidation of a primary alcohol to aldehyde?

Options: (a) Acidified dichromate (b) Acidified chromate (c) Acidified permanganate (d) PCC

Correct answer: PCC

Q: Q7. Which one is an aromatic alcohol?

Options: (a) methyl alcohol (b) ethyl alcohol (c) benzyl alcohol (d) p-cresol

Correct answer: benzyl alcohol

Q: Q8. Compound which is added to natural gas to make gas leakage detectable?

Options: (a) phenol (b) ethanthiol (c) methanol (d) hydrogen sulphide

Correct answer: ethanthiol

Q: Q9. Which of the following is more reactive toward Lucas Reagent?

Options: (a) methanol (b) ethanol (c) 2-methyl-2-propanol (d) 2-butanol

Correct answer: 2-methyl-2-propanol

Q: Q10. Ethoxyethane when treated with conc. H2SO4 produces

Options: (a) carbocation (b) oxonium ion (c) carbanion (d) oxalate ion

Correct answer: oxonium ion

Q: Q11. Lucas Reagent is

Options: (a) Zn-Hg/HCl (b) ZnCl2 + HCl (c) Zn + H2O (d) Na + liq.NH3

Correct answer: ZnCl2 + HCl

Q: Q12. The reaction of an alcohol with sodium produces

Options: (a) ethane (b) ethene (c) alkoxide (d) aldehyde

Correct answer: alkoxide

Q: Q13. Benzene diazonium salt is a reactive salt and upon hydrolysis yields

Options: (a) phenol (b) benzene (c) diazobenzene (d) benzoic acid

Correct answer: phenol

Q: Q14. Oxidation of secondary alcohol gives

Options: (a) carboxylic acid (b) ether (c) aldehyde (d) ketone

Correct answer: ketone

Q: Q15. The appearance of cloudiness in the Lucas test for alcohol is due to formation of

Options: (a) alkyl chloride (b) acid chlorides (c) aldehydes (d) ketones

Correct answer: alkyl chloride

mcqs.why: An oxygen carrying a positive charge and bonded to three other atoms is an oxonium ion, formed when alcohols or ethers are protonated.

mcqs.why: A secondary alcohol has one alpha-hydrogen and is oxidised to a ketone, e.g. isopropyl alcohol gives acetone.
