lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • An alcohol has -OH on an aliphatic sp3 carbon, while a phenol has -OH directly on an aromatic ring carbon.
  • Four isomeric alcohols exist for C4H9OH: butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol.
  • In the Lucas test tertiary alcohols turn cloudy at once, secondary alcohols in a few minutes, and primary alcohols stay clear at room temperature.
  • Phenol (pKa 10) is far more acidic than alcohols (pKa 16-18) because the phenoxide ion is resonance stabilised.
  • Phenol is hard to protonate because an oxygen lone pair is delocalised into the ring, unlike the localised lone pairs in alcohols and ethers.
  • Mixed ethers are made by Williamson's synthesis because dehydrating two different alcohols gives a mixture of three ethers.
  • Phenol discharges bromine water and gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol; an alkene only decolourises it with no precipitate.
  • A tertiary alcohol cannot be oxidised because it has no hydrogen on the carbon carrying the -OH group.

Solved Exercises

Exercise: Q2. Write Short Answers of the Following Questions

Q: Q1 (i). What is the basic difference between an alcohol and phenol, although both have same functional group?

Ans: Both contain the hydroxyl (-OH) functional group, but in an alcohol the -OH group is attached to an aliphatic (sp3) carbon atom, R-OH, while in a phenol the -OH group is attached directly to an aromatic ring carbon, Ar-OH. This difference changes their chemistry: phenols are much more acidic than alcohols because the phenoxide ion is resonance-stabilised by the ring, phenols give electrophilic substitution reactions of the ring and do not undergo the typical substitution and dehydration reactions of alcohols in the same way.

Q: Q2 (ii). How many isomeric alcohols are possible for C4H9OH? Draw their structural formulae and write both common and IUPAC names.

Ans: Four isomeric alcohols are possible for C4H9OH. (1) CH3-CH2-CH2-CH2-OH: common name n-butyl alcohol, IUPAC name butan-1-ol (primary). (2) CH3-CH2-CH(OH)-CH3: common name sec-butyl alcohol, IUPAC name butan-2-ol (secondary). (3) (CH3)2CH-CH2-OH: common name isobutyl alcohol, IUPAC name 2-methylpropan-1-ol (primary). (4) (CH3)3C-OH: common name tert-butyl alcohol, IUPAC name 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tertiary). They differ in the carbon skeleton (straight or branched) and in the position of the -OH group.

Q: Q3 (iii). What is Lucas test? How Lucas test is used to distinguish alcohols?

Ans: Lucas reagent is a mixture of concentrated hydrochloric acid and anhydrous zinc chloride (conc. HCl + ZnCl2). Alcohols react with it to form the corresponding alkyl chlorides, which are insoluble in the reagent and make the mixture cloudy: R-OH + HCl (ZnCl2) -> R-Cl + H2O. The time taken for cloudiness to appear shows the class of alcohol: a tertiary alcohol reacts immediately and cloudiness appears at once, a secondary alcohol reacts after some time (cloudiness in a few minutes), while primary and methyl alcohols do not react at room temperature and the solution stays clear. The test therefore distinguishes primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols.

Q: Q4 (iv). Why phenol is more acidic than alcohols?

Ans: Phenol has Ka about 10^-10 (pKa 10) while alcohols have Ka 10^-16 to 10^-18 (pKa 16-18). On losing a proton, phenol forms the phenoxide ion in which the negative charge is delocalised over the benzene ring through resonance, so the ion is stabilised and the equilibrium shifts towards ionisation. In an alkoxide ion from an alcohol the negative charge stays localised on oxygen and is further destabilised by the electron-donating alkyl group. Hence phenol is much more acidic: it reacts with NaOH and KOH to form salts, while alcohols do not react with aqueous NaOH.

Q: Q5 (v). What is meant by primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols?

Ans: Alcohols are classified by the carbon atom carrying the -OH group. In a primary (1 degree) alcohol the -OH group is attached to a carbon which is bonded to only one other carbon (or none), e.g. CH3-CH2-OH. In a secondary (2 degree) alcohol that carbon is bonded to two other carbons, e.g. isopropyl alcohol (CH3)2CH-OH. In a tertiary (3 degree) alcohol it is bonded to three other carbons, e.g. tert-butyl alcohol (CH3)3C-OH. The class decides their reactivity, e.g. in the Lucas test and in oxidation.

Q: Q6 (vi). Why alcohol and ethers are easily protonated unlike phenol?

Ans: In alcohols and ethers the oxygen atom carries two lone pairs localised on it, and the alkyl groups push electrons towards oxygen (+I effect), so oxygen is electron rich and readily donates a lone pair to a proton, forming oxonium ions. In phenol one lone pair of oxygen is delocalised into the benzene ring by conjugation (resonance), so it is much less available for protonation, and the ring carbon-oxygen bond also has partial double-bond character. Phenol is therefore protonated only with difficulty, unlike alcohols and ethers.

Q: Q7 (vii). Why intermolecular dehydration of alcohol is not a suitable method for synthesis of asymmetric ethers?

Ans: Intermolecular dehydration works well only for a single alcohol, giving a symmetrical ether, e.g. 2C2H5OH (conc. H2SO4, 140 degrees C) -> C2H5-O-C2H5 + H2O. If two different alcohols are dehydrated together, both alcohols react with themselves as well as with each other, giving a mixture of three ethers (two symmetrical and one unsymmetrical) which is very difficult to separate. Asymmetric (mixed) ethers are therefore prepared by Williamson's synthesis instead, by reacting a sodium alkoxide with an alkyl halide.

Q: Q8 (viii). How bromine water test in alkene differ from bromine water test for phenol?

Ans: With an alkene, bromine water is decolourised because Br2 adds across the carbon-carbon double bond (electrophilic addition) to give a colourless dibromoalkane; no precipitate is formed. With phenol, the reddish brown colour of bromine water is also discharged, but by electrophilic substitution on the activated ring, and a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol is formed along with HBr: C6H5OH + 3Br2 -> C6H2Br3OH (white ppt) + 3HBr. The white precipitate, not mere decolourisation, is the positive test for phenol.

Q: Q9 (ix). Why benzene diazonium salt is not much stable and hydrolyse to phenol easily?

Ans: Benzenediazonium chloride contains the -N2+ Cl- group, and molecular nitrogen is an exceptionally stable and good leaving group. The salt is therefore unstable, especially on warming, and even in cold aqueous solution it slowly decomposes; on warming with water at about 100 degrees C it hydrolyses readily, nitrogen gas escapes and phenol is formed: C6H5-N2+ Cl- + H2O -> C6H5-OH + N2 + HCl. Loss of gaseous N2 drives the reaction forward, which is why the hydrolysis is so easy.

Q: Q10 (x). Why tertiary alcohol can not be oxidized?

Ans: Oxidation of an alcohol requires removal of a hydrogen atom from the carbon carrying the -OH group (the alpha-hydrogen): primary alcohols have two such hydrogens and give aldehydes and then acids, and secondary alcohols have one and give ketones. A tertiary alcohol has no hydrogen on its hydroxyl-bearing carbon, (R)3C-OH, so there is no alpha-hydrogen to remove and it does not undergo oxidation under normal conditions, as shown in Section 18.1.7.5.

mcqs.q: What is the basic difference between an alcohol and a phenol?
options: Alcohol -OH is on an aromatic carbon; phenol -OH is aliphatic
Alcohol -OH is on an aliphatic sp3 carbon; phenol -OH is directly on an aromatic ring carbon
mcqs.why: Both contain -OH, but in an alcohol it is attached to an aliphatic (sp3) carbon, R-OH, while in a phenol it is attached directly to an aromatic ring carbon, Ar-OH.

mcqs.q: How many isomeric alcohols are possible for C4H9OH?
mcqs.why: Four isomers exist: butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol, differing in skeleton and in the position of the -OH group.

mcqs.q: What is Lucas reagent?
mcqs.why: Lucas reagent is a mixture of concentrated hydrochloric acid and anhydrous zinc chloride; alcohols form insoluble alkyl chlorides with it.

mcqs.q: In the Lucas test, how does a tertiary alcohol respond at room temperature?
options: It stays clear and does not react
It forms an aldehyde at once
mcqs.why: A tertiary alcohol reacts immediately with Lucas reagent and cloudiness appears at once; a secondary alcohol takes a few minutes and primary alcohols stay clear.

mcqs.q: What are the approximate pKa values of phenol and alcohols?
mcqs.why: Phenol has Ka about 10^-10 (pKa 10) while alcohols have Ka 10^-16 to 10^-18 (pKa 16-18), so phenol is much more acidic.

mcqs.q: Why is the phenoxide ion more stable than an alkoxide ion?
options: Its charge is increased by the alkyl group
Its negative charge stays fixed on oxygen
Its negative charge is delocalised over the benzene ring by resonance
It forms hydrogen bonds with water only
mcqs.why: In the phenoxide ion the negative charge is delocalised over the ring through resonance, stabilising the ion; in an alkoxide ion the charge stays localised on oxygen.

mcqs.q: Why is Williamson's synthesis preferred for asymmetric (mixed) ethers?
options: Dehydration of two different alcohols gives a mixture of three ethers that is hard to separate
Dehydration gives no ether at all
Williamson's synthesis dehydrates two alcohols together
mcqs.why: Two different alcohols dehydrated together give two symmetrical ethers plus the mixed ether, a mixture very difficult to separate, so Williamson's synthesis is used instead.

mcqs.q: How does the bromine water test for phenol differ from that for an alkene?
options: Phenol gives no change with bromine water
Alkene gives a white precipitate; phenol does not
Phenol gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol; an alkene only decolourises the bromine water
mcqs.why: An alkene decolourises bromine water by addition, giving a colourless dibromoalkane with no precipitate; phenol undergoes substitution and forms white 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

mcqs.q: Why does benzenediazonium chloride hydrolyse so easily to phenol?
options: Chloride is a very strong base
Molecular nitrogen is an exceptionally stable and good leaving group, and its escape drives the reaction
Water attacks the ring carbon directly
Phenol is a stronger acid than the salt
mcqs.why: The -N2+ Cl- group loses N2, an exceptionally stable leaving group; on warming with water at about 100 degrees C phenol forms and loss of gaseous N2 drives the reaction forward.

mcqs.q: Why can a tertiary alcohol not be oxidised under normal conditions?
options: It has no hydrogen on the carbon carrying the -OH group
Its -OH group is attached to a ring
It is too soluble in water
mcqs.why: Oxidation requires removal of an alpha-hydrogen from the -OH carbon; a tertiary alcohol, (R)3C-OH, has none, so it does not oxidise under normal conditions.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Diethyl ether is made by heating ethanol with concentrated H2SO4 at 140 degrees C, or by Williamson's synthesis from sodium ethoxide and ethyl iodide.
  • Above 140 degrees C, intramolecular dehydration of ethanol to ethene is favoured instead of ether formation.
  • Ethers form oxonium salts with cold concentrated acids and are cleaved by hot concentrated HI to an alcohol and an alkyl iodide.
  • Phenol is prepared by the Dow process, from benzenesulphonic acid, by cumene oxidation and by hydrolysis of diazonium salts.
  • In phenol the C-O bond (136 pm) is shorter than in methanol (142 pm) because of partial double-bond character from conjugation with the ring.
  • Phenol with concentrated nitric acid gives 2,4,6-trinitrophenol (picric acid), and with K2Cr2O7/H2SO4 it gives p-benzoquinone.
  • Alcohols are very weak acids (pKa 16-18), weaker than water, and react with sodium but not with aqueous NaOH.
  • Alcohols dehydrate with concentrated H2SO4 at 170 degrees C to alkenes, with ease tertiary > secondary > primary.

Solved Exercises

Exercise: Q3. Write Detail Answers of the Following Questions

Q: Q1. (a) Describe the reaction for preparation of diethyl ether, by dehydration of alcohol and Williamson's synthesis. (b) Write two chemical reactions of diethyl ether. (c) Enlist the physical properties of ether.

Ans: (a) By dehydration of alcohol: two molecules of ethyl alcohol are heated with concentrated sulphuric acid at 140 degrees C; one molecule loses -OH and the other loses H, giving diethyl ether: C2H5-OH + HO-C2H5 (conc. H2SO4, 140 degrees C) -> C2H5-O-C2H5 + H2O. The temperature must be controlled, because above 140 degrees C intramolecular dehydration to ethene is favoured. By Williamson's synthesis: sodium ethoxide is treated with ethyl iodide (an alkyl halide): C2H5-ONa + I-C2H5 -> C2H5-O-C2H5 + NaI. The alkoxide is first made by reacting ethanol with sodium metal. (b) Two reactions of diethyl ether: (1) Formation of oxonium salt: with cold concentrated H2SO4 or HCl it donates a lone pair to H+ and forms diethyloxonium hydrogen sulphate or chloride, e.g. C2H5-O-C2H5 + conc. H2SO4 -> [C2H5-O+H-C2H5] HSO4-. (2) Cleavage of ether linkage: with hot concentrated HI it is cleaved to ethyl alcohol and ethyl iodide: C2H5-O-C2H5 + HI -> C2H5-OH + C2H5-I; on prolonged heating with dilute H2SO4 under pressure it hydrolyses back to ethanol. (c) Physical properties of ethers: dimethyl ether and ethyl methyl ether are gases at room temperature, while the others (including diethyl ether) are colourless, volatile liquids with pleasant odours; they are highly flammable; they have much lower boiling points than alcohols of comparable molecular mass because they cannot form hydrogen bonds among themselves; low molecular weight ethers show some solubility in water through hydrogen bonding with water, and they are readily soluble in organic solvents; they are generally less dense than water and are chemically quite stable, which makes them good solvents.

Q: Q2. (a) What are phenols? Give method of preparation of phenol. (b) Discuss the acidic behaviour of phenol.

Ans: (a) Phenols are organic compounds in which a hydroxyl group is attached directly to an aromatic ring carbon; the parent compound is phenol itself, C6H5OH (benzenol). Phenol is prepared by: (1) From benzenesulphonic acid: benzene is sulphonated with fuming H2SO4 to benzenesulphonic acid, converted to sodium benzenesulphonate, which is fused with solid NaOH at 300-350 degrees C to give sodium phenoxide, and acidification with dilute HCl gives phenol. (2) Dow process: chlorobenzene is hydrolysed with aqueous NaOH (10%) at 350 degrees C and 150 atm pressure to sodium phenoxide, which on treatment with dilute HCl gives phenol. (3) Acidic oxidation of cumene: cumene (isopropylbenzene) is oxidised by air to cumene hydroperoxide, which with dilute acid (H2SO4/H2O, 70 degrees C) gives phenol along with acetone. (4) Hydrolysis of diazonium salts: benzenediazonium chloride solution is warmed with water at 100 degrees C to give phenol with loss of N2. (b) Acidic behaviour: phenol is a weak acid (Ka about 10^-10, pKa 10), more acidic than water and alcohols but less acidic than carboxylic acids (Table 18.2). It turns blue litmus slightly red, reacts with NaOH and KOH to form sodium phenoxide and water, and reacts with sodium metal to form sodium phenoxide with evolution of hydrogen: C6H5OH + Na -> C6H5ONa + 1/2 H2. Its acidity is due to resonance stabilisation of the phenoxide ion, in which the negative charge is delocalised over the ring, whereas in phenol itself the charge separation in the resonance forms makes the O-H bond easier to break. Electron-withdrawing groups on the ring increase its acidity further.

Q: Q3. Give detail description of structure and chemical properties of phenols.

Ans: Structure: in phenol the -OH group is attached to an sp2 carbon of the benzene ring; the molecule is planar, the C-O-H bond angle is 109 degrees, the C-O bond length is 136 pm (shorter than in methanol, 142 pm) and the O-H bond length is 96 pm. The shorter C-O bond is due to partial double-bond character, which results from conjugation of the unshared electron pair of oxygen with the aromatic ring, as shown by its dipolar resonance structures; each ring carbon is sp2 hybridised with internal angles of 120 degrees. Chemical properties: phenol shows reactions of the hydroxyl group and reactions of the ring. (1) Acidity: it forms salts (phenoxides) with NaOH, KOH and sodium metal. (2) Electrophilic aromatic substitution: the -OH group strongly activates the ring and directs incoming groups to ortho and para positions: nitration with dilute HNO3 gives mainly o- and p-nitrophenol, while concentrated HNO3 gives 2,4,6-trinitrophenol (picric acid); halogenation with excess bromine water gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol, while in a non-polar solvent (CCl4 or CS2) at low temperature it gives a mixture of o- and p-bromophenol; sulphonation, Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation also occur readily. (3) Oxidation: phenol is oxidised even more readily than primary and secondary alcohols; with K2Cr2O7/H2SO4 it gives p-benzoquinone. Phenol is also used as a disinfectant and germicide.

Q: Q4. (a) Discuss the structure, synthesis and chemical reactions of alcohols. (b) How alcohols are slightly acidic?

Ans: (a) Structure: alcohols are alkyl derivatives of water; the oxygen is sp3 hybridised with a geometry similar to water, the C-O-H angle in methyl alcohol is 108.9 degrees, and the C-O and O-H bond lengths are 142 pm and 96 pm respectively. Hydrogen bonding between alcohol molecules gives them relatively high boiling points and good miscibility of the lower members with water. Synthesis (preparation) of alcohols: (1) hydration of alkenes with H2SO4/H2O; (2) hydrolysis of alkyl halides with water or aqueous alkali; (3) reaction of Grignard reagents with aldehydes, ketones and esters followed by workup; (4) reduction of aldehydes and ketones by H2/Ni, Pt or Pd, or by LiAlH4 or NaBH4 in ether followed by workup (formaldehyde gives methanol, higher aldehydes give primary alcohols, ketones give secondary alcohols); (5) reduction of carboxylic acids and esters by the powerful reducing agent LiAlH4 to primary alcohols. Chemical reactions: (1) with halogen acids (HX) they give alkyl halides (Lucas test conditions for HCl); (2) with PX3 and SOCl2 they give alkyl halides; (3) acid-catalysed dehydration with conc. H2SO4 at 170 degrees C gives alkenes (ease: tertiary > secondary > primary); (4) esterification with carboxylic acids in conc. H2SO4 (Fischer esterification) gives esters; (5) oxidation gives aldehydes or carboxylic acids from primary alcohols (PCC stops at the aldehyde), ketones from secondary alcohols, while tertiary alcohols resist oxidation; (6) with sodium metal they give alkoxides and hydrogen; (7) oxidative cleavage of 1,2-diols with periodic acid (HIO4) gives two carbonyl compounds. (b) Slight acidity of alcohols: the O-H bond in alcohols is polar (O delta- - H delta+), so the hydrogen can be released as a proton: R-OH + H2O ⇌ R-O- + H3O+, with pKa 16-18, so alcohols are very weak acids, even weaker than water (pKa 15.7). They react with active metals like sodium to give alkoxides and hydrogen, 2ROH + 2Na -> 2RONa + H2, but they are not acidic enough to react with aqueous NaOH or KOH. Acidity decreases from methyl alcohol to tertiary alcohols because electron-donating alkyl groups destabilise the alkoxide ion.

Q: Q5. (a) How alcohol can be prepared from Grignard reagents. (b) Mention the reaction for the formation of following compounds from alcohol: (i) ethene (ii) ethylacetate (iii) acetone (iv) formaldehyde. (c) Write the systematic names for the following organic compounds: (i) H3C-C(OH)(CH3)-CH2-CH3 (ii) H3C-C(OH)(CH3)-CH(OH)-CH2-CH3 (iii) H3C-C(OH)(CH3)-CH2-CH=CH2 (iv) a benzene ring bearing -OH at position 1, -Br at position 2, -F at position 3 and -CH3 at position 4 (v) H3C-CH(OCH3)-CH(OCH3)-CH3 (d) Draw the structural formula of the following organic compounds: (i) pentan-2-ol (ii) 3,4-dimethylhexan-2-ol (iii) 4-methylpent-3-en-2-ol (iv) 3,4-dimethyl-2-nitrophenol (v) 2,3-dimethoxy-4-methylpentane.

Ans: (a) A Grignard reagent adds to the carbonyl group of an aldehyde or ketone to form an addition product (alkoxide salt), which on acid workup (H3O+) gives an alcohol: R-MgX + R'-CHO -> addition product -> R-CH(OH)-R'. Formaldehyde gives a primary alcohol, higher aldehydes give secondary alcohols and ketones give tertiary alcohols. With esters, formate esters give secondary alcohols and higher esters give tertiary alcohols, because the ketone formed first reacts with a second molecule of the reagent. (b) (i) Ethene: ethanol is dehydrated with concentrated H2SO4 at 170 degrees C: CH3-CH2-OH (conc. H2SO4, 170 degrees C) -> CH2=CH2 + H2O. (ii) Ethyl acetate: ethanol reacts with acetic acid in the presence of concentrated H2SO4 (Fischer esterification): CH3-COOH + HO-C2H5 (H+) ⇌ CH3-COO-C2H5 + H2O. (iii) Acetone: isopropyl alcohol (a secondary alcohol) is oxidised: (CH3)2CH-OH + [O] -> CH3-CO-CH3 + H2O. (iv) Formaldehyde: methanol (a primary alcohol) is oxidised with PCC in CH2Cl2, which stops the oxidation at the aldehyde stage: CH3-OH + [O] (PCC) -> H-CHO + H2O. (c) (i) 2-methylbutan-2-ol. (ii) 2-methylpentane-2,3-diol. (iii) 2-methylbut-3-en-2-ol (the right-hand end of this structure is cut off at the edge of the printed page in the scan; it reads as -CH=CH2, which alone completes the carbon valency). (iv) 2-bromo-3-fluoro-4-methylphenol. (v) 2,3-dimethoxybutane. (d) (i) CH3-CH(OH)-CH2-CH2-CH3. (ii) CH3-CH(OH)-CH(CH3)-CH(CH3)-CH2-CH3. (iii) CH3-CH(OH)-CH=C(CH3)-CH3. (iv) A benzene ring with -OH at carbon 1, -NO2 at carbon 2, -CH3 at carbon 3 and -CH3 at carbon 4. (v) CH3-CH(OCH3)-CH(OCH3)-CH(CH3)-CH3.

mcqs.q: At what temperature does dehydration of ethanol with concentrated H2SO4 give diethyl ether?
mcqs.why: Two molecules of ethanol heated with concentrated H2SO4 at 140 degrees C give diethyl ether; the temperature must be controlled to avoid alkene formation.

mcqs.q: What happens if the dehydration of ethanol is heated above 140 degrees C?
options: Intramolecular dehydration to ethene is favoured
Ethanol is oxidised to acetic acid
mcqs.why: Above 140 degrees C intramolecular dehydration is favoured, and at 170 degrees C ethanol gives ethene instead of diethyl ether.

mcqs.q: What does diethyl ether form with cold concentrated H2SO4?
options: An oxonium salt, diethyloxonium hydrogen sulphate
mcqs.why: Diethyl ether donates a lone pair to H+ and forms diethyloxonium hydrogen sulphate with cold concentrated H2SO4.

mcqs.q: In the Dow process, how is chlorobenzene converted to phenol?
options: It is hydrolysed with aqueous NaOH (10%) at 350 degrees C and 150 atm to sodium phenoxide, then acidified
It is reduced with H2/Ni to phenol
It is oxidised by air to a hydroperoxide
It is fused with solid NaOH at 300 degrees C directly
mcqs.why: In the Dow process chlorobenzene is hydrolysed with 10% aqueous NaOH at 350 degrees C and 150 atm pressure to sodium phenoxide, which gives phenol with dilute HCl.

mcqs.q: What is produced along with phenol in the cumene process?
mcqs.why: Cumene is oxidised by air to cumene hydroperoxide, which with dilute acid gives phenol along with acetone.

mcqs.q: Why is the C-O bond in phenol (136 pm) shorter than in methanol (142 pm)?
options: Phenol has a triple C-O bond
The ring carbon is sp3 hybridised
It has partial double-bond character from conjugation of the oxygen lone pair with the ring
mcqs.why: Conjugation of the unshared electron pair of oxygen with the aromatic ring gives the C-O bond partial double-bond character, shortening it to 136 pm.

mcqs.q: What does phenol give with concentrated HNO3?
mcqs.why: The -OH group strongly activates the ring: dilute HNO3 gives mainly o- and p-nitrophenol, while concentrated HNO3 gives 2,4,6-trinitrophenol, picric acid.

mcqs.q: What is the C-O-H bond angle in methyl alcohol?
mcqs.why: In alcohols the oxygen is sp3 hybridised with a geometry similar to water; the C-O-H angle in methyl alcohol is 108.9 degrees.

mcqs.q: What is the order of ease of acid-catalysed dehydration of alcohols to alkenes?
mcqs.why: Acid-catalysed dehydration with concentrated H2SO4 at 170 degrees C gives alkenes with ease tertiary > secondary > primary.

mcqs.q: How can methanol be converted to formaldehyde without further oxidation?
options: By oxidation with PCC in CH2Cl2, which stops at the aldehyde stage
By Fischer esterification with acetic acid
mcqs.why: Methanol, a primary alcohol, is oxidised with PCC in CH2Cl2 to formaldehyde; PCC stops the oxidation at the aldehyde stage.

lessons.title: Project
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The test dissolves a few drops or one small crystal of the substance in 10 mL of ethyl alcohol or methyl alcohol.
  • Bromine water is added drop-wise while stirring vigorously.
  • Phenol rapidly discharges the reddish brown colour of bromine water.
  • A white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol forms: C6H5OH + 3Br2 gives C6H2Br3OH + 3HBr, confirming phenol because the -OH group activates the 2, 4 and 6 positions.

Solved Exercises

Project

Q: Project. Dissolve few drops or one small crystal of phenol in 10 mL of ethyl alcohol or methyl alcohol. Stir vigorously while adding bromine water, drop-wise. Rapid loss of reddish brown color of bromine water and formation of white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol suggests the presence of phenol (Section 18.2.7.1).

Ans: Step 1: Dissolve a few drops or one small crystal of the given substance in 10 mL of ethyl alcohol or methyl alcohol. Step 2: Add bromine water drop-wise while stirring vigorously. Step 3: Observe that the reddish brown colour of bromine water is rapidly discharged. Step 4: A white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol appears: C6H5OH + 3Br2 -> C6H2Br3OH (white ppt) + 3HBr. Discharge of the bromine colour together with the white precipitate confirms that the substance is phenol, because the -OH group strongly activates the 2, 4 and 6 positions of the ring towards electrophilic substitution.

chapters.title: Unit 19: Carbonyl Compounds 1: Aldehydes and Ketones

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The carbon of the carbonyl group is sp2-hybridized.
  • Reduction of a carbonyl group to methylene is carried out by the Clemmensen method.
  • Formaldehyde with methyl magnesium iodide gives, after hydrolysis, ethyl alcohol.
  • Ethanal gives a silver mirror with ammoniacal silver nitrate (Tollen's reagent), while acetone does not.
  • The IUPAC name of acetone is propanone.
  • Formalin is a 40% aqueous solution of formaldehyde.
  • Ozonolysis of but-2-ene gives only one type of aldehyde, acetaldehyde.
  • Formaldehyde is the aldehyde most reactive towards nucleophilic addition.

Solved Exercises

Q1. Choose the correct one from the given options

Q: 1. The carbon of the carbonyl group is

Options: (a) sp3-hybridized. (b) sp2-hybridized. (c) sp-hybridized. (d) dsp2-hybridized.

Correct answer: sp2-hybridized.

Q: 2. The reduction of carbonyl to methylene is carried out with

Options: (a) catalytic reduction (b) Metal hydride (c) Clemmensen method (d) Lindlar's catalyst

Correct answer: Clemmensen method

Q: 3. Formaldehyde gives an addition product with methyl magnesium iodide which on hydrolysis gives

Options: (a) n-propyl alcohol. (b) isopropyl alcohol. (c) methyl alcohol. (d) ethyl alcohol.

Correct answer: ethyl alcohol.

Q: 4. Which of the following compounds can react with ammoniacal silver nitrate solution to form silver mirror?

Options: (a) Acetone (b) Ethanol (c) Dimethyl ether (d) Ethanal

Correct answer: Ethanal

Q: 5. Which of the following compounds will form a precipitate of cupric oxide from Fehling's reagent but does not react with sodium metal?

Options: (a) C2H5OH (b) C2H5CHO (c) CH3CH(OH)CH3 (d) CH3COCH3

Correct answer: C2H5CHO

Q: 6. IUPAC name of acetone is

Options: (a) ethanone. (b) propanone. (c) ethanal. (d) ethanoic acid.

Correct answer: propanone.

Q: 7. Formalin is

Options: (a) 10% aq. solution of formaldehyde. (b) 20% aq. solution of formaldehyde. (c) 40% aq. solution of formaldehyde. (d) 5% aq. solution of formaldehyde.

Correct answer: 40% aq. solution of formaldehyde.

Q: 8. An alkene upon ozonolysis gives only one type of aldehyde in product. Identify that alkene.

Options: (a) but-1-ene (b) propene (c) but-2-ene (d) 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene

Correct answer: but-2-ene

Q: 9. Which of the following alkyne would not yield a ketone upon hydration?

Options: (a) acetylene (b) propyne (c) but-1-yne (d) but-2-yne

Correct answer: acetylene

Q: 10. Geminal diol can be obtained by

Options: (a) hydration of alcohol. (b) hydration of aldehyde. (c) hydrogenation of ketone. (d) hydration of both aldehyde and ketone.

Correct answer: hydration of both aldehyde and ketone.

Q: 11. Schiff base can be obtained by reaction of ______ amine with ketone

Options: (a) primary (b) secondary (c) tertiary (d) quaternary

Correct answer: primary

Q: 12. A hemiacetal contains both

Options: (a) alcohol and aldehyde functional groups. (b) alcohol and ether functional groups. (c) aldehyde and ether functional groups. (d) alcohol and carboxylic acid functional groups.

Correct answer: alcohol and ether functional groups.

Q: 13. Which aldehyde is more reactive towards nucleophilic addition?

Options: (a) Formaldehyde (b) Acetaldehyde (c) Butyraldehyde (d) Propionaldehyde

Correct answer: Formaldehyde

Q: 14. Which type of reaction is involved in the formation of acetals from alcohols on treatment with aldehydes?

Options: (a) Nucleophilic substitution (b) Electrophilic substitution (c) Oxidation (d) Nucleophilic addition

Correct answer: Nucleophilic addition

Q: 15. Which of the following method does not give ketones?

Options: (a) Hydration of alkyne (b) Oxidation of primary alcohol (c) Oxidation of secondary alcohols (d) Friedel-Crafts acylation

Correct answer: Oxidation of primary alcohol

mcqs.q: The carbon of the carbonyl group is
mcqs.why: The carbonyl carbon and oxygen are both sp2-hybridized, giving a trigonal planar carbonyl group with bond angles of about 120 degrees.

mcqs.q: The reduction of carbonyl to methylene is carried out with
mcqs.why: Clemmensen reduction with zinc-mercury amalgam and concentrated HCl reduces the carbonyl group all the way to a methylene (-CH2-) group.

mcqs.q: Formaldehyde gives an addition product with methyl magnesium iodide which on hydrolysis gives
mcqs.why: Formaldehyde reacts with methyl magnesium iodide and the addition product on hydrolysis gives ethyl alcohol, a primary alcohol with one extra carbon.

mcqs.q: Which of the following compounds can react with ammoniacal silver nitrate solution to form silver mirror?
mcqs.why: Ethanal is an aldehyde, and aldehydes reduce Tollen's reagent (ammoniacal silver nitrate) to metallic silver, deposited as a silver mirror; ketones do not.

mcqs.q: Which of the following compounds will form a precipitate of cupric oxide from Fehling's reagent but does not react with sodium metal?
mcqs.why: Propanal, C2H5CHO, is an aldehyde, so it reduces Fehling's solution to a red precipitate of Cu2O, and having no hydroxyl group it does not react with sodium metal.

mcqs.q: IUPAC name of acetone is
mcqs.why: Acetone, CH3-CO-CH3, is the three-carbon ketone, so its systematic IUPAC name is propanone.

mcqs.q: Formalin is
mcqs.why: Formalin is the 40% aqueous solution of formaldehyde, the form in which formaldehyde is stored and used.

mcqs.q: An alkene upon ozonolysis gives only one type of aldehyde in product. Identify that alkene.
mcqs.why: But-2-ene is symmetrical, so ozonolysis cleaves it into two molecules of the same aldehyde, acetaldehyde, giving only one type of aldehyde.

mcqs.q: Which of the following alkyne would not yield a ketone upon hydration?
mcqs.why: Acetylene on hydration gives vinyl alcohol, which tautomerizes to acetaldehyde, an aldehyde and not a ketone; higher alkynes give ketones.

mcqs.q: Geminal diol can be obtained by
options: hydration of both aldehyde and ketone.
mcqs.why: Addition of water across the carbonyl group of either an aldehyde or a ketone gives a geminal diol, a carbon bearing two hydroxyl groups.

mcqs.q: Schiff base can be obtained by reaction of ______ amine with ketone
mcqs.why: A primary amine reacts with a ketone with loss of water to give an N-substituted imine, which is called a Schiff base.

mcqs.q: A hemiacetal contains both
options: alcohol and carboxylic acid functional groups.
mcqs.why: A hemiacetal carbon carries both a hydroxyl (-OH) group and an alkoxy (-OR) group, so it contains alcohol and ether functional groups together.

mcqs.q: Which aldehyde is more reactive towards nucleophilic addition?
mcqs.why: Formaldehyde has no electron-donating alkyl group and the least steric hindrance, so its carbonyl carbon is the most electrophilic and most reactive towards nucleophiles.

mcqs.q: Which type of reaction is involved in the formation of acetals from alcohols on treatment with aldehydes?
mcqs.why: Acetal formation begins with nucleophilic addition of an alcohol to the carbonyl group of the aldehyde, forming a hemiacetal first and then the acetal.

mcqs.q: Which of the following method does not give ketones?
mcqs.why: Oxidation of a primary alcohol gives an aldehyde and then a carboxylic acid, never a ketone; ketones come from oxidation of secondary alcohols.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • In an aldehyde the carbonyl carbon carries at least one hydrogen as the formyl group -CHO at the end of the chain, while in a ketone it carries two carbon groups.
  • Acid protonates the carbonyl oxygen to an oxonium ion, making the carbonyl carbon much more electrophilic.
  • The C=O bond is polarized, so carbonyl compounds undergo nucleophilic addition while alkenes undergo electrophilic addition.
  • Aldehydes oxidize easily because their carbonyl carbon carries a hydrogen; ketones resist oxidation and need C-C bond cleavage.
  • HCN addition is base-catalysed only, because the base generates the CN- ions that actually attack the carbonyl carbon.
  • Ketones are less reactive than aldehydes because two alkyl groups donate electrons and cause more steric crowding.
  • Lower aldehydes and ketones dissolve in water because the carbonyl oxygen forms hydrogen bonds with water.
  • Tollen's reagent distinguishes aldehydes from ketones: aldehydes give a silver mirror, ketones do not.

Solved Exercises

Q2. Write short answers of the following questions

Q: i. Both aldehydes and ketones contain carbonyl group, then what is the basic difference between an aldehyde and a ketone?

Ans: In an aldehyde the carbonyl carbon is attached to at least one hydrogen atom and one alkyl (or aryl) group, i.e. it carries the formyl group -CHO, which is always at the end of the chain, e.g. CH3-CHO. In a ketone the carbonyl carbon is attached to two carbon groups (alkyl or aryl) and has no hydrogen on it, so the -CO- group lies inside the chain, e.g. CH3-CO-CH3. Because of the hydrogen attached to it, an aldehyde is easily oxidized to a carboxylic acid, while a ketone resists oxidation.

Q: ii. How acid catalyst increases the electrophilic character of carbonyl carbon?

Ans: Carbonyl compounds are weak Lewis bases, so in acid the carbonyl oxygen is protonated to give an oxonium ion, >C=O + H+ -> >C=OH+. Protonation pulls the pi electrons of C=O still more towards oxygen and puts a full positive character on the carbonyl carbon. The carbon thus becomes much more electrophilic and is attacked even by weak nucleophiles, which could not attack the neutral carbonyl group.

Q: iii. Addition reaction is the characteristic of a double bond. Aldehydes and ketones undergo nucleophilic addition to carbon-oxygen double bond, while alkenes undergo electrophilic addition to carbon-carbon double bond. Why?

Ans: The C=C bond of an alkene is non-polar, so it is electron-rich and is attacked first by an electrophile. The C=O bond, however, is strongly polarized because oxygen is much more electronegative than carbon: the oxygen carries a partial negative charge and the carbon a partial positive charge. The positively charged carbonyl carbon is therefore attacked by a nucleophile, and the pi electrons shift onto oxygen to form an alkoxide ion, which is then protonated. Hence aldehydes and ketones give nucleophilic addition, not electrophilic addition.

Q: iv. Aldehydes are oxidized easily than ketones. Why?

Ans: In an aldehyde the carbonyl carbon carries a hydrogen atom. Oxidation simply converts this C-H into C-OH, giving a carboxylic acid with the same number of carbon atoms, and even mild oxidizing agents like Tollen's reagent and Fehling's solution can do it. A ketone has no hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon, so it can be oxidized only by breaking a C-C bond with strong oxidizing agents under drastic conditions. That is why aldehydes are oxidized easily and ketones are resistant to oxidation.

Q: v. Hydration of aldehyde and ketone can be catalyzed by both acid and base, but addition of hydrogen cyanide can only be catalysed by base. Why?

Ans: Water is a reasonably good nucleophile: acid catalysis helps by protonating the carbonyl oxygen, and base catalysis helps by converting water into the stronger nucleophile OH-, so hydration works with either catalyst. HCN, however, is a very weak acid and contains almost no CN- ions, and CN- is the real nucleophile in cyanohydrin formation. A base removes H+ from HCN and generates CN- ions (HCN + OH- -> CN- + H2O), so the addition is catalysed by base only; an acid would suppress the formation of CN- and stop the reaction.

Q: vi. Why addition of Grignard reagent to a carbonyl generally do not require any catalyst?

Ans: A Grignard reagent (R-MgX) is itself a very strong nucleophile and a strong base, because its carbon carries a large partial negative charge and acts as a carbanion. It attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon directly and irreversibly, forming a new C-C bond and an alkoxide intermediate, which on acid workup gives the alcohol. Since the nucleophile is already so reactive, neither acid nor base catalysis is needed to activate it or the carbonyl group.

Q: vii. How ketones are somewhat less reactive than aldehydes towards nucleophile?

Ans: Two factors work together. (1) Electronic effect: a ketone has two electron-donating alkyl groups on the carbonyl carbon, which neutralize its partial positive charge more than the single alkyl group of an aldehyde, so the ketone carbon is less electrophilic. (2) Steric effect: the carbonyl carbon of a ketone is more crowded by two bulky alkyl groups, and in the tetrahedral addition product the groups are pushed still closer, so attack by a nucleophile is hindered. Aldehydes, with one small hydrogen atom, are less crowded and more reactive.

Q: viii. Why lower aldehydes and ketones are highly soluble in water, although there is no acidic hydrogen available in these compounds?

Ans: Solubility in water does not need an acidic hydrogen; it needs hydrogen bonding with water. The carbonyl oxygen of aldehydes and ketones has lone pairs and accepts hydrogen bonds from water molecules, so the lower members (up to about four carbon atoms) dissolve well. They cannot form hydrogen bonds among themselves, because they have no hydrogen on oxygen, but they form them readily with water. As the non-polar alkyl chain grows, this effect is outweighed and solubility decreases.

Q: ix. The carboxylic acid(s) formed upon oxidation of ketones, must have carbon atoms less than parent ketone. Why?

Ans: A ketone has no hydrogen on its carbonyl carbon, so oxidation cannot take place at that carbon without breaking the molecule. Strong oxidizing agents therefore cleave one of the C-C bonds next to the carbonyl group, and the carbonyl carbon goes with one fragment only. Each acid so formed contains fewer carbon atoms than the parent ketone, e.g. acetone (3 carbons) on oxidation with acidified K2Cr2O7 gives acetic acid (2 carbons) and CO2.

Q: x. Briefly explain a test that can be used for detection of aldehydes from ketones in laboratory.

Ans: Tollen's reagent (silver mirror) test is used. Tollen's reagent is ammoniacal silver nitrate, [Ag(NH3)2]OH, prepared by adding dilute NH4OH to AgNO3 solution until the precipitate of silver oxide just dissolves. On warming an aldehyde with it, the aldehyde is oxidized to the carboxylate ion and Ag+ is reduced to metallic silver, which deposits as a bright silver mirror on the walls of the test tube: RCHO + 2[Ag(NH3)2]OH -> RCOONH4 + 2Ag + 3NH3 + H2O. Ketones are not oxidized by this reagent and give no mirror, so the test distinguishes aldehydes from ketones. Fehling's and Benedict's solutions (red precipitate of Cu2O with aldehydes only) are also used for the same purpose.

mcqs.q: In an aldehyde, the carbonyl carbon is attached to
options: two alkyl or aryl groups and no hydrogen
at least one hydrogen atom, forming the formyl group -CHO
one hydroxyl group and one hydrogen atom
mcqs.why: An aldehyde carries the formyl group -CHO at the end of the chain, so its carbonyl carbon has at least one hydrogen; a ketone carbonyl carbon carries two carbon groups instead.

mcqs.q: How does an acid catalyst make the carbonyl carbon more electrophilic?
options: It removes the carbonyl oxygen as water
It converts the carbonyl carbon into a carbanion
It protonates the carbonyl oxygen to give an oxonium ion, >C=OH+
It reduces the C=O bond to a single bond
mcqs.why: Protonation of the carbonyl oxygen pulls the pi electrons still more towards oxygen and puts full positive character on the carbonyl carbon, so even weak nucleophiles can attack it.

mcqs.q: Aldehydes and ketones undergo nucleophilic addition to C=O because
options: oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so the carbonyl carbon carries a partial positive charge
the C=O bond is non-polar like the C=C bond of alkenes
the carbonyl oxygen carries a partial positive charge
the carbonyl carbon is electron-rich and attracts electrophiles
mcqs.why: Because oxygen is much more electronegative than carbon, the carbonyl carbon is electron-deficient and is attacked by a nucleophile, the pi electrons shifting onto oxygen to form an alkoxide ion.

mcqs.q: Aldehydes are oxidized much more easily than ketones because
options: aldehydes contain more oxygen atoms than ketones
aldehydes have a weaker carbon-carbon bond
the aldehyde carbonyl carbon carries a hydrogen that is converted from C-H to C-OH
mcqs.why: Oxidation of an aldehyde simply converts the carbonyl C-H bond into C-OH, giving an acid with the same carbon number, while a ketone has no such hydrogen and needs C-C bond cleavage.

mcqs.q: Addition of HCN to a carbonyl compound is catalysed by base only because
options: the base protonates the carbonyl oxygen
the base removes H+ from HCN and generates CN- ions, the real nucleophile
HCN is a strong acid full of CN- ions
the base converts HCN into water
mcqs.why: HCN is a very weak acid containing almost no CN- ions; a base generates CN- from HCN, and CN- is the nucleophile that attacks the carbonyl carbon in cyanohydrin formation.

mcqs.q: A Grignard reagent needs no catalyst for addition to a carbonyl group because
options: it is a very weak nucleophile
it reacts only in presence of strong acid
its carbon carries a large partial negative charge and acts as a strong nucleophile (carbanion)
it first converts the ketone into an alkene
mcqs.why: In R-MgX the carbon carries a large partial negative charge and behaves as a carbanion, attacking the electrophilic carbonyl carbon directly and irreversibly without any catalysis.

mcqs.q: Ketones are less reactive than aldehydes towards nucleophiles because of
options: two electron-donating alkyl groups reducing the positive charge on carbon, plus greater steric crowding
the absence of a carbonyl group in ketones
the presence of a hydrogen atom on the ketone carbonyl carbon
mcqs.why: Two alkyl groups donate electrons towards the ketone carbonyl carbon and crowd it sterically, whereas an aldehyde has only one alkyl group and one small hydrogen atom.

mcqs.q: Lower aldehydes and ketones dissolve in water because
options: they contain an acidic hydrogen atom
they form hydrogen bonds among themselves
the carbonyl oxygen accepts hydrogen bonds from water through its lone pairs
mcqs.why: Solubility needs hydrogen bonding with water, not an acidic hydrogen: the lone pairs on the carbonyl oxygen accept hydrogen bonds from water, so members up to about four carbons dissolve well.

mcqs.q: Acetone on oxidation with acidified K2Cr2O7 gives
mcqs.why: A ketone can be oxidized only by cleaving a C-C bond next to the carbonyl group, so three-carbon acetone gives two-carbon acetic acid plus CO2; the acid always has fewer carbons than the ketone.

mcqs.q: Tollen's reagent, used to distinguish aldehydes from ketones, is
options: a solution of bromine in carbon tetrachloride
mcqs.why: Tollen's reagent is ammoniacal silver nitrate; an aldehyde reduces its Ag+ to metallic silver, forming a bright silver mirror, while ketones give no mirror.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • C5H10O has seven carbonyl isomers: four aldehydes and three ketones.
  • The carbonyl group is trigonal planar, with sp2 hybridization, bond angles near 120 degrees and a C=O length of 1.23 Angstrom.
  • In nucleophilic addition the carbonyl carbon changes from sp2 to sp3 and the product is tetrahedral.
  • Cyanohydrins, oximes, imines, hydrazones and acetals are all formed from aldehydes and ketones with HCN, hydroxylamine, amines, hydrazine and alcohols respectively.
  • Grignard reagents give primary alcohols from formaldehyde, secondary alcohols from other aldehydes and tertiary alcohols from ketones.
  • PCC oxidizes a primary alcohol only as far as the aldehyde, while strong oxidants continue to the carboxylic acid.
  • Friedel-Crafts acylation with an acyl chloride and AlCl3 prepares aromatic ketones such as acetophenone.
  • Lower aldehydes and ketones are soluble in water up to about C4, and their boiling points lie between those of alkanes and the corresponding alcohols.

Solved Exercises

Q3. Write detail answers of the following questions

Q: 1(a). Write the structural formulae and give IUPAC names for all possible aldehydes and ketones isomers of the molecular formula C5H10O.

Ans: C5H10O gives four aldehydes and three ketones (seven isomers in total).
Aldehydes: (1) CH3-CH2-CH2-CH2-CHO, pentanal. (2) CH3-CH2-CH(CH3)-CHO, 2-methylbutanal. (3) (CH3)2CH-CH2-CHO, 3-methylbutanal. (4) (CH3)3C-CHO, 2,2-dimethylpropanal.
Ketones: (5) CH3-CO-CH2-CH2-CH3, pentan-2-one. (6) CH3-CH2-CO-CH2-CH3, pentan-3-one. (7) CH3-CO-CH(CH3)-CH3, 3-methylbutan-2-one.
Aldehydes and ketones with the same molecular formula are functional group isomers of each other.

Q: 1(b). Explain the structure and reactivity of carbonyl compounds.

Ans: Structure: In aldehydes and ketones the carbonyl carbon and oxygen are both sp2-hybridized. The C=O bond consists of one sigma bond (sp2-sp2 overlap) and one pi bond (sideways overlap of p orbitals). The carbonyl carbon and the three atoms attached to it lie in one plane with bond angles of about 120 degrees (trigonal planar), and the C=O bond length is 1.23 Angstrom, shorter than a C-O single bond (1.43 Angstrom).
Reactivity: Oxygen is much more electronegative than carbon, so the pi electrons are pulled towards oxygen; the oxygen gets a partial negative charge and the carbon a partial positive charge. The carbonyl group is therefore highly polar and the carbon is electrophilic. Most reactions of aldehydes and ketones are nucleophilic additions across C=O: the nucleophile attacks the carbonyl carbon, the hybridization changes from sp2 to sp3 and the geometry from trigonal planar to tetrahedral, giving an alkoxide ion which is protonated to the addition product. They can also be oxidized (aldehydes easily, ketones with difficulty) and reduced to hydrocarbons or alcohols.

Q: 2(a). Give a reaction for the formation of the following from aldehydes and ketones: i. Cyanohydrin ii. Oxime iii. Imine iv. Hydrazone v. Acetal

Ans: i. Cyanohydrin: addition of HCN in presence of KCN (base). CH3-CHO + H-CN --KCN--> CH3-CH(OH)-CN (acetaldehyde cyanohydrin, 2-hydroxypropanenitrile).
ii. Oxime: reaction with hydroxylamine in acid medium. CH3-CHO + H2N-OH --H+--> CH3-CH=N-OH + H2O (acetaldoxime).
iii. Imine: reaction with ammonia or a primary amine. R-CHO + H2N-R' --H+--> R-CH=N-R' + H2O (an N-substituted imine; with ammonia itself a simple imine is formed).
iv. Hydrazone: reaction with hydrazine. CH3-CO-CH3 + H2N-NH2 --H+--> (CH3)2C=N-NH2 + H2O (acetone hydrazone).
v. Acetal: reaction with excess alcohol in presence of acid catalyst; first a hemiacetal forms, which reacts with a second molecule of alcohol. R-CHO + 2R'-OH --H+--> R-CH(OR')2 + H2O.

Q: 2(b). Using appropriate Grignard reagent and aldehyde or ketone, how each of the following can be prepared? i. butan-1-ol ii. ethyl alcohol iii. butan-2-ol iv. 2-methylbutan-2-ol

Ans: The Grignard reagent adds to the carbonyl carbon and the alkoxide formed is hydrolysed (workup with dilute HCl) to the alcohol. Formaldehyde gives primary alcohols, other aldehydes give secondary alcohols and ketones give tertiary alcohols.
i. butan-1-ol (1 degree alcohol): formaldehyde + propylmagnesium bromide. HCHO + CH3CH2CH2-MgBr -> CH3CH2CH2CH2-O-MgBr --H3O+--> CH3CH2CH2CH2-OH.
ii. ethyl alcohol: formaldehyde + methylmagnesium iodide. HCHO + CH3-MgI -> CH3CH2-O-MgI --H3O+--> CH3CH2-OH.
iii. butan-2-ol (2 degree alcohol): acetaldehyde + ethylmagnesium bromide. CH3-CHO + CH3CH2-MgBr -> CH3-CH(O-MgBr)-CH2CH3 --H3O+--> CH3-CH(OH)-CH2CH3.
iv. 2-methylbutan-2-ol (3 degree alcohol): acetone + ethylmagnesium bromide. CH3-CO-CH3 + CH3CH2-MgBr -> (CH3)2C(O-MgBr)CH2CH3 --H3O+--> (CH3)2C(OH)CH2CH3.

Q: 3(a). Write any three methods for preparation of aldehydes.

Ans: (1) Ozonolysis of alkenes: ozone adds to an alkene to form an unstable ozonide, which is reduced directly by zinc and water to aldehydes (and ketones). For example, but-2-ene gives two molecules of acetaldehyde: CH3-CH=CH-CH3 --1. O3, 2. Zn/H2O--> 2CH3-CHO.
(2) Hydration of acetylene: acetylene adds water in presence of H2SO4 and HgSO4 at 100 degree C to give vinyl alcohol, which rearranges (tautomerizes) to acetaldehyde: HC triple-bond CH + H-OH --H2SO4, HgSO4--> CH2=CH-OH -> CH3-CHO. (Higher alkynes give ketones, so this is specific for acetaldehyde.)
(3) Oxidation of primary alcohols with a mild/controlled oxidizing agent: strong agents like acidified KMnO4 or K2Cr2O7 carry a primary alcohol through the aldehyde to the carboxylic acid, but a good yield of aldehyde is obtained with pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC) in CH2Cl2, which stops the oxidation at the aldehyde stage: R-CH2-OH + [O] --PCC--> R-CHO.

Q: 3(b). How does acetaldehyde react with the following reagents? i. Ethyl magnesium iodide ii. Zinc-mercury amalgam in HCl iii. Lithium aluminium hydride iv. Acidified dichromate

Ans: i. Ethyl magnesium iodide (Grignard reagent): nucleophilic addition gives, after hydrolysis, the secondary alcohol butan-2-ol. CH3-CHO + C2H5-MgI -> CH3-CH(O-MgI)-C2H5 --H3O+--> CH3-CH(OH)-C2H5 (butan-2-ol).
ii. Zinc-mercury amalgam in HCl (Clemmensen reduction): the carbonyl group is reduced to methylene, giving ethane. CH3-CHO --Zn-Hg, conc. HCl--> CH3-CH3 + H2O.
iii. Lithium aluminium hydride: a hydride reducing agent; acetaldehyde is reduced to the primary alcohol ethanol. CH3-CHO --1. LiAlH4, ether, 2. H2O--> CH3-CH2-OH.
iv. Acidified dichromate: a strong oxidizing agent; acetaldehyde is oxidized to acetic acid with the same number of carbon atoms. CH3-CHO + [O] --K2Cr2O7, H2SO4--> CH3-COOH.

Q: 4(a). How aromatic ketones are prepared by Friedel-Craft acylation?

Ans: The introduction of an acyl group (R-CO-) into an aromatic ring in the presence of an acyl halide and anhydrous AlCl3 (a Lewis acid) is called Friedel-Crafts acylation. The acyl chloride first forms an acylium ion with AlCl3, which attacks the benzene ring as an electrophile and replaces a ring hydrogen. For example, benzene reacts with acetyl chloride in presence of AlCl3 to give the aromatic ketone acetophenone: C6H6 + CH3-CO-Cl --AlCl3--> C6H5-CO-CH3 + HCl. In this way aromatic ketones such as acetophenone and benzophenone are prepared.

Q: 4(b). Starting from acetone, how will you prepare each of the following? i. propane ii. propan-2-ol iii. acetone cyanohydrin iv. acetone hydrazone v. acetic acid

Ans: i. Propane: Clemmensen reduction reduces the carbonyl group of acetone to methylene. CH3-CO-CH3 --Zn-Hg, conc. HCl--> CH3-CH2-CH3 + H2O. (Wolff-Kishner reduction with NH2NH2/KOH also gives propane.)
ii. Propan-2-ol: reduction with LiAlH4 or NaBH4, or catalytic hydrogenation (H2/Ni), converts the ketone into the secondary alcohol. CH3-CO-CH3 --LiAlH4, then H2O--> CH3-CH(OH)-CH3.
iii. Acetone cyanohydrin: addition of HCN in presence of KCN. CH3-CO-CH3 + H-CN --KCN--> (CH3)2C(OH)-CN (2-hydroxy-2-methylpropanenitrile).
iv. Acetone hydrazone: reaction with hydrazine in acid medium with loss of water. CH3-CO-CH3 + H2N-NH2 -> (CH3)2C=N-NH2 + H2O.
v. Acetic acid: oxidation with a strong oxidizing agent breaks a C-C bond next to the carbonyl group. CH3-CO-CH3 + 4[O] --K2Cr2O7, H2SO4--> CH3-COOH + CO2 + H2O.

Q: 5(a). Explain the acid and base-catalysed mechanism of nucleophilic addition to carbonyl group.

Ans: Base-catalysed addition: this takes place with a strong nucleophile. The base reacts with the reagent H-Nu and generates the nucleophile Nu-. The nucleophile attacks the carbonyl carbon, the pi electrons of C=O move onto oxygen and an alkoxide ion is formed. The alkoxide then abstracts a proton from H-Nu, giving the addition product and regenerating Nu-, so the base acts as a catalyst and increases the nucleophilic character of the reagent. Example: addition of HCN (KCN) to form cyanohydrins.
Acid-catalysed addition: carbonyl compounds are weak Lewis bases and are protonated on oxygen to form an oxonium ion, >C=OH+. Protonation increases the positive (electrophilic) character of the carbonyl carbon, so even a weak nucleophile (water, alcohol, ammonia derivatives) can attack it. The addition product then loses a proton to give the neutral product and regenerate the acid. Addition of water, alcohols, ammonia and its derivatives generally follows this acid-catalysed mechanism.

Q: 5(b). Discuss the physical properties of aldehydes and ketones.

Ans: (1) State and odour: formaldehyde is a gas at room temperature; acetaldehyde and the other lower members are colourless volatile liquids, and higher members are also colourless liquids with characteristic odour. Lower aldehydes like formaldehyde and acetaldehyde have a very sharp pungent odour, whereas higher aldehydes and most ketones have a pleasant odour. Formaldehyde is stored and used as its 40% aqueous solution, formalin; acetone, the simplest ketone, is a liquid (bp 56 degree C).
(2) Solubility: lower aldehydes and ketones (up to C4) are soluble in water because the carbonyl oxygen forms hydrogen bonds with water; solubility decreases as the size of the non-polar alkyl group increases, and higher members are insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents.
(3) Polarity and boiling points: aldehydes and ketones are polar compounds due to the high dipole moment of C=O, so their boiling points are higher than those of the corresponding alkanes and non-polar compounds like ethers, but lower than those of the corresponding alcohols, because they cannot form hydrogen bonds with each other (there is no hydrogen on the carbonyl oxygen). Boiling points increase with molecular mass, e.g. methanal boils at -21 degree C and ethanal at 21 degree C.

Q: 5(c). Write the systematic names for the following organic compounds: i. CH3-C(=O)-CH=CH-CH3 ii. CH3-CH2-C(=O)-CH(CH3)-CH(CH3)-CH3 iii. H-C(=O)-CH(CH3)-CH(CH3)-CH3 iv. H-C(=O)-CH(CH3)-CH(Br)-C(=O)-H v. H-C(=O)-C(CH3)=CH-C(=O)-H

Ans: i. pent-3-en-2-one. ii. 4,5-dimethylhexan-3-one. iii. 2,3-dimethylbutanal. iv. 3-bromo-2-methylbutanedial. v. 2-methylbut-2-enedial.

Q: 5(d). Draw the structural formulae for the following organic compounds: i. 2,4-dimethylpent-2-enal ii. 2,2-dimethylbutanal iii. 3,3-dimethylhex-4-en-2-one iv. 4-methylhex-5-en-3-one v. pent-4-yn-2-one

Ans: i. 2,4-dimethylpent-2-enal: OHC-C(CH3)=CH-CH(CH3)-CH3, the chain being numbered from the -CHO carbon (C-1), with a methyl group on C-2 and on C-4 and the double bond between C-2 and C-3.
ii. 2,2-dimethylbutanal: OHC-C(CH3)2-CH2-CH3, i.e. the C-2 next to the -CHO group carries two methyl groups.
iii. 3,3-dimethylhex-4-en-2-one: CH3-C(=O)-C(CH3)2-CH=CH-CH3.
iv. 4-methylhex-5-en-3-one: CH2=CH-CH(CH3)-C(=O)-CH2-CH3, with the carbonyl carbon numbered 3 from the end nearer to it.
v. pent-4-yn-2-one: HC triple-bond C-CH2-C(=O)-CH3.

mcqs.q: How many aldehyde and ketone isomers in total have the molecular formula C5H10O?
mcqs.why: C5H10O has four aldehydes (pentanal, 2-methylbutanal, 3-methylbutanal and 2,2-dimethylpropanal) and three ketones, making seven functional-group isomers in total.

mcqs.q: The geometry of the carbonyl group in aldehydes and ketones is
options: tetrahedral with bond angles of 109.5 degrees
linear with bond angles of 180 degrees
trigonal planar with bond angles of about 120 degrees
square planar with bond angles of 90 degrees
mcqs.why: The carbonyl carbon and oxygen are both sp2-hybridized, so the carbonyl carbon and the three atoms attached to it lie in one plane with bond angles of about 120 degrees.

mcqs.q: The length of the C=O bond in carbonyl compounds is
mcqs.why: The C=O double bond is 1.23 Angstrom long, distinctly shorter than a C-O single bond, which is 1.43 Angstrom long.

mcqs.q: During nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl group, the carbonyl carbon changes from
options: sp2 to sp3 hybridization, and the geometry becomes tetrahedral
mcqs.why: The nucleophile adds to the planar sp2 carbonyl carbon, so the hybridization changes from sp2 to sp3 and the geometry changes from trigonal planar to tetrahedral in the addition product.

mcqs.q: Acetaldehyde cyanohydrin, formed by addition of HCN to acetaldehyde in presence of KCN, is systematically named
mcqs.why: CH3-CH(OH)-CN has a three-carbon chain including the nitrile carbon, with the hydroxyl group on carbon 2, so it is 2-hydroxypropanenitrile.
