options: a primary amine in acid medium
excess alcohol in presence of acid
mcqs.why: Reaction with hydroxylamine, H2N-OH, replaces the carbonyl oxygen by =N-OH with loss of water, giving an oxime such as acetaldoxime from acetaldehyde.

mcqs.q: Acetone hydrazone is the product of acetone reacting with
options: hydrazine, with loss of a water molecule
mcqs.why: Acetone reacts with hydrazine, H2N-NH2, in acid medium to give (CH3)2C=N-NH2, acetone hydrazone, plus water.

mcqs.q: Formaldehyde on reaction with a Grignard reagent followed by hydrolysis always gives
mcqs.why: Formaldehyde has two hydrogens on the carbonyl carbon, so Grignard addition and hydrolysis give primary alcohols; other aldehydes give secondary and ketones give tertiary alcohols.

mcqs.q: 2-Methylbutan-2-ol, a tertiary alcohol, is prepared from
mcqs.why: A ketone gives a tertiary alcohol with a Grignard reagent: acetone plus ethylmagnesium bromide, on hydrolysis, gives (CH3)2C(OH)CH2CH3, which is 2-methylbutan-2-ol.

mcqs.q: Ozonolysis of but-2-ene with Zn/H2O work-up gives
mcqs.why: Cleavage of the symmetrical double bond of but-2-ene at the middle gives two identical two-carbon fragments, both acetaldehyde.

mcqs.q: Pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC) is used to oxidize a primary alcohol because it
options: oxidizes it directly to the carboxylic acid
stops the oxidation at the aldehyde stage
mcqs.why: Strong oxidants carry a primary alcohol through the aldehyde to the acid, but PCC in CH2Cl2 stops at the aldehyde, giving a good yield of R-CHO.

mcqs.q: Benzene reacts with acetyl chloride in presence of anhydrous AlCl3 to give
mcqs.why: Friedel-Crafts acylation introduces the acetyl group onto the ring through an acylium ion, giving the aromatic ketone acetophenone, C6H5-CO-CH3.

mcqs.q: Clemmensen reduction of acetone gives
mcqs.why: Zinc-mercury amalgam in concentrated HCl reduces the carbonyl group of acetone to a methylene group, giving propane; Wolff-Kishner reduction gives the same product.

mcqs.q: The systematic name of CH3-C(=O)-CH=CH-CH3 is
mcqs.why: The five-carbon chain is numbered to give the carbonyl carbon the lowest locant, 2, and the double bond then falls at carbon 3, giving pent-3-en-2-one.

mcqs.q: The boiling points of aldehydes and ketones are lower than those of the corresponding alcohols because
options: they have smaller molecular masses than the alcohols
they cannot form hydrogen bonds with each other, having no hydrogen on the carbonyl oxygen
mcqs.why: Aldehydes and ketones are polar and boil higher than alkanes and ethers, but with no hydrogen attached to oxygen they cannot hydrogen-bond to each other, so they boil lower than alcohols.

lessons.title: Project
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Tollen's reagent is prepared by adding NH4OH to silver nitrate until the brown silver(I) oxide precipitate just dissolves, giving the clear diamminesilver(I) complex.
  • Glucose contains an aldehyde group, so it reduces Ag+ of Tollen's reagent to metallic silver.
  • The metallic silver deposits as a bright mirror on the inner wall of the flask, which is the positive test for an aldehyde.
  • Ketones do not reduce Tollen's reagent and give no mirror, so the test identifies aldehydes and distinguishes them from ketones.

Solved Exercises

Project

Q: Identify aldehydes and ketones in the laboratory tests. Add 50 mL of 0.1 M AgNO3 to the beaker and add NH4OH to this. A brown precipitate will form. Continue adding NH4OH until the solution becomes clear. To this, add 25 mL of 0.8 M KOH. Again, add NH4OH until solution becomes clear. To perform demonstration, add 5 mL of glucose solution to a flask (or test tube) and to this add 25 mL of Tollen's reagent. Stopper the flask and swirl the solution so that the whole of the inner surface of the flask is wetted. The solution will turn yellow and brown then become cloudy and dark before silver begins to form on the inside of the flask. This should take a couple of minutes. When a satisfactory mirror has formed, rinse the flask and analyse the silver mirror.

Ans: The reagent prepared is Tollen's reagent, ammoniacal silver nitrate [Ag(NH3)2]OH; the brown precipitate first formed is silver(I) oxide, which dissolves in excess NH4OH to give the clear diamminesilver(I) complex. Glucose contains an aldehyde group (-CHO), so it reduces Ag+ to metallic silver while itself being oxidized to the carboxylate (gluconate) ion. The metallic silver deposits uniformly on the inner wall of the flask as a bright silver mirror. Formation of the silver mirror is the positive test for an aldehyde; ketones do not reduce Tollen's reagent and give no mirror, which is how aldehydes are identified and distinguished from ketones in the laboratory.

chapters.title: Unit 20: Carbonyl Compounds 2: Carboxylic Acids and Functional Derivatives

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • C6H5COOH, benzoic acid, is the formula of an aromatic carboxylic acid.
  • The acid found in rancid butter is butyric acid, C4H8O2.
  • Acetic acid has the highest boiling point among acetic acid, water, ethyl alcohol and diethyl ether.
  • The carbon atom of methanol is not sp2-hybridized; it is sp3-hybridized.
  • Fluoroacetic acid is the strongest acid among ethanol, acetic acid, chloroacetic acid and fluoroacetic acid.
  • Acetic acid can be prepared by the hydrolysis of methyl cyanide.
  • Acyl chloride is prepared from a carboxylic acid with thionyl chloride.
  • Hydrolysis is the one common reaction that converts all acid derivatives back into the corresponding acid.

Solved Exercises

Q1. Choose the correct one from the given options

Q: 1. Which of the following represents the formula of an aromatic carboxylic acids?

Options: (a) HCOOH (b) C6H5OH (c) C6H5COOH (d) C6H5CH2OH

Correct answer: C6H5COOH

Q: 2. Which of the following acids is found in rancid butter?

Options: (a) C2H4O2 (b) C3H6O2 (c) C4H8O2 (d) C5H10O2

Correct answer: C4H8O2

Q: 3. The compound with highest boiling point is

Options: (a) acetic acid. (b) water. (c) ethyl alcohol. (d) diethyl ether.

Correct answer: acetic acid.

Q: 4. In which of the following compounds, the carbon atom does not show sp2-hybridization?

Options: (a) Methanal (b) Methanol (c) Methanoic acid (d) Acetone

Correct answer: Methanol

Q: 5. Which is the strongest acid?

Options: (a) Ethanol (b) Acetic acid (c) Chloroacetic acid (d) Fluoroacetic acid

Correct answer: Fluoroacetic acid

Q: 6. Acetic acid can be prepared by the hydrolysis of

Options: (a) methyl cyanide. (b) methylmagnesium chloride. (c) ethanal. (d) ethanol.

Correct answer: methyl cyanide.

Q: 7. Fischer esterification is the reaction between

Options: (a) an acid and ester. (b) an acid and alcohol. (c) an acid halide and ester. (d) an ester and sodium hydroxide.

Correct answer: an acid and alcohol.

Q: 8. Acyl chloride can be prepared by the reaction of a carboxylic acid with

Options: (a) phosphorous pentoxide. (b) soda lime. (c) hydrochloric acid. (d) thionyl chloride.

Correct answer: thionyl chloride.

Q: 9. The hydrolysis of an ester in presence of alkali is known as

Options: (a) saponification. (b) decarboxylation. (c) esterification. (d) transesterification.

Correct answer: saponification.

Q: 10. All the acid derivatives can be converted back into the corresponding acid by one common reaction.

Options: (a) ammonolysis (b) alcoholysis (c) reduction (d) hydrolysis

Correct answer: hydrolysis

mcqs.q: Which of the following represents the formula of an aromatic carboxylic acids?
mcqs.why: C6H5COOH is benzoic acid, a carboxylic acid with the -COOH group attached directly to a benzene ring; C6H5OH is phenol and C6H5CH2OH is an alcohol.

mcqs.q: Which of the following acids is found in rancid butter?
mcqs.why: The acid present in rancid butter is butyric (butanoic) acid, a four-carbon carboxylic acid with molecular formula C4H8O2.

mcqs.q: The compound with highest boiling point is
mcqs.why: Acetic acid boils at 118 degree C because its molecules form strong hydrogen-bonded cyclic dimers, higher than water, ethanol and diethyl ether.

mcqs.q: In which of the following compounds, the carbon atom does not show sp2-hybridization?
mcqs.why: In methanol the carbon is bonded to four atoms by single bonds and is sp3-hybridized, while the carbonyl carbons of methanal, methanoic acid and acetone are sp2.

mcqs.q: Which is the strongest acid?
mcqs.why: Fluorine is the most electronegative halogen, so its -I effect stabilizes the carboxylate ion most strongly, making fluoroacetic acid the strongest of these acids.

mcqs.q: Acetic acid can be prepared by the hydrolysis of
mcqs.why: Hydrolysis of methyl cyanide (ethanenitrile) with aqueous acid or base on heating passes through acetamide and gives acetic acid.

mcqs.q: Fischer esterification is the reaction between
mcqs.why: Fischer esterification is the reaction of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol in presence of concentrated sulphuric acid to form an ester and water.

mcqs.q: Acyl chloride can be prepared by the reaction of a carboxylic acid with
mcqs.why: Thionyl chloride replaces the -OH group of a carboxylic acid by -Cl, giving the acyl chloride along with SO2 and HCl.

mcqs.q: The hydrolysis of an ester in presence of alkali is known as
mcqs.why: Hydrolysis of an ester with an alkali gives an alcohol and the salt of the carboxylic acid, the soap-making reaction called saponification.

mcqs.q: All the acid derivatives can be converted back into the corresponding acid by one common reaction.
mcqs.why: All acid derivatives - acyl halides, anhydrides, esters, amides and nitriles - are converted back into the corresponding carboxylic acid by hydrolysis.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Pure acetic acid freezes near 17 degree C into ice-like crystals, so it is called glacial acetic acid.
  • Carboxylic acids form cyclic dimers through two hydrogen bonds, so they boil higher than the corresponding alcohols.
  • The carboxylate ion is resonance-stabilized over two oxygen atoms, making carboxylic acids stronger than phenols, alcohols and water.
  • Electron-withdrawing groups such as chlorine increase acid strength, while electron-donating alkyl groups decrease it.
  • Carboxylic acids react with nucleophiles only by nucleophilic acyl substitution, because resonance lowers the positive charge on the carboxyl carbon.
  • The reactivity order of acid derivatives is acyl halides, then anhydrides, then esters, then amides.
  • Alkaline hydrolysis of an ester is called saponification because it is the reaction used to make soap from fats and oils.

Solved Exercises

Q2. Write short answers of the following questions

Q: i. Why anhydrous acetic acid is known as glacial acetic acid?

Ans: Pure (anhydrous) acetic acid freezes at about 17 degree C into a colourless, ice-like crystalline solid. Because it looks like ice (a glacier), it is called glacial acetic acid. Ordinary acetic acid contains water and does not freeze in this way.

Q: ii. The boiling points of carboxylic acids are higher than corresponding alcohols. Explain briefly.

Ans: Carboxylic acids form very strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds and exist largely as cyclic dimers, in which two molecules are held together by two hydrogen bonds. The effective molecular mass is thus doubled and much more heat is needed to break these bonds. Alcohols form weaker, single hydrogen-bonded aggregates, so carboxylic acids boil higher than alcohols of comparable molecular mass, e.g. acetic acid boils at 118 degree C while ethanol boils at 78 degree C.

Q: iii. How carboxylic acids are stronger acids than phenol, alcohols and water?

Ans: A carboxylic acid ionizes to give a carboxylate ion, R-COO-, which is stabilized by resonance: the negative charge is delocalized equally over two oxygen atoms (the ion is a resonance hybrid of two equivalent forms). In an alcohol, the alkoxide ion formed on ionization has its negative charge localized on one oxygen and is not stabilized, so alcohols hardly ionize (Ka of ethanol = 10^-16, against Ka of acetic acid = 1.8 x 10^-5). Phenoxide ion is resonance stabilized too, but less effectively than carboxylate, and water's hydroxide ion is not resonance stabilized. Hence carboxylic acids are much stronger acids than phenols, alcohols and water.

Q: iv. Why methanoic acid is stronger acid than ethanoic acid?

Ans: In ethanoic (acetic) acid the -CH3 group is an electron-donating group (+I effect). It pushes electron density towards the carboxylate carbon, increases the negative charge on the acetate ion and destabilizes it, so the acid ionizes less (pKa = 4.76). Methanoic (formic) acid has only a hydrogen atom attached to the carboxyl carbon and no electron-donating alkyl group, so the formate ion is comparatively more stable and the acid ionizes more (pKa = 3.68). Therefore methanoic acid is stronger than ethanoic acid.

Q: v. Chloroacetic acid is a derivative of acetic acid. Why chloroacetic acid is stronger acid than acetic acid?

Ans: Chlorine is a strongly electron-withdrawing substituent (-I effect). It pulls electron density away from the carboxyl group and disperses the negative charge of the chloroacetate ion formed on ionization, thus stabilizing the conjugate base and promoting dissociation of the acid. Acetic acid has instead an electron-donating -CH3 group, which destabilizes its anion. Hence chloroacetic acid (pKa = 2.86) is much stronger than acetic acid (pKa = 4.76).

Q: vi. How carboxylic acids can be obtained readily by the oxidation of primary alcohols?

Ans: A primary alcohol is oxidized by a strong oxidizing agent such as acidified potassium permanganate or acidified potassium dichromate, first to the aldehyde and then, with the same number of carbon atoms, to the carboxylic acid: R-CH2-OH --[O]--> R-CHO --[O]--> R-COOH. For example, ethanol is oxidized through acetaldehyde to acetic acid: C2H5-OH + 2[O] --K2Cr2O7, H2SO4--> CH3-COOH + H2O. The reaction is carried out under reflux so that the intermediate aldehyde is not distilled off before further oxidation.

Q: vii. Carboxylic acids are less reactive towards nucleophile, compared to aldehydes. Why?

Ans: Although the carboxyl group contains a carbonyl group, its carbon is much less electrophilic than the carbonyl carbon of an aldehyde. One lone pair of the hydroxyl oxygen is delocalized into the carbonyl group by resonance, which reduces the partial positive charge on the carboxyl carbon. As a result, a nucleophile cannot simply add to the C=O of a carboxylic acid as it does in aldehydes; carboxylic acids react with nucleophiles only by nucleophilic acyl substitution, in which the -OH group is replaced, and this is comparatively slow.

Q: viii. Why amides are the least reactive derivatives of carboxylic acid, towards nucleophile?

Ans: In an amide the lone pair of the nitrogen atom is strongly delocalized into the carbonyl group by resonance, so the carbonyl carbon has the least positive character among all acid derivatives and is least attractive for a nucleophile. In addition, -NH2 is a very poor leaving group (it would have to leave as the strong base NH2-). Both factors make amides the least reactive derivatives; their hydrolysis needs strong acid or base, heat and a long time. The reactivity order is: acyl halides > acid anhydrides > esters > amides.

Q: ix. Esters can be hydrolysed in both acidic and basic conditions. Why base hydrolysis of esters is also called saponification?

Ans: Saponification literally means soap-making. When an ester is hydrolysed with an alkali such as NaOH, the products are an alcohol and the sodium salt of the carboxylic acid, and the reaction is irreversible because the acid is removed as its salt. This is exactly the reaction used to make soap: fats and oils (glyceryl esters of long-chain fatty acids) on boiling with NaOH give glycerol and sodium salts of the fatty acids, which are soaps. Because of this use, alkaline hydrolysis of esters in general is called saponification.

Q: x. Acid halides are the most reactive of all acid derivatives towards nucleophiles. Explain briefly.

Ans: Two reasons make acyl halides the most reactive. (1) The halogen is strongly electron-withdrawing (-I effect), so the carbonyl carbon of an acyl halide carries the largest partial positive charge and is most strongly attacked by nucleophiles; the lone pairs of chlorine are poorly delocalized into the carbonyl group, so this positive character is not neutralized. (2) The halide ion (e.g. Cl-) is an excellent leaving group, being a very weak base, so the substitution step is fast. Hence acyl halides react vigorously even with weak nucleophiles like water, and they are used to prepare the other derivatives.

mcqs.q: Pure acetic acid is called glacial acetic acid because it
options: freezes at about 17 degree C into an ice-like crystalline solid
is always sold as a gas
mcqs.why: Anhydrous acetic acid freezes at about 17 degree C into a colourless, ice-like crystalline solid that looks like a glacier, hence the name glacial acetic acid.

mcqs.q: Carboxylic acids boil higher than the corresponding alcohols because they
options: have no hydrogen bonds at all
exist largely as cyclic dimers held together by two hydrogen bonds
mcqs.why: Two carboxylic acid molecules form a cyclic dimer through two strong hydrogen bonds, doubling the effective molecular mass; acetic acid boils at 118 degree C against 78 degree C for ethanol.

mcqs.q: A carboxylic acid is a much stronger acid than an alcohol because
options: the carboxylate ion is resonance-stabilized, its negative charge delocalized over two oxygen atoms
the alkoxide ion is resonance-stabilized over two oxygens
carboxylic acids contain two carbon atoms
alcohols cannot form any ions at all
mcqs.why: The carboxylate ion is a resonance hybrid of two equivalent forms with the charge spread over both oxygens, while an alkoxide ion has its charge localized on one oxygen; acetic acid has Ka 1.8 x 10^-5 against 10^-16 for ethanol.

mcqs.q: The pKa of methanoic (formic) acid, which is a stronger acid than ethanoic acid, is
mcqs.why: Formic acid has no electron-donating methyl group to destabilize its anion, so it ionizes more than acetic acid: its pKa is 3.68, against 4.76 for ethanoic acid.

mcqs.q: Chloroacetic acid is stronger than acetic acid because chlorine
options: donates electrons towards the carboxyl group (+I effect)
withdraws electrons (-I effect) and disperses the negative charge of the chloroacetate ion
adds a second carboxyl group to the molecule
removes the hydroxyl group of the acid
mcqs.why: The electron-withdrawing chlorine stabilizes the conjugate base by dispersing its negative charge, so chloroacetic acid has pKa 2.86 compared with 4.76 for acetic acid.

mcqs.q: Ethanol is converted into acetic acid by
options: oxidation with acidified K2Cr2O7 under reflux, through acetaldehyde
mcqs.why: A strong oxidizing agent oxidizes a primary alcohol first to the aldehyde and then to the acid with the same carbon number; reflux keeps the intermediate acetaldehyde in the flask until it is fully oxidized.

mcqs.q: Carboxylic acids are less reactive than aldehydes towards nucleophiles because
options: a lone pair of the hydroxyl oxygen is delocalized into the carbonyl group, reducing the positive charge on the carboxyl carbon
the carboxyl carbon carries a full positive charge
carboxylic acids contain no carbonyl group
nucleophiles add to carboxylic acids faster than to aldehydes
mcqs.why: Resonance donation from the -OH oxygen into the C=O lowers the electrophilicity of the carboxyl carbon, so acids react only by slower nucleophilic acyl substitution, not by simple addition.

mcqs.q: Amides are the least reactive carboxylic acid derivatives towards nucleophiles because
options: the nitrogen lone pair is not delocalized at all
the halide ion is their leaving group
the nitrogen lone pair is strongly delocalized into the carbonyl group and -NH2 is a very poor leaving group
mcqs.why: Strong resonance from nitrogen gives the amide carbonyl carbon the least positive character of all derivatives, and NH2- would be a very poor leaving group, so amide hydrolysis needs strong acid or base, heat and time.

mcqs.q: Alkaline hydrolysis of an ester (saponification) gives
options: an alcohol and the sodium salt of the carboxylic acid
mcqs.why: With NaOH the ester gives an alcohol plus the sodium carboxylate; applied to fats and oils this gives glycerol and sodium salts of fatty acids, which are soaps - hence the name saponification.

mcqs.q: The correct order of reactivity of acid derivatives towards nucleophiles is
options: acyl halides > acid anhydrides > esters > amides
mcqs.why: Acyl halides have the most electrophilic carbonyl carbon and the best leaving group, while amides are the least reactive, giving the order acyl halides, anhydrides, esters, then amides.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Acetic acid has Ka = 1.8 x 10^-5 (pKa 4.76), far larger than ethanol's Ka of 10^-16, because the carboxylate ion is resonance-stabilized.
  • Acid strength rises with more, stronger and closer electron-withdrawing groups: trichloroacetic acid has pKa 0.65.
  • Acetic acid can be prepared by hydrolysing a nitrile, carbonating a Grignard reagent, or oxidizing an alcohol, an aldehyde or an acid halide route.
  • Carbonation of a Grignard reagent gives a carboxylic acid with one carbon more than the Grignard reagent.
  • From acetic acid, thionyl chloride gives acetyl chloride, P2O5 gives acetic anhydride, ammonia and heat give acetamide, and ethanol with concentrated H2SO4 gives ethyl acetate.
  • LiAlH4 reduces an ester to two alcohols and an amide to a primary amine.
  • Heating a sodium carboxylate with soda lime decarboxylates it to an alkane with one carbon less.

Solved Exercises

Q3. Write detail answers of the following questions

Q: 1. Explain the acidity of carboxylic acids. How their acid strength is affected by electron donating and withdrawing substitutions?

Ans: Carboxylic acids ionize in water to give a carboxylate ion and a hydronium ion: R-COOH + H2O <-> R-COO- + H3O+. Acetic acid has Ka = 1.8 x 10^-5 (pKa = 4.76), while ethanol has Ka = 10^-16 (pKa = 16), so carboxylic acids are far stronger acids than alcohols. The reason is the resonance stabilization of the carboxylate ion: it is a resonance hybrid of two equivalent canonical forms, and the negative charge is delocalized over both oxygen atoms instead of remaining localized on one oxygen, as in an alkoxide ion.
Effect of substituents: any substituent that stabilizes the carboxylate ion increases the acid strength, and any that destabilizes it decreases the strength. Electron-withdrawing groups (e.g. -X, -NO2) pull electron density away, disperse the negative charge of the anion and increase acidity; the effect is larger when there are more such groups, when the group is more strongly withdrawing, and when it is closer to the -COOH group. Thus pKa values decrease in the order: propionic acid 4.87, acetic acid 4.76, bromoacetic acid 2.90, chloroacetic acid 2.86, fluoroacetic acid 2.59, dichloroacetic acid 1.29, trichloroacetic acid 0.65. Electron-donating groups (alkyl groups) push electron density towards the anion, destabilize it and decrease acidity, e.g. propionic acid (4.87) is weaker than acetic acid (4.76), which is weaker than formic acid (3.68).

Q: 2. How will you prepare acetic acid by using: i. a nitrile ii. a Grignard reagent iii. an alcohol iv. an aldehyde v. an acid halide

Ans: i. From a nitrile: hydrolysis of methyl cyanide (ethanenitrile) with aqueous acid or base on heating gives acetic acid, through acetamide as intermediate. CH3-C triple-bond N + 2H2O --H+ or OH-, heat--> CH3-COOH + NH3.
ii. From a Grignard reagent (carbonation): methylmagnesium bromide is treated with carbon dioxide in dry ether and the addition product is hydrolysed. CH3-MgBr + CO2 --dry ether--> CH3-C(=O)-O-MgBr --H3O+--> CH3-COOH. The acid obtained has one carbon more than the Grignard reagent.
iii. From an alcohol: oxidation of ethanol with a strong oxidizing agent (acidified K2Cr2O7 or KMnO4). C2H5-OH + 2[O] -> CH3-COOH + H2O.
iv. From an aldehyde: oxidation of acetaldehyde with an oxidizing agent. CH3-CHO + [O] --K2Cr2O7, H2SO4--> CH3-COOH.
v. From an acid halide: hydrolysis of acetyl chloride with water. CH3-CO-Cl + H-OH -> CH3-COOH + HCl.

Q: 3. Starting from acetic acid, how will you prepare each of the following? i. acetyl chloride ii. acetic anhydride iii. acetamide iv. ethyl acetate v. ethyl alcohol

Ans: i. Acetyl chloride: replace the -OH of acetic acid by -Cl using thionyl chloride (or PCl5). CH3-COOH + SOCl2 -> CH3-CO-Cl + SO2 + HCl.
ii. Acetic anhydride: dehydrate two molecules of acetic acid with a strong dehydrating agent such as phosphorus pentaoxide (P2O5) on heating. 2CH3-COOH --P2O5, heat--> (CH3-C(=O))-O-(C(=O)-CH3) + H2O.
iii. Acetamide: treat acetic acid with ammonia to form ammonium acetate, then heat it; loss of water gives the amide. CH3-COOH + NH3 -> CH3-COO-NH4+ --heat--> CH3-CO-NH2 + H2O.
iv. Ethyl acetate: Fischer esterification - heat acetic acid with ethanol in presence of concentrated H2SO4. CH3-COOH + C2H5-OH <-> CH3-COO-C2H5 + H2O.
v. Ethyl alcohol: reduce acetic acid with lithium aluminium hydride in ether, followed by hydrolysis. CH3-COOH --1. LiAlH4, ether, 2. H2O--> CH3-CH2-OH.

Q: 4. Write an equation for: i. Hydrolysis of acetyl chloride ii. Reaction of benzoyl chloride with methanol iii. Esterification of butan-1-ol with acetic anhydride iv. Ammonolysis of butanoyl chloride v. Fischer esterification of pentanoic acid with ethanol

Ans: i. Hydrolysis of acetyl chloride: CH3-CO-Cl + H-OH -> CH3-COOH + HCl.
ii. Benzoyl chloride with methanol: C6H5-CO-Cl + CH3-OH -> C6H5-COO-CH3 (methyl benzoate) + HCl. (The reaction is carried out in presence of pyridine, which absorbs the HCl.)
iii. Esterification of butan-1-ol with acetic anhydride: CH3CH2CH2CH2-OH + (CH3-C(=O))-O-(C(=O)-CH3) -> CH3-COO-CH2CH2CH2CH3 (butyl acetate) + CH3-COOH.
iv. Ammonolysis of butanoyl chloride: CH3CH2CH2-CO-Cl + 2NH3 -> CH3CH2CH2-CO-NH2 (butanamide) + NH4Cl.
v. Fischer esterification of pentanoic acid with ethanol: CH3CH2CH2CH2-COOH + C2H5-OH --conc. H2SO4, heat--> CH3CH2CH2CH2-COO-C2H5 (ethyl pentanoate) + H2O.

Q: 5(a). Describe three methods for preparation of carboxylic acids.

Ans: (1) Carbonation (carboxylation) of Grignard reagent: an alkyl or aryl magnesium halide reacts with carbon dioxide in dry ether to give an addition product, which on acid workup yields a carboxylic acid having one carbon atom more than the Grignard reagent. R-MgX + CO2 --dry ether--> R-C(=O)-O-MgX --H3O+--> R-COOH.
(2) Hydrolysis of nitriles: alkyl nitriles (alkyl cyanides) are hydrolysed by aqueous acid or base on heating, through an amide intermediate, to carboxylic acids. In base the product is actually the salt of the acid. R-C triple-bond N + 2H2O --H+ or OH-, heat--> R-COOH + NH3; e.g. ethanenitrile gives acetic acid.
(3) Oxidation of primary alcohols: strong oxidizing agents like acidified KMnO4 or K2Cr2O7 oxidize a primary alcohol first to an aldehyde and then to the carboxylic acid with the same number of carbon atoms. R-CH2-OH --[O]--> R-CHO --[O]--> R-COOH; e.g. ethanol gives acetic acid. (Aldehydes are likewise oxidized to acids, and alkyl benzenes are oxidized to benzoic acid.)

Q: 5(b). Write the systematic names for the following organic compounds: i. HO-C(=O)-CH(CH3)-CH2-C(=O)-OH ii. CH3-CH2-CH(CH3)-CH2-C(=O)-OH iii. CH3-CH2-CH(CH3)-CH2-C(=O)-OC2H5 iv. H2C=CH-CH2-CH2-C(=O)-NH2 v. HC triple-bond C-CH2-CH2-C(=O)-OH

Ans: i. 2-methylbutanedioic acid. ii. 3-methylpentanoic acid. iii. ethyl 3-methylpentanoate. iv. pent-4-enamide. v. pent-4-ynoic acid.

Q: 5(c). Draw the structural formula of the following organic compounds: i. 3-ethyl-4-methylpentanoic acid ii. ethyl 3-methylbutanoate iii. 2-chloropropanoyl bromide iv. ethanoic propanoic anhydride v. 3,3-dimethylbutanenitrile

Ans: i. 3-ethyl-4-methylpentanoic acid: HO-C(=O)-CH2-CH(C2H5)-CH(CH3)-CH3, the carboxyl carbon being C-1, an ethyl group on C-3 and a methyl group on C-4.
ii. ethyl 3-methylbutanoate: (CH3)2CH-CH2-C(=O)-O-C2H5.
iii. 2-chloropropanoyl bromide: CH3-CH(Cl)-C(=O)-Br.
iv. ethanoic propanoic anhydride: CH3-C(=O)-O-C(=O)-CH2-CH3, formed from one molecule each of ethanoic acid and propanoic acid with loss of water.
v. 3,3-dimethylbutanenitrile: (CH3)3C-CH2-C triple-bond N, the nitrile carbon being C-1 and C-3 carrying two methyl groups.

Q: 5(d). Complete the following reactions: i. CH3CH2CH2COOH + PCl5 -> ii. CH3CH2COOH + SOCl2 -> iii. CH3CH2CONH2 + LiAlH4 -> iv. CH3COOCOCH3 + NH3 -> v. CH3CH2COOCH3 + NaOH -> vi. CH3CH2COONa + NaOH --CaO--> vii. CH3CH2COOC2H5 + LiAlH4 -> viii. CH3CH2MgBr + CH3CH2CN ->

Ans: i. CH3CH2CH2-COOH + PCl5 -> CH3CH2CH2-CO-Cl (butanoyl chloride) + POCl3 + HCl.
ii. CH3CH2-COOH + SOCl2 -> CH3CH2-CO-Cl (propanoyl chloride) + SO2 + HCl.
iii. CH3CH2-CO-NH2 --LiAlH4, then H2O--> CH3CH2-CH2-NH2 (propan-1-amine); the amide is reduced to the primary amine.
iv. (CH3-C(=O))-O-(C(=O)-CH3) + NH3 -> CH3-CO-NH2 (acetamide/ethanamide) + CH3-COOH (ammonolysis of the anhydride).
v. CH3CH2-COO-CH3 + NaOH -> CH3CH2-COO-Na+ (sodium propanoate) + CH3-OH (saponification).
vi. CH3CH2-COO-Na+ + NaOH --CaO, heat--> CH3-CH3 (ethane) + Na2CO3 (decarboxylation; the alkane has one carbon less than the acid).
vii. CH3CH2-COO-C2H5 --LiAlH4, then H2O--> CH3CH2-CH2-OH (propan-1-ol) + C2H5-OH; the ester is reduced to two alcohols.
viii. CH3CH2-MgBr + CH3CH2-C triple-bond N -> imine salt --H3O+--> CH3CH2-C(=O)-CH2CH3 (pentan-3-one); a Grignard reagent adds to a nitrile and hydrolysis of the imine salt gives a ketone.

mcqs.q: The acid dissociation constant Ka of acetic acid is
mcqs.why: Acetic acid has Ka = 1.8 x 10^-5, corresponding to pKa 4.76; ethanol by contrast has Ka = 10^-16, showing how much stronger a carboxylic acid is than an alcohol.

mcqs.q: Which of the following acids is the strongest, judging by its pKa value?
mcqs.why: Three electron-withdrawing chlorine atoms stabilize the trichloroacetate ion most strongly, giving the lowest pKa, 0.65, and therefore the strongest acid in the list.

mcqs.q: Hydrolysis of methyl cyanide on heating with aqueous acid gives acetic acid through the intermediate
mcqs.why: Ethanenitrile adds two molecules of water, passing through acetamide, to give acetic acid and ammonia; in base the product is obtained as the salt of the acid.

mcqs.q: When a Grignard reagent is treated with carbon dioxide and then hydrolysed, the carboxylic acid obtained has
options: the same number of carbons as the Grignard reagent
two carbons more than the Grignard reagent
one carbon less than the Grignard reagent
one carbon more than the Grignard reagent
mcqs.why: The carbon of CO2 becomes the carboxyl carbon of the product, so carbonation of CH3MgBr, for example, gives two-carbon acetic acid - one carbon more than the Grignard reagent.

mcqs.q: Acetyl chloride is prepared from acetic acid using
mcqs.why: Thionyl chloride replaces the -OH of acetic acid by -Cl, giving CH3-CO-Cl together with SO2 and HCl; PCl5 can be used for the same conversion.

mcqs.q: Acetic anhydride is prepared by dehydrating two molecules of acetic acid with
mcqs.why: A strong dehydrating agent such as P2O5 removes a molecule of water from two molecules of acetic acid, linking them through an oxygen atom as (CH3CO)2O.

mcqs.q: Benzoyl chloride reacts with methanol to give
mcqs.why: Methanol replaces the chlorine of benzoyl chloride by -OCH3, giving the ester methyl benzoate; pyridine is used to absorb the HCl formed.

mcqs.q: Ammonolysis of butanoyl chloride with ammonia gives
mcqs.why: Two molecules of ammonia are used: one converts CH3CH2CH2-CO-Cl into the amide butanamide, and the second neutralizes the HCl as NH4Cl.

mcqs.q: The systematic name of HO-C(=O)-CH(CH3)-CH2-C(=O)-OH is
mcqs.why: The compound is a four-carbon dicarboxylic acid (both carboxyl carbons counted in the chain) with a methyl group on carbon 2, so it is 2-methylbutanedioic acid.

mcqs.q: Sodium propanoate heated with soda lime (NaOH/CaO) undergoes decarboxylation to give
options: ethane, which has one carbon less than the acid
mcqs.why: Decarboxylation removes the carboxyl carbon as sodium carbonate, so the three-carbon propanoate gives the two-carbon alkane ethane.

lessons.title: Self-Assessment
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Every derivative of acetic acid gives acetic acid (ethanoic acid) on hydrolysis.
  • The acid halide is acetyl chloride, IUPAC name ethanoyl chloride, CH3-CO-Cl.
  • The anhydride is acetic anhydride (ethanoic anhydride), (CH3CO)2O, and it gives two molecules of acetic acid on hydrolysis.
  • The amide is acetamide (ethanamide) and the nitrile is acetonitrile (ethanenitrile).
  • Common esters giving acetic acid on hydrolysis include ethyl acetate (ethyl ethanoate) and methyl acetate (methyl ethanoate).

Solved Exercises

Self-Assessment

Q: Write the common and IUPAC names of derivatives of carboxylic acids, which yield acetic acid upon hydrolysis.

Ans: All derivatives of acetic acid give acetic acid (ethanoic acid) on hydrolysis. The main ones are: (1) Acid halide: common name acetyl chloride, IUPAC name ethanoyl chloride, CH3-CO-Cl. (2) Acid anhydride: common name acetic anhydride, IUPAC name ethanoic anhydride, (CH3CO)2O (it gives two molecules of acetic acid). (3) Esters, e.g. common name ethyl acetate, IUPAC name ethyl ethanoate, CH3-COO-C2H5; and methyl acetate / methyl ethanoate, CH3-COO-CH3. (4) Amide: common name acetamide, IUPAC name ethanamide, CH3-CO-NH2. (5) Nitrile: common name acetonitrile (methyl cyanide), IUPAC name ethanenitrile, CH3-C triple-bond N.

lessons.title: Project
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Carboxylic acids decompose sodium bicarbonate with brisk effervescence of carbon dioxide.
  • The reaction is R-COOH + NaHCO3 -> R-COO-Na+ + CO2 + H2O.
  • The carbon dioxide evolved turns lime water milky, confirming the gas.
  • Phenols and alcohols do not decompose NaHCO3, so the test distinguishes carboxylic acids from them.

Solved Exercises

Project

Q: Add few drops or a small crystal of available carboxylic acid with about 2-3 mL of aq. NaHCO3 and shake well. Formation of bubbles of carbon dioxide is positive test, for presence of carboxylic acid.

Ans: Carboxylic acids are stronger acids than carbonic acid, so they decompose sodium bicarbonate with brisk effervescence of carbon dioxide: R-COOH + NaHCO3 -> R-COO-Na+ + CO2 + H2O. The bubbles of CO2, which turn lime water milky, are the positive test for a carboxylic acid. Weaker organic acids such as phenols and alcohols do not decompose NaHCO3, so this test also distinguishes carboxylic acids from them.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The optimum pH of pepsin is around 2.0.
  • Cellulose is the most abundant carbohydrate found in nature.
  • Steroids belong to the family of lipids.
  • Haemoglobin has a quaternary protein structure.
  • Humans are unable to digest cellulose.
  • In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine and guanine pairs with cytosine.
  • Proteins are polymers of amino acids.

Solved Exercises

Exercise: Q1. Choose the correct one from the given options

Q: 1. The optimum pH of pepsin is around

Options: (a) 3.0 (b) 3.5 (c) 2.0 (d) 2.5

Correct answer: 2.0

Q: 2. The most abundant carbohydrate found in nature is

Options: (a) cellulose (b) glycogen (c) pectin (d) chitin

Correct answer: cellulose

Q: 3. The glycosidic linkage is present between the molecules of

Options: (a) glucose (b) glycine (c) fatty acid (d) none of these

Correct answer: glucose

Q: 4. Steroid belong to family of

Options: (a) carbohydrates (b) proteins (c) lipids (d) enzymes

Correct answer: lipids

Q: 5. Protein present in haemoglobin has the structure known as

Options: (a) primary structure (b) secondary structure (c) tertiary structure (d) quaternary structure

Correct answer: quaternary structure

Q: 6. Which carbohydrate does not conform the general formula Cn(H2O)n?

Options: (a) Deoxyribose (b) Ribose (c) Glucose (d) Fructose

Correct answer: Deoxyribose

Q: 7. Ethanol is produced from starch by the process of

Options: (a) hydrolysis (b) hydrogenation (c) decomposition (d) fermentation

Correct answer: fermentation

Q: 8. Human are unable to digest

Options: (a) glucose (b) cellulose (c) starch (d) denatured protein

Correct answer: cellulose

Q: 9. Which one of the following term is not related to term aldohexose?

Options: (a) Aldehyde (b) Ketone (c) Six (d) Sugar

Correct answer: Ketone

Q: 10. Slow healing of wounds is due the deficiency of

Options: (a) Ca (b) P (c) Zn (d) Fe

Correct answer: Zn

Q: 11. RNA is primarily seen in

Options: (a) nucleus (b) cytoplasm (c) cell wall (d) cell membrane

Correct answer: cytoplasm

Q: 12. In which of following disaccharides both the basic structural units are the same?

Options: (a) Maltose (b) Lactose (c) Sucrose (d) All of these

Correct answer: Maltose

Q: 13. In competitive inhibition, the inhibitor

Options: (a) competes with enzyme (b) irreversibly binds with the enzyme (c) binds with substrate (d) competes with substrate

Correct answer: competes with substrate

Q: 14. In DNA, adenine forms a complementary pair with which other nitrogen base?

Options: (a) Uracil (b) Cytosine (c) Thymine (d) Guanine

Correct answer: Thymine

Q: 15. Proteins are polymers of

Options: (a) glucose (b) disulphide bridges (c) amino acids (d) peptide bonds

Correct answer: amino acids

mcqs.q: The optimum pH of pepsin is around
mcqs.why: The solved answers state that pepsin is best active in the acidic stomach and its optimum pH is around 2.0.

mcqs.q: The most abundant carbohydrate found in nature is
mcqs.why: The unit identifies cellulose as the most abundant carbohydrate in nature, ahead of glycogen, pectin and chitin.

mcqs.q: The glycosidic linkage is present between the molecules of
mcqs.why: Two monosaccharide units such as glucose join through an oxygen atom by a glycosidic linkage, as the classification answer explains.

mcqs.q: Steroid belong to family of
mcqs.why: The lipids answer lists steroids among the non-saponifiable lipids, so steroids belong to the lipid family.

mcqs.q: Protein present in haemoglobin has the structure known as
mcqs.why: Haemoglobin shows quaternary structure, the association of protein sub-units each with its own tertiary structure into one functional unit.

mcqs.q: Which carbohydrate does not conform the general formula Cn(H2O)n?
mcqs.why: Deoxyribose (C5H10O4) is named in the detailed answer as a carbohydrate that does not follow the general formula Cn(H2O)n.

mcqs.q: Ethanol is produced from starch by the process of
mcqs.why: Starch is used for making ethanol by fermentation, as stated in the cellulose and starch comparison in the short answers.

mcqs.q: Human are unable to digest
mcqs.why: Cellulose has no food value for humans and cannot be digested by them; it only serves as roughage in the diet.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following term is not related to term aldohexose?
mcqs.why: Aldohexose combines aldehyde, six carbons and sugar; a ketone group would make it a ketose, not an aldose.

mcqs.q: Slow healing of wounds is due the deficiency of
mcqs.why: The zinc answer states that deficiency of zinc results in slow healing of wounds, so Zn is the deficient element.

mcqs.q: RNA is primarily seen in
mcqs.why: The nucleic acid answers state that genetic information is transmitted to the cytoplasm as messenger RNA, so RNA is primarily seen in the cytoplasm.

mcqs.q: In which of following disaccharides both the basic structural units are the same?
mcqs.why: Maltose gives two units of the same monosaccharide, glucose only, on hydrolysis, while sucrose and lactose give different units.

mcqs.q: In competitive inhibition, the inhibitor
mcqs.why: In competitive inhibition the inhibitor resembles the substrate and competes with the substrate for the active site of the enzyme.

mcqs.q: In DNA, adenine forms a complementary pair with which other nitrogen base?
mcqs.why: In DNA, adenine joins only to thymine by two hydrogen bonds, while guanine joins only to cytosine by three hydrogen bonds.

mcqs.q: Proteins are polymers of
mcqs.why: Proteins are made up of amino acid subunits joined together by peptide bonds, so they are polymers of amino acids.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Vegetable oils become rancid because atmospheric oxygen attacks the C=C double bonds of their unsaturated fatty acids.
  • Saturated fatty acids pack closely with strong van der Waals forces, so they melt at higher temperatures than unsaturated fatty acids.
  • Sucrose hydrolyses to one molecule of glucose and one molecule of fructose, while maltose gives two glucose units.
  • Denaturation breaks the cross linkages of a protein, so it loses its structure and biological activity.
  • Each nucleotide consists of a nitrogenous base, a five-carbon sugar and a phosphate group.
  • Natural fats are insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents such as benzene, ether and chloroform.

Solved Exercises

Exercise: Q2. Write short answers of the following questions

Q: i. Why vegetable oil is sensitive to rancidity?

Ans: Vegetable oils are rich in unsaturated fatty acids, i.e. they contain C=C double bonds in their fatty acid chains. Atmospheric oxygen attacks these double bonds (oxidative rancidity / autoxidation) by free radical reactions, and the fats also undergo partial hydrolysis and oxidation in the presence of the enzyme lipase. This produces volatile carboxylic acids, aldehydes and ketones of sour taste and unpleasant smell, so the oil becomes rancid quickly.

Q: ii. Why melting point of saturated fatty acid is higher than unsaturated fatty acid?

Ans: Saturated fatty acids have straight hydrocarbon chains with no double bonds, so their molecules pack closely and regularly together and are held by strong van der Waals forces; more heat is therefore needed to melt them. Unsaturated fatty acids contain one or more C=C double bonds which bend (kink) the chain, so the molecules cannot pack closely, the attractive forces are weaker and the melting point is lower. This is why fats rich in saturated fatty acids are solid at room temperature while oils rich in unsaturated fatty acids are liquid.

Q: iii. Make at least one point difference in each compound in the given pairs. Differentiate between the following compounds. (a) Glucose and fructose (b) Sucrose and maltose (c) Cellulose and starch

Ans: (a) Glucose and fructose: Glucose is an aldose; it has an aldehyde group at carbon atom number one. Fructose is a ketose; it has a keto group at carbon atom number two. (b) Sucrose and maltose: On hydrolysis sucrose gives two different monosaccharides, glucose and fructose (C12H22O11 + H2O -> C6H12O6 + C6H12O6), while maltose gives two units of the same monosaccharide, glucose only (C12H22O11 + H2O -> 2C6H12O6). (c) Cellulose and starch: Starch is a food polysaccharide stored in plants (bread, potatoes, rice) and is used as food and for making ethanol by fermentation, while cellulose has no food value for humans; it is used as roughage in the diet to promote peristaltic motion of the digestive tract and for making paper, cotton cloth and wood products.

Q: iv. Write down at least three important functions of nucleic acids.

Ans: 1. Storage of genetic information: DNA is the ultimate carrier of heredity in all living organisms; genes are composed of DNA, which contains genetic information in the form of codes. 2. Protein synthesis: nucleic acids are the main information-carrying molecules of the cell and, by directing the process of protein synthesis, they determine the inherited characteristics of every living thing; the information is transmitted to the cytoplasm as messenger RNA (mRNA) and read by transfer RNA (tRNA) during translation. 3. Transfer of heredity: nucleic acids allow organisms to transfer genetic information from one generation to the next and are the essential substance of the genes.

Q: v. Write down the products of hydrolysis of sucrose with reaction.

Ans: On hydrolysis sucrose gives two different types of monosaccharides, i.e. one molecule of glucose and one molecule of fructose.
C12H22O11 + H2O -> C6H12O6 + C6H12O6
sucrose + water -> glucose + fructose

Q: vi. What happens when protein is denatured?

Ans: Denaturation is the change in the properties of a protein or loss of its biological activity. When a protein is denatured by denaturing agents such as vigorous shaking, heat, light or low pH, some or all the cross linkages which normally keep the molecular structure are broken, so the protein loses its structural organization (secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure) and its biological function. Denatured proteins are called primary derived proteins; for example, strongly heated proteins coagulate and lose their biological functions.

Q: vii. What are chemical components that compose the nucleic acid?

Ans: The monomer that makes up a nucleic acid is called a nucleotide. Each nucleotide is composed of three components: (1) a nitrogenous base, which is either a purine (adenine and guanine) or a pyrimidine (cytosine, thymine and uracil); (2) a five-carbon monosaccharide sugar, deoxyribose in DNA and ribose in RNA; and (3) an inorganic phosphate group (from phosphoric acid). On complete breakdown, nucleic acids yield phosphoric acid, sugars and a mixture of these organic bases (purines and pyrimidines).

Q: viii. Describe briefly the primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure of protein.

Ans: Primary structure: it simply shows the sequence and number of different amino acids in a polypeptide chain, and whether the chain is open, branched or cyclic, e.g. the hormone insulin has two polypeptide chains, A and B. Secondary structure: the long polypeptide chains twist or coil upon themselves in a special pattern; this folding is held together by strong hydrogen bonding and may take the alpha-helix form or the beta-pleated sheet form. Tertiary structure: the long polypeptide chain undergoes folding and re-folding on itself to give a definite three dimensional structure, which makes proteins rounded and somewhat rigid molecules. Quaternary structure: it shows the association of many individual protein sub-units, each with its own tertiary structure, into a complex functional unit, e.g. myoglobin (oxygen storage) and haemoglobin (oxygen carrier).

Q: ix. Differentiate between non-competitive and uncompetitive inhibitions.

Ans: Non-competitive inhibition: the inhibitor has no structural resemblance with the substrate, does not compete with the substrate for the active site and does not bind to the active site; instead it binds to a site other than the active site (allosteric site) of the enzyme and forms an enzyme-substrate-inhibitor complex, changing the shape of the active site. Uncompetitive inhibition: these inhibitors are like non-competitive inhibitors, but the uncompetitive inhibitor combines with the enzyme-substrate complex rather than directly with the free enzyme, to give an inactive enzyme-inhibitor complex.

Q: x. Write down the physical and chemical properties of lipids.

Ans: Physical properties: natural fats are colourless, odourless and tasteless; they are insoluble in water but highly soluble in organic solvents like benzene, ether and chloroform; they have well defined melting and solidifying points; they have low specific gravity and therefore float on the surface of water. Chemical properties: (1) Hydrolysis: natural fats undergo hydrolysis with acids or bases in boiling water and produce free fatty acids and glycerol; base hydrolysis gives salts of fatty acids called soap, and the process is called saponification. (2) Addition reaction: unsaturated fatty acids of fats and oils undergo addition reactions at the points of unsaturation; oils containing more unsaturation are hydrogenated to produce solid ghee. (3) Oxidation: fats rich in unsaturated fatty acids undergo spontaneous oxidation at their double bonds and produce aldehydes, ketones and resins. (4) Rancidification: in the presence of lipase and atmospheric oxygen, fats undergo partial hydrolysis and oxidation producing volatile carboxylic acids of sour taste and unpleasant smell.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or polyhydroxy ketones, or compounds that give them on hydrolysis.
  • Monosaccharides contain one sugar unit, oligosaccharides two to ten units, and polysaccharides more than ten units.
  • One gram of sucrose produces 4 kilo calories of energy, while one gram of lipid produces 9.3 kcal on complete oxidation.
  • Simple proteins yield only amino acids on hydrolysis, while conjugated proteins also contain a non-protein prosthetic group.
  • In DNA, adenine joins thymine by two hydrogen bonds and guanine joins cytosine by three hydrogen bonds.
  • Most animal enzymes have an optimum temperature around 37 C, and zinc's recommended daily amount for an adult is 10 mg.

Solved Exercises

Exercise: Q3. Write detail answers of the following questions

Q: 1. (a) What are carbohydrates? Explain the basis of classification of carbohydrate. (b) How would you evaluate the role of various carbohydrates in health and diseases?

Ans: (a) Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes (aldoses) or polyhydroxy ketones (ketoses), or compounds that give such compounds on hydrolysis. The hydroxyl group and the carbonyl group are the major functional groups in carbohydrates. The name arose because the molecular formulae of these compounds can be expressed as hydrates of carbon, e.g. glucose C6H12O6 can be written as C6(H2O)6, although some carbohydrates like 2-deoxyribose (C5H10O4) do not follow the general formula Cn(H2O)n. Basis of classification: carbohydrates are classified on the basis of the number of simple sugar units present per molecule into three classes. 1. Monosaccharides (simple sugars): they contain only one sugar unit per molecule and cannot be broken down into simpler carbohydrates on hydrolysis, e.g. glucose and fructose. They are further subdivided on the basis of the functional group (aldoses and ketoses) and the number of carbon atoms (trioses, tetroses, pentoses, hexoses). 2. Oligosaccharides: they contain two to ten monosaccharide units covalently bonded to each other; disaccharides (two units) are the most common, e.g. sucrose, lactose and maltose, while those with three and four units are called trisaccharides and tetrasaccharides. Two monosaccharide units join through an oxygen atom with the elimination of one water molecule; this linkage is called a glycosidic linkage or glycosidic bond. 3. Polysaccharides: they contain many (above ten to hundreds of) monosaccharide units covalently bonded to each other and produce monosaccharides on hydrolysis, e.g. starch and cellulose. Monosaccharides and oligosaccharides are collectively called sugars; polysaccharides are non-sugars. (b) Role in health: Sucrose (table sugar) is a caloric carbohydrate and an efficient source of energy; 1 gram of sucrose produces 4 kilo calories of energy when metabolised, and it is used as a sweetening agent in sweets, soft drinks and energy drinks. Lactose, the milk sugar made of glucose and galactose, is the universal food of new born mammals; its galactose serves in neural and immunological processes, is a component of nerve cell membranes and of the molecules on blood cells that determine ABO blood types, and it helps in the absorption of calcium and minerals such as copper and zinc during infancy. Glucose is the most common monosaccharide, used by living bodies for the production of instant energy; normal human blood contains about 70-110 mg of glucose per 100 cm3, it regulates body temperature, and surplus glucose is converted to glycogen and stored in the liver and muscles. Role in diseases: excess of sucrose may cause tooth decay, obesity, plaque formation on teeth and gum diseases. Many human adults are unable to digest milk due to deficiency of the enzyme lactase, a condition called lactose intolerance, which results in intestinal discomfort such as cramps, flatulence, colic pains, nausea and watery diarrhoea. Defects in the metabolism of glucose raise the blood glucose level and result in diabetes mellitus, whose unchecked consequences include hardening of blood vessels, dysfunction of kidney and diabetic coma that causes premature death.

Q: 2. (a) Describe various classes of protein along with examples. (b) Enlist the properties of protein.

Ans: (a) Proteins have been classified into the following three major classes. 1. Simple proteins: these are made up of amino acid subunits joined together by peptide bonds. When hydrolysed by enzymes, simple proteins yield only the amino acids and their derivatives from which they are formed. Examples: albumins, globulins, collagens, histones, glutelins and albuminoids. 2. Compounds or conjugated proteins: these are complex proteins composed of a simple protein and a non-protein substance referred to as a prosthetic group or cofactor; most prosthetic groups are small organic molecules formed from vitamins. On hydrolysis they yield the amino acids plus some other chemical component. Examples with their prosthetic groups: nucleoproteins (DNA or RNA), phosphoproteins (phosphoric acid), lipoproteins (lipids), glycoproteins (carbohydrates), chromoproteins (coloured compounds) and haemoglobins. 3. Derived proteins: these are proteins derived by partial to complete hydrolysis of simple or conjugated proteins by the action of acids, alkalies or enzymes. They are of two types: (i) Primary derived proteins, also called denatured proteins, in which some or all cross linkages which normally keep the molecular structure are broken by physical or chemical agents such as vigorous shaking, heat, light and low pH; they include proteins and meta-proteins. (ii) Secondary derived proteins, formed by hydrolysis of simple or conjugated proteins by acid or enzymes, e.g. proteoses and peptones. (b) Properties of proteins. Physical properties: proteins are colourless and usually tasteless; they generally have high molecular weights; they range in shape from simple crystalloid spherical (globular) structures to long fibrillar (thread-like) structures; protein denaturation is the change in properties of a protein or loss of biological activity; like amino acids, proteins are amphoteric in nature because they contain both acidic (-COOH) and basic (amino) groups; their solubility is influenced by pH; all protein solutions rotate the plane of polarized light to the left, i.e. they are levorotatory. Chemical properties: (1) Hydrolysis: proteins are hydrolysed by a variety of hydrolytic agents, such as acidic agents and basic (alkaline) agents, ultimately to amino acids. (2) They react with both acids and bases (amphoteric behaviour). (3) They can be precipitated from their solutions by salts of heavy metals, heat and alcohols etc. (4) Coagulation: when proteins are strongly heated or treated with certain reagents, they lose their structural organization and their biological functions; this is known as coagulation of proteins.

Q: 3. (a) What are lipids? Explain the basis of classification of lipids. (b) Discuss in detail the structure and nutritional and biological importance of lipids.

Ans: (a) Lipids are a heterogeneous group of organic compounds. They are greasy substances which are relatively insoluble in water and soluble in non-polar organic solvents like ether and benzene. They may be saponifiable (fats, oils and waxes, which have ester linkages and are easily hydrolysed in basic conditions such as sodium hydroxide) or non-saponifiable (terpenes and steroids, which have no ester bonds and cannot be hydrolysed by sodium hydroxide). Basis of classification: lipids have been classified into three major classes. 1. Simple lipids: these are the esters of fatty acids with different types of alcohols. They include (i) fats and oils, which yield fatty acids and glycerol upon hydrolysis (both are triacylglycerols or triglycerides, esters composed of three fatty acids joined to glycerol; fat is solid at room temperature while oil is liquid), and (ii) waxes, which yield fatty acids and long-chain alcohols upon hydrolysis, e.g. bees wax and carnauba wax. 2. Compound lipids: these are the esters of fatty acids with alcohols containing some additional groups as well. They are further divided into (i) phospholipids, which contain fatty acids, phosphoric acid and nitrogenous bases (also called phosphatides); (ii) glycolipids, which contain fatty acid, alcohol and carbohydrates, present in large amount in the white matter of brain and in the myelin sheaths of nerves; (iii) sulpholipids, which contain a sulphate group in addition to fatty acids, alcohol and carbohydrates; and (iv) lipo-proteins, which are complexes of lipids with proteins. 3. Derived lipids: these are the substances derived by the hydrolysis of simple and compound lipids; they include fatty acids, alcohols, steroids, terpenes and arytenoids etc. (b) Structure: a lipid has no common structure; the most common occurring lipids are triglycerides and phospholipids. Triglycerides are fats and oils having a glycerol backbone bonded to three fatty acids; if the three fatty acids are similar the fat is a simple triglyceride, and if they are not similar it is a mixed triglyceride. Fatty acids are long chain carboxylic acids containing usually 12-18 carbon atoms per molecule, e.g. stearic acid CH3(CH2)14COOH (saturated) and oleic acid (unsaturated). Phospholipids, the second most common lipids, are found in the cell membranes of animals and plants and contain glycerol and fatty acids as well as a phosphoric (phosphate) group and a nitrogenous base such as choline. Nutritional and biological importance: (1) Lipids provide food which is highly rich in calorific value; one gram of lipid on complete oxidation produces 9.3 kcal of heat, about double the amount produced by carbohydrates and proteins. (2) Being insoluble in water, lipids can be stored easily in the body as food reserves, which organisms use during hibernation periods. (3) Lipids in association with different proteins form the important constituents of cell membranes, and they act as structural components of membranes, as protective and insulating coatings, and are rich in nervous tissues. (4) Fats have high insulating capacity; great quantities of fat deposited in the sub-cutaneous layers of aquatic mammals such as whale and in animals of cold climates protect them from severe cold and temperature changes. (5) Some lipids, especially phospholipids, play a key role in the absorption and transportation of fatty acids in the body. (6) Sex hormones, adrenocorticoids and cholic acids are synthesized from a steroidal lipid known as cholesterol. (7) Lipids serve as carriers of fat soluble vitamins such as vitamins A, D and E in the body.

Q: 4. (a) Explain the role of inhibitors of enzyme catalysed reactions. (b) Identify the different structural components of DNA and RNA.

Ans: (a) The process by which the activity of an enzyme is decreased or inhibited by the addition of certain substances is called enzyme inhibition, and the substances which inhibit the activity of enzymes are known as inhibitors; poisons and drugs are examples of inhibitors. Inhibitors control enzyme catalysed reactions in the body by switching enzymes off where their activity is not needed, and they are also useful as drugs and poisons that block specific enzymes. According to the similarity between the inhibitor and the substrate, enzyme inhibition is classified as follows. 1. Irreversible inhibition: when the inhibitor reacts and forms a strong covalent bond with the active site of the enzyme, it is termed irreversible inhibition; the inhibitor forms a stable and irreversible complex with the enzyme which cannot be broken down by physical or chemical methods to restore the active form of the enzyme. 2. Reversible inhibition: it is a temporary type of inhibition in which the inhibitor binds non-covalently (weak interaction) with the enzyme; if the inhibitor is removed, the activity of the enzyme is fully restored, e.g. by dialysis. Reversible inhibition is sub-divided into competitive inhibition (the inhibitor resembles the substrate, competes with it for the active site and blocks it), non-competitive inhibition (the inhibitor binds at a site other than the active site and changes the shape of the active site) and uncompetitive inhibition (the inhibitor combines with the enzyme-substrate complex to give an inactive complex). (b) Both DNA and RNA are formed by the polymerization of a large number of units known as nucleotides, so DNA and RNA are polynucleotides. Each nucleotide, the structural component of DNA and RNA, is composed of three parts: (1) A nitrogenous base: the bases are of two types, purines and pyrimidines. There are two purine derivatives, adenine and guanine, and three pyrimidine derivatives, cytosine, thymine (present only in DNA) and uracil (present only in RNA). (2) A sugar: DNA and RNA contain two different types of sugars; one is deoxyribose (in DNA) and the other is ribose (in RNA), both in cyclic furanose form. (3) A phosphate group: the third component of nucleic acid is phosphoric acid. In DNA the two antiparallel long polydeoxyribonucleotide chains wind around each other and are held together by hydrogen bonding between their nitrogenous bases; adenine joins only to thymine by two hydrogen bonds while guanine joins only to cytosine by three hydrogen bonds. RNA consists of ribonucleotides and is single stranded.

Q: 5. (a) Assess the role of enzyme as biocatalyst and relate this role to various functions such as digestion of food. (b) Evaluate the factors that affect enzyme activity such as effect of temperature and pH.

Ans: (a) Enzymes are complex organic substances (biocatalysts) which alter the rate of an already initiated biological reaction without themselves being altered permanently during the reaction. They are organic catalysts produced by living cells but are capable of acting independently outside the cells. Most enzymes are protein in nature, are non-hydrolysable with nitrogen contents of about 16%, are de-activated by extreme alteration of pH and high temperature, and are highly specific: an enzyme can work only for one type of reaction in the body, and the substance upon which an enzyme acts is called the substrate of that enzyme. Hundreds of biological reactions for obtaining energy, synthesizing protoplasmic and structural materials, digestion, absorption and assimilation of food are catalysed by enzymes. Role in digestion of food: (i) Digestion of carbohydrates: after ingestion, food meets saliva, which contains the enzyme salivary amylase or ptyalin; this enzyme catalyzes the hydrolysis of carbohydrates of food without affecting proteins and fats. When food reaches the stomach, the action of amylase comes to an end due to the acidic pH of the stomach; when food enters the intestine, pancreatic juice containing pancreatic amylase, which has the same action as salivary amylase, is secreted. (ii) Digestion of fats: there is only slight hydrolysis of fats in the mouth and stomach because no lipase is secreted by the salivary glands, while the lipase of the gastric juice is weak; lingual lipase secreted by Ebner's glands on the tongue can hydrolyse about 30% of the ingested fats, and when fats reach the intestine, pancreatic lipase (steapsin) in pancreatic juice completely hydrolyses all the fats of the food. (iii) Digestion of proteins: digestion of proteins starts in the stomach because saliva contains no enzyme for protein digestion; the first enzyme is pepsin present in the gastric juice of the stomach, which is best active in the acidic pH of 1-2 and also has milk-curdling properties. In the intestine, pancreatic juice contains trypsin, chymotrypsin, carboxypeptidases A and B, elastase and collagenase, which are secreted in inactive forms and then activated by other enzymes, e.g. inactive trypsinogen is activated to active trypsin by enterokinase. (b) Factors affecting enzyme activity include temperature, pH, enzyme concentration, substrate concentration and the presence of any inhibitor or activator. Effect of temperature: the protein nature of enzymes makes them extremely sensitive to thermal changes; enzyme activity occurs within a narrow range of temperature. Each enzyme has a certain temperature at which it is more active and shows maximum activity, called the optimum temperature; for most animal enzymes the optimum temperature is around body temperature (37 C), while some plant enzymes such as urease have optimum temperature even up to 60 C. As the temperature rises above the optimum, the enzyme activity gradually lowers until it stops completely due to the change of its natural structure and composition (denaturation of enzyme). Below the optimum temperature, activity decreases until a minimum temperature is reached; the enzyme activity stops completely at 0 C, but if the temperature rises again the enzyme is reactivated, and enzymes can be stored for years in frozen state. Effect of pH: enzyme activity is also effected by pH; some enzymes work best in alkaline pH while others in acidic pH. As the pH is decreased or increased, the nature of the various acid and amino groups on the side chains is altered, which results in a change in the overall shape and structure of the enzyme. Each enzyme has a pH at which it shows maximum activity, called its optimum pH; for example, the optimum pH of pepsin is around 2.0 while that of trypsin varies from 8-9 pH. The pH below which the enzyme loses its activity and at which the enzyme shows the lowest activity is called minimum pH. Most of the enzymes have optimum activities in the range 5-9 pH; pepsin is an exception to this rule.

Q: 6. (a) Why zinc is important for human being? (b) State the medical problems that may relate to calcium and phosphorus deficiency and excess.

Ans: (a) Zinc is an antioxidant and is important for the maintenance of a healthy immune system. It is an important element for the normal growth, reproduction and longevity of animals. The recommended daily amount of zinc for an adult is 10 mg. Zinc is a constituent of several types of enzymes such as alkaline phosphatase and carbonic anhydrase etc. It also forms a complex with insulin and helps in its storage and release according to the needs of the body, and it is required for maintaining the plasma concentration of vitamin A. Its sources include meat, liver, eggs, fish, milk and cereals. Deficiency of zinc results in slow healing of wounds, impairment of acuity of taste and skin problems, while excess intake of zinc can cause gastrointestinal discomfort and, when chronic, may disrupt the balance of other chemicals in the body, including copper and iron. (b) Calcium: calcium is essential for strong bones and teeth, is the main constituent of bones and teeth, accounts for 1 to 2 percent of adult human body weight (99% of which is present in bones in the form of hydroxyapatite crystals), plays an active role in the body's immune system, and is required for cellular activities, muscle and nerve functions, hormonal action, blood coagulation and cell motility; the recommended daily amount for an adult is around 800 mg. Deficiency: a decrease of calcium in the diet contributes to osteoporosis, a condition that causes brittle bones in adults, and a decrease of calcium level in plasma leads to hypocalcemia. Excess: an increase in the concentration of calcium in plasma leads to hyperparathyroidism. Phosphorus: phosphorus is also a major constituent of bones and teeth, is present in all body cells in association with proteins, lipids and carbohydrates as phosphoproteins and phospholipids, forms the bone component hydroxyapatite with calcium (80% of the phosphorus in the body is present as calcium salts in the skeleton) and has a unique role in the storage and transformation of energy in the body; an adult requires about 800 mg per day. Deficiency: deficiency of phosphorus leads to joint and bone pain, loss of appetite, irritability or anxiety, fatigue and poor bone development in children, and in children it leads to renal rickets. Excess: too much phosphate can be toxic; an excess can cause diarrhoea as well as hardening of organs and soft tissues, and an increase in the plasma phosphate level due to decrease in its excretion leads to kidney dysfunction.

lessons.title: Project
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Adding lemon juice or vinegar curdles milk, separating white solid curds from the watery whey.
  • The curdling is a chemical change because the acid lowers the pH and denatures and coagulates the milk protein casein.
  • The product obtained is curd, from which paneer (cheese) is prepared by pressing out the whey.
  • Curd and paneer retain milk protein and calcium, so they are nutritious foods used in dishes such as lassi, raita and sweets.

Solved Exercises

Project

Q: Project: Take 250 cm3 milk in a beaker. Gently warm the milk (not boil), add small amount of lemon juice or vinegar (acetic acid) in it and observe it. 1. What happen to the state of the milk?

Ans: On adding lemon juice or vinegar, the liquid milk curdles: it separates into white solid curds (clots) and a watery liquid (whey). The milk protein casein coagulates and comes out of solution as a solid mass.

Q: Project: 2. Is there any chemical change occur in it?

Ans: Yes, it is a chemical change. The acid lowers the pH of the milk and denatures and coagulates its protein (casein); a new substance, curd, is formed and the change cannot be reversed simply by removing the acid.

Q: Project: 3. Does the change in pH affect the milk?

Ans: Yes. Milk protein remains dispersed at the normal pH of milk; when the pH falls due to the added acid, the protein loses its structural organization (denaturation, as also happens at low pH in the stomach where pepsin has milk-curdling properties) and precipitates out as curd.

Q: Project: 4. Name the product obtained during the process.

Ans: The product obtained is curd (coagulated milk protein, casein), from which paneer (cheese) is prepared by pressing out the whey.

Q: Project: 5. Is this product has any nutritional importance?

Ans: Yes. The curd/paneer retains the milk protein and calcium, so it is a nutritious food: proteins are the most significant biological compounds needed for growth and repair of the body, and calcium is the main constituent of bones and teeth.

Q: Project: 6. Name some products in which it is used.

Ans: The curdled product is used as paneer (cheese) in cooking, and curd is used for making yogurt-based dishes, lassi, raita and sweets; coagulated milk protein is also the basis of cheese making.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Nylon 6,6 is formed from hexamethylene diamine and adipic acid.
  • Petroleum is called black gold.
  • Cellulose is not a petrochemical.
  • Cracking breaks large molecules down into smaller ones.
  • Rexine is the manipulated form of PVC plastic.
  • Polythene is a synthetic polymer, while cellulose, starch and silk are natural.
  • Acrylate base polymers are pressure sensitive adhesives.

Solved Exercises

Exercise: Q1. Choose the correct one from the given options

Q: 1. The monomer pair required for the formation of Nylon 6,6 is

Options: (a) hexamethylene diamine + adipic acid (b) hexamethylene diamine + sebacoyl chloride (c) hexamethylene diamine + decanoic acid (d) hexamethylene amine + ethanedioic acid

Correct answer: hexamethylene diamine + adipic acid

Q: 2. Which one is true for DDT?

Correct answer: Non-degradable

Options: (a) coal (b) carbon black (c) petroleum (d) coal tar

Correct answer: petroleum

Correct answer: cellulose

Q: 5. Multipart adhesive is an example of

Options: (a) reactive adhesives (b) contact adhesives (c) hot adhesives (d) pressure sensitive adhesives

Correct answer: reactive adhesives

Q: 6. Nail polish removers are mainly composed of

Options: (a) propyne (b) propanone (c) propanal (d) propene

Correct answer: propanone

Q: 7. In the process of cracking

Options: (a) small molecule unite together (b) large molecules unite together (c) large molecules are broken down (d) small and large molecules unite together

Correct answer: large molecules are broken down

Q: 8. Rexine is the manipulated form of

Options: (a) plastic (PVC) (b) nylon (c) lipstick (d) nail polish

Correct answer: plastic (PVC)

Q: 9. Identify the petrochemical which is not obtained from benzene

Options: (a) alkyl benzenes (b) cyclohexane (c) nitrobenzene (d) vinyl chloride

Correct answer: vinyl chloride

Q: 10. Which of the following is condensation polymer

Correct answer: nylon

Q: 11. (-NH-(CH2)6-CONHCO(CH2)4CO-)n is an example of

Options: (a) addition polymer (b) thermosetting polymer (c) condensation copolymer (Nylon-6,6) (d) homo-polymer

Correct answer: condensation copolymer (Nylon-6,6)

Q: 12. Which one of the following is synthetic polymer?

Options: (a) cellulose (b) starch (c) silk (d) polythene

Correct answer: polythene

Q: 13. Hair dyes are commonly classified into groups

Options: (a) 3 (b) 4 (c) 5 (d) 6

Correct answer: 4

Q: 14. All are synthetic adhesives except

Options: (a) casein glues (b) polyurethanes (c) cyanoacrylates (d) polyimides

Correct answer: casein glues

Q: 15. Acrylate base polymers are

Options: (a) drying adhesives (b) pressure sensitive adhesives (c) contact adhesives (d) hot adhesives

Correct answer: pressure sensitive adhesives
