lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Non-reactive adhesives harden by a physical change, while reactive adhesives harden by a chemical reaction.
  • Nail polish remover, usually acetone (propanone), dissolves the hardened film of polish so it can be wiped off.
  • Temporary hair dyes only coat the hair shaft weakly and wash out with a single shampooing.
  • PVC is used for rexine, pipes, wire insulation and bottles.
  • About 10% of petroleum is used to prepare petrochemicals.
  • Addition polymers form without elimination of any small molecule, while condensation polymers form with elimination of water, HCl, ammonia or methanol.
  • The main goal of petroleum refining is the production of gasoline.

Solved Exercises

Exercise: Q2. Write short answers of the following questions

Q: i. Differentiate between reactive and non-reactive adhesives.

Ans: Non-reactive adhesives harden by a physical change, not by chemical reaction: they include drying adhesives (which harden as the solvent evaporates), pressure-sensitive adhesives, contact adhesives and hot (hot-melt) adhesives, and they may be of natural or synthetic origin; their classification is based on their method of adhesion. Reactive adhesives harden by a chemical reaction with the material: they chemically react when they harden and are divided into multipart adhesives, which harden by mixing two or more components that chemically react, and one-part adhesives, which harden through a chemical reaction with an external energy source such as radiation, heat or moisture.

Q: ii. How nail-polish remover removes the nail polish?

Ans: Nail polish remover is an organic solvent (most commonly acetone, i.e. propanone). Nail polish remover works only when the nail polish and the remover both contain similar organic solvents: the organic solvent present in the remover dissolves the hardened film of polish on the nail, so the polish softens, dissolves and can be wiped off from the nail.

Q: iii. Why temporary hair dyes are removed with single shampooing?

Ans: Temporary hair dyes contain molecules that are too large to penetrate the hair cortex and have low affinity for hair, meaning that the binding forces between the hair cuticle and the dye molecules are low. As a result, the temporary dyes only provide a weak coating on the hair shaft, which is easily washed out with a single shampooing.

Q: iv. Write down at least four uses of PVC.

Ans: PVC is durable, inexpensive and resistant to heat, water and chemicals. Its uses include: (1) it is manipulated to create a leather-like material called rexine; (2) PVC pipes, which are strong, lightweight and less reactive, and do not wear, rot or rust; (3) insulating material on electrical wires (wire and cable insulation); (4) manufacture of bottles; (5) other uses include medical tubing and devices, PVC window frames, flexible packaging, blood bags, resilient flooring, vinyl panelling, drainage pipes, gramophone records and carpet backing; it is also widely used in the building and construction industry and for drinking and wastewater pipes.

Q: v. What is the difference between petrochemical and chemicals derived from them?

Ans: Petrochemicals are the group of chemicals produced directly or indirectly from the hydrocarbons of petroleum or natural gas; about 10% of the petroleum is used to prepare this range of chemicals. The primary petrochemicals obtained from feedstocks are simple building-block chemicals: from natural gas, ethene, propene and ethyne; from naphtha, ethene, propene and butadiene; and from reformed naphtha, benzene, toluene and the xylenes. The chemicals derived from them are the large number of useful products manufactured by further processing of these primary petrochemicals, such as plastics, rubbers, fibres, paints, solvents and detergents, on which almost every area of human activity depends.

Q: vi. Differentiate between addition and condensation polymers.

Ans: Addition polymers are formed by the polymerization of monomers containing double or triple bonds (unsaturated compounds); they result from the self-combination of many monomer units into a substance whose molecular weight is a multiple of the monomer, no small molecule is eliminated, and the addition polymer has the same empirical formula as its monomer, e.g. polythene from ethene and PVC from vinyl chloride. Condensation polymers are formed by the combination of two or more monomers with the elimination of small molecules such as water, hydrogen chloride (HCl), ammonia (NH3) or methanol (CH3OH); the monomer units must carry two functional groups, and the polymer does not have the same empirical formula as the monomers, e.g. nylon 6,6 formed by the condensation of hexamethylene diamine with adipic acid (hexanedioic acid) with the loss of water.

Q: vii. How would you justify that non-acetone base nail polish remover is better than acetone base nail polish remover?

Ans: The most common remover contains acetone, which is powerful and effective but is harsh on skin and nails and can even make them more brittle; acetone also dehydrates the skin, causes irritation to eyes and makes nails dry and brittle, and it cannot be used on artificial nails. The non-acetone remover usually contains ethyl acetate, which is a less aggressive solvent; it is gentler on skin and nails and can therefore be used to remove nail polish from artificial nails (which are usually made of acrylic). Hence, for regular use and for artificial nails, the non-acetone base remover is better.

Q: viii. How important the safety consideration for the workers in industry?

Ans: Safety considerations in the process industry are very important and must be kept in view before launching an industrial activity. All procedures must be carried out in a non-hazardous manner to ensure the safety of workers and the plant; proper material of construction must be selected so the factory does not corrode away; careful process control by periodic analysis, modern instrumentation and automatic control avoids harmful impurities and secures the requisite yield and purity of products; suitable containers must be used to transmit goods in a clean and economical manner; factories must avoid discharge of toxic material into the air and water of their localities to prevent contamination; and chemicals that can help in identifying the more hazardous chemicals must be labelled. Neglect of these considerations can cost workers their health and lives and can damage the plant and the environment.

Q: ix. What is main goal of petroleum refining?

Ans: According to the book, the main goal of refinery operations is the production of gasoline. By fractional distillation, crude oil is separated into useful fractions of different boiling ranges, such as refinery gas, petroleum ether, naphtha, gasoline (petrol), kerosene, diesel oil, lubricating oil, fuel oil and residue, and further processes such as cracking and reforming convert less useful heavy fractions and low octane naphtha into more gasoline and other valuable products.

mcqs.q: Non-acetone nail polish remover is preferred for artificial nails because it
options: usually contains ethyl acetate, a less aggressive and gentler solvent
mcqs.why: Non-acetone remover usually contains ethyl acetate, which is gentler on skin and nails and can be used on artificial nails, whereas acetone is harsh, dehydrating and cannot be used on them.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Cracking dissociates raw material molecules into smaller ones, while reforming converts heavy naphtha into aromatics and low octane naphtha into high octane gasoline components.
  • Thermal steam cracking of ethane and propane gives ethene and propene, while catalytic cracking of gas oil and fuel oil gives gasoline and kerosene.
  • Nail polish contains a nitrocellulose film former, plasticizers such as camphor, solvents and colouring pigments.
  • Hot adhesives are applied molten at 65-180 C and solidify on cooling to form strong bonds.
  • Fractional distillation separates crude oil into fractions such as gasoline (80-180 C), kerosene (160-300 C) and diesel oil (250-350 C).
  • Oil and gas are the source of 90% of world organic chemical production.

Solved Exercises

Exercise: Q3. Write detail answers of the following questions

Q: 1. (a) Explain the Petrochemical Process Technology. (b) Describe the different types of cracking in detail.

Ans: (a) Petrochemical process technology is the technology by which chemicals are produced directly or indirectly from the hydrocarbons of petroleum or natural gas. Petroleum is a complex mixture of hydrocarbons formed by the decomposition of fossil remains; it exists as a gas (natural gas), liquid (crude oil) or as solids (oil shales) and is found deep underground or below the seabed. The raw materials (feedstocks) are obtained from natural gas processing plants (methane, ethane, propane and butanes) and from petroleum refineries (gas oil and naphtha; benzene, toluene and xylene are also primarily obtained from petroleum refineries), and methane, benzene, toluene and xylene are used directly as feedstocks for producing petrochemicals. From these feedstocks the primary petrochemicals are obtained: natural gas gives ethene (CH2=CH2), propene (CH3-CH=CH2) and ethyne (CH triple bond CH); naphtha gives ethene, propene and butadiene (CH2=CH-CH=CH2); and reformed naphtha gives benzene, toluene and o-, m- and p-xylene. These primary petrochemicals are produced by the basic building block processes, which are divided into two groups: the cracking process and the reforming process. Cracking dissociates the molecules of raw material into smaller ones, while in reforming, hydrocarbons are treated with heat, pressure and/or catalyst to obtain desired products; heavy naphtha is converted into aromatics such as benzene, toluene and xylene with hydrogen as by-product, and low octane rating naphtha is broken down into high octane gasoline blending components (reformates). The primary petrochemicals are then converted into the vast range of end products such as plastics, rubbers, fibres, paints, solvents and detergents. (b) Cracking is a process in which molecules of raw material are dissociated into smaller ones. There are two types of cracking process. 1. Thermal steam cracking: steam cracking is the breaking of raw material such as ethane and propane (by heat, in the presence of steam) yielding important petrochemical products such as ethene and propene; methane and hydrogen are also some of the major by-products. 2. Catalytic cracking: breaking of larger, stable molecules requires catalysis. Refinery products such as gas oil and fuel oil are passed through a catalytic cracker to obtain gasoline and kerosene oil as major products and propene as by-product. Thus thermal steam cracking mainly supplies the light olefins (ethene, propene) from light feedstocks, while catalytic cracking converts heavy, less useful fractions into valuable lighter fuels.

Q: 2. (a) Discuss the preparation and applications of lipsticks. (b) Write down in detail the composition of nail polish.

Ans: (a) Lipsticks are basically dispersions of colouring matter in a base containing a suitable blend of oils, fats and waxes, suitably perfumed and flavoured, moulded in the form of a stick and enclosed in a case. Lipstick is a cosmetic product containing pigments, oils, waxes and emollients that apply colour, texture and protection to the lips; it is the cosmetic which is generally formulated to provide both protection and colour, and some lipsticks are also lip balms, to add colour and hydration. In preparation, the mixture of non-volatile oils (e.g. castor, vegetable, mineral or wool fat, lanolin oil) and waxes (e.g. bee wax or carnauba) forms the base; the oil makes the wax-based product soft and easy to apply, and to reduce the 'stickiness', esters of fatty acids (like 2-propyl myristate) are also added. Colours are a key ingredient: the dyes are water-insoluble because lipsticks are made from hydrophobic materials; water-soluble dyes such as green or blue food dyes are first combined with metal oxides such as aluminium hydroxide, Al(OH)3, to form an insoluble precipitate that is then suspended in the oil base of the lipstick. Antioxidants and preservatives are added, perfumes are added in very small quantity to combat the unpleasant fatty odour of the oil, and silicones and oily materials are also added to reflect light and provide shine. The mass is moulded into sticks and enclosed in cases. A good lipstick should be nontoxic, non-irritant to the lips and insoluble in water so that it cannot dissolve with saliva. Applications: lipsticks are applied to the lips to add colour, texture and protection, to beautify the appearance, and (as lip balms) to give hydration and protection to the lips. (b) There is no single formula for nail polish; a number of ingredients are used in its preparation. The basic components include film forming agents, resins and plasticizers, solvents and colouring agent. In detail: (a) Lacquer base: (1) Film former: nail polishes are made up of nitrocellulose dissolved in a solvent (e.g. butyl acetate or ethyl acetate); it forms a thin film on the nail after application, and this film is hard and water-proof and abrasion resistant. Adhesive polymers (e.g. tosylamide/formaldehyde resin) are added to make sure that the nitrocellulose adheres to the nail surface. (2) Plasticizers: plasticizers (e.g. camphor) are used to avoid the brittle film formed by nitrocellulose; they are chemicals that link between polymer chains and add to impart flexibility and adhesive property to the film. (3) Solvent: low levels of solvents, including ethyl acetate, butyl acetate, isopropyl alcohol and toluene, are used to help products flow smoothly; quick evaporation of the solvent is important, because slow evaporation causes uneven and streaky application. (b) Colouring agents: pigments, which have non-toxic, non-irritating and non-staining properties; sparkling particles such as mica are added for reflecting properties to nail polishes. (c) Other formulating agents: suspending agents, which avoid sedimentation of the insoluble pigments that tend to settle down at the bottom; thickening agents, added to maintain the sparkling particles in suspension within the bottle; ultraviolet stabilizers, which resist colour changes when the dry film is exposed to direct sunlight; and perfumes, used to mask the odour of other ingredients.

Q: 3. (a) What are adhesives? Classify the adhesives on the basis of reactiveness. (b) Discuss the importance of adhesive in our daily life.

Ans: (a) An adhesive is a substance usually in liquid or semi-liquid state that is used in binding two or more objects together and resists their separation. Adhesives come from either natural or synthetic sources; a large number of materials can be joined by means of adhesives, and they are especially useful for binding thin materials. Adhesives cure (harden) either by evaporating a solvent or by chemical reactions that occur between two or more constituents. Classification on the basis of reactiveness: adhesives are mainly classified into two classes on reactiveness, and the basis of this classification is their method of adhesion. 1. Non-reactive adhesives: these may be of natural or synthetic origin and harden without a chemical reaction. They include (i) drying adhesives, of two types: solvent based adhesives, a mixture of ingredients (typically polymers) dissolved in a solvent, e.g. white glue, contact adhesives and rubber cements, used for binding woods and papers; and polymer dispersion adhesives, also known as emulsion adhesives, milky white dispersions often based on polyvinyl acetate (PVAc), extensively used in the woodworking and packaging industries and with fabrics and engineered products such as loudspeaker cones; (ii) pressure sensitive adhesives (PSA), which form a bond by the application of light pressure, the major raw material being acrylate-based polymers, mainly used in safety labels for power equipment and automotive interior trim assembly; (iii) contact adhesives, used in strong bonds with high shear-resistance like laminates, e.g. bonding formica to a wooden counter and in footwear for attaching outsoles to uppers, e.g. natural rubber and polychloroprene (neoprene); and (iv) hot adhesives, also known as hot melt adhesives (HMA) or thermoplastics, applied in molten form (65-180 C range) which solidify on cooling to form strong bonds, commonly used in bookbinding, packaging, coatings, diapers, other sanitary products and tapes. 2. Reactive adhesives: these adhesives chemically react with the material when they harden. They are of two types: (i) multipart adhesives, which harden by mixing two or more components which chemically react, e.g. polyester resin-polyurethane resin, polyols-polyurethane resins and acrylic polymers-polyurethane resins; and (ii) one part adhesives, which harden through a chemical reaction with an external energy source such as radiation, heat or moisture: light curing adhesives are generally acrylic based and are significantly used in electronics, telecommunications, medical, aerospace, glass and optics; heat curing adhesives include epoxies, urethanes and polyimides; and moisture curing adhesives cure when they react with moisture present on the substrate surface or in the air, and include cyanoacrylates and urethanes. (Adhesives are also classified by origin into synthetic adhesives, e.g. epoxies, polyurethanes, cyanoacrylates, polyimides, silicones, acrylics, polyacrylates, polyvinyl acetate (PVA) and neoprene, and natural adhesives or glues obtained from natural resources such as plants or animals, starch, casein glues or natural rubber.) (b) A number of miscellaneous tasks in our world require gluing together of things. Industrial adhesives are extremely strong and they can be used in place of more complicated repair works, so adhesives reduce the cost. Adhesives are efficient: they do not tamper with the integrity of the substance; in fact, they only make it stronger. They can be applied to any kind of material and are especially useful for binding thin materials, joining materials like wood, paper, fabrics, laminates, footwear and packaging, and in bookbinding, coatings, tapes, labels and sanitary products.

Q: 4. (a) Write down the raw materials in Pakistan for various chemical and petrochemical industries. (b) Discuss the Safety Considerations in Process Industries in detail.

Ans: (a) Raw materials for chemical industries in Pakistan are oil, natural gas, metals, minerals, coal and salt etc. Raw materials for petrochemical industries are methane, ethane, propane and butanes; these are obtained primarily from natural gas processing plants. Gas oil and naphtha are obtained from petroleum refineries, and benzene, toluene and xylene are also primarily obtained from petroleum refineries. Methane, benzene, toluene and xylene are used directly as feedstocks for producing petrochemicals. In general, chemicals are produced from these raw materials (principally minerals, metals and hydrocarbons) in a series of processing steps; oil and gas are today the source of 90% of world organic chemical production, while inorganic chemicals are derived chiefly from mineral sources, e.g. sulphur and chlorine. (b) The following safety considerations in the process industry must be kept in view before launching an industrial activity. (1) To keep away the factory itself from corroding away, proper material of construction should be selected by the designing chemical engineers. (2) To avoid harmful impurities in raw materials, to follow the course of chemical reactions and to secure the requisite yield and purity of products, careful process control by periodic analysis is required, as well as modern instrumentation and automatic control. (3) To transmit goods in a clean and economical manner from the manufacturer to the customer, suitable containers must be used. (4) To ensure the safety of workers and the plant, all procedures must be carried out in a non-hazardous manner. (5) To guarantee progress, to continue profits and to replace obsolescent processes and equipments, much attention and money must be spent upon continuing research and development. (6) To prevent the contamination of water and air, factories must avoid discharge of toxic material into the air and water of their localities. (7) To label the chemicals that can help in identifying the more hazardous chemicals.

Q: 5. (a) Explain the fractional distillation of petroleum. (b) Discuss in detail the importance of the chemical industries in the economy of Pakistan.

Ans: (a) Petroleum in the unrefined form is called crude oil. It is a naturally occurring thick viscous brown or greenish black liquid obtained from the earth's crust. The crude oil consists of different substances (hydrocarbons) which are miscible, so they do not separate out into layers; therefore fractional distillation, carried out in fractionating towers, is used in refining petroleum. Fractional distillation is the process of heating up a mixture containing different substances with different boiling points and after condensation drawing the different fractions off. Each fraction is not a pure compound but a mixture of different hydrocarbons with similar boiling points. Crude oil is first treated to remove the sulphur or sulphur compounds that may be present; the cleaned hydrocarbon material is then heated in a furnace and distilled, and fractions with various boiling ranges are collected from the fractionating column (cooler at the top, about 25 C, hotter at the bottom). The principal fractions are: refinery gas (below 20 C, C1 to C4, used as a fuel and for making other organic compounds); petroleum ether (20-60 C, C5-C6, used as a solvent); light naphtha (60-100 C, C6-C7, used as a solvent and as a raw material for making other petrochemicals); gasoline/petrol (80-180 C, C7-C10, used as a motor fuel); kerosene/paraffin oil (160-300 C, C11-C15, used as a jet fuel and for oil fired domestic heating); heavy oil, i.e. diesel oil and gas oil (250-350 C, C15-C18, used as a fuel for diesel engines and for making greases, vaseline and candles); lubricating oil (300-370 C, C18-C50, used for lubricating heavy machinery); fuel oil (400-600 C, C50-C70, used as fuel for ships and factories and as industrial fuel); and residue/solid mass (above 600 C, more than C70, used for metalling roads). The main goal of refinery operations is the production of gasoline. (b) The chemical industry is the industry involved in the business of making different products from raw materials through chemical reactions, and the chemical sector plays a fundamental role in the economic development of any nation. It converts essential raw materials into more than seventy thousand variety products for industry as well as the goods of consumers that people depend upon in their daily lives. Pakistan trades in chemicals with other countries to earn foreign exchange in the field of chemical industry such as fertilizer, plastics, rubber, medicine, cement, dyes and pigments, soaps and detergents. Chemical industries supply the farmers the pesticides and fertilizers which are essential for crop growing, so the chemical industry contributes to agriculture and food self-sufficiency of the country. In our everyday life we use many industrial products and most of them are related to the chemical industry in some way or the other; the chemical industry produces the synthetic fibres and dyes which are used in the textile industry, it supplies the synthetic sweeteners and synthetic flavours used by food manufacturing companies, and it indirectly helps the pharmaceutical industry and health care industry by providing the essential chemical components. The main sectors of the industry include basic inorganics (acids, alkalies, salts and industrial gases such as oxygen, nitrogen and acetylene), basic organics (feedstocks for plastics, resins, synthetic rubbers and synthetic fibres; solvents and detergent raw materials; dyestuffs and pigments), fertilizers and pesticides, plastics, resins, synthetic rubbers and fibres, pharmaceuticals, paints, varnishes and lacquers, soaps, detergents, cleaning preparations, perfumes and cosmetics, and miscellaneous chemicals such as polishes, explosives, adhesives, inks and photographic film. In short, the chemical industry contributes indirectly to almost every sector of the economy of Pakistan.

mcqs.q: Cracking is a process in which
options: raw material molecules are dissociated into smaller ones
small molecules unite into large ones
naphtha is converted into aromatics only
mcqs.why: The detailed answer defines cracking as a process in which molecules of raw material are dissociated into smaller ones, one of the two basic building block processes.

mcqs.q: Thermal steam cracking of ethane and propane mainly yields
mcqs.why: Steam cracking breaks ethane and propane by heat in the presence of steam, yielding important petrochemical products such as ethene and propene, with methane and hydrogen as by-products.

mcqs.q: In catalytic cracking, gas oil and fuel oil are converted mainly into
mcqs.why: Refinery products such as gas oil and fuel oil are passed through a catalytic cracker to obtain gasoline and kerosene oil as major products and propene as by-product.

mcqs.q: In lipstick preparation, water-soluble dyes are made usable by combining them with
options: aluminium hydroxide, Al(OH)3, to form an insoluble precipitate
mcqs.why: Lipstick dyes must be water-insoluble, so water-soluble dyes are first combined with metal oxides such as aluminium hydroxide to form an insoluble precipitate suspended in the oil base.

mcqs.q: The film former in nail polish is
options: nitrocellulose dissolved in a solvent such as butyl acetate
mcqs.why: Nail polishes are made up of nitrocellulose dissolved in a solvent (e.g. butyl acetate or ethyl acetate), which forms a hard, water-proof, abrasion resistant film on the nail.

mcqs.q: Plasticizers such as camphor are added to nail polish to
options: stop the nitrocellulose film from being brittle and add flexibility
mcqs.why: Plasticizers link between polymer chains and are used to avoid the brittle film formed by nitrocellulose, imparting flexibility and adhesive property to the film.

mcqs.q: Hot adhesives are applied
options: as a solvent solution that dries in air
in molten form at 65-180 C and solidify on cooling
mcqs.why: Hot melt adhesives are thermoplastics applied in molten form in the 65-180 C range which solidify on cooling to form strong bonds, e.g. in bookbinding and packaging.

mcqs.q: The major raw material of pressure sensitive adhesives is
mcqs.why: Pressure sensitive adhesives form a bond by light pressure and the major raw material used in them is acrylate-based polymers, as the adhesives answer states.

mcqs.q: In fractional distillation of petroleum, the gasoline (petrol) fraction has the boiling range
mcqs.why: The fraction table gives gasoline/petrol the boiling range 80-180 C with C7-C10 hydrocarbons, between light naphtha (60-100 C) and kerosene (160-300 C).

mcqs.q: Raw materials for petrochemical industries in Pakistan are obtained primarily from
options: natural gas processing plants and petroleum refineries
mcqs.why: Methane, ethane, propane and butanes come primarily from natural gas processing plants, while gas oil, naphtha, benzene, toluene and xylene come primarily from petroleum refineries.

lessons.title: Project
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Petroleum is a complex mixture of hydrocarbons formed by the decomposition of fossil remains.
  • Petroleum is refined by fractional distillation in fractionating towers into fractions of different boiling ranges.
  • Petrochemicals are produced from feedstocks by cracking and reforming into primary petrochemicals such as ethene, propene, butadiene, benzene, toluene and xylenes.
  • Petrochemicals are the building blocks for plastics, rubbers, fibres, paints, solvents and detergents used in daily life.

Solved Exercises

Project

Q: Project: Use the library or internet to research the petrochemicals. Write a newspaper article about petrochemicals. 1. What are the origin of petroleum?

Ans: Petroleum is a complex mixture of hydrocarbons formed by the decomposition of fossil remains. It exists as a gas (natural gas), liquid (crude oil) or as solids (oil shales) and is found deep underground or below the seabed.

Q: Project: 2. How petroleum is refined? Also, give a touch to the different fractions.

Ans: Petroleum is refined by fractional distillation in fractionating towers: crude oil is first treated to remove sulphur compounds, then heated and separated into fractions of different boiling ranges, namely refinery gas (below 20 C), petroleum ether (20-60 C), naphtha (60-100 C), gasoline (80-180 C), kerosene (160-300 C), diesel oil (250-350 C), lubricating oil (300-370 C), fuel oil (400-600 C) and residue (above 600 C). Further refining processes include cracking and reforming.

Q: Project: 3. How petrochemicals are produced?

Ans: Petrochemicals are produced directly or indirectly from the hydrocarbons of petroleum or natural gas. Feedstocks from natural gas processing plants (methane, ethane, propane, butanes) and from refineries (naphtha, gas oil, benzene, toluene, xylene) are converted by the basic building block processes, cracking and reforming, into primary petrochemicals such as ethene, propene, butadiene, benzene, toluene and xylenes, which are then processed into finished petrochemical products.

Q: Project: 4. Write down the names of some famous petrochemicals.

Ans: Famous petrochemicals and products made from them include ethene, propene, ethyne, butadiene, benzene, toluene and xylenes, and the materials made from petrochemicals: plastics (e.g. polythene, PVC, polypropylene), rubbers, synthetic fibres (e.g. nylon), paints, solvents and detergents.

Q: Project: 5. What are the functions of petrochemicals?

Ans: Petrochemicals serve as the raw materials and building blocks for manufacturing plastics, rubbers, fibres, paints, solvents, detergents and many other chemicals and consumer goods; only about 10% of the petroleum is used to prepare this range of chemicals, the rest being used mainly as fuels.

Q: Project: 6. Why the petrochemicals are so much important in our life?

Ans: Since every area of human activity makes use of petrochemicals or the materials made from them, our life without petrochemicals would be very different and less comfortable: clothing, packaging, transport, housing, medicines, cosmetics and countless daily-use articles depend on petrochemicals and the products derived from them.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Ozone (O3) in the stratosphere absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation and protects life on Earth.
  • Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) destroy the ozone layer and are more dangerous for it than CO2, CO or oxides of nitrogen.
  • The mesosphere is the coldest region of the atmosphere, and the thermosphere is its thickest layer.
  • Photochemical smog is primarily caused by NO2, and the photochemical oxidant PAN forms by the action of oxides of nitrogen on hydrocarbons in the presence of sunlight.
  • Acid rain contains H2SO4 and HNO3; acetic acid (CH3COOH) is not present in acid rain.
  • The quality of water is measured by dissolved oxygen (DO), biological oxygen demand (BOD) and chemical oxygen demand (COD).
  • Alum is the flocculating agent used in the purification of water.
  • Green chemistry works to prevent waste creation, maximize atom economy and create less hazardous synthetic chemicals.

Solved Exercises

Exercise: Multiple Choice Questions

Q: Which one of the following is not a secondary pollutant?

Options: (a) O3 (b) H2CO3 (c) H2SO4 (d) CO2

Correct answer: CO2

Q: The coldest region of atmosphere is

Options: (a) troposphere (b) thermosphere (c) stratosphere (d) mesosphere

Correct answer: mesosphere

Q: Ozone layer in upper atmosphere is being destroyed by

Options: (a) chlorofluorocarbons (b) SO2 (c) smog (d) photochemical oxidant

Correct answer: chlorofluorocarbons

Q: Drained sewage has BOD

Options: (a) more than that of water (b) less than that of water (c) equal to that of water (d) none of above

Correct answer: more than that of water

Q: Photochemical smog is primarily caused by

Options: (a) CO (b) CO2 (c) O3 (d) NO2

Correct answer: NO2

Q: Result of ozone hole is

Options: (a) acid rain (b) global warming (c) increased amount of CO2 (d) greater exposure of Earth to U.V.

Correct answer: greater exposure of Earth to U.V.

Q: Which one of the following substances is not present in acid rain?

Options: (a) H2SO4 (b) HNO3 (c) H2SO3 (d) CH3COOH

Correct answer: CH3COOH

Q: Photochemical oxidant PAN is formed by

Options: (a) the action of oxide of nitrogen on hydrocarbons in presence of sunlight (b) action of carbon dioxide on hydrocarbon in presence of sunlight (c) action of hydrogen sulphide on hydrocarbon in presence of sunlight (d) action of SO2 and hydrocarbons

Correct answer: the action of oxide of nitrogen on hydrocarbons in presence of sunlight

Q: Which two main gases are produced when you burn a piece of wood?

Options: (a) Oxygen and nitrogen (b) Carbon dioxide and oxygen (c) Carbon dioxide and steam (d) Carbon dioxide and nitrogen

Correct answer: Carbon dioxide and steam

Q: The temperature range of troposphere is

Options: (a) 15 to -56 (b) 56 to -2 (c) -2 to -92 (d) -92 to 1200

Correct answer: 15 to -56

Q: In which of the following layer of atmosphere there is more thickness of the layer? (Note: the printed answer key gives (b) for this question, which is wrong.)

Options: (a) Troposphere (b) Stratosphere (c) Mesosphere (d) Thermosphere

Correct answer: Thermosphere

Q: Which of the following is more dangerous for the ozone layer?

Options: (a) CFCs (b) CO2 (c) CO (d) Oxides of nitrogen

Correct answer: CFCs

Q: Which of the following factors help to measure the quality of water?

Options: (a) DO (b) BOD (c) COD (d) All of the above

Correct answer: All of the above

Q: In the purification of water the flocculating agent used is

Options: (a) alum (b) nickel sulphate (c) copper sulphate (d) barium sulphate

Correct answer: alum

Q: The basic principle of green chemistry is/are

Options: (a) to prevent waste creation (b) to maximize the atom economy (c) to create less hazardous synthetic chemicals (d) all of the above

Correct answer: all of the above

mcqs.q: Which one of the following is not a secondary pollutant?
mcqs.why: CO2 is a primary pollutant released directly from combustion, whereas O3, H2CO3 and H2SO4 are secondary pollutants formed later by reactions in the atmosphere.

mcqs.q: The coldest region of atmosphere is
mcqs.why: The mesosphere (50-85 km) has the lowest temperature range, falling to -92 deg C, so the book's solved answers call it the coldest region of the atmosphere.

mcqs.q: Ozone layer in upper atmosphere is being destroyed by
mcqs.why: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) rise into the stratosphere, are broken down by UV rays and release halogen radicals that destroy ozone catalytically, as explained in the unit's detailed answers.

mcqs.q: Drained sewage has BOD
options: about half that of clean water
mcqs.why: Drained sewage carries a heavy load of biodegradable organic matter, so the oxygen demanded by organisms to oxidize it (its BOD) is more than that of ordinary water.

mcqs.q: Photochemical smog is primarily caused by
mcqs.why: Photochemical smog forms when nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds react in sunlight; NO2 is photolysed by UV to give the oxygen atoms that form ozone, the primary component of the smog.

mcqs.q: Result of ozone hole is
options: greater exposure of Earth to U.V.
mcqs.why: Thinning of the ozone layer (the ozone hole) lets more harmful ultraviolet radiation reach the Earth's surface, creating health problems for humans and harming plants and animals.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following substances is not present in acid rain?
mcqs.why: Acid rain is formed from SO2 and NOx and contains the strong acids H2SO4 and HNO3 (with H2SO3 as an intermediate); acetic acid, CH3COOH, is not a constituent of acid rain.

mcqs.q: Photochemical oxidant PAN is formed by
options: the action of oxide of nitrogen on hydrocarbons in presence of sunlight
action of carbon dioxide on hydrocarbon in presence of sunlight
action of hydrogen sulphide on hydrocarbon in presence of sunlight
mcqs.why: Peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN), a constituent of photochemical smog, forms when oxides of nitrogen react with hydrocarbons (VOCs) in the presence of sunlight: NO2 + VOC -> PAN.

mcqs.q: Which two main gases are produced when you burn a piece of wood?
mcqs.why: Wood is an organic (carbon and hydrogen containing) fuel; its combustion produces carbon dioxide from its carbon and steam (water vapour) from its hydrogen.

mcqs.q: The temperature range of troposphere is
mcqs.why: The troposphere extends from 0-14 km and its temperature falls from 15 deg C at the surface to -56 deg C at its top, as given in the unit's table of atmospheric layers.

mcqs.q: In which of the following layer of atmosphere there is more thickness of the layer?
mcqs.why: The printed answer key gives (b) Stratosphere for this question, which is wrong. From the book's own Table 23.1 thicknesses: troposphere 0-14 km, stratosphere 10-50 km (about 40 km), mesosphere 50-85 km (35 km), but the thermosphere spans 85-500 km (about 415 km), so the thermosphere is by far the thickest layer.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is more dangerous for the ozone layer?
mcqs.why: CFCs are very stable, reach the stratosphere and release halogen radicals that destroy ozone catalytically, so one CFC molecule can destroy many ozone molecules; they are the most dangerous of the listed gases for the ozone layer.

mcqs.q: Which of the following factors help to measure the quality of water?
mcqs.why: Water quality is measured through dissolved oxygen (DO), biological oxygen demand (BOD) and chemical oxygen demand (COD) together, since each of these factors shows how much oxygen the water holds or demands.

mcqs.q: In the purification of water the flocculating agent used is
mcqs.why: In primary water treatment, alum, aluminium sulphate Al2(SO4)3, is added with lime to form a gelatinous Al(OH)3 precipitate that traps colloidal particles and bacteria so they can be filtered out.

mcqs.q: The basic principle of green chemistry is/are
options: to create less hazardous synthetic chemicals
Preventing waste creation, maximizing the atom economy and creating less hazardous synthetic chemicals
mcqs.why: The basic principles of green chemistry include all three listed ideas together: preventing waste instead of cleaning it up later, maximizing atom economy so the product contains the maximum proportion of starting material, and designing less hazardous chemical syntheses.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Acid rain is precipitation with pH less than 5.6; normal rain has pH about 5.6 because dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid.
  • Acid rain contains H2SO4 and HNO3, which attack the CaCO3 of marble and limestone in historical monuments.
  • BOD is the amount of oxygen required by living organisms for the oxidation of biodegradable organic matter in water under aerobic conditions.
  • Dissolved oxygen is essential for aquatic aerobic organisms, and sewage discharge and thermal pollution lower its level.
  • SO2 pollution is reduced by using low-sulphur fuels and by controlling and treating industrial and power-station emissions before release.
  • CFCs are more effective greenhouse gases than CO2 because they absorb infrared radiation strongly and stay in the atmosphere for a long time.
  • A 3-way catalytic converter changes NOx, CO and hydrocarbons into the harmless gases N2, CO2 and H2O.

Solved Exercises

Exercise: Short Answer Questions

Q: Q2 (i) Why is acid rain considered as a threat to historical monuments?

Ans: Acid rain contains H2SO4 and HNO3 formed from SO2 and NOx. These acids attack the calcium carbonate (CaCO3) of marble and limestone used in historical buildings and monuments: CaCO3(s) + H2SO4(aq) -> CaSO4(ppt) + CO2 + H2O. The stone surface is slowly eaten away, so buildings, monuments and statues are corroded and damaged, as has happened to the Taj Mahal.

Q: Q2 (ii) Define the following: (a) Contaminants (b) Pollutant (c) Acid rain (d) Biological oxygen demand (BOD) (e) Smog

Ans: (a) Contaminants: The unwanted substances present in a substance or in the environment which make it impure and unfit for use, e.g. the chemicals, bacteria and other pollutants present in wastewater. (b) Pollutant: Any substance which contaminates our environment is called a pollutant, e.g. CO, SO2, NOx and VOCs in air. (c) Acid rain: All precipitation (rain, snow or dew) having pH less than 5.6 is called acid rain. It is produced mainly by the emission of SO2 and NOx, which form H2SO4 and HNO3 in rain water. (d) Biological oxygen demand (BOD): It is the amount of oxygen required by living organisms to survive and for the oxidation of biodegradable organic matter present in water under aerobic conditions. It is an indirect measurement of the quantity of biodegradable organic matter in water. (e) Smog: Smog is the combination of smoke and fog. It produces a yellow-brown colour in the atmosphere near the ground level, which results in poor visibility in the area.

Q: Q2 (iii) What is importance of dissolved oxygen in water?

Ans: Dissolved oxygen (DO) provides a source of oxygen for aquatic aerobic (oxygen-requiring) organisms like fish and aerobic bacteria, so it is essential for aquatic life. An important aspect of water quality is the amount of dissolved oxygen in it. Discharge of sewage and organic waste reduces the dissolved oxygen, and thermal pollution also lowers its level, which affects the biological activity, growth and survival of the organisms living in natural water bodies.

Q: Q2 (iv) How we can reduce pollution due to SO2?

Ans: SO2 is produced mainly by the burning of coal and the smelting of metals, because the sulphur present in coal is converted to SO2 during combustion. Its pollution can be reduced by using low-sulphur fuels: the sulphur content of refined petroleum is generally quite low, while that of coal is quite high, so replacing coal with low-sulphur fuels cuts SO2 emission. SO2 emission from industries and power stations should also be controlled and treated before release, because SO2 is oxidized to the sulphuric acid aerosol which is the major contributor to acid rain and damages the lungs.

Q: Q2 (v) Write any four principles of Green Chemistry.

Ans: Any four of the twelve principles are: (1) Prevent waste: design a process to prevent the generation of waste instead of later on treating and cleaning up the waste. (2) Atom economy: design syntheses so that the final product contains the maximum proportion of the starting material, i.e. maximize the incorporation of all materials used in the process into the final product. (3) Design less hazardous chemical syntheses: wherever possible, design to use and generate substances that possess little or no toxicity to humans or to the environment. (4) Designing safer chemicals: chemical products should be designed to deliver their desired function while minimizing their toxicity.

Q: Q2 (vi) Name four major greenhouse gases.

Ans: Four major greenhouse gases are carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O) and ozone (O3). The unit also lists SO2 and CFCs among the gases contributing to the greenhouse effect; CO2 alone contributes about 50% to the greenhouse effect.

Q: Q2 (vii) Out of CFCs and CO2 which one has higher potential to cause global warming and why?

Ans: CFCs have the higher potential. Apart from destroying the ozone layer, CFCs are also greenhouse gases and are more effective than CO2 as greenhouse gases, molecule for molecule. They absorb the infrared radiation emitted by the Earth very strongly and, being very stable, they stay in the atmosphere for a long time, so even a small amount of CFCs traps much more heat than the same amount of CO2.

Q: Q2 (viii) Why does the rain water normally have pH of about 5.6 and when does it change into acid rain?

Ans: Rain water is normally slightly acidic (pH = 5.6) because the CO2 present in the atmosphere (0.036%) dissolves in it and forms carbonic acid: H2O + CO2 -> H2CO3. When pollutants such as SO2 and NOx (NO and NO2), emitted mainly by the burning of fossil fuels, also dissolve and react with water and oxygen to form the much stronger acids H2SO4 and HNO3 (SO2 + H2O + 1/2 O2 -> H2SO4; 4NO2 + 2H2O + O2 -> 4HNO3), the pH falls below 5.6 and the rain is then called acid rain.

Q: Q2 (ix) Which gases are converted to harmless gases by 3-way catalytic converter?

Ans: The three automobile exhaust pollutants NOx, CO and hydrocarbons (HCs) are converted into the relatively harmless gases nitrogen (N2), carbon dioxide (CO2) and water (H2O). The reduction catalyst (platinum and rhodium) converts oxides of nitrogen to N2 and O2: 2NO -> N2 + O2 and 2NO2 -> N2 + 2O2. The oxidation catalyst (platinum and palladium) then converts CO and hydrocarbons to CO2 and water: 2CO + O2 -> 2CO2 and HC + O2 -> CO2 + H2O.

mcqs.q: Acid rain damages marble and limestone monuments mainly because its acids react with which substance in the stone?
mcqs.why: The H2SO4 and HNO3 of acid rain attack the calcium carbonate (CaCO3) of marble and limestone: CaCO3 + H2SO4 -> CaSO4 + CO2 + H2O, so the stone surface is slowly eaten away, as happened to the Taj Mahal.

mcqs.q: Precipitation is called acid rain when its pH is
mcqs.why: All precipitation (rain, snow or dew) having pH less than 5.6 is called acid rain; it is produced mainly by emissions of SO2 and NOx, which form H2SO4 and HNO3 in rain water.

mcqs.q: Biological oxygen demand (BOD) is an indirect measurement of
options: the quantity of biodegradable organic matter in water
the amount of dissolved oxygen in water
mcqs.why: BOD is the amount of oxygen required by living organisms for the oxidation of biodegradable organic matter in water under aerobic conditions, so it indirectly measures the quantity of that biodegradable matter.

mcqs.q: Smog, the combination of smoke and fog, produces which colour in the atmosphere near ground level?
mcqs.why: Smog is the combination of smoke and fog and produces a yellow-brown colour in the atmosphere near ground level, which results in poor visibility in the area.

mcqs.q: Which of the following lowers the dissolved oxygen level of natural water bodies?
options: Discharge of sewage and organic waste
mcqs.why: Dissolved oxygen is essential for aquatic aerobic organisms; discharge of sewage and organic waste reduces it, and thermal pollution also lowers its level, affecting the growth and survival of aquatic organisms.

mcqs.q: SO2 is produced mainly by
options: burning of coal and smelting of metals
mcqs.why: SO2 is produced mainly by the burning of coal and the smelting of metals, because the sulphur present in coal is converted to SO2 during combustion.

mcqs.q: SO2 pollution can be reduced by using low-sulphur fuels because
options: the sulphur content of coal is quite low
the sulphur content of refined petroleum is generally quite low while that of coal is quite high
sulphur is removed by the chimney
mcqs.why: Replacing coal with low-sulphur fuels cuts SO2 emission because the sulphur content of refined petroleum is generally quite low, while that of coal is quite high.

mcqs.q: Which greenhouse gas alone contributes about 50% to the greenhouse effect?
mcqs.why: The four major greenhouse gases are CO2, CH4, N2O and O3, and CO2 alone contributes about 50% to the greenhouse effect.

mcqs.q: CFCs have a higher global-warming potential than CO2 because they
options: are present in larger amounts than CO2
absorb infrared radiation very strongly and stay in the atmosphere for a long time
mcqs.why: Apart from destroying ozone, CFCs are more effective greenhouse gases than CO2 molecule for molecule: they absorb the infrared radiation emitted by the Earth very strongly and, being very stable, remain in the atmosphere for a long time.

mcqs.q: In a 3-way catalytic converter, the reduction catalyst that converts oxides of nitrogen to N2 and O2 is made of
mcqs.why: The reduction catalyst (platinum and rhodium) converts oxides of nitrogen to N2 and O2 (2NO -> N2 + O2), while the oxidation catalyst (platinum and palladium) converts CO and hydrocarbons to CO2 and water.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Green chemistry, based on the 12 principles of Anastas and Warner, prevents pollution at the source instead of cleaning it up afterwards.
  • Greenhouse gases absorb the infrared radiation emitted by the Earth and redirect it back, causing the greenhouse effect and global warming.
  • The atmosphere has five layers: troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere.
  • Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin 320 times more tightly than O2, and above 750 ppm it may cause loss of consciousness or death.
  • Ozone forms in the stratosphere by photodissociation of O2 (wavelength less than 242 nm) followed by O + O2 -> O3, most suitably at 25-30 km altitude.
  • Wastewater treatment has four stages: screening, primary treatment, secondary treatment and tertiary (final) treatment.
  • One CFC molecule can destroy many ozone molecules because the halogen radical is regenerated in the catalytic cycle.

Solved Exercises

Exercise: Detailed Answer Questions

Q: Q3. 1 (i) 'Green Chemistry is a new route to the protection of environment'. Comment on it.

Ans: The statement is correct. Green chemistry (sustainable chemistry) is defined as the invention, design and application of chemical products and processes to reduce or eliminate the use and generation of substances hazardous to humans, animals, plants and the environment. Its aim is to reduce the chemical-related impact on human health and to virtually eliminate contaminants of the environment through dedicated sustainable prevention programs. Instead of cleaning up pollution after it is produced, green chemistry prevents it at the source: it searches for alternative, environmentally friendly reaction media, and at the same time strives to increase the reaction rate and lower the reaction temperature. It is based on the 12 principles proposed by Anastas and Warner, such as prevention of waste, maximum atom economy, less hazardous chemical syntheses, safer chemicals and solvents, energy efficiency, use of renewable feedstock, use of catalysts, designing chemicals that degrade after use, real-time analysis to prevent pollution and minimizing the potential for accidents. Following these principles in designing new chemical products, syntheses and processes is therefore a new and effective route to the protection of the environment.

Q: Q3. 1 (ii) What is greenhouse effect? How is it causing global warming?

Ans: The Earth receives mostly visible radiation from the sun and gets heated. It emits most of its heat in the form of infrared (IR) radiation. Some gases present in the atmosphere, the greenhouse gases (CO2, CH4, SO2, N2O, O3 and others), absorb this heat and redirect it back to the Earth. These gases trap the heat into the atmosphere, which results in an increase in the Earth's temperature. This is called the greenhouse effect, because these gases behave like the glass cover of a greenhouse, which maintains the temperature of the greenhouse used to cultivate vegetation in cold climate regions. Global warming is the gradual increase in the average temperature of the Earth's atmosphere and its oceans. Human activities are increasing the atmospheric concentration of CO2 (which contributes about 50% to the greenhouse effect) and other greenhouse gases, thereby strengthening the greenhouse effect. The Earth's average temperature is thus being increased (global warming), which ultimately changes our climates; the most serious outcomes would be a rise in sea level, floods and a changed pattern of rainfall.

Q: Q3. 2 (i) What is meant by atmosphere? Explain the various layers of atmosphere.

Ans: Atmosphere is the envelope (blanket) of gases surrounding the Earth's surface. It plays a key role to sustain life on Earth and saves it from the hazardous environment of outer space: it absorbs most of the cosmic rays from outer space and harmful radiations such as U.V. through the ozone (O3) layer, and it maintains the heat balance of the Earth through absorption of energy from the sun and its re-emission. Based on temperature and characteristics, the atmosphere is divided into five layers. (1) Troposphere: altitude 0-14 km, temperature range 15 to -56 deg C; it contains N2, O2, CO2, H2O and Ar, and is the part we live in. (2) Stratosphere: altitude 10-50 km, temperature range -56 to -2 deg C; it contains the ozone (O3) layer, N2 and O2. (3) Mesosphere: altitude 50-85 km, temperature range -2 to -92 deg C; it contains NO+ and O2+; it is the coldest region of the atmosphere. (4) Thermosphere: altitude 85-500 km, temperature range -92 to 1200 deg C; it contains O2+, NO+, O and O+. (5) Exosphere: altitude 500-10,000 km, temperature above 1500 deg C; it contains H, He, N2, O2 and CO2.

Q: Q3. 2 (ii) Define air pollution and discuss its effects.

Ans: Air pollution is the contamination of air by pollutants. An air pollutant generally refers to substances that on local and regional scales directly harm animals, plants and people and their artifacts. The main air pollutants released by the combustion of hydrocarbon-based fuels and other human activities are CO, SO2 (SOx), nitrogen oxides (NOx), volatile organic compounds (VOCs) and ground-level O3. Their effects are serious. Carbon monoxide from incomplete combustion is a colourless, odourless, toxic gas; it binds to haemoglobin 320 times more tightly than O2, and at concentrations above 750 ppm it may cause loss of consciousness or death. SO2 is a lung irritant; its oxidation product, sulphuric acid aerosol, swells and blocks the fine vessels of the pulmonary region and is the major contributor to acid rain. NOx causes respiratory diseases, forms smog and the typical brown haze over large cities, contributes to acid rain and forms ground-level ozone, which damages animal and plant life and causes forest damage. Ground-level ozone produces cracks in rubber, destroys plants and causes respiratory distress and eye irritation in humans at about 100 ppb. Pollutants also form industrial and photochemical smog, and increased CO2 causes the greenhouse effect, global warming and climate change.

Q: Q3. 3 (i) What is role of ozone layer in upper atmosphere?

Ans: The ozone layer lies in the stratosphere (11-50 km above the Earth's surface), where ozone (O3) is formed by photodissociation of oxygen: O2 + hv (wavelength less than 242 nm) -> 2O, followed by O + O2 -> O3. The ozone layer acts as a protective shield (layer) for the survival of life on Earth: it absorbs the harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiations from the sun and does not allow them to reach the Earth's surface, thus protecting us from the harmful effects of these radiations. Its concentration depends on the relative rates of its formation and destruction reactions (O3 + hv -> O2 + O, and O3 + O -> 2O2), which keep a natural balance.

Q: Q3. 3 (ii) What will happen if ozone is no more present in upper atmosphere?

Ans: If ozone is no more present in the upper atmosphere, the harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiations of the sun will no longer be absorbed in the stratosphere and will reach the Earth's surface in much greater amount. This greater exposure of the Earth to U.V. creates human health problems, such as increased risk of skin diseases and other radiation damage, and also harms plants and animals. This is exactly what happens on ozone depletion (the ozone hole): the gradual thinning of the ozone layer by CFCs and other halocarbons increases the amount of U.V. radiation reaching the Earth's surface, which creates health problems for humans and disturbs life on Earth.

Q: Q3. 4 What is water pollution? What are the main sources of water pollution?

Ans: Water pollution is any change in the physical, chemical or biological properties of water that will have harmful effects on humans, the environment and the ecosystem. It is the contamination of water bodies (lakes, oceans, seas, rivers and groundwater), usually caused by human activities such as agricultural, industrial and mining activities. The main sources of water pollution are: (i) Domestic effluents and sewage: municipal sewage from houses, commercial buildings and institutions contains soap and detergent remains, biodegradable organic matter, coliform bacteria and pathogens; it reduces the dissolved oxygen content and makes water unfit for drinking and public use. (ii) Industrial effluents: industries such as sugar mills, pulp and paper mills, textile, oil refineries and tanneries discharge non-degradable organic substances and toxic pollutants like asbestos, lead, mercury, arsenic, cadmium, nitrates, phosphates and sulphates into natural waterways. (iii) Agricultural effluents: soil and silt removed by erosion, run-off of synthetic fertilizers, herbicides, pesticides and insecticides, and drainage from poultry farms. (iv) Radioactive waste and mining: ore-washings, acid drainage from mines, arsenic residues from gold mines, and radioactive waste from mining and refining of uranium and thorium. (v) Thermal pollution: heavy industries discharge hot water used as coolant into natural water bodies, which decreases the dissolved oxygen level. (vi) Oil pollution.

Q: Q3. 5 (a) Write note on: Acid rain

Ans: Acid rain, also called acid precipitation or acid deposition, is precipitation possessing a pH of about 5.6 or below. Rain water is generally slightly acidic (pH = 5.6) due to the dissolved CO2, which forms carbonic acid (H2O + CO2 -> H2CO3). Acid rain is primarily produced from the emission of sulphur dioxide (SO2) and nitrogenous oxides (NOx; the combination of NO and NO2) from human activities, mainly the burning of fossil fuels. These react with water, oxygen and other chemicals to form sulphuric acid and nitric acid: SO2 + H2O + 1/2 O2 -> H2SO4 and 4NO2 + 2H2O + O2 -> 4HNO3, which then mix with water and fall on the ground as acid rain, sometimes quite far from the source of pollution due to long-range transport by wind. Its effects are severe: it contaminates drinking water, is a serious threat to plants, animals and aquatic life (high acidity kills fish, reduces their growth, causes reproductive failure, prevents hatching of fish eggs and kills green algae and beneficial bacteria), it dissolves heavy metals e.g. Cu, Hg and Pb producing toxic effects, it inhibits plant growth, and it corrodes buildings, monuments, statues and metals, e.g. H2SO4 destroys the CaCO3 of building material.

Q: Q3. 5 (b) Write note on: Smog

Ans: The word smog is the combination of smoke and fog. It produces a yellow-brown colour in the atmosphere near the ground level, which results in poor visibility in the area. There are two major types of smog. (1) Industrial smog: it forms in areas with high water vapours and is caused by the burning of coal, vehicular emission and industrial fumes. It contains carbon particles like smoke, sulphur dioxide (SO2) and other compounds; SO2 gradually reacts further to form SO3, which in the presence of water vapours forms droplets of H2SO4 (SO3 + H2O -> H2SO4), which is corrosive to materials like building stones and to the human respiratory tract. Soot (primarily particles of carbon) gives smoke its persistent dark colour. (2) Photochemical smog: it forms when pollutants from automobile and industrial exhausts, such as nitrogen oxides and organic compounds (VOCs), react together in the presence of sunlight and produce ozone gas, a primary component of photochemical smog: NO + VOC -> NO2; NO2 + UV -> NO + O; O + O2 -> O3; NO2 + VOC -> PAN etc.; net reaction NO + VOC + O2 + UV -> O3 + PAN. It is characterized by an accumulation of brown, hazy fumes over the horizon. Peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN) is a relatively common smog constituent; it irritates the lungs and eyes, and ground-level ozone is hazardous to human health and, being a greenhouse gas, produces global warming.

Q: Q3. 5 (c) Write note on: Water treatment

Ans: Wastewater is full of contaminants such as chemicals, bacteria and other pollutants. Wastewater treatment is the process used to remove contaminants from wastewater or sewage and convert it into an effluent that can be returned to the water cycle with minimum impact on the environment. It takes place in a wastewater treatment plant in four stages. Stage-I, Screening: screening or filtering removes large floating solid objects like broken bottles, plastic objects, shopping bags, cloth pieces and stones that may block or damage the equipment. Stage-II, Primary treatment: the wastewater is put into large settlement tanks; the finer colloidal particles that make water turbid cannot be removed by simple filtration, so a flocculating agent, commonly aluminium sulphate Al2(SO4)3 (alum), is added with some lime Ca(OH)2 to produce a gelatinous precipitate of aluminium hydroxide: Al2(SO4)3 + 3Ca(OH)2 -> 2Al(OH)3(ppt) + 3CaSO4. This precipitate traps both inorganic solid particles and bacteria in the large curd-like particles, which are then easily removed by filtration through a sand-bed or charcoal; heavy particles sink to the bottom as sludge and are treated separately. Stage-III, Secondary treatment: the water is put into large rectangular tanks, where air is pumped into the water so that the bacteria break down the tiny bits of sludge. Stage-IV, Tertiary or final treatment: the almost treated wastewater is passed through a settlement tank, more sludge is formed and scraped off, and the water is filtered to remove additional particles. After that the filtered water is discharged into a river. If the water is treated for drinking purposes, it is disinfected by chlorination, ozone treatment or ultraviolet light to eliminate disease-causing organisms; air is sometimes blown through the water to improve its odour and taste, and a fluoride compound is added in some plants to help fight tooth decay. The result of a thorough water treatment operation is water that is as good as new.

Q: Q3. 5 (d) Write note on: Chemistry of stratosphere

Ans: The stratosphere is the part of the atmosphere which extends from 11-50 km above the Earth's surface, and its temperature ranges from -56 deg C to -2 deg C, increasing with increasing altitude. The important chemical species that exists in this sphere is ozone (O3), which acts as a protective shield (layer) for the survival of life on Earth from the harmful effects of the sun's UV radiations. Production of ozone results from the breaking of the chemical bond of the oxygen molecule (O2) by high-energy solar (UV) radiations; this process, called photodissociation, releases single oxygen atoms: O2 + hv (wavelength less than 242 nm) -> 2O. The oxygen atoms then combine with oxygen molecules to form ozone: O + O2 -> O3. Conditions most suitable for ozone formation are found at intermediate altitude (between 25 and 30 km). Ozone is also destroyed by solar radiation: O3 + hv -> O2 + O, and O3 + O -> 2O2, so its concentration depends on the relative rates of the formation and destruction reactions. Depletion of the ozone layer is the gradual thinning of Earth's ozone layer in the upper atmosphere due to the release of chemical compounds containing chlorine or bromine (CFCs and other halocarbons) from industries and other human activities. CFCs are very stable molecules; they rise into the stratosphere, where they are eventually broken down by UV rays, releasing a free halogen atom or free radical (X.). The free halogen atom reacts with ozone and destroys it catalytically: X. + O3 -> XO + O2; XO + O -> X. + O2; overall reaction O3 + O -> 2O2. Because the radical is regenerated, one CFC molecule can destroy many ozone molecules, increasing the amount of U.V. radiation reaching the Earth's surface.

mcqs.q: Green chemistry is based on how many principles proposed by Anastas and Warner?
mcqs.why: Green chemistry is based on the 12 principles proposed by Anastas and Warner, such as prevention of waste, maximum atom economy, less hazardous syntheses, energy efficiency and use of catalysts.

mcqs.q: In the greenhouse effect, greenhouse gases trap heat in the atmosphere by absorbing
options: infrared radiation emitted by the Earth
mcqs.why: The Earth emits most of its heat as infrared (IR) radiation; greenhouse gases such as CO2, CH4, N2O and O3 absorb this heat and redirect it back to the Earth, raising its temperature.

mcqs.q: Which layer of the atmosphere contains the ionic species NO+ and O2+ and spans 50-85 km?
mcqs.why: The mesosphere spans 50-85 km with temperature range -2 to -92 deg C and contains NO+ and O2+; it is the coldest region of the atmosphere.

mcqs.q: Carbon monoxide is dangerous because it binds to haemoglobin
options: at the same strength as O2
only in the presence of sunlight
mcqs.why: CO from incomplete combustion is a colourless, odourless, toxic gas that binds to haemoglobin 320 times more tightly than O2, and at concentrations above 750 ppm it may cause loss of consciousness or death.

mcqs.q: Ozone is formed in the stratosphere when O2 undergoes photodissociation by radiation of wavelength
mcqs.why: Ozone formation begins with photodissociation of oxygen: O2 + hv (wavelength less than 242 nm) -> 2O, followed by O + O2 -> O3.

mcqs.q: Conditions most suitable for ozone formation are found at an altitude of
mcqs.why: The unit's note on the chemistry of the stratosphere states that conditions most suitable for ozone formation are found at intermediate altitude, between 25 and 30 km.

mcqs.q: In industrial smog, the corrosive droplets of H2SO4 form by the reaction
mcqs.why: In industrial smog, SO2 gradually reacts further to form SO3, which in the presence of water vapours forms droplets of H2SO4 (SO3 + H2O -> H2SO4), corrosive to building stones and the human respiratory tract.

mcqs.q: In primary wastewater treatment, adding alum with lime produces a gelatinous precipitate of
mcqs.why: Al2(SO4)3 + 3Ca(OH)2 -> 2Al(OH)3 (ppt) + 3CaSO4; the gelatinous aluminium hydroxide precipitate traps inorganic solid particles and bacteria in large curd-like particles that are removed by filtration.

mcqs.q: During secondary wastewater treatment, air is pumped into the water so that
options: bacteria break down the tiny bits of sludge
fluoride is dissolved in the water
mcqs.why: In Stage-III (secondary treatment) the water is put into large rectangular tanks where air is pumped in so that bacteria break down the tiny bits of sludge; disinfection by chlorination comes later, in treatment for drinking purposes.

mcqs.q: One CFC molecule can destroy many ozone molecules because
options: each CFC molecule contains many chlorine atoms
the halogen radical is regenerated in the cycle X. + O3 -> XO + O2 and XO + O -> X. + O2
CFCs convert ozone into oxygen permanently
mcqs.why: The free halogen atom destroys ozone catalytically: X. + O3 -> XO + O2, then XO + O -> X. + O2; because the radical X. is regenerated, one CFC molecule can destroy many ozone molecules (overall: O3 + O -> 2O2).

lessons.title: Project
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • In the bottle filtration apparatus, the upper cut part of the bottle works as a funnel and the lower part as the receiving part.
  • Cotton is placed at the mouth of the bottle as a plug and washed, dried sand is put above the cotton plug.
  • The sand layer and cotton plug act as a filter and trap the suspended solid particles, mud and other undissolved impurities of the muddy water.
  • The water collected in the receiving part is filtered water, seen as clean and transparent as fresh water, just as suspended solids are removed by filtration in water treatment.

Solved Exercises

Project

Q: Project: To build a water filtration apparatus. Take a soft drink plastic bottle, cut it in the middle leaving the lower part a little longer than the upper one. The upper part will be used as funnel and the lower part as receiving part. Put some cotton at the mouth of the bottle as a plug and some sand above the cotton plug (the sand must be washed and dried beforehand so as to remove any dust or water-soluble substances). Put this funnel in the receiving part and add some muddy water slowly in it. What do you observe?

Ans: The muddy water slowly passes through the sand layer and the cotton plug. The sand and cotton act as a filter: the suspended solid particles, mud and other undissolved impurities of the water are trapped in the sand bed and the cotton plug, just as suspended solids are removed by filtration in water treatment. The water collected in the lower (receiving) part is the filtered water, which is seen as clean and transparent as the fresh water.
