lessons.title: Practice Problem 12.1
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • In combustion analysis, %C = (mass of CO2 / mass of compound) x (12.011 / 44.010) x 100.
  • In combustion analysis, %H = (mass of H2O / mass of compound) x (2.0158 / 18.0153) x 100, and %O is found by difference from 100.
  • For vanillin, combustion of 2.50 g gives %C = 63.20, %H = 5.32 and %O = 31.48.
  • Dividing the mole numbers by the smallest value and multiplying to whole numbers gives vanillin the empirical formula C8H8O3.
  • The empirical formula mass of vanillin is 152.15 amu, equal to its molecular mass, so n = 1 and its molecular formula is also C8H8O3.
  • For glucose, the mole ratio C : H : O is 1 : 2 : 1, giving the empirical formula CH2O of mass 30.03 amu.
  • For glucose, n = 180 / 30.03 = 6, so the molecular formula is C6H12O6.

Solved Exercises

Practice Problem 12.1

Q: Vanillin, a flavoring agent, is made up of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen atoms. When a sample of vanillin weighing 2.50 g burns in oxygen, 5.79 g of carbon dioxide and 1.188 g of water are obtained. The molecular mass of vanillin determined from mass spectrometry is 152.15 amu. Calculate the empirical and molecular formulae of vanillin.

Ans: Given: mass of vanillin sample = 2.50 g
Mass of CO2 produced = 5.79 g
Mass of H2O produced = 1.188 g
Molecular mass of vanillin = 152.15 amu
Formula: %C = (mass of CO2 produced / mass of organic compound) x (12.011 / 44.010) x 100
Substitution: %C = (5.79 / 2.50) x (12.011 / 44.010) x 100 = 63.20%
Formula: %H = (mass of H2O produced / mass of organic compound) x (2.0158 / 18.0153) x 100
Substitution: %H = (1.188 / 2.50) x (2.0158 / 18.0153) x 100 = 5.32%
Formula: %O = 100 - (%C + %H)
Substitution: %O = 100 - (63.20 + 5.32) = 31.48%
Moles of C = 63.20 / 12.011 = 5.26
Moles of H = 5.32 / 1.0079 = 5.28
Moles of O = 31.48 / 15.9994 = 1.97
Simplest ratio (dividing each by the smallest, 1.97): C : H : O = 2.67 : 2.68 : 1
Multiplying by 3 to get whole numbers: C : H : O = 8 : 8 : 3
Empirical formula = C8H8O3
Empirical formula mass = 8(12.011) + 8(1.0079) + 3(15.9994) = 152.15 amu
Formula: n = molecular mass / empirical formula mass = 152.15 / 152.15 = 1
Molecular formula = n x empirical formula = 1 x (C8H8O3)
Answer: Empirical formula = C8H8O3, Molecular formula = C8H8O3

Q: Glucose has C = 39.99%, H = 6.72% and O = 53.2%. Molecular mass of glucose is 180 amu. Calculate its empirical and molecular formulae.

Ans: Given: %C = 39.99%, %H = 6.72%, %O = 53.2%
Molecular mass of glucose = 180 amu
Moles of C = 39.99 / 12.011 = 3.33
Moles of H = 6.72 / 1.0079 = 6.67
Moles of O = 53.2 / 15.9994 = 3.33
Simplest ratio (dividing each by the smallest, 3.33): C : H : O = 1 : 2 : 1
Empirical formula = CH2O
Empirical formula mass = 12.011 + 2(1.0079) + 15.9994 = 30.03 amu
Formula: n = molecular mass / empirical formula mass = 180 / 30.03 = 6
Molecular formula = n x empirical formula = 6 x (CH2O) = C6H12O6
Answer: Empirical formula = CH2O, Molecular formula = C6H12O6

mcqs.q: A 2.50 g sample of vanillin burns to give 5.79 g of CO2. What is the percentage of carbon in vanillin?
mcqs.why: Given: mass of vanillin = 2.50 g, mass of CO2 = 5.79 g. Formula: %C = (mass of CO2 / mass of compound) x (12.011 / 44.010) x 100. Substitution: %C = (5.79 / 2.50) x (12.011 / 44.010) x 100 = 2.316 x 0.27289 x 100 = 63.20%. Answer: %C = 63.20%.

mcqs.q: A 2.50 g sample of vanillin burns to give 1.188 g of H2O. What is the percentage of hydrogen in vanillin?
mcqs.why: Given: mass of vanillin = 2.50 g, mass of H2O = 1.188 g. Formula: %H = (mass of H2O / mass of compound) x (2.0158 / 18.0153) x 100. Substitution: %H = (1.188 / 2.50) x (2.0158 / 18.0153) x 100 = 0.4752 x 0.11190 x 100 = 5.32%. Answer: %H = 5.32%.

mcqs.q: Vanillin contains 63.20% carbon and 5.32% hydrogen, the rest being oxygen. What is the percentage of oxygen in vanillin?
Using %C = 63.20, %H = 5.32 and %O = 31.48 for vanillin, what is the simplest whole-number mole ratio C : H : O?
mcqs.why: Given: %C = 63.20, %H = 5.32, %O = 31.48. Formula: moles = percentage / atomic mass. Substitution: C = 63.20 / 12.011 = 5.26; H = 5.32 / 1.0079 = 5.28; O = 31.48 / 15.9994 = 1.97. Dividing each by the smallest (1.97): 2.67 : 2.68 : 1. Multiplying by 3 to get whole numbers: 8 : 8 : 3. Answer: C : H : O = 8 : 8 : 3.

mcqs.q: What is the empirical formula of vanillin, whose simplest mole ratio is C : H : O = 8 : 8 : 3?
mcqs.why: Given: simplest whole-number ratio C : H : O = 8 : 8 : 3 (from moles C = 5.26, H = 5.28, O = 1.97, divided by 1.97 and multiplied by 3). Formula: empirical formula is written using the simplest ratio as subscripts. Substitution: C8 H8 O3. Answer: Empirical formula = C8H8O3.

mcqs.q: The molecular mass of vanillin is 152.15 amu and its empirical formula is C8H8O3. What is its molecular formula?
mcqs.why: Given: molecular mass = 152.15 amu, empirical formula = C8H8O3. Formula: empirical formula mass = 8(12.011) + 8(1.0079) + 3(15.9994) = 96.088 + 8.063 + 47.998 = 152.15 amu; n = molecular mass / empirical formula mass. Substitution: n = 152.15 / 152.15 = 1. Molecular formula = 1 x (C8H8O3). Answer: Molecular formula = C8H8O3.

mcqs.q: Glucose contains C = 39.99%, H = 6.72% and O = 53.2%. What is the simplest mole ratio C : H : O in glucose?
mcqs.why: Given: %C = 39.99, %H = 6.72, %O = 53.2. Formula: moles = percentage / atomic mass. Substitution: C = 39.99 / 12.011 = 3.33; H = 6.72 / 1.0079 = 6.67; O = 53.2 / 15.9994 = 3.33. Dividing each by the smallest (3.33): 1 : 2 : 1. Answer: C : H : O = 1 : 2 : 1.

mcqs.q: What is the empirical formula of glucose, whose simplest mole ratio is C : H : O = 1 : 2 : 1?
mcqs.why: Given: simplest whole-number ratio C : H : O = 1 : 2 : 1 (from moles C = 3.33, H = 6.67, O = 3.33, divided by 3.33). Formula: empirical formula is written using the simplest ratio as subscripts. Substitution: C1 H2 O1. Answer: Empirical formula = CH2O.

mcqs.q: What is the empirical formula mass of CH2O, the empirical formula of glucose?
mcqs.why: Given: empirical formula = CH2O. Formula: empirical formula mass = sum of (atoms x atomic mass). Substitution: 12.011 + 2(1.0079) + 15.9994 = 12.011 + 2.0158 + 15.9994 = 30.03 amu. Answer: Empirical formula mass = 30.03 amu.

mcqs.q: The molecular mass of glucose is 180 amu and its empirical formula CH2O has mass 30.03 amu. What is the molecular formula of glucose?
mcqs.why: Given: molecular mass = 180 amu, empirical formula mass = 30.03 amu. Formula: n = molecular mass / empirical formula mass; molecular formula = n x empirical formula. Substitution: n = 180 / 30.03 = 6 (5.99); molecular formula = 6 x (CH2O) = C6H12O6. Answer: Molecular formula = C6H12O6.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Titration is a quantitative chemical analysis, while salt analysis, flame test and bromine-water test are qualitative.
  • IR spectroscopy is mainly used for the determination of functional groups in a compound.
  • Two different compounds always give different absorption peaks in the fingerprint region (1500-625 cm-1) of the IR spectrum.
  • NMR spectroscopy gives relatively more information about the structure of an organic compound than the other listed methods.
  • The wavelength range of the UV region is 10-400 nm.
  • In combustion analysis, water is absorbed by Mg(ClO4)2 and carbon dioxide by aqueous sodium or potassium hydroxide.
  • Scissoring is an in-plane bending vibration, while wagging and twisting are out-of-plane bending vibrations.
  • 16O is an NMR inactive nucleus, while 13C, 1H and 15N are NMR active.

Solved Exercises

Exercise: Multiple Choice Questions

Q: Which one of the following is quantitative chemical analysis?

Options: (a) Salt analysis (b) Titration (c) Flame test (d) Bromine-water test

Correct answer: Titration

Q: C2H6O is the molecular formula of (i) ethanol (ii) methanol (iii) dimethyl ether (iv) diethyl ether

Options: (a) (i) and (ii) (b) (ii) and (iii) (c) (i) and (iii) (d) (ii) and (v)

Correct answer: (i) and (iii)

Q: Which one of the following techniques is mainly used for determination of functional group in a compound?

Options: (a) IR Spectroscopy (b) NMR (c) UV/Visible spectroscopy (d) Mass spectroscopy

Correct answer: IR Spectroscopy

Q: Two different compounds will always give different absorption peak in ______ region of IR.

Options: (a) 1500-625 cm^-1 (b) 4000-1500 cm^-1 (c) 3000-2500 cm^-1 (d) 3500-1500 cm^-1

Correct answer: 1500-625 cm^-1

Q: Which one of the following methods, relatively gives more information about the structure of an organic compound?

Options: (a) Mass Spectroscopy (b) NMR Spectroscopy (c) IR Spectroscopy (d) UV-Visible Spectroscopy

Correct answer: NMR Spectroscopy

Q: A mass spectrum is shown below. (The graph of relative abundance against m/z shows small peaks at m/z 12, 16 and 28 and the tallest peak at m/z 44.) Which one of the following compound gives complete mass spectrum illustrated?

Options: (a) CO2 (b) N2 (c) C3H8 (d) Mixture of CH4 and N2

Correct answer: CO2

Q: The wavelength range of UV region is from

Options: (a) 400-800 nm (b) 800-1200 nm (c) 1200-1600 nm (d) 10-400 nm

Correct answer: 10-400 nm

Q: Which one of the following hydrocarbon produces a proton NMR spectrum with more than one peak?

Options: (a) Methane (b) Ethane (c) Butane (d) Cyclobutane

Correct answer: Butane

Q: How many signals/peaks would you expect in the proton NMR spectrum of 1,1-dichloroethane?

Options: (a) 2 (b) 4 (c) 6 (d) 8

Correct answer: 2

Q: How many types of protons are there in butanoic acid?

Options: (a) 8 (b) 2 (c) 6 (d) 4

Correct answer: 4

Q: In combustion analysis water is absorbed by

Options: (a) Mg(ClO4)2 (b) NaOH (c) CuO (d) CuSO4

Correct answer: Mg(ClO4)2

Q: Modern methods of analysis are superior to classical one because

Options: (a) they give more accurate results (b) small amounts of chemicals are used (c) less time consuming (d) all of the above

Correct answer: all of the above

Q: Which one is an in-plane bending vibration?

Options: (a) Wagging (b) Scissoring (c) Twisting (d) None of these

Correct answer: Scissoring

Q: Pi to pi star transition occurs in

Options: (a) ethane (b) ethene (c) ethyl alcohol (d) methyl chloride

Correct answer: ethene

Q: Which one is NMR inactive nucleus?

Options: (a) 13C (b) 1H (c) 15N (d) 16O

Correct answer: 16O

mcqs.q: Which one of the following is quantitative chemical analysis?
mcqs.why: Titration measures the exact amount or concentration of a substance, so it is quantitative analysis; salt analysis, flame test and bromine-water test only identify what is present, so they are qualitative.

mcqs.q: C2H6O is the molecular formula of (i) ethanol (ii) methanol (iii) dimethyl ether (iv) diethyl ether
mcqs.why: Ethanol, CH3CH2OH, and dimethyl ether, CH3OCH3, are isomers that both have the molecular formula C2H6O; methanol is CH4O and diethyl ether is C4H10O.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following techniques is mainly used for determination of functional group in a compound?
mcqs.why: IR spectroscopy is mainly used for the determination of functional groups in a compound, because each functional group absorbs at characteristic wavenumbers in the functional group region (4000-1500 cm-1).

mcqs.q: Two different compounds will always give different absorption peak in ______ region of IR.
mcqs.why: The fingerprint region (1500-625 cm-1) contains the complex vibrations of the whole molecule, so two different compounds (except enantiomers) never show the same frequencies for all of them there.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following methods, relatively gives more information about the structure of an organic compound?
mcqs.why: NMR is the most powerful tool for organic structure determination: its spectrum shows the number of types of protons, their environments and their amounts, giving relatively more structural information than the other methods.

mcqs.q: A mass spectrum is shown below. (The graph of relative abundance against m/z shows small peaks at m/z 12, 16 and 28 and the tallest peak at m/z 44.) Which one of the following compound gives complete mass spectrum illustrated?
mcqs.why: The tallest peak at m/z 44 is the molecular ion of CO2 (12 + 16 + 16 = 44), and the small peaks at m/z 12 (C+), 16 (O+) and 28 (CO+) are its fragments, so the spectrum is that of CO2.

mcqs.q: The wavelength range of UV region is from
mcqs.why: Absorption in the ultraviolet region (10-400 nm) and the visible region (400-750 nm) causes electronic transitions, which is why UV-Visible spectroscopy is also called electronic spectroscopy.

mcqs.q: Which one of the following hydrocarbon produces a proton NMR spectrum with more than one peak?
mcqs.why: In butane, CH3-CH2-CH2-CH3, the CH3 protons and the CH2 protons are in different environments, so it gives two signals; in methane, ethane and cyclobutane all the protons are equivalent and give only one signal each.

mcqs.q: How many signals/peaks would you expect in the proton NMR spectrum of 1,1-dichloroethane?
mcqs.why: 1,1-Dichloroethane, CH3-CHCl2, has two types of protons: the three equivalent CH3 protons and the single CH proton, so its proton NMR spectrum shows 2 signals.

mcqs.q: How many types of protons are there in butanoic acid?
mcqs.why: Butanoic acid, CH3-CH2-CH2-COOH, has four types of protons: the CH3 protons, the two different CH2 groups and the COOH proton, so there are 4 types of protons.

mcqs.q: In combustion analysis water is absorbed by
mcqs.why: In combustion analysis the water produced is absorbed in magnesium perchlorate, Mg(ClO4)2, of known mass, while the CO2 is absorbed by aqueous sodium or potassium hydroxide.

mcqs.q: Modern methods of analysis are superior to classical one because
options: small amounts of chemicals are used
More accurate results, use of small amounts of chemicals and less time consumption
mcqs.why: Modern spectroscopic methods are superior to classical methods for all three listed reasons together: they give more accurate and rapid results, they need only a small (tiny) amount of sample, and they are less time consuming and nondestructive.

mcqs.q: Which one is an in-plane bending vibration?
mcqs.why: Bending vibrations are of two types: in-plane bending (scissoring and rocking) and out-of-plane bending (twisting and wagging); scissoring is therefore an in-plane bending vibration, while symmetrical stretching is a stretching vibration, not a bending one.

mcqs.q: Pi to pi star transition occurs in
mcqs.why: Pi to pi star transitions occur in molecules containing double or triple bonds or aromatic rings; ethene contains a C=C double bond and absorbs at 171 nm for this transition, while the other listed compounds have only sigma bonds or heteroatoms.

mcqs.q: Which one is NMR inactive nucleus?
mcqs.why: Only nuclei with odd atomic number, odd mass number, or both, have a quantized nuclear spin and can be detected in NMR; 16O has even atomic number (8) and even mass number (16), so it is NMR inactive.

lessons.title: Short Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • Stretching vibrations change the bond length at regular intervals and are symmetrical or asymmetrical; bending vibrations change the bond angle and are also called deformation vibrations.
  • Percent transmittance is %T = (Is / Ir) x 100; 100% transmittance means the sample does not absorb radiation at that wavenumber.
  • Lambda max is the wavelength at which absorption is maximum, and each chromophore absorbs at a characteristic wavelength.
  • Beer-Lambert's Law, A = epsilon x c x l, is used for quantitative analysis in UV-Visible spectroscopy.
  • Tetramethylsilane (TMS) is the NMR standard: its protons are all equivalent and shielded, its shift is taken as 0 ppm, and it is inert, miscible and highly volatile.
  • In the ionization chamber of a mass spectrometer, the gaseous sample is bombarded with high-energy electrons to form positively charged radical cations.
  • The mass spectrum of neon shows three peaks at m/z 20, 21 and 22; neon-20 is the most abundant isotope (90.92%) and neon-21 the least (0.57%).

Solved Exercises

Exercise: Short Answer Questions

Q: Q2 (i) What is meant by stretching and bending vibrations?

Ans: In stretching vibrations, the bond length is increased or decreased at regular intervals; there are two types of stretching vibrations, symmetrical stretching and asymmetrical stretching. In bending vibrations, a change in bond angle occurs between bonds with a common atom; bending vibrations are also called deformation vibrations and are of two types, in-plane bending (scissoring and rocking) and out-of-plane bending (twisting and wagging).

Q: Q2 (ii) If a compound shows 100% transmittance, what do we infer from it?

Ans: Percent transmittance (%T) = (Is / Ir) x 100, where Is is the intensity of the sample beam and Ir is the intensity of the reference beam. In many parts of the spectrum the transmittance is nearly 100%, meaning that the sample is nearly transparent (no absorbance) to radiation of that wavenumber. So, if a compound shows 100% transmittance, we infer that it does not absorb the radiation at that wavenumber, i.e. there is no absorption.

Q: Q2 (iii) What does lambda max mean to you?

Ans: The UV-Visible spectrum is a plot of absorbance (A) against wavelength. The wavelength at which absorption is maximum is referred to as lambda max, and the intensity of absorption at this wavelength is referred to as epsilon max. Each chromophore absorbs at a characteristic wavelength, so lambda max is used to identify an unknown compound by comparing its lambda max with that of a known compound.

Q: Q2 (iv) Define and explain Beer-Lambert's Law.

Ans: Beer-Lambert's Law is used for quantitative analysis in UV-Visible spectroscopy. It states that the absorbance (A) of a solution is given by A = epsilon x c x l, where A is the absorbance, c is the molar concentration of the solution, l is the path length of the sample solution in centimetres, and epsilon is the molar absorptivity (formerly called molar extinction coefficient), a constant characteristic of the solute at a given wavelength. By measuring the absorbance (A) of a solution at the wavelength of maximum absorption (lambda max), its concentration (c) can be calculated if epsilon max and l are known; the concentration of an unknown solution can also be found from a working (calibration) curve plotted from the absorbances of solutions of known concentrations.

Q: Q2 (v) Why tetramethyl silane is used as a standard in NMR spectroscopy?

Ans: Tetramethylsilane (TMS) is used as a standard in NMR spectroscopy because all of its protons are equivalent and shielded due to the electropositive nature of silicon, and show a single absorption at the lowest delta value; its chemical shift has been chosen as zero (0 ppm) arbitrarily, and the chemical shifts of other compounds are compared with this reference value. Moreover, it is chemically inert to most of the organic compounds, miscible with most of the organic solvents, and highly volatile, so it can easily be separated from the compound after its spectrum has been recorded.

Q: Q2 (vi) Explain the use of ionization chamber in mass spectrometer.

Ans: The ionization chamber is the part of the mass spectrometer where the gaseous sample is ionized. The gaseous sample is bombarded with high-energy electrons from an electron-gun, and the resulting positively charged ions (which are radical cations) are produced there. These ions are then directed into an analyzer tube surrounded by a magnet, where they are sorted according to their mass-to-charge ratio (m/z).

Q: Q2 (vii) Why magnesium perchlorate is used as H2O absorber?

Ans: In combustion analysis, the organic compound on burning produces carbon dioxide and water vapours, which are swept out of the furnace and trapped in a pair of absorbers. Water is absorbed in a sample of magnesium perchlorate, Mg(ClO4)2, of known mass, while carbon dioxide is absorbed by aqueous sodium or potassium hydroxide. The increase in the mass of the magnesium perchlorate absorber is the mass of water produced during combustion, from which the percentage of hydrogen in the compound is calculated. Magnesium perchlorate is therefore used because it strongly absorbs water vapours.

Q: Q2 (viii) Why modern method of analysis is superior over classical method of analysis?

Ans: Modern (spectroscopic) methods are superior because, unlike chemical tests (the classical methods of analysis), most of the spectroscopic and chromatographic techniques are nondestructive, require only a small (tiny) amount of sample and are less time consuming, and they provide more accurate and rapid results. These methods are simple and do not involve much chemistry as compared to the classical methods, which are impractical for compounds that are difficult to obtain, because a relatively large sample is required to complete the elemental analysis and all the functional group tests.

Q: Q2 (ix) Mass spectrum of an element can give information of number of isotopes, atomic masses and natural abundance of each isotope. Explain with an example.

Ans: A mass spectrum of an element is a graph of m/z values on the x-axis and the relative number (abundance) of ions of each mass on the y-axis; the higher the peak of a species, the higher is its abundance. Each peak corresponds to one isotope, so the number of peaks gives the number of isotopes, the m/z value of each peak gives the atomic (isotopic) mass, and the height of each peak gives the natural abundance of that isotope. For example, the mass spectrum of neon shows three peaks with m/z equal to 20, 21 and 22, which correspond to 20Ne, 21Ne and 22Ne respectively. Neon-20 is the most abundant isotope (90.92%) and Neon-21 is the least abundant (0.57%), as is clear from the heights of their peaks, while 22Ne is 8.82% abundant.

Q: Q2 (x) Explain the nuclear spin flipping briefly.

Ans: Like electrons, the atomic nucleus proton also has the property of spin, and spinning charged bodies produce a magnetic field. In an external magnetic field, each proton assumes either the low-energy alpha-spin state (magnetic field aligned with the applied field) or the high-energy beta-spin state (aligned against the applied field). When such a nucleus is irradiated with radio-frequency photons having energy equal to the energy difference between the two spin states (delta E = E beta - E alpha = h nu), a proton in the alpha-spin state can absorb a photon and flip to the beta-spin state. This absorption of energy and change of spin orientation with respect to the applied field is called nuclear spin flipping, and it is the basis of the NMR phenomenon.

mcqs.q: In a stretching vibration, what changes at regular intervals?
mcqs.why: In stretching vibrations the bond length is increased or decreased at regular intervals; a change in bond angle, by contrast, is a bending (deformation) vibration.

mcqs.q: Bending vibrations are also called
mcqs.why: In bending vibrations a change in bond angle occurs between bonds with a common atom; bending vibrations are also called deformation vibrations and are of in-plane and out-of-plane types.

mcqs.q: Which pair gives the two in-plane bending vibrations?
mcqs.why: Bending vibrations are of two types: in-plane bending (scissoring and rocking) and out-of-plane bending (twisting and wagging), as stated for the methylene group vibrations.

options: it absorbs all the radiation at that wavenumber
it does not absorb the radiation at that wavenumber
it is present in a very large amount

the wavelength at which absorption is maximum
the path length of the sample cell
mcqs.why: The UV-Visible spectrum is a plot of absorbance against wavelength; the wavelength at which absorption is maximum is called lambda max, and the intensity of absorption there is epsilon max.

mcqs.q: In Beer-Lambert's Law, A = epsilon x c x l, the symbol epsilon stands for
mcqs.why: In A = epsilon x c x l, A is the absorbance, c is the molar concentration, l is the path length in centimetres, and epsilon is the molar absorptivity (formerly molar extinction coefficient), a constant characteristic of the solute at a given wavelength.

mcqs.q: Tetramethylsilane (TMS) is taken as the NMR standard with chemical shift
mcqs.why: All the protons of TMS are equivalent and shielded due to the electropositive nature of silicon and show a single absorption at the lowest delta value; its chemical shift has been chosen as zero (0 ppm) arbitrarily.

mcqs.q: TMS can easily be separated from the sample after recording the spectrum because it is
mcqs.why: TMS is used as the NMR standard because it is chemically inert to most organic compounds, miscible with most organic solvents, and highly volatile, so it can easily be separated from the compound after its spectrum has been recorded.

mcqs.q: In the ionization chamber of a mass spectrometer, the gaseous sample is bombarded with
mcqs.why: The ionization chamber is where the gaseous sample is ionized: it is bombarded with high-energy electrons from an electron-gun, and the resulting positively charged ions (radical cations) are then sorted by their m/z values.

mcqs.q: In the mass spectrum of neon, the least abundant isotope is
mcqs.why: Neon shows three peaks at m/z 20, 21 and 22; the peak heights give the abundances: 20Ne is the most abundant (90.92%), 22Ne is 8.82% abundant and 21Ne is the least abundant (0.57%).

lessons.title: Numerical Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • The percentage of oxygen in a C, H, O compound is found by difference: %O = 100 - (%C + %H).
  • Moles of each element = percentage / atomic mass, and dividing by the smallest mole value gives the simplest ratio.
  • A compound with 32% C and 4% H has 64% O, empirical formula C2H3O3 and molecular formula C4H6O6 at molecular mass 150 amu.
  • A compound with 27.3% C and 72.7% O has the empirical formula CO2.
  • Combustion of 5 g of acetic acid gives %C = 40.0, %H = 6.71 and %O = 53.29, with empirical formula CH2O.
  • Isoprene (88.17% C, 11.83% H) has empirical and molecular formula C5H8, since n = 1 at molecular mass 68.11 amu.
  • Combustion of 1.26 g of polyethylene gives %C = 85.34 and %H = 14.30, with empirical formula CH2.

Solved Exercises

Exercise: Numerical Questions

Q: Q3 (i) A compound containing C, H and O, is found to contain 32% carbon and 4% hydrogen. Its molecular mass is 150 amu. Find its molecular formula.

Ans: Given: %C = 32%, %H = 4%
Percentage of O = 100 - (32 + 4) = 64%
Molecular mass = 150 amu
Moles of C = 32 / 12.011 = 2.66
Moles of H = 4 / 1.0079 = 3.97
Moles of O = 64 / 15.9994 = 4.00
Simplest ratio (dividing each by the smallest, 2.66): C : H : O = 1 : 1.49 : 1.50
Multiplying by 2 to get whole numbers: C : H : O = 2 : 3 : 3
Empirical formula = C2H3O3
Empirical formula mass = 2(12.011) + 3(1.0079) + 3(15.9994) = 75.04 amu
Formula: n = molecular mass / empirical formula mass
Substitution: n = 150 / 75.04 = 2
Molecular formula = n x empirical formula = 2 x (C2H3O3) = C4H6O6
Answer: Molecular formula = C4H6O6

Q: Q3 (ii) Calculate the empirical formula of the compound that contains 27.3% carbon and 72.7% oxygen.

Ans: Given: %C = 27.3%, %O = 72.7%
Moles of C = 27.3 / 12.011 = 2.27
Moles of O = 72.7 / 15.9994 = 4.54
Simplest ratio (dividing each by the smallest, 2.27): C : O = 1 : 2
Answer: Empirical formula = CO2

Q: Q3 (iii) Acetic acid contains only C, H and O. A 5 g sample of acetic acid is completely burnt. It gives 7.33 g of carbon dioxide and 3 g of water. What is the mass percentage of each element in acetic acid? Also calculate the empirical formula of acetic acid.

Ans: Given: mass of acetic acid sample = 5 g
Mass of CO2 produced = 7.33 g
Mass of H2O produced = 3 g
Formula: %C = (mass of CO2 produced / mass of organic compound) x (12.011 / 44.010) x 100
Substitution: %C = (7.33 / 5) x (12.011 / 44.010) x 100 = 40.0%
Formula: %H = (mass of H2O produced / mass of organic compound) x (2.0158 / 18.0153) x 100
Substitution: %H = (3 / 5) x (2.0158 / 18.0153) x 100 = 6.71%
Formula: %O = 100 - (%C + %H)
Substitution: %O = 100 - (40.0 + 6.71) = 53.29%
Moles of C = 40.0 / 12.011 = 3.33
Moles of H = 6.71 / 1.0079 = 6.66
Moles of O = 53.29 / 15.9994 = 3.33
Simplest ratio (dividing each by the smallest, 3.33): C : H : O = 1 : 2 : 1
Answer: Mass percentage: C = 40.0%, H = 6.71%, O = 53.29%; Empirical formula of acetic acid = CH2O

Q: Q3 (iv) Isoprene is a liquid compound that can be polymerized to form synthetic rubber. It is composed of 88.17% carbon and 11.83% hydrogen. Its molecular mass is 68.11 amu. What are its empirical and molecular formulae?

Ans: Given: %C = 88.17%, %H = 11.83%
Molecular mass of isoprene = 68.11 amu
Moles of C = 88.17 / 12.011 = 7.34
Moles of H = 11.83 / 1.0079 = 11.74
Simplest ratio (dividing each by the smallest, 7.34): C : H = 1 : 1.60
Multiplying by 5 to get whole numbers: C : H = 5 : 8
Empirical formula = C5H8
Empirical formula mass = 5(12.011) + 8(1.0079) = 68.12 amu
Formula: n = molecular mass / empirical formula mass
Substitution: n = 68.11 / 68.12 = 1
Molecular formula = n x empirical formula = 1 x (C5H8) = C5H8
Answer: Empirical formula = C5H8, Molecular formula = C5H8

Q: Q3 (v) Polyethylene is a hydrocarbon polymer used to produce food-storage bags and many other flexible plastic items. A combustion analysis of a 1.26 g sample of polyethylene yields 3.94 g of carbon dioxide and 1.61 g of water. What is the empirical formula of polyethylene?

Ans: Given: mass of polyethylene sample = 1.26 g
Mass of CO2 produced = 3.94 g
Mass of H2O produced = 1.61 g
Formula: %C = (mass of CO2 produced / mass of organic compound) x (12.011 / 44.010) x 100
Substitution: %C = (3.94 / 1.26) x (12.011 / 44.010) x 100 = 85.34%
Formula: %H = (mass of H2O produced / mass of organic compound) x (2.0158 / 18.0153) x 100
Substitution: %H = (1.61 / 1.26) x (2.0158 / 18.0153) x 100 = 14.30%
Moles of C = 85.34 / 12.011 = 7.11
Moles of H = 14.30 / 1.0079 = 14.19
Simplest ratio (dividing each by the smallest, 7.11): C : H = 1 : 2
Answer: Empirical formula of polyethylene = CH2

mcqs.q: A compound contains 32% carbon and 4% hydrogen, the rest being oxygen. What is the percentage of oxygen in the compound?
mcqs.why: Given: %C = 32%, %H = 4%, compound contains only C, H and O. Formula: %O = 100 - (%C + %H). Substitution: %O = 100 - (32 + 4) = 100 - 36 = 64. Answer: %O = 64%.

mcqs.q: A compound contains 32% C, 4% H and 64% O and has molecular mass 150 amu. What is its molecular formula?
mcqs.why: Given: %C = 32, %H = 4, %O = 64; molecular mass = 150 amu. Formula: moles = percentage / atomic mass; n = molecular mass / empirical formula mass. Substitution: moles C = 32 / 12.011 = 2.66, H = 4 / 1.0079 = 3.97, O = 64 / 15.9994 = 4.00; dividing by 2.66 gives 1 : 1.49 : 1.50, and multiplying by 2 gives 2 : 3 : 3, so empirical formula = C2H3O3, of mass 2(12.011) + 3(1.0079) + 3(15.9994) = 75.04 amu; n = 150 / 75.04 = 2. Answer: Molecular formula = 2 x (C2H3O3) = C4H6O6.

mcqs.q: What is the simplest mole ratio C : O in a compound containing 27.3% carbon and 72.7% oxygen?
mcqs.why: Given: %C = 27.3, %O = 72.7. Formula: moles = percentage / atomic mass. Substitution: moles C = 27.3 / 12.011 = 2.27; moles O = 72.7 / 15.9994 = 4.54. Dividing each by the smallest (2.27): C = 1, O = 4.54 / 2.27 = 2. Answer: Simplest ratio C : O = 1 : 2.

mcqs.q: What is the empirical formula of the compound that contains 27.3% carbon and 72.7% oxygen?
mcqs.why: Given: %C = 27.3, %O = 72.7. Formula: moles = percentage / atomic mass, then simplest ratio as subscripts. Substitution: moles C = 27.3 / 12.011 = 2.27; moles O = 72.7 / 15.9994 = 4.54; dividing by 2.27 gives C : O = 1 : 2. Answer: Empirical formula = CO2.

mcqs.q: A 5 g sample of acetic acid is completely burnt and gives 7.33 g of CO2. What is the mass percentage of carbon in acetic acid?
mcqs.why: Given: mass of acetic acid = 5 g, mass of CO2 = 7.33 g. Formula: %C = (mass of CO2 / mass of compound) x (12.011 / 44.010) x 100. Substitution: %C = (7.33 / 5) x (12.011 / 44.010) x 100 = 1.466 x 0.27289 x 100 = 40.0%. Answer: %C = 40.0%.

mcqs.q: A 5 g sample of acetic acid is completely burnt and gives 3 g of H2O and 7.33 g of CO2. What is the empirical formula of acetic acid?
Isoprene is composed of 88.17% carbon and 11.83% hydrogen. By what number must the simplest ratio C : H = 1 : 1.60 be multiplied to get whole numbers?
mcqs.why: Given: %C = 88.17, %H = 11.83. Formula: moles = percentage / atomic mass. Substitution: moles C = 88.17 / 12.011 = 7.34; moles H = 11.83 / 1.0079 = 11.74; dividing by 7.34 gives C : H = 1 : 1.60. Since 1.60 = 8/5, multiplying the ratio by 5 gives 5 : 8. Answer: Multiply by 5, giving C : H = 5 : 8.

mcqs.q: Isoprene (88.17% C, 11.83% H) has molecular mass 68.11 amu. What are its empirical and molecular formulae?
mcqs.why: Given: %C = 88.17, %H = 11.83, molecular mass = 68.11 amu. Formula: moles = percentage / atomic mass; n = molecular mass / empirical formula mass. Substitution: moles C = 7.34, H = 11.74, ratio 1 : 1.60, multiplied by 5 gives 5 : 8, so empirical formula = C5H8, of mass 5(12.011) + 8(1.0079) = 68.12 amu; n = 68.11 / 68.12 = 1. Answer: Empirical formula = C5H8, Molecular formula = 1 x (C5H8) = C5H8.

mcqs.q: A 1.26 g sample of polyethylene yields 3.94 g of CO2 on combustion. What is the percentage of carbon in polyethylene?
mcqs.why: Given: mass of polyethylene = 1.26 g, mass of CO2 = 3.94 g. Formula: %C = (mass of CO2 / mass of compound) x (12.011 / 44.010) x 100. Substitution: %C = (3.94 / 1.26) x (12.011 / 44.010) x 100 = 3.127 x 0.27289 x 100 = 85.34%. Answer: %C = 85.34%.

mcqs.q: Combustion of 1.26 g of polyethylene yields 3.94 g of CO2 and 1.61 g of H2O. What is the empirical formula of polyethylene?
mcqs.why: Given: mass of sample = 1.26 g, CO2 = 3.94 g, H2O = 1.61 g. Formula: %C = (3.94 / 1.26) x (12.011 / 44.010) x 100 = 85.34%; %H = (1.61 / 1.26) x (2.0158 / 18.0153) x 100 = 14.30%. Substitution for moles: C = 85.34 / 12.011 = 7.11, H = 14.30 / 1.0079 = 14.19; dividing by 7.11 gives C : H = 1 : 2. Answer: Empirical formula of polyethylene = CH2.

lessons.title: Detailed Answers
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A mass spectrometer ionizes gaseous atoms and molecules in a high vacuum, sorts the ions by mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) and records the abundance of ions of each mass.
  • In a mass spectrum, ions of small m/z are deflected more by the magnet than ions of larger m/z, and the higher the peak of a species, the higher its abundance.
  • The molecular ion (M+) has the highest m/z value and gives the molecular mass of a compound directly; the fragmentation pattern gives an idea of its structure.
  • Emission spectroscopy studies radiation emitted by excited atoms, while absorption spectroscopy studies radiation absorbed by ground-state atoms; each element's spectrum is a unique fingerprint.
  • In flame photometry and atomic absorption spectroscopy, the emitted intensity or absorbance is directly proportional to the concentration of the element, found from a working curve.
  • Shielded protons absorb at low delta values in the upfield region, while deshielded protons absorb at high delta values in the downfield region.
  • UV-Visible spectroscopy involves electronic transitions: sigma to sigma star, n to sigma star, pi to pi star and n to pi star.
  • For a vibration to be IR active, the dipole moment of the molecule must change; the fingerprint region (1500-625 cm-1) establishes the identity of a compound.

Solved Exercises

Exercise: Detailed Answer Questions

Q: Q4. 1 (a) Define mass spectroscopy. Explain the construction and working of mass spectrometer.

Ans: Mass spectroscopy (mass spectrometry) is a highly sensitive instrumental technique by which atomic and molecular masses are determined. A mass spectrometer ionizes gaseous atoms and molecules in a high vacuum, sorts the ions according to their masses, and records the abundance of ions of each mass. Construction and working: the gaseous sample is bombarded with high-energy electrons from an electron-gun in the ionization chamber, and the resulting positively charged ions (radical cations) are directed into an analyzer tube surrounded by a magnet. This magnet deflects the ions from their original trajectory, causing them to adopt a circular path, the radius of which depends on their mass-to-charge ratio (m/z); ions of small m/z values are deflected more than those of larger m/z. By varying the magnetic field strength, ions of a particular m/z can be selectively focused through a narrow slit onto a detector, where they are counted. The graph plotted by the mass spectrometer, with the m/z values on the x-axis and the relative number of ions of each mass on the y-axis, is the mass spectrum; the higher the peak of a species, the higher will be its abundance.

Q: Q4. 1 (b) How a mass spectrum of an element and compound can give information about atomic mass and molecular mass, respectively?

Ans: For an element, the mass spectrum shows a separate peak for each isotope at its own m/z value, and the height of each peak shows the relative abundance of that isotope; from the positions and heights of the peaks the atomic (isotopic) masses and the relative atomic mass of the element can be found. For example, the mass spectrum of neon shows three peaks at m/z 20, 21 and 22 for 20Ne, 21Ne and 22Ne, with abundances 90.92%, 0.57% and 8.82%. For a compound, when a molecule is introduced into the mass spectrometer, the molecular ion (M+) is produced due to loss of an electron; the molecular ion has the highest m/z value and represents the molecular mass of the molecule, so the molecular mass of the compound is obtained directly. In addition, more ions are produced due to fragmentation of the molecule, and the fragmentation pattern gives an idea of the structure of the molecule. For example, the mass spectrum of chlorine shows peaks for 35Cl (m/z = 35) and 37Cl (m/z = 37) and for the three types of chlorine molecules 35Cl-35Cl (m/z = 70), 35Cl-37Cl (m/z = 72) and 37Cl-37Cl (m/z = 74).

Q: Q4. 2 (a) Differentiate between atomic emission and absorption spectroscopy.

Ans: In atomic emission spectroscopy, the atoms of an element are excited (for example in a flame), and when the excited atoms lose energy they emit radiations of characteristic wavelength; the study of this emitted radiation gives the emission spectrum. In atomic absorption spectroscopy, the atoms are mostly in the ground state (as atomic vapour in a flame), and when light of a particular wavelength from a hollow cathode lamp is passed through these atoms, they absorb the light for excitation from the ground state to a higher energy state; the study of this absorbed radiation gives the absorption spectrum. In short, emission spectroscopy deals with radiation emitted by excited atoms, while absorption spectroscopy deals with radiation absorbed by ground-state atoms. Every element has a unique emission or absorption spectrum, so these atomic spectra are used as a fingerprint to identify the elements.

Q: Q4. 2 (b) Explain the working of flame photometer and atomic absorption spectrometer.

Ans: Flame photometer (flame atomic emission spectrophotometer): an aqueous analyte (sample solution) is introduced into the flame through an atomizer. Water evaporates and solid salt is left behind; the salt breaks into constituent atoms, and the gaseous atoms get excited in the flame. The excited atoms lose energy of characteristic wavelength, which is dispersed by a grating or prism and detected in the spectrophotometer (through lens, slit, filter, amplifier and photo detector). The intensity of light emitted by the atoms is directly proportional to the concentration of the analyte. Atomic absorption spectrometer: the sample solution is evaporated in a flame and the sample is converted to atomic vapour; some of the atoms in the flame get excited, but the majority of them are in the ground state. When light of a particular wavelength from the hollow cathode lamp is passed through these atoms, they absorb the light for excitation from the ground state to a higher energy state. The absorbance of light by the atoms is directly proportional to the concentration of atomic vapours in the flame. For the analysis of different elements, different types of lamps are used, which produce light of different wavelengths, because each element shows absorption of a particular wavelength.

Q: Q4. 2 (c) How atomic emission and absorption spectrophotometry is used for qualitative and quantitative analysis of elements?

Ans: Qualitative analysis: every element has a unique emission or absorption spectrum, thus the emission or absorption atomic spectra are used as a fingerprint to identify the elements; for example, a flame photometer with monochromators emits radiations of characteristic wavelengths which help to detect the presence of a particular metal in the sample. Quantitative analysis: the intensity of light emitted by the atoms in flame photometry, and the absorbance of light by the atoms in atomic absorption spectroscopy, are each directly proportional to the concentration of the element. Before introducing the sample of unknown concentration, solutions of known concentrations of that element are aspirated into the flame one by one, their absorbances (or emission intensities) are recorded and a working curve is constructed between concentration and absorbance; then the sample of unknown concentration is aspirated and its concentration is determined from its absorbance using the working curve. In this way flame photometry is used to find the concentration of various alkali and alkaline earth metals in soil samples and of Na+ and K+ ions in biological samples, and atomic absorption spectroscopy is used for the estimation of over sixty metals in polluted water, body fluids and soft drinks.

Q: Q4. 3 (a) What is meant by proton NMR spectroscopy?

Ans: Proton NMR spectroscopy is the nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy carried out with proton (1H) nuclei. Nuclei which possess either odd atomic number, odd mass number, or both, have a quantized nuclear spin and a magnetic moment and can be detected in NMR spectroscopy. In proton NMR, the protons of a sample are placed in an external magnetic field, where they take up the alpha-spin or beta-spin states, and the absorption of radio-frequency radiation at the resonance frequency (where the absorbed energy equals the difference between the two spin states) is recorded as a spectrum of absorption against chemical shift. NMR is the most powerful tool available for organic structure determination: like infrared spectroscopy, it can be used with a very small amount of sample, it does not harm the sample, and the NMR spectrum provides a great deal of information about the structure of the compound.

Q: Q4. 3 (b) Explain how chemical shift varies with shielding?

Ans: Protons in a molecule are surrounded by electrons and exist in slightly different electronic (magnetic) environments from one another, and the electron densities vary from one proton to another. The net field felt by a proton in a molecule is always less than the applied field, and the proton is said to be shielded. All the protons of a molecule are shielded from the applied field by the electrons, but some are less shielded than others because they may have less surrounding electron cloud; these are termed deshielded protons. Deshielded protons are generally in the vicinity of electronegative atoms in a molecule. More shielded protons absorb low radio-frequency radiations and their signals appear on the right side of the spectrum, the upfield region, at low chemical shift (delta) values; while deshielded protons absorb high radio-frequency radiations and their signals appear on the left side of the spectrum, the downfield region, at high delta values. Thus the chemical shift of a proton increases as its shielding decreases, i.e. deshielding moves the signal downfield to higher delta. Chemical shift (delta) = [shift from TMS (Hz) / operating frequency of spectrometer (Hz)] x 10^6, expressed in ppm with reference to TMS, which is defined to be 0 ppm.

Q: Q4. 3 (c) From proton NMR spectrum of a molecule, how would you know about presence of different types of protons in molecule?

Ans: Protons in identical chemical environments, with the same shielding, have the same chemical shift and are called equivalent protons. In general, the number of NMR signals corresponds to the number of types of protons present in different electronic environments in the molecule. So, from the proton NMR spectrum of a molecule, we count the number of signals: each signal corresponds to one type (set of equivalent) protons, and the position (chemical shift) of each signal tells us about the environment of that type of proton. For example, methyl alcohol has two types of protons, therefore its 1H NMR spectrum has only two signals: an upfield signal for the three equivalent and shielded methyl protons, and a downfield signal for the deshielded proton of the hydroxyl group.

Q: Q4. 4 (a) Explain the principle of UV-Visible spectroscopy.

Ans: The principle of UV-Visible spectroscopy is that absorption of electromagnetic radiation by a molecule in the ultraviolet (10-400 nm) and visible (400-750 nm) region leads to electronic transitions, i.e. the excitation of an electron from the ground state to an excited state. It is therefore also called electronic spectroscopy. A normal UV-Visible spectrometer uses the near ultraviolet region of wavelength range 200 nm to 400 nm, together with visible light. The UV-Visible spectrum is a plot of absorbance (A) against wavelength; the wavelength at which absorption is maximum is lambda max. Different chromophores (structural features responsible for the absorption) absorb different wavelengths, so a compound can be identified by comparing its lambda max with that of a known compound, the presence of conjugated systems and groups like carbonyl groups can be detected, and the technique is also used for quantitative analysis using Beer-Lambert's Law (A = epsilon x c x l). The d-d transitions of transition metal complexes occur usually in the visible region, so the colour of a transition metal complex can also be predicted from its UV-Visible spectrum.

Q: Q4. 4 (b) Explain different types of electron transitions in organic molecules.

Ans: The common electronic transitions associated with the absorption of UV-Visible radiation by organic molecules are of four types. (i) sigma to sigma star transitions: these occur in saturated hydrocarbons such as alkanes and cycloalkanes, which contain only sigma bonds. This transition requires greater energy; thus the C-C bond absorbs at 135 nm and the C-H bond absorbs at about 125 nm. (ii) n to sigma star transitions: these occur in saturated molecules containing heteroatoms, such as oxygen, sulphur, nitrogen or halogens. This transition requires slightly less energy than the sigma to sigma star transition; for example, methyl alcohol shows n to sigma star absorption at 183 nm. (iii) pi to pi star transitions: these occur in molecules containing double or triple bonds or aromatic rings; for example, ethylene absorbs at 171 nm for the pi to pi star transition. However, a conjugated system of unsaturated bonds absorbs at much longer wavelength, e.g. buta-1,3-diene and isoprene show maximum absorption at 217 nm and 222 nm respectively. (iv) n to pi star transitions: these occur in molecules that contain double or triple bonds involving heteroatoms, such as aldehydes, ketones and nitriles; e.g. the n to pi star absorption band for acetone appears at 279 nm. In addition, the d-d transitions of transition metal complexes occur in the visible region and are responsible for their colours.

Q: Q4. 5 (a) What is IR spectroscopy?

Ans: IR (infrared) spectroscopy is the spectroscopic technique in which organic compounds are exposed to infrared radiations in the range of 4000-625 cm^-1. Infrared photons do not have enough energy to cause electronic transitions, but they can cause groups of atoms to vibrate with respect to the bonds that connect them. Like electronic transitions, these vibrational transitions correspond to distinct energies, and molecules absorb infrared radiations only at certain wavelengths and frequencies. The plot of wavenumber (cm^-1) versus percent transmittance (%T) is called the infrared spectrum. IR spectroscopy is mainly used for the determination of functional groups in a compound and for establishing the identity of a compound.

Q: Q4. 5 (b) Explain different types of molecular vibrations in a molecule.

Ans: Absorption of a photon of infrared radiation excites a molecule from its lowest, or ground, vibrational state to a higher one. For a vibration to be IR active, the dipole moment of the molecule must be changed. There are two main types of molecular vibrations. (1) Stretching vibrations: the bond length is increased or decreased at regular intervals. There are two types of stretching vibrations: symmetrical stretching and asymmetrical stretching. (2) Bending vibrations (deformation vibrations): a change in bond angle occurs between bonds with a common atom. Deformation vibrations are of two types: (a) in-plane bending vibrations, e.g. scissoring and rocking; and (b) out-of-plane bending vibrations, e.g. twisting and wagging. These different types of vibrations are shown in the unit for the methylene (-CH2-) group.

Q: Q4. 5 (c) Explain the significance of functional group and fingerprint regions in IR spectrum.

Ans: In using infrared spectroscopy for structure determination, the spectrum is divided into two regions. (1) The functional group region (4000-1500 cm^-1): peaks in this range are usually emphasized because this is the region in which the vibrations characteristic of particular functional groups are found; therefore, by examining which absorption bands are present in this region, the functional groups present in the molecule can be identified, e.g. O-H of alcohols at 3200-3600 cm^-1, C=O of aldehydes and ketones at 1710-1750 cm^-1 and C=C at 1620-1680 cm^-1. (2) The fingerprint region (1500-625 cm^-1): this region contains the complex vibrations of the whole molecule. It is highly unlikely that the IR spectra of two different compounds (except enantiomers) will show the same frequencies for all of their various complex vibrations; hence this region of the infrared spectrum provides a 'fingerprint' of a molecule, and the identity of a compound can be established by comparing the fingerprint region of its infrared spectrum with that of a known compound.

mcqs.q: In a mass spectrometer, the magnet deflects ions of small m/z values
options: less than ions of larger m/z
more than ions of larger m/z
the same as ions of larger m/z
only when the field is switched off
mcqs.why: The magnet deflects the ions into a circular path whose radius depends on m/z; ions of small m/z values are deflected more than those of larger m/z, and by varying the field, ions of a particular m/z are focused onto the detector.

mcqs.q: The molecular ion (M+) of a compound is important because it
options: has the lowest m/z value in the spectrum
gives the number of isotopes of the compound
has the highest m/z value and represents the molecular mass of the molecule
shows the natural abundance of carbon
mcqs.why: When a molecule is introduced into the mass spectrometer, the molecular ion (M+) is produced by loss of an electron; it has the highest m/z value and represents the molecular mass, so the molecular mass is obtained directly.

mcqs.q: The mass spectrum of chlorine shows peaks for the three types of chlorine molecules at m/z
mcqs.why: Chlorine has isotopes 35Cl (m/z = 35) and 37Cl (m/z = 37), so its molecules appear at m/z = 70 (35Cl-35Cl), 72 (35Cl-37Cl) and 74 (37Cl-37Cl).

mcqs.q: Atomic absorption spectroscopy deals with radiation
mcqs.why: In atomic absorption spectroscopy the atoms are mostly in the ground state as atomic vapour in a flame and absorb light of a particular wavelength from a hollow cathode lamp for excitation; emission spectroscopy, in contrast, deals with radiation emitted by excited atoms.

mcqs.q: In a flame photometer, the intensity of light emitted by the atoms is
options: inversely proportional to the concentration of the analyte
directly proportional to the concentration of the analyte
independent of the concentration of the analyte
proportional to the square of the concentration
mcqs.why: In flame photometry the aqueous analyte is introduced into the flame through an atomizer, the gaseous atoms get excited and emit light of characteristic wavelength, and the intensity of the emitted light is directly proportional to the concentration of the analyte.

mcqs.q: Atomic absorption spectroscopy is used for the estimation of
options: over sixty metals in polluted water, body fluids and soft drinks
mcqs.why: Atomic absorption spectroscopy is used for the estimation of over sixty metals in polluted water, body fluids and soft drinks, while flame photometry finds alkali and alkaline earth metals in soil and Na+ and K+ ions in biological samples.

mcqs.q: Nuclei that can be detected in NMR spectroscopy are those which possess
options: only even atomic and mass numbers
odd atomic number, odd mass number, or both
an even number of protons only
mcqs.why: Nuclei which possess either odd atomic number, odd mass number, or both, have a quantized nuclear spin and a magnetic moment and can be detected in NMR spectroscopy; this is why 16O is NMR inactive.

mcqs.q: Deshielded protons appear in the spectrum in the
options: upfield region at low delta values
downfield region at high delta values
mcqs.why: More shielded protons absorb low radio-frequency radiations and appear upfield at low delta values, while deshielded protons (near electronegative atoms) absorb high radio-frequency radiations and appear downfield at high delta values; the chemical shift increases as shielding decreases.

mcqs.q: The chemical shift (delta) is expressed in ppm with reference to
mcqs.why: Chemical shift delta = [shift from TMS (Hz) / operating frequency of spectrometer (Hz)] x 10^6, expressed in ppm with reference to TMS, which is defined to be 0 ppm.

mcqs.q: The proton NMR spectrum of methyl alcohol (methanol) has only two signals because methanol has
options: two types of protons: the methyl protons and the hydroxyl proton
mcqs.why: Methyl alcohol has two types of protons, so its 1H NMR spectrum has only two signals: an upfield signal for the three equivalent, shielded methyl protons and a downfield signal for the deshielded hydroxyl proton.

mcqs.q: UV-Visible spectroscopy is also called electronic spectroscopy because absorption in this region leads to
options: electronic transitions, the excitation of an electron from the ground state to an excited state
mcqs.why: The principle of UV-Visible spectroscopy is that absorption of radiation in the ultraviolet (10-400 nm) and visible (400-750 nm) region leads to electronic transitions, i.e. excitation of an electron from the ground state to an excited state.

mcqs.q: Sigma to sigma star transitions occur in saturated hydrocarbons such as alkanes, and the C-C bond absorbs at
mcqs.why: Sigma to sigma star transitions occur in saturated hydrocarbons containing only sigma bonds and require the greatest energy; the C-C bond absorbs at 135 nm and the C-H bond at about 125 nm.

mcqs.q: The n to pi star absorption band of acetone appears at
mcqs.why: N to pi star transitions occur in molecules with double or triple bonds involving heteroatoms, such as aldehydes and ketones; the n to pi star absorption band for acetone appears at 279 nm, while methyl alcohol shows n to sigma star absorption at 183 nm.

mcqs.q: For a molecular vibration to be IR active, it is necessary that
options: the dipole moment of the molecule must be changed
the molecule must contain a double bond
mcqs.why: Absorption of an infrared photon excites a molecule from its ground vibrational state to a higher one, and for a vibration to be IR active the dipole moment of the molecule must be changed.

mcqs.q: In the functional group region (4000-1500 cm-1) of the IR spectrum, the C=O absorption of aldehydes and ketones appears at
mcqs.why: In the functional group region, the functional groups present can be identified from their characteristic bands: O-H of alcohols at 3200-3600 cm-1, C=O of aldehydes and ketones at 1710-1750 cm-1 and C=C at 1620-1680 cm-1; 1500-625 cm-1 is the fingerprint region.

lessons.title: Project
lessons.notes_html:
Key Points

  • A single proton NMR signal for C3H6O means all six hydrogen atoms are equivalent, which fits acetone, (CH3)2C=O, whose two CH3 groups are equivalent.
  • 1-Bromobutane and 2-bromobutane each have four types of protons and give 4 NMR signals.
  • 1-Bromo-2-methylpropane has three types of protons, because its two CH3 groups are equivalent, and gives 3 signals.
  • 2-Bromo-2-methylpropane has only one type of proton, because all three CH3 groups are equivalent, and gives 1 signal.

Solved Exercises

Project

Q: Project: The molecular formula of a compound determined from combustion analysis and mass spectrometry is C3H6O. Proton NMR spectrum of compound has only one signal. Draw the possible structure of compound.

Ans: One signal in the proton NMR spectrum means that all six hydrogen atoms of C3H6O are equivalent, i.e. all the protons are in the same electronic environment. This is true for acetone (propanone), CH3-CO-CH3: its two CH3 groups are equivalent, so all six protons are equivalent and give only one signal. The possible structure of the compound is therefore (CH3)2C=O, acetone.

Q: Project: Draw the structures of four isomeric butyl bromides (C4H9Br) and predict the number of signals in proton NMR spectrum of each of the isomer.

Ans: The four isomeric butyl bromides (C4H9Br) are: (1) 1-bromobutane, CH3-CH2-CH2-CH2Br: it has four types of protons (the CH3 protons, two different CH2 groups and the CH2Br protons), so it gives 4 signals. (2) 2-bromobutane, CH3-CHBr-CH2-CH3: it also has four types of protons (two different CH3 groups, the CHBr proton and the CH2 protons), so it gives 4 signals. (3) 1-bromo-2-methylpropane (isobutyl bromide), (CH3)2CH-CH2Br: the two CH3 groups are equivalent, so it has three types of protons (the equivalent CH3 protons, the CH proton and the CH2Br protons), giving 3 signals. (4) 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (tert-butyl bromide), (CH3)3CBr: all three CH3 groups are equivalent, so it has only one type of proton and gives 1 signal.
